# Architecture

This document describes only what is implemented. Proposals live in `spec/`. When a spec is implemented, its content moves here in the same commit (CLAUDE.md "Design docs").

**State**: Built as of 2026-10-30: the Phase 0 foundations, Phase 1 compatibility core, Phase 2 non-agentic chat features and Phase 3 LCM implementation. This describes code, not owner acceptance of the daily-use milestone. The build includes worker-isolated storage, the message graph and independent forks, library editing and card forks, protected drafts and recycle bin (§3); auth and settings (§4–§5); registered providers, normalized usage/cost rollups and image token estimates (§6); card, lorebook and preset formats, macros and import/export (§8–§11); streaming chat, versions, guidance, notes, image editing/toggles and group-only greetings (§12); ST folder import (§13); library editors, snippets and raw-source selection copy (§14); registered context assembly, exact historical request inspection, image/cache estimates and cache-aware history (§15); and LCM planning, generation, condensation, editable summaries and approved backfill (§16). Message insertion is built through all nine units: storage, fork inheritance, positional reads and assembly, the bin, generation, LCM, history edits and ST re-import, and the registered insertion UI (§3.8, §3.10, §3.11, §3.13, §5, §13, §15–§16). Built agentic RP rollouts, workshops and plugin installation are documented in §16–§17; proposals for later work remain in `spec/`.

---

## 1. Repository

npm workspaces, TypeScript, ESM throughout.

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `packages/shared` | Code used by both server and client: the client-facing RPC contract (`api.ts`), its errors (`errors.ts`), and the domain schemas and pure logic (users, chats and state, library and merge, card and lorebook documents, drafts, the bin, providers and usage), plus UUIDv7 ids (`id.ts`). Imported as `@rp/shared/<file>.ts`. |
| `packages/server` | The Node server: HTTP, RPC over WebSocket, authentication, the database workers. |
| `packages/client` | The React single-page app, built with Vite and served by the server. |
| `spikes/` | Throwaway experiments with their findings (not part of the build). |
| `spec/` | Proposals and design records. |

**Runtime.** Node 24 runs the server's TypeScript directly through type stripping, so the code must use erasable syntax only (`erasableSyntaxOnly`). The client is bundled, and so are the database workers for production (§3.6). The server's main thread runs from source.

Bun was measured as an alternative (2026-10-10) and not adopted. On this server it gave the same RPC latency and throughput and 13% less memory, but it has no `node:sqlite`, stubs the event-loop delay API, and Effect's Node HTTP layer errors under it. Bundling the workers saves far more memory on Node.

**Toolchain.**
- TypeScript 6.0 (`tsc --noEmit` per package). TypeScript 7's native compiler isn't used yet, because typescript-eslint doesn't support it. The two projects that check the server's sources (`packages/server`, `packages/server/test/protocol`) run with an 8 GB heap (`NODE_OPTIONS` in the `typecheck` script): with the threads, tool-loading and workshop operations together (merge-batch9) they need about 5 GB, above Node's default of about 4.2 GB on the dev host, mostly in the RPC groups' handler layers (`db/writer.ts` `WriteOps.toLayer`, `server.ts`, `db/Database.ts`).
- ESLint with typescript-eslint, plus `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` including the React Compiler rules.
- Prettier.
- knip: fails on unused files, exports and dependencies, the shared package's exports included (`knip.jsonc` says why each exception exists).
- Vitest with `@effect/vitest`, and Playwright for the browser tests (§5).
- `npm run check` runs all of them at once (`scripts/check.ts`: each tsc project, ESLint, Prettier, knip and `npm test`, the fast tests), so it takes as long as its slowest step: about 8 minutes on the 48-core host at a load average of 30 to 90, the tests 7.5 of them. `npm run test:slow` runs the rest, which `npm test` leaves out: the files `vitest.config.ts` lists (`SLOW_SERVER_FILES`: model-based runs over many seeds, scale fixtures, performance measurements, process spawns), as the `server-slow` project, then the tests tagged `slow` in the other files (timing and memory budgets, large fixtures, process spawns, seeds past the first). The `server-slow` project allows 60 s for setup/cleanup hooks, set before modules register them, so multi-gigabyte fixtures can be removed. A test that measures time, or takes minutes, is registered with `slowIt` (`test/support/slow.ts`, `it` with the tag) instead of `it`, or gets `tags: ["slow"]` among its options. Vitest runs one test process per free core (the cores less the load average, less 2), but at least a quarter of the cores; `VITEST_MAX_WORKERS` overrides it. Tests may take 30 s each, so a busy host and Vite's first transform of a large module graph don't fail them. CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) also builds the client and the workers, runs the browser tests, and builds the Docker image (without pushing it). It checks that the image refuses to start without exposure settings, and runs it with an admin password until its health check passes.
- Plugin checks that launch compiler and sandbox processes use the slow tier: `test/pluginApiDocs.test.ts`, `test/pluginSettings.test.ts`, the compiler/sandbox cases in `test/pluginWorkshop.test.ts`, and the six complete macro-family checks in `test/pluginCopy.test.ts` use literal `tags: ["slow"]` options. Pure copy/provenance/rewriting tests remain fast, as do routing and setup-continuity workflows. Their assertions and per-case deadlines are unchanged.
- `npm run test:live` (the `server-live` project, `packages/server/test/live/`) sends real requests to Anthropic, OpenAI (Chat Completions and Responses), DeepSeek, Google's Gemini API (`google.test.ts`) and OpenRouter, so neither `npm test` nor `npm run check` runs it. Every file is skipped unless `RP_LIVE_KEY_DIR` names a directory holding one API key file per provider (`anthropic`, `openai`, `openrouter`, `deepseek`, `google`). `RP_LIVE_BASE_URL_<PROVIDER>` (`ANTHROPIC`, `OPENAI`, `OPENROUTER`, `DEEPSEEK`, `GOOGLE`) optionally sends one provider's requests to another endpoint that speaks the same API, with the route's path appended; the default is the provider's public origin. Each test starts the app's server (database workers from source, no bundle build) and drives it only through its RPCs: a connection whose base URL is a loopback recorder in front of the provider's own API (`support/live.ts`), which keeps each request body, status, request-id headers and response and never stores the key. It compares the app's ledger counts, cost, cache markers and next-context estimate with what the provider reported, over growing chats, swipes, deep edits, TTLs and cache minimums (`support/scenarios.ts`), and covers reasoning, prefill, continue, vision, agent tools, errors, stop, OpenRouter upstreams pinned by the model's routing setting (`provider.only`, which OpenRouter honors; `openrouterProviders.test.ts` adds DeepSeek, MiMo and an OpenAI model on Bedrock through several providers, and one image per pair) and prompt shapes (`shapes.test.ts`). Fixtures are synthetic. Findings and spend go to `RP_LIVE_OUT` as JSON per file, with the recorded exchanges; OpenRouter stops at `RP_LIVE_OPENROUTER_CAP` dollars of reported cost (default 2). `RP_LIVE_WAIT_TTL=1` adds the 5-minute expiry check (a 330 s wait). A test fails when any of its checks fails.
- Server test directories created by `support/tempDir.ts` are tracked per file. Running files remove them in `afterAll`, after scopes close and before Vitest reports the file finished; large removals must finish before the coordinator checks leftovers. Environment teardown is the fallback for wholly skipped files and collection failures, where suite hooks do not run. The global setup still rejects any remaining entries in the run’s scratch directory. Search scale fixtures record each version’s actual authoring fork, including side replies on their own branches.
- Timing-sensitive assertions use the state they need: prompt-regex correctness and output-limit tests inject a deadline independently of host scheduling (the real VM interruption has a separate test), and the browser `saveRevision` helper waits for Saved state and a cleared pending flag, since a pending save also disables its button and a no-op save keeps the revision number. Exposure-gate socket tests bind the selected peer address but dial loopback, keeping the policy check independent of LAN intermediaries.
- Browser readiness checks use the content they exercise: `e2e/csp.spec.ts` waits for each route's heading rather than network idleness, and `pendingChatPanel.spec.ts` waits for the overflow menu's items before collecting its tab names. `composerRow.spec.ts` moves the pointer away from a clicked guidance toggle before hovering it again, so the hover check actually re-enters the control after clicking dismissed its explanation. `qaAttribution.spec.ts` waits for the ready branch label before measuring group titles, so a narrower loading label cannot hide clipping. `connections.spec.ts` waits for the form to become clean after Load the latest before typing a fresh change; a shared draft can already display the remote name while its discard is still queued. Shared labels such as sort direction and message versions are scoped to their library or message surface. `snippets.spec.ts` waits for the Send selection button, which shows the editor has published its selection, before pressing the shortcut; `editors2.spec.ts` waits for the closing Cast menu to unmount before reopening it by keyboard, and for focus to enter the Export submenu before pressing keys there. The timeline mounts only the rows in view and two beyond, so specs count messages through the server and scroll to a message outside that window before reading it (`insertMessage`, `naming`, `presentationContributions`); `chatFlash.spec.ts` requires branch rows only while its sidebar section is unfolded.
- Menu and image explanations (suitegreen4, 2026-11-05): request-inspector and library-update menu links pass their router links directly to the shared menu item; its own explanation supplies the tooltip, so render composition retains the link and menu role. Message images use one tooltip that explains exclusion when applicable.
- Browser suite repairs (suitegreen4, 2026-11-05): card-family rows separate the name and chat count, and revision restore actions retain their revision-specific accessible names when a known name clash disables them. The character-scoped New chat action has the scrollport’s standard top inset. Browser assertions scope sent text to messages, pin chats globally through `SetChatPin`, and follow the approved version-free pickers, full-portrait rows, focusable overflow tiles, pre-read chat handover and lorebook help presentation. Field geometry checks leave independent sidebar recovery notices out of the editor measurement. The focused dialog audit includes the card-family picker. The Vite-backed composition probe compiles and mounts in file setup before timing composition assertions, matching the contribution probes; dependency optimization can otherwise consume the first test’s minute before its editor exists.
- Vite dev-server specs (suitegreen5, 2026-11-06): the Playwright global setup `e2e/support/viteDeps.ts` pre-bundles the client's dependencies once (`vite optimize`), unless the cache is newer than the lockfile and `vite.config.ts`. Started cold, each Vite spec scanned and bundled every dependency itself, and parallel specs cleared one another's half-written cache. `chatContributions` and `presentationContributions` load the routes they use once in `beforeAll`, so the dev server's first compile of those modules doesn't count against a test's steps.
- Composition probe cache reuse (fix-codeeditorcomposition, 2026-11-07): `codeEditorComposition.spec.ts` serves its synthetic HTML through middleware with Vite's custom app mode. Adding a harness-only plugin changed Vite's dependency-cache hash, deleted global setup's completed pre-bundle and started another bundle inside the setup timeout. Middleware keeps the production plugin list and shared pre-bundle intact; the composition assertions and editor behavior are unchanged.
- Browser server ownership (suitegreen3, 2026-11-04): `e2e/support/server.ts` waits for its child’s IPC confirmation that the configured port is listening before accepting HTTP health. The child-only `serverReady.ts` preload forwards the listening event without changing application handlers; each restart has its own readiness generation. An occupied port therefore follows the existing EADDRINUSE retry instead of borrowing another test’s server and losing it when that test ends. `serverPort.spec.ts` holds a healthy foreign listener on the first port in a fresh-process probe and requires a different, healthy app port. The same occupied-port probe reproduces the original failure on reference 3bfac8d4.
- `npm run size` prints one line of sizes: code lines in sources and in tests, comment lines, and doc lines (`scripts/size.ts`, tracked files outside `spikes/`). CI prints it too, so growth shows per commit.

**Native build allocation (plugintests1, 2026-11-14).** `scripts/check.ts` sets `MIMALLOC_ALLOW_THP=0` for its validation subprocesses, including Vitest's one-time worker-bundle setup. Docker's build-stage command applies the same setting only while running `npm run build`; it is not a production-image environment variable. This avoids rolldown/mimalloc's synchronous huge-page compaction stalls before any plugin test starts. The unchanged application build stage took 770.6 seconds with allocator defaults and 44.6 seconds with this setting on the shared host. Runtime plugin child allocation is fixed independently in §17, so direct callers and restarts receive the same policy. Checks and generated inputs remain complete. The `build`, `test`, `test:slow` and `test:perf` scripts set it too (review-finalwipe, 2026-11-16): `stReimportCrashScale` bundles the writer from source inside its 180 s budget, and that one rolldown build took 189 s with allocator defaults and 0.2 s with the setting at load 15–20 (a standalone repeat: over 60 s, nearly all kernel time, against 0.27 s). Vitest's own startup in `test:slow` took about 9 minutes before the first test for the same reason.

**Final-image smoke check** (imagesmoke1, 2026-11-13). `npm run smoke:image -- BASE_URL CONTAINER` (`scripts/image-smoke.ts`, typechecked with the server) checks an already running, disposable production container with a fresh synthetic data directory. Supply its synthetic admin password through `IMAGE_SMOKE_PASSWORD` (or the third argument). The caller builds, starts and removes that container/image. Bind only to `127.0.0.1`, on a caller-selected port. The script requires `FAKE_CARD_SOURCE=off` and every development generator/decision switch set on that normal launch: `FAKE_GENERATOR_TPS=100`, `FAKE_GENERATOR_TOKENS=10`, `FAKE_GENERATOR_SEED=1`, `FAKE_GENERATOR_BURST_MS=10`, `FAKE_GENERATOR_REASONING=10`, `FAKE_GENERATOR_SECTION=10`, `FAKE_GENERATOR_COT=10`, `DECISION_TIMEOUT_MS=1`. These values exercise the switches; production ignores them. It requires `/healthz` to identify the actual provider generator (§12).

The check verifies health and matching client build ids; index/deep-link/panel-bootstrap/font/hashed-JS responses and content types; no `__rpPerf` or development-only UI marker anywhere in the built JS/CSS/HTML; admin login and baseline/default settings; generated PNG and JSON card imports, avatar media/thumbnail retrieval and chats with attached cards; and the first Workshop's lazily seeded Assistant/preset and their attachments. It creates a synthetic connection pointing at closed loopback port 9, adds model ids for every finite local encoding, and counts distinct text twice through authenticated `CountTokens`, requiring exact counts rather than the fallback estimate. No provider request or generation is made. There is no supported external format-worker restart operation; the output explicitly records that restart was not exercised.

Read-only `docker exec` checks the final filesystem exclusions, worker bundles, all tokenizer data and licence texts in source and beside the bundles, the built-in preset, and `node -e` resolution of bundle externals. The only containers the script launches are two unique `docker run --rm` negative probes of the supplied container's immutable image id: fake card source and fake saved media. Both have networking disabled, bind fresh directories under `<work>/artifacts/imagesmoke1/`, and must fail with the plain startup message, without paths/stacks or listening. Cleanup removes only their exact names and temporary directories, including on SIGINT/SIGTERM; no image is removed. A 175-second watchdog bounds the run, with bounded HTTP/RPC/Docker calls and cleanup. Failures print a plain one-line step reason and exit nonzero; successes print a short pass list. `test/imageSmoke.test.ts` checks the PNG, refusal validation, and real/fake generator health identity.

The slow startup refusal tests preserve the shipped `packages/server` and sibling `packages/plugin-api` source layout while excluding `server/src/dev`. The plugin documentation and editable story tools use relative imports of the runtime plugin API; a flattened server-only fixture fails at those imports before reaching either guarded development loader. The final-image negative launches exercise the actual workspace layout and retain their plain-message, no-loader-stack assertions.

**Dependencies are pinned to exact versions.** The owner's machine enforces a 5-day cooldown on newly published packages.

**Effect 4** (`effect` 4.0.x) is used on the server and in the client's data layer. Its RPC, HTTP, SQL, worker and reactivity modules are tagged `unstable` upstream (EFFECT.md §2), which is another reason versions are pinned exactly.

## 2. Server

`packages/server/src/main.ts` reads configuration from the environment and launches `ServerLive` (`server.ts`). That's one HTTP server with these parts:
- **`/rpc`:** the RPC endpoint (`AppApi` from `@rp/shared/api.ts`) over a WebSocket, JSON-serialized. Every UI action is meant to become an RPC in this group (DESIGN §7.7). Today it has `Health`, `Whoami`, the account RPCs (§4), the provider-kind, connection, credential, model, network-settings and usage RPCs (§6), `ListLibrary` (§11), the chat RPCs (§12), the editor RPCs (§14), the recycle bin (§3.11), composer-draft and notice RPCs (§12), and the request inspector (§15). `AppApi` is `AppCoreApi` merged with the authenticated `ForkMergeApi` (§3.9), `SplitChatApi`, `GalleryApi`, `ChatEventsApi` (`SubscribeChat`, whose event union tipped `AppCoreApi` over), `AgentApi` (§16, "Agent rollouts"), `DecisionApi` (§16, "Decision models"), `ChatContextsApi` (§3.8, "Away rows in the timeline") and `DraftPreviewApi` (§12, "The first request of a chat not sent yet"), and `server.ts` builds one handler layer for each: a single `toLayer` over every RPC exceeds TypeScript's instantiation depth (TS2589). New RPCs that tip it over go in a group of their own the same way.
- **`/healthz`:** a plain-text liveness route, used by the Docker health check.
- **`/auth/login`, `/auth/logout`** (§4), **`/library/import`, `/library/export`** (§11.4) and **`/library/avatar`, `/library/media`** (§14.5): plain HTTP, for what a WebSocket message can't do well, a cookie and a file.
- **Everything else:** the client build, served as a single-page app (unknown paths return `index.html`, so deep links work).

**Content-Security-Policy.** `RequestGuard` puts one on every response: `default-src 'self'`; `script-src 'self'` (the build's own modules, nothing inline, nothing from elsewhere, so markup that got past sanitizing can't run script); `style-src 'self'` (a message's `<style>` applies through a constructed stylesheet, which the directive doesn't govern, §12); `font-src 'self' blob: data:` (bounded embedded message fonts and the approved media queue's app-created font blobs, §12; no direct remote fonts); `img-src 'self' blob: data:` (local attachment previews use blob URLs; `data:` images in message HTML make no request, §12; an image URL in a message could report on the chat to its server, so remote ones stay blocked, and Markdown blocks them too); `connect-src 'self'` plus `ws://` and `wss://` on the Host the browser used, when it's a plain host name (`'self'` covers the WebSocket in current browsers; the explicit origins, older ones); `object-src 'none'`, `base-uri 'none'`, `form-action 'none'` (every form of the app's handles its own submit, so a form that slipped past sanitizing, or a script's, can't post to the app's routes: htmlboundary), `frame-ancestors 'none'`. One page has its own: `/frame/panel`, the frame a message's document block loads (§12), gets `default-src 'none'; script-src 'nonce-<n>'` (a fresh nonce on the page's one script tag, the bootstrap's, so no other script of the app's runs there, whatever the Host) `; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; img-src data: blob:; font-src data:; connect-src 'none'; form-action 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'self'`, set by the route itself (`RequestGuard` sets the same policy without a nonce, running nothing, on its refusals). With `?scripts` (a panel whose sources allowed scripts, §12) `script-src` is `'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval' <host>/frame/bootstrap.js <host>/frame/lib/` (by the Host the browser used, as http and https: a nonce would turn `'unsafe-inline'` off; a bracketed IPv6 Host, which no source expression can name, gets `'self'` instead, adding nothing to a block that runs any code already; a missing or malformed Host gets the page without scripts), and `style-src`, `img-src` and `font-src` add `<host>/frame/lib/`; with `&network` too, those four add `https:`, `connect-src` becomes `https:` and `media-src data: blob: https:` is added (`network` without `scripts` is the plain page). `GET`/`HEAD` under `/frame/lib/` with `Origin: null` (a panel's fonts are CORS requests from its opaque origin) are let through with `access-control-allow-origin: *`: they're public library files; every other route still refuses `Origin: null`. The app's own pages allow it as a frame through `default-src 'self'`. The browser tests run every screen under it and fail on any violation, and check a native form submission is refused before any request (`e2e/csp.spec.ts`). What an inline-HTML sanitizer failure could still do under this policy: run no script (no inline script or handler, no `javascript:`; `'self'` scripts are the build's modules and the `/frame/` files, which on the app's page only define functions, but for the Tailwind runtime, whose generated `<style>` the policy refuses); load nothing from another site (images, media, fonts, frames and connections are the app's own or `data:`/`blob:`); make same-origin GET requests by image or frame address (the app's GET routes only read, and `/media/external` fetches only for a scope the user allowed); and draw inside its message box (containment, §12). Trusted Types are not required: message HTML never reaches an HTML string sink (§12, `test/htmlTree.test.ts`), and the app's own sinks (workers' script URLs, React DOM) would need a policy first. The Vite development server doesn't send it.

**Configuration** (`config.ts`, environment variables):

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `HOST`, `PORT` | `127.0.0.1`, `8080` | Listen address. `PORT=0` takes a free port, which the startup log names |
| `DATA_DIR` | `./data` | Database, instance lock, media files (§11.1) |
| `DB_READERS` | `2` | Reader worker count, at least 1 (§3) |
| `FORMAT_WORKERS` | `1` | Format worker count, at least 1: how many uploads are parsed, or exports written, at once (§11.3) |
| `THUMBNAIL_WORKERS` | `1` | Thumbnail worker count, at least 1: how many thumbnails are made at once on request, in workers apart from the format workers (§14.5b) |
| `DB_ALLOW_NETWORK_FS` | `false` | Override the refusal of filesystems not known to be local (§3.4) |
| `SHELL_PASS_PAUSE_MS` | `0` | A wait before the shell's summary parts but a library pass's first; tests hold a pass half done with it (§12, "Branch lists while the first pass runs") |
| `DB_WORKERS` | `bundle` in production, else `source` | Worker entry points, the format workers' too (§3.6) |
| `AUTH_MODE` | `single` | `single` or `proxy` (§4) |
| `AUTH_PROXY_HEADER` | `remote-user` | Identity header in proxy mode |
| `ALLOWED_IPS` | unset | IPs, CIDR ranges and host names besides loopback that may connect in single mode (§4) |
| `TRUSTED_PROXIES` | unset (loopback) | The only addresses that may connect in proxy mode: IPs, CIDR ranges and host names, e.g. `proxy,127.0.0.1` (§4) |
| `ALLOW_INSECURE_EXPOSURE` | `false` | Serve every address without protection (§4) |
| `LOOPBACK_REQUIRES_LOGIN` | `true` | Once an account has a password, loopback needs a login too (§4) |
| `ADMIN_PASSWORD_FILE`, `ADMIN_PASSWORD`, `ADMIN_USER` | unset | The first admin's password, for headless servers. Applies only while no enabled admin has one (§4) |
| `PUBLIC_ORIGINS` | unset | Origins the app is served at by name, e.g. `https://rp.example.com` (§4) |
| `CLIENT_DIST` | `packages/client/dist` | Static files to serve |
| `SECRET_KEY`, `SECRET_KEY_FILE` | unset | The server secret (below). Generated into `DATA_DIR/secret.key` when neither is set |
| `KEY_HOST_BINDING` | `true` | Keys go only to the hosts their credential was entered for (§3.12). A security setting, so it's set only here, never from inside the app |
| `FAKE_GENERATOR_SEED` | unset | Development entry point only: fix the synthetic reply's prose seed for deterministic fixtures; otherwise each version supplies its seed |
| `FAKE_GENERATOR_TPS`, `FAKE_GENERATOR_TOKENS` | unset, `400` | Read only by the development entry point (`src/dev/main.ts`): chats generate synthetic text at this rate, about this many tokens each (§12). `main.ts` ignores them |
| `DECISION_TIMEOUT_MS` | unset | Development entry point only (tests): every decision point waits this many milliseconds for its answer instead of its own deadline (`DecisionEngine.layerWith({ timeoutMs })`, §16), so a browser test can hold a decision while it looks at the page. `main.ts` ignores it |

**Data directory** (`dataDirectory.ts`). Before opening storage or generating the server secret, startup creates missing path components once and checks directory write/search access. An unusable `DATA_DIR` exits with the path and filesystem cause. Recursive Node mkdir is avoided: on `/proc/nope` it loops on `ENOENT` instead of returning. `startup.test.ts` spawns the real server for missing, non-directory and unwritable paths, with generated and configured secrets.

**Secrets** (`secrets.ts`). Connection secrets (API keys, header values, proxy URLs) are encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM, under a key derived (HKDF-SHA256) from the server secret.
- **Bound to where they belong.** Each ciphertext is bound to what it belongs to (`credential:<id>:key`, `connection:<id>:headers`, `connection:<id>:proxy_url`), so it doesn't decrypt anywhere else.
- **Format:** a version byte, a fresh 12-byte nonce, the tag, then the ciphertext.
- **Only the main thread holds the secret.** The database workers only ever see ciphertext.
- **The secret is automatic** (owner, 2026-10-10: setup must be trivial). It comes from `SECRET_KEY` or `SECRET_KEY_FILE` (a Docker secret) when set. Otherwise it's generated at first start into `DATA_DIR/secret.key`, mode 0600 (tightened if a restore loosened it), and never overwritten.
- **Honest scope:** with the key file next to the database, encryption protects a leaked database or backup on its own, not a copy of the whole data directory.
- **A changed secret** makes stored secrets unreadable (`SecretUnreadable`), which surfaces as "enter the key again". It never surfaces as a crash.

**Outgoing requests** (`net/`, spec/PROVIDERS.md §6.2). Every request the server sends goes through the `Network` service. ESLint forbids the global `fetch`, `undici` and `node:https` anywhere else in `packages/server/src`, so nothing can skip the proxy by accident.
- **The instance settings** are an optional proxy (HTTP, HTTPS or SOCKS5) and a bypass list of hostnames, `*.domain` suffixes, IPs and CIDR ranges. Local ranges are on the bypass list by default (loopback, RFC 1918, link-local, CGNAT, IPv6 ULA and link-local). A hostname bypasses by address only if every address it resolves to is on the list, and its connection is then pinned to those addresses (`bypassOnlyLookup`), so a second lookup can't land elsewhere. A host the admin listed by name or suffix goes direct whatever it resolves to, unpinned. With `forceProxy`, non-admins can't send direct or through their own proxy (§6).
  - They're stored in app-scoped `settings`, with the proxy URL encrypted, since it can hold credentials.
  - The proxy is only ever shown as scheme, host and port.
  - Unusable settings are refused with `InvalidNetworkSettings`.
- **Each connection overrides the route** with `inherit`, `direct` or its own proxy. The route for a request (`route.ts`, pure and unit-tested):
  - the override wins
  - otherwise a target on the bypass list goes direct, matched by name, by literal IP, or by its resolved addresses (IPv4-mapped IPv6 counts as IPv4)
  - otherwise the instance proxy is used
  - a failed DNS lookup leaves the target to the proxy
- **The route is reported:** `fetchFor(override, onRoute)` gives a `fetch` for one connection's requests and reports each request's route, e.g. "direct: 192.168.1.20 is in the bypass list" or "via proxy socks5://vpn:1080".
- **One undici dispatcher per route** (`Agent`, `ProxyAgent`, `Socks5ProxyAgent`), reused across requests and closed with the layer. undici marks its SOCKS5 support experimental. SOCKS5 sends the hostname to the proxy, so DNS for proxied targets resolves remotely.
- **A response may stay silent for 30 minutes,** before its headers and between body chunks, on every route (an interceptor sets undici's `headersTimeout` and `bodyTimeout` per request, since proxy agents don't pass their options to their per-origin pools). undici's default of 300 s cut off local models still reading a long prompt, and the retry started the prompt again. Stopping a generation aborts at once, as before.
- `test/network.test.ts` runs real requests through a local HTTP proxy (CONNECT and absolute-URI forwarding) and a SOCKS5 proxy with credentials (`test/support/proxies.ts`), counting the tunnels.
- **pi-ai:** all four built-in wire adapters use our `fetch`. Startup removes SDK environment defaults; the app-owned Gemini REST adapter uses the same controlled transport (§6). Node environment proxies cannot choose a provider route.

**Stopping** (`SIGTERM`, `docker stop`). Node's `server.close()` waits for every connection, and an open tab's WebSocket never ends on its own, so a stop used to hang until it was killed, with the database workers mid-flight. Closing the server now:
- ends idle HTTP connections, and drops RPC requests that arrive from then on, unanswered, so nothing starts that the stop could cut off between its commit and its reply
- waits up to 2 seconds for the RPCs in flight to reply (the serialization layer counts requests in and exits out)
- sends each WebSocket a close frame with code 1001 ("going away"; the client reconnects), and destroys whatever is left a second later
- exits 0: an interruption by signal is how the server is meant to stop, and the default 130 would count as a failure to systemd (`main.ts`)

`shutdown.test.ts` stops a real server with a socket open (it exits 0 within seconds and leaves no WAL behind, the sign that the workers closed the database), and during a burst of writes (every committed write was acknowledged).

**Event-loop monitoring** (`eventLoop.ts`). A 10 ms timer measures how late each tick runs, into one-second buckets. `Health` reports the last minute: the longest single delay (`eventLoopMaxMs`) and the worst one-second p99 (`eventLoopP99Ms`). Reading them resets nothing, so callers don't affect each other. Node's `monitorEventLoopDelay` isn't used: it discards the first interval after a reset, so a 300 ms stall starting just after a bucket change showed as 0.3 ms. Tested: a single 300 ms block shows in the max, including 2, 10 and 25 ms after a bucket change, and still does after another read and a bucket change. Anything that blocks the loop delays every live stream, so this is a budgeted metric (CLIENT-FRAMEWORK §7).

---

## 3. Database

SQLite through Node's built-in `node:sqlite` and Effect's driver (`@effect/sql-sqlite-node`); see STORAGE.md for why not Turso. Code is in `packages/server/src/db/`.

### 3.1 SQLite never runs on the main thread

`node:sqlite` is synchronous: a query blocks the thread that runs it, for its full duration. On the main thread, that would stall every WebSocket stream for as long as any query runs. So all SQL runs in worker threads:
- **One writer worker** (`writer.ts`) holds the **only read-write connection**. It runs migrations at startup, then serves `WriteOps` one at a time (`concurrency: 1`). A crashed writer is respawned every second by Effect's worker pool, which logs nothing, so `writerProtocol` logs it on the main thread: the first stop with its cause, then failed restarts as a count (after 1, 2, 4, 8, … of them), then the recovery (`test/readerPool.test.ts`).
- **A pool of reader workers** (`reader.ts`, `DB_READERS`) each hold one **read-only** connection (opened with `readOnly`, plus `PRAGMA query_only`). They serve `ReadOps`. A request goes to an idle reader, so one slow query doesn't hold up the others. **Background reads** (`BACKGROUND_READS` in `Database.ts`: the shell's shared `ShellMaterialize` and legacy shell reads, `CacheWarmth` and `AssembleDraftChat`, the first-request preview of a chat not sent yet, which a card with a huge greeting makes take minutes; what browsing asks for and can take seconds at scale) hold at most all readers but one, and reads queued behind a held-back one go first, so a reply's reads (context assembly) never wait for both readers to finish browsing reads (`test/readerPool.test.ts`). With one reader there's nothing to reserve. **Reply reads** (`REPLY_READS`: `GetSlot`, `AssembleContext`, the provider layer's `ResolveConnection`, `GetModel` and `GetCostSettings`, and `CachePrefixWarm`, what a reply waits on before its request goes out) have bounded priority over ordinary queued reads, such as the history pages a chat reads after each change; the eight-bypass rule below preserves older work’s progress.
- **The main thread** talks to both through typed Effect RPC over `worker_threads` (`Database.ts`: the `Writer` and `Reader` services). Errors cross the boundary typed: `StorageError { reason: busy | constraint | corrupt | other }` from the operation, `RpcClientError` if the worker itself fails.
  - `StorageError.message` carries SQLite's own message (e.g. `UNIQUE constraint failed: users.handle`). `corrupt` is `SQLITE_CORRUPT` or `SQLITE_NOTADB`; unique, check, not-null and foreign-key failures are `constraint`. The worker logs every one. The message never leaves the server: every client-facing handler turns storage failures into `ServerError` with a fixed message.

**Summary-planning admission** (planperf1, 2026-11-14). `PlanSummaries` without a reason is a reply-priority read. The same operation with `reason: reply | completion` goes to one additional, isolated read-only reader, outside `DB_READERS`. Even `DB_READERS=1` therefore leaves its ordinary reader available during maintenance. The isolated reader has the same crash, interruption, transaction and retry rules; it never serves ordinary reads, and ordinary readers never serve its maintenance requests. Startup still requires an ordinary reader. No new storage operation or RPC is introduced. The summarizer runs at most one coalesced maintenance pass at a time in a scoped fiber; its reconciliation and claim loop continues while that pass reads, including for already queued jobs in another chat. `afterReply` still only schedules and returns. Waiting maintenance passes retain their existing per-branch coalescing and within-plan job order. `readerPool.test.ts` holds maintenance until an ordinary read completes, with one and two ordinary readers; `lcmPool.test.ts` holds planning until a next-send check and a queued job claim complete.

**Planning reader affinity** (review-planperf2, 2026-11-14). Successful plans remember their reader by owner/chat and admission class (reply or isolated maintenance), in at most 4,096 routing hints. An idle preferred reader takes the next plan; a busy or unavailable one causes immediate fallback to another eligible reader. Hints neither reserve a reader nor change reply priority, background admission or maintenance isolation. A crash removes its hints; a retried plan warms the surviving reader. Dispatch revisits earlier idle readers after assigning a preferred reader later in the pool. This avoids an unnecessary cold fact read without waiting for affinity. `readerAffinity.test.ts` checks idle reuse, busy fallback and crash/retry; the existing pool tests retain interruption, priority and isolation coverage.

**The reader pool** (`readerPool.ts`) is our own RPC transport, not Effect's worker pool (`RpcClient.layerProtocolWorker`, still used for the single writer):

- **A reader is busy until it answers.** `node:sqlite` can't stop a running query. Effect's pool freed a reader as soon as its caller gave up (a timeout, a closed tab), so the next read went to the reader still running the old query. Measured with 2 readers: after a 2 s read timed out at 200 ms, the next light read waited 1,843 ms while the other reader idled. Here an interrupted read is forwarded to its reader, which stops at its next statement at best, and the reader takes nothing new until it answers.
- **A crashed reader gets nothing until it's back.** Effect's pool kept routing to it until it respawned (a light read waited 1,651 ms). Here it's out of the rotation from the crash until the respawned thread is ready, about a second later.
- **A crash fails no read.** It touches only the read its reader was running, which goes first in line to the next free reader, the respawned one included (`retryCrashed`, which the database readers opt into: reads are idempotent). A read that stops a second reader fails and isn't retried again, so a poison query costs two restarts, not a crash loop. Nor is a read whose caller gave up on it. Reads on other readers, and reads queued meanwhile, never notice.
- **What fails a request is typed:** `RpcClientError`, which the handlers turn into `ServerError` with a fixed message. An rpc's exit can only fail with the errors it declares, and a protocol error fails every request of the client, so the pool sends the error as an encoded defect of that one request, and `ReaderPool.client`, which builds the `Reader` service, restores it. A reader's own defect stays a defect.
- **Every crash is logged** on the main thread with the worker's error (e.g. its exit code) and what happens to its read, and the reader is respawned every second.
- **While no reader is up, queued reads fail** (`RpcClientError`) at each failed respawn, instead of waiting for a respawn that may never succeed. With every respawn failing, a read fails within about a second. A spawn that throws (a stale bundle, §3.6) is respawned like any other.
- **Startup waits for one reader to be ready**, and fails if every reader dies before any is.
- Reply reads have bounded priority; bounded independent reads (`SHORT_READS`: `GetSessionUser`, `GetDisplayPrefs`, `ListStImports`, `ShellEpoch`, `GetSplitChatsFast`, `ThreadsOfFast`) go next; after eight priority bypasses the oldest eligible request gets the next dispatch. Eligibility always respects the background allowance, including priority tags. It is one predicate for the reply, short and oldest candidates alike, and it also holds the maintenance isolation and planning affinity below: a maintenance plan never reaches an ordinary reader through the reply or burst lanes, and a plan whose preferred reader is idle goes to it under every lane (`readerPool.test.ts` holds a reply-tagged and a short-tagged maintenance read behind another). This prevents a sustained reply/short-read stream from starving older browsing work; the indexed session lookup is in the same short lane so authentication cannot strand another account’s otherwise short RPC behind a history queue; FIFO within each class also prevents short reads from starving behind later arrivals. With at least two readers, background work still leaves one reader available. A running SQLite statement is not preempted; short-read priority applies when a reader becomes available. `readerPool.test.ts` holds a long read indefinitely and queues eight more, then requires every short read to finish before releasing the long read. It also checks queued short reads precede earlier ordinary reads, with one reader. A request whose send fails fails alone. Sent to a ready thread, it gets a defect, and its reader is released. Sent first to a new thread, Effect's worker holds it until the thread is ready, and its failure stops the thread like a crash. Effect's worker keeps a message it couldn't send for its next thread, so each thread gets a new one. A buffer listed twice among a request's transferables fails a send, so they're listed once.
- An answer to a request its reader isn't running is dropped, with a warning. The workers answer a handler's defect with its request's Exit (`disableFatalDefects`), so a `Defect` message, which names no request, is the protocol failing: the pool treats it as a crash of that reader.
- Tested (`test/readerPool.test.ts`) with a test reader whose requests block like queries, without a clock. A reader can be held, in a request or before it starts, until the test releases it, and light reads must finish first: one sent to a held reader would wait for a release that never comes. After an interrupted read, every light read goes to the other reader. A read that stops its reader once is retried, on the reader that's up, or on the replacement while the other reader's held read finishes. A read that stops every reader fails with a typed `RpcClientError` after two stops. An interrupted read that then stops its reader stops only that one. A stray Exit from a reader finishes nothing, and a read whose reader sends a `Defect` is retried. With readers that die as they start, startup fails, and a read sent once every reader is down fails with the failed respawn's error. An earlier version asserted that light reads took under 300 ms, and waited 300 ms for both crashes to be handled.

Measured: the same CPU-heavy 800 ms query blocks the main event loop for **795 ms** when run on the main thread, and **0.8 ms** when run through a reader worker. `test/database.test.ts` checks this without a clock, through a test-only reader pool with the readers' connection setup (`test/support/diagnostics.ts`). The query on the main thread blocks the loop for over 100 ms. One reader is then held blocked until the test releases it, and 20 light reads through the other reader must finish first. If the blocked reader blocked the main thread, they never would. An earlier version asserted under 30 ms of main-thread lag, which failed at load averages of 40 to 60.

### 3.2 Storage operations are named commands

Operations (`ops.ts`) are declared as RPC groups and implemented inside the workers. **A write operation is one synchronous transaction executed entirely inside the writer.** You can't send a closure to a worker thread, so a transaction structurally can't span an `await`, a network call or an LLM request. That's the usual way transactions grow long and hold locks.

Operations that run over 25 ms are logged (`timed.ts`): a write holds the writer, so a slow one delays all writes.

**How code types itself from the groups.** An operation is declared as before: one `Rpc.make` entry in `WriteOps` (either of its halves, `WriteOpsChat` or `WriteOpsLibrary`, which `WriteOps` merges; the split is only a grouping) or `ReadOps`, and one handler in the worker, typed with `WriteOps.of`/`ReadOps.of`. The `Writer` and `Reader` clients and every type that names an operation's RPC read the union off the group's `requests` map with `OpsOf` (`db/opsOf.ts`), never `RpcClient.FromGroup` or `RpcGroup.Rpcs`: those infer it by matching the group against the whole `RpcGroup` interface, which passed TypeScript's instantiation limit (TS2589) once `WriteOps` passed about 200 operations (two more writes in the cardex2 merge), and every user of the writer then saw `unknown` (about 2,000 errors). Through `OpsOf`, one client over all 364 storage operations checks; `test/opsTyping.test.ts` types that client and fails on either inferring form anywhere in the sources. The client API does the same (`AppRpcs` in `api.ts`). The writer also builds its shared handler set once, then registers it through `WriteOpsChat.toLayer` and `WriteOpsLibrary.toLayer`; its one RPC server is explicitly typed with `OpsOf<typeof WriteOps>`. This avoids the combined operation group exceeding handler-layer inference depth without duplicating the connection, bin, attribution or import-prefix state. Handler layers are a separate limit: `toLayer`'s handler inference over the whole `AppApi` is too deep, so `server.ts` builds one layer for `AppCoreApi` (225 RPCs) and one per merged `Authenticated*Api` group. A new family of RPCs gets its own group, merged into `AppApi` and given its own `toLayer`, not more entries in `AppCoreApi`; if `AppCoreApi.toLayer` reports TS2589, move one of its merged groups (`.merge(EditorApi)` and the like) out to `AppApi` with its own layer. The storage workers hit the same two limits when merge-batch8 combined the side-chat and workshop-context writes: the writer's client is made as `RpcClient.make<OpsOf<typeof WriteOps>>(WriteOps)` (`db/Database.ts`), so the union comes from `OpsOf` rather than being inferred against the group, and the writer worker builds `WriteOps.toLayer(...)` as its own constant before `RpcServer.layer(WriteOps).pipe(Layer.provide(handlers), ...)` (`db/writer.ts`), so the handler object is not inferred inside the pipe's contextual type.

**A read operation is one read transaction** (`query` in `tx.ts`, a deferred `BEGIN` on the read-only connection), so all its statements see the same snapshot. Readers still never block the writer or each other. Measured cost on a trivial point read through the workers: about 40 µs per read (≈190 µs to ≈230 µs sequential) and about 8% fewer reads per second at saturation; no difference on a list read.

### 3.3 Why `SQLITE_BUSY` can't happen inside the process

`SQLITE_BUSY` ("database is locked") means one connection needs a lock another connection holds. The setup rules out every in-process way for that to happen:

| Possible conflict | Why it can't occur |
|---|---|
| Two writers | There is exactly one read-write connection, and the writer worker serializes its operations. Within it, Effect's driver serializes statements and holds the connection for a whole transaction. |
| A writer and a reader | The database is in WAL mode, where readers never block the writer and the writer never blocks readers. Reader connections are read-only and can't take write locks. |
| A read transaction upgrading to a write | Readers can't write, and the writer opens transactions with `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, so there's no upgrade. |
| Checkpoints | Only automatic PASSIVE checkpoints run (the writer, at commit). PASSIVE never waits on or blocks readers. `journal_size_limit` bounds the WAL file. |
| Readers opening before the file exists or is migrated | Readers are spawned only after the writer answers `Ready`, which it does only after migrations. |

Tested (`test/database.test.ts`): 500 concurrent writes and 500 concurrent reads complete with no errors, and every completed write is visible to readers.

### 3.4 Outside the process

Other processes are the remaining risk, so they're kept out:
- **Instance lock.** At startup the main thread takes an exclusive SQLite lock on `DATA_DIR/instance.lock` (`locking_mode = EXCLUSIVE` + `BEGIN EXCLUSIVE`) and holds it for the process lifetime. It's an OS file lock, so the kernel releases it if the process dies; there's no stale lock file to clean up. A second instance on the same data directory exits immediately with `InstanceLocked`, instead of contending for the database. Examples: a second `npm start`, or two containers on one volume. This is tested both in-process and from a separate process.
- **Only filesystems known to be local are accepted** (`statfs` on Linux): ext2/3/4, XFS, Btrfs, ZFS, F2FS, tmpfs and overlayfs (Docker's container filesystem). Network and FUSE filesystems (NFS, CIFS/SMB, sshfs, rclone, virtiofs, Docker Desktop file sharing, WSL2's 9p `/mnt/c`, Ceph, AFS) may not provide the POSIX locks SQLite relies on, and WAL can corrupt there. Anything else is refused as unrecognized. `DB_ALLOW_NETWORK_FS=1` overrides this, and is also what a local filesystem not on the list needs (e.g. exFAT or NTFS on a USB disk, bcachefs, eCryptfs).
- **Nothing else should open the live database.** There is no built-in backup operation yet; the app holds its instance lock for the life of its database workers.
- **Backstop.** If an outside process does take a lock anyway, the workers' 5 s `busy_timeout` applies. It blocks only that worker thread, never the main thread, and anything that still fails surfaces as `StorageError { reason: "busy" }`.

### 3.5 Connection settings

| | Writer | Readers |
|---|---|---|
| Mode | read-write, `journal_mode = WAL` | `readOnly`, `query_only = ON` |
| Durability | `synchronous = FULL`: a committed transaction survives power loss | n/a |
| Other | `foreign_keys = ON`, `temp_store = MEMORY`, 64 MiB cache, `journal_size_limit` 64 MiB | `temp_store = MEMORY`, 256 MiB cache (allocated as pages are read: a long path's slot, version and step pages at hundreds of forks, spec/FORK-COST.md §2.3), `mmap_size` 2 GiB (eligible main-database pages can be read from the OS mapping without copying into SQLite's page cache; WAL pages still use the ordinary read path, planperf2) |

### 3.6 Worker bundles

Each worker thread is a separate V8 isolate that loads its own copy of every module it imports. Loading Effect's module graph from source costs about 85 MB per worker. `npm run build` therefore bundles the worker entry points into single tree-shaken files with rolldown (`packages/server/scripts/build-workers.ts` writes `packages/server/dist/workers/{writer,reader,formats}.mjs`; the format worker is §11.3). A bundled worker costs about 19 MB (measured in `test/database.test.ts`, which fails above 40 MB).

`DB_WORKERS` selects the entry points:
- `source` is the default outside production, so development never runs a stale bundle.
- `bundle` is the default when `NODE_ENV=production`. The server refuses to start if the bundles are missing (`WorkerBundleMissing`) or stale (`WorkerBundleStale`), with a message to run `npm run build`.

**Stale bundles are refused.** The build writes `stamp.json` next to the bundles (`workerStamp.ts`): the repository files among the bundled modules (43 today) plus `package-lock.json`, and a SHA-256 of their contents. At startup the server hashes the same files again, in about 3 ms, and again before spawning each worker thread, so a crashed worker isn't replaced by code from an `npm run build` run after the server started (`WorkerBundleStale`; the reader is retried every second, and reads fail meanwhile). Without it, `git pull && npm start` would run new main-thread code against old workers: migrations wouldn't run, and a new operation would fail every in-flight request with "Unknown request tag".

The tests run the core operations against both. Every other server test runs bundled workers from the run's own build (`test/support/bundles.ts`, through the `WorkerBundleDir` reference in `Database.ts`, which defaults to `dist/workers`). A bundled worker starts in about a fifth of the CPU time a source one takes: measured at a load average of 110, a writer and reader took 0.7 s against 3.5 s, a format worker 0.4 s against 1.6 s. `TEST_DB_WORKERS=source` runs those tests on the source entry points instead. The bundles are built once per test run, from the sources as they are, into a temporary directory, by a Vitest global setup (`test/support/globalSetup.ts`), so a run never uses an older build; in watch mode, a source edited after the build makes the stamp refuse the bundles rather than run old code. A run of both server projects (`server` and `server-slow`) shares one directory and one build. A build usually takes about 2 s and 10 to 17 s of CPU, since rolldown uses every core. Once, at a load average of 85, a build in a test file's hook overran the hook's 60 s limit. The same setup points `TMPDIR` at a directory of the run's own. Tests get temporary directories only from `tempDir()` (`test/support/tempDir.ts`), which removes them when the test file ends, and anything left at the end of the run fails it.

The LCM SQL fixture worker (`test/support/lcmFixtureWorker.ts`) is bundled once by the same test setup, as `lcmFixture.mjs`. Vitest selects it through `RP_TEST_LCM_FIXTURE_WORKER`; browser fixtures keep the source entry point. Each fixture batch still runs in a worker transaction, and resolves only after that worker closes its connection and exits; repeated batches no longer start Node's TypeScript loader. The pause/cap tests observe the real wait's job escalation and its return before answering held summaries, and poll the generated version's state instead of sleeping. The fork-generation regression finishes the preceding reply's summary planning before recording the swipe's exact before/after calls.

**The server tests run with `--no-wasm-code-gc`** (`vitest.config.ts`). Node's type stripping is WebAssembly, so every source-mode worker runs Wasm. In Node 24's V8, Wasm code GC can free an import wrapper twice while another isolate is tiering it up ([nodejs/node#66366](https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/66366), fixed upstream in V8 `9b8ca54d5a` and not yet in a 24.x release). The tests create and terminate workers constantly, so without the flag about 1 run in 14 of the database test files died with SIGSEGV or `Check failed: jit_page.has_value()`. With the flag, none did in 70 runs. Node 22 has a V8 version older than the bug. The server isn't exposed in production: its bundled workers run no Wasm, so only the main thread does. In development, the source workers also run Wasm, but they live as long as the server.

Measured whole-server memory with the main thread, the writer and 2 readers: about 380 MB from source, and **188 MB** with bundles (Docker image, idle). The main thread still runs from source.

### 3.7 Schema

The writer initializes the schema through Effect's `SqliteMigrator`, with only `0001_baseline` (`db/baseline.ts`): a list of statements (tables, indexes, triggers, views, FTS tables), because `node:sqlite` prepares one statement at a time. It seeds no rows. `test/migrations.test.ts` compares `sqlite_master` against the recorded current schema (`test/fixtures/preSquashSchema.json`).

**The baseline is frozen; schema changes are numbered migrations after it** (`db/migrations.ts`): `0003_subagents` (§16, "Subagents") adds three nullable `rollouts` columns, an index and four triggers, and leaves existing rows as they were. `migrations.test.ts` migrates a synthetic database made at the baseline. Before the freeze: **schema changes went into baseline.ts and required a fresh deploy.** No migration or backfill is added during this period. Schemaclean (2026-11-06) folds the stray composer-guidance, branch-added-characters and global-chat-pin migrations into the baseline. Before the separate STRICT, extensibility and thread-cleanup edits, the folded baseline matched all 494 `sqlite_master` objects of the old baseline plus those three migrations (excluding the ledger; SQL whitespace, punctuation spacing and identifier quotes normalized). `npm run check:schema-fold -- <old-statements.json> <folded-statements.json>` runs the comparison in a worker; its frozen inputs and output are under `<work>/artifacts/schemaclean/`.

**Cold shell reads (perfred1, 2026-11-13).** `slots_chat_depth` covers the plain tree's slot metadata; `slots_shell_chain` covers the same fields on an overridden path without changing the unique chain/depth constraint. `versions_shell` covers retained swipes by slot (their seqs, which `version_participants_seq` joins; no ids since stack4), and `versions_shell_meta` the selected version's shell fields by id (perfshell3 split them; §12 *Indexes*). Shell queries join the selected version by slot and version id, which the id-keyed one answers. A partial covering index holds human authors separately from model alternatives. This avoids fetching scattered slot/version records across a dense swipe history and repeatedly evicting them from each reader's 256 MiB page cache. Historical participation still includes unselected retained alternatives, excludes purged ones, and uses the slot's authoring time for edits. Evidence retains alternative order explicitly, independent of the index SQLite chooses. `participationQuery.test.ts` checks those results and SQLite's bytecode: the shared-tree query opens neither record table, and the path query never opens version records. On overridden paths the view reads its fork-label point once, carries it through chain segments, and joins selection/replacement overrides against the already-covered slot; it does not reopen the slot or fork label per message. `shellSelection.test.ts` counts actual slot/label visits and checks selected, replaced, deleted and frozen-point results. The recorded baseline schema is updated; a fresh database is required. `chatForkSummaries` uses a separate outline projection for previews, split markers and threads: it omits participation and human-author evidence that those fields never consume, and never stores that partial result as a complete shell summary. Its regression compares all four returned fields with the complete projection.

Summary-stamp settlement starts from the sparse TEMP touch rows before resolving versions and slots (`CROSS JOIN`, `db/summaryValidity.ts`). A covering version index otherwise let SQLite choose a full index scan for each streamed text write. `summarySettlementPlan.test.ts` checks the real statement's query plan on a worker connection; the existing shell-summary model and mutation tests check that untouched frozen forks remain valid. `settlementDifferential.test.ts` additionally compares each optimized reach statement with the frozen pre-3a47fa35 scanning statement inside a rolled-back savepoint, on the same touches and stored summaries, across seeded forks, shared-ancestor rewrites, swipes, multi-deletes, tip moves, merges and separate histories; stored shell answers are checked against full recomputation after every step. The children of touched forks and of shifted slots are found from the touches too (perfshell3): in the other order SQLite scanned every fork and probed the touches for each, 300 ms of a 5,000-message rename's settlement (40 ms now, replayed on the rename's own database and touches); the plan test also refuses a fork scan. A touched slot reaches a fork when one of the fork's path segments holds it, checked once per segment (`EXISTS`) instead of once per touch and segment: with 5,000 touched slots in a 200-branch chat, 476 ms against 55 ms.

**A split chat's picture** (families1, 2026-11-15; **BASELINE CHANGED**, fresh deploy). `forks.cover_media_id TEXT REFERENCES media_assets(id)` holds the picture of the chat split off at that fork (`split_chat = 1`); the original chat's is the existing `chats.cover_media_id`. Both are optional and written only by `SetChatPicture` (§12). No migration or backfill. Both columns are in the shell's display epoch (`shellEpoch.ts`), so a picture change refreshes shared snapshots, and `GetSplitChats`'s metadata-only answer for an unsplit chat carries the chat's own picture (stack4: before, merged with the progressive shell, lists kept the old picture and the split header lost it; `chatPicture.test.ts`).

**MCP storage** (spec/MCP.md §12, M0; finalwipe1, 2026-11-16; **BASELINE CHANGED**, fresh deploy, no migration). `db/mcpSchema.ts`, in the baseline: `mcp_connections` (one MCP server, owned by one user: name, a key fixed for life (`mcp_<key>_<tool>`), what it's for, transport with its URL or argv, encrypted environment, headers and proxy with only names in the clear, a credential of the owner's (`ON DELETE SET NULL`), timeout, loading, sharing, the last tool listing with its revision, row and cache revisions, bin fields, and a purge tombstone that keeps no address, program or secret), `mcp_connection_shares` (the users an admin chose), `mcp_uses` (each user's switches for stories and workshops, tool allow list, last reviewed catalog revision, offered key, own sign-in) and `mcp_calls` (one row per request sent, opened `running` and closed once, with no arguments or results). Triggers: a connection's id, owner, key and creation time never change; it uses only its owner's credentials; only an admin owns a local program or shares one, on insert and on update; a share never names the owner; a use needs a connection its user owns or was given and not purged, and keeps its key; a call needs a connection its user may use and only its user's chat, its identity never changes except that its rollout can be cleared, and a closed call is a record. Deleting a chat or a rollout clears a call's attribution (`chat_id`, `rollout_id`; `tool_call_id` stays) under running and closed calls alike, and a connection or a user can't go while calls or connections name them. `storageKinds` adds the bin kind `mcp_connection` and the effect kind `mcp.call`; effect target kinds have no registry, so `mcp_connection` needs none. No operations, client or UI yet (M1+). `test/mcpSchema.test.ts` checks every trigger, the rule-carrying CHECKs, the unique keys and the cascades on a bare connection.

**Extensible storage kinds** (`db/storageKinds.ts`). Entity/chat kinds, revision/version/event/changeset origins, rollout kinds, request purposes, attachment kinds, draft/changeset targets, bin kinds, version marks and fork override kinds/origins have no stored `CHECK ... IN` list. Each column has a registered, replaceable entry in `storageKinds`, using the shared scoped registry; plugins extend its `values`, replace it or disable it. The writer installs TEMP capture triggers for inserts and changed discriminator columns, including bulk imports and copy paths. Its transaction validates the distinct captured values against the current registry before commit; an unknown value returns `StorageError` with reason `constraint` and rolls back the whole write. These TEMP objects never enter the baseline or reader schema. Trusted `StateModules` installers receive the worker's storage registry as a second argument, so scoped registrations and worker restarts work in source and bundled workers. Existing feature-specific DTOs still describe their own supported shapes; version origins accept strings and defer membership validation to the writer. Kernel enums (statuses, booleans, human/model writers, template/verbatim macros, scheduler classes, ref roles, queue actions and draft-history edit mechanics) remain database CHECKs. `test/storageKinds.test.ts` covers validation, replacement, disablement, plugin registration, scope removal and atomic worker rollback.

**Removed unused thread scaffolding** (owner, 2026-11-06). The never-built lane/multi-parent design's `lanes`, `slots.lane_id`, `slot_parents`, `slots.placement_group_id`, `chats.current_leaf_slot_id` and `slots.branch_name`/`branch_name_user` are gone, along with their indexes, triggers and LCM guards. Paths and siblings are bounded by chat and parent; alternate labels come from `forks.name`. Every implemented slot has one parent; intentional conversation joins retain their existing soft source references in `chat_merges`. A future in-chat thread design will get its own schema. The live `chats.active_leaf_slot_id`, fork pins and library-ref labels/subtitles remain in use. All application tables, including `chat_pins` and `settings`, are STRICT; the schema test checks this.

**Consolidated settings** (settingsdb, owner 2026-11-06; BASELINE CHANGED). `settings(scope, scope_id, key, value_json, revision, updated_at)` is the only settings table, keyed by `(scope, scope_id, key)`. The five former preference/settings tables are removed from the baseline; a fresh deploy is required, with no migrations or backfill. **New settings must go into this table through the settings registry, never a new table.**

`db/settings.ts` registers each key's scope and Effect schema in `settingsRegistry`. Registrations can be added, replaced or disabled for a scope; trusted `StateModules` installers receive this registry as their third argument, including in source and bundled workers. `writeSetting` validates the active declaration, compares a replacement's expected row revision (absent row = 0), increments it, and timestamps the row inside the caller's synchronous writer transaction. Cost formulas (`cost`) and global regex (`regex.global`) use that common check; their JSON no longer carries its own revision. Patch operations read/merge/write in one transaction, preserving concurrent edits to unrelated fields; resets store JSON null where applicable, keeping revision history to prevent a stale pre-reset replacement. Existing typed worker operations and client hooks retain their API shapes and ownership checks.

- `app`: `scope_id = ''`, key `network`; the encrypted proxy and network-cache invalidation remain unchanged.
- `user`: `scope_id = userId`; display, notices, shell pins fold, costs, persona/generation defaults, global regex, card favourites, bin limits, decision models, token-counting choices and imported summary settings.
- `device`: `scope_id` is the collision-free JSON pair `[userId, deviceId]`, so accounts on the same browser remain isolated. No key uses it since the workbench layout moved to each browser tab (homeopen, 2026-11-07).

Split-chat markers are chat state on `forks.split_chat`, not settings. They are owner-scoped through the fork's chat and cascade with the fork. The unchanged split/group/pin/bin APIs now read that flag. `test/settings.test.ts` covers validation, registration replacement/disablement, scope/owner/device separation, revisions, reset/stale-write protection, atomic rollback and plugin loading in both worker modes; existing display, shell, costs, regex, decisions, import and LCM tests exercise the feature paths.

**Planning indexes** (planperf1, 2026-11-14; **BASELINE CHANGED**, fresh deploy, no migration). `slots_chain_cover(chain_id, depth, id, parent_slot_id)` covers metadata path spans; `versions_lcm_inputs(id, slot_id, status, content_length, deleted_at, purged_at)` covers effective-input proofs; `summaries_status(chat_id, status, level)` bounds the complete/failed existence probes. The unique `slots_chain` and version-identity indexes remain their integrity constraints. Readers drive summary metadata from requested ids, and ending-slot candidates from selected path segments; they do not scan every branch's summaries before filtering.

**LCM stamp** (planperf2, 2026-11-14; **BASELINE CHANGED**, fresh deploy, no migration). `chats.lcm_stamp` moves, by the `lcm_stamp_*` triggers (`baseline.ts` `lcmStamp`), on every write that can change what a reader knows of a sealed summary in any fork of the chat: an update or delete of a slot or version that is some summary's input, its text, amendments or attachments; every fork override except stars and picker hides, and the message kinds (`select`, `replace`, `delete_slot`, `delete_version`, `hide`) only for a slot that is an input (or none named); revisions, inputs or parents of a sealed summary; a sealed summary's update or a summary's delete; summary choices, changesets and their items, chat merges, published LCM ranges and their slots; a completed explicit rerun job (it marks its source replaced); a fork's lineage, deletion or purge; the chat's owner or deletion; and dropped fork labels (with their fork, or by `rebuildForkLabels`, which rewrites every step). Appending, new versions, writing, swiping or editing a message no summary covers, settings, and job status changes move nothing. `db/lcmFactStore.ts` reads it (§16 "Kept planning facts").

**Version metadata and payloads** (versiontext, 2026-11-06; **BASELINE CHANGED**, fresh deploy). `versions` holds the integer `seq`, public id, slot/ordinal, status, author, macro mode, origin/source, rollout/model/connection/changeset references, flags, fork, timestamps and the payload-maintained `content_length`. All prose and JSON live in `version_texts(version_seq PRIMARY KEY)`: content, reasoning, raw content/reasoning/sections, reply sections, context/display forms, rewrite evidence, frozen macros, direction, greeting reference, cast snapshot, errors, usage and imported generation attribution. The payload references `versions.seq` with delete cascade; a reverse deferred FK requires exactly one payload per metadata row at commit. Payload ownership cannot change and a payload cannot be removed while its version exists.

Text readers and writers use `version_records`, a flattened join view, for inner/point reads and writes. Optional payload reads use separate indexed `LEFT JOIN`s on metadata and text: SQLite otherwise materializes the entire joined view, even for a small window. LCM joins payloads only for effective nonempty messages; its scale test counts the real projection’s metadata and payload reads from 2,000 to 100,000 slots. Its `INSTEAD OF` insert trigger writes both tables in the same SQL statement, including bulk `INSERT ... SELECT` imports and fork/merge/history copies. Its update trigger saves the amendment timestamp and purge authorization first, writes changed payloads while generation is still open, then finalizes metadata/status. Read back persisted rows when defaults or the generated integer key are needed: SQLite's view `RETURNING` reports supplied values. Operations and DTOs keep their public shapes. Structural path walks, version flags/counts, fork lineage, membership/activity projections and inspector source ordinals use the narrow table; only message bodies/previews, assembly, history/search/export and payload writes join text. Emptiness, token estimates and eligibility/freshness checks use `content_length` without joining prose; SQLite maintains and guards that count on payload insert/change. The search candidate walk also stays narrow until fetching matched bodies.

FTS5 retains `versions.seq` as its document key but takes external content from `version_texts.version_seq`. Payload inserts/content changes and metadata status transitions maintain it; generating text stays unindexed. The parent’s before-delete trigger removes the index entry before cascading its payload. Model-content freezing and amendment history run on the payload table and read their version's status/author, timestamp and bin authorization. Failed versions require an error payload. Cast insert/update and speaker changes maintain `version_participants`; shell stamp/touch triggers track changed content and cast separately, preserving fork-local summary validity. Purges also empty the raw text and rewrite evidence and include those bytes in their size estimate. `test/schema.test.ts` covers the physical split, one-to-one ownership, direct payload guards and FTS/history behavior; the recorded baseline schema is updated with the code.

**Bounded preview reads.** Shell summary walks carry selected version keys and content counts, then fetch only each fork's newest candidate excerpt in batches, sharing equal selections across forks; whitespace-only 160-character prefixes fall back to earlier candidates using the existing JavaScript trim semantics. History, participation, activity and split calculations never join payloads. `lastText` finds each chain range's newest visible nonblank version with a descending indexed walk, then reads the winning excerpt, rather than sorting every path body before `LIMIT 1`. Its full-text whitespace test retains the existing ASCII trim semantics. Both skip failed/deleted messages and retain empty fallbacks.

**Measurements.** `test/versionFlagsScale.test.ts` uses the same synthetic 2,000-message/20-swipe and 5,000-message/50-swipe fixtures before/after the split: alternating human/model turns, 5% fork-owned edited copies, 142-character short replies versus 2–8k reply characters plus 5–20k reasoning (400-character human turns). It measures real reader path/shell/assembly calls and worker SQL with a 256 MiB cache. SQL's first call follows `PRAGMA shrink_memory` (SQLite-cold, OS cache uncontrolled), followed by seven warm samples; application timings are first-call and five-call warm medians. Assembly retains its fixed 32k budget, so long replies fit fewer messages. A disposable narrow flag table remains an ideal control. Schemaclean's original realistic 5k/50 all-swipe flags cost 2,044 ms warm versus 75 ms in the control, and full shell SQL 2,102 ms. The paired versiontext runs and query plans are under `<work>/artifacts/versiontext/`; the brief's report records before/after numbers. These measurements do not establish physical cold-disk behavior or a reply-generation speedup.

**Old databases are refused.** Before the migrator runs, the ledger (`effect_sql_migrations`) is read: if it holds an id this code doesn't know (any database made before the squash, or by a newer build), startup fails with a message to start from an empty data directory, and nothing is run or changed. Migration numbers named elsewhere in this file (`0052`, `0053`, …) refer to steps of the replaced chain.

Conventions:
- **Tables:** all `STRICT`, with JSON columns guarded by `json_valid` CHECKs and timestamps in epoch milliseconds.
- **Ids:** UUIDv7 (`@rp/shared/id.ts`), so `ORDER BY id` follows creation order.
- **Concurrency:** mutable rows carry `row_version` for optimistic concurrency.
- **Mutual references** (`slots.selected_version_id` ↔ `versions.slot_id`, a summary ↔ its selected revision) use deferred foreign keys. The version row is inserted first, then the slot, in one transaction.

**Invariants enforced by the database** (`db/baseline.ts`). Triggers check each statement, so no single statement can break these, and `test/schema.test.ts` checks each one on a bare connection. A sequence of statements still can, for example deleting a selected model version and inserting another under its id in one transaction: no trigger can tell that from a legitimate insert. The writer is the only code path that writes, and these back it up:
- **Edits are non-destructive.** Changing content creates new rows; it never overwrites. Deliberate deletion is allowed, and foreign keys keep it consistent: for example, a slot can't be left selecting a deleted version, and deleting a chat removes everything in it, its chat-local overrides and drafts included.
  - Model-written versions are frozen once they stop generating, and a version never goes back to generating. Only deleting for good from the recycle bin empties one: `purged_at` set, under a bin item of the chat's owner that the version, or its slot, carries (a swipe, message or branch item; an import's copy carries the original's, migration 0042). `purged_at` is never cleared on versions and slots.
  - Amending a user-written version copies the previous content into `version_history` automatically, with its thinking as `reasoning_json` (JSON: the text, or null for none; NULL in a row that didn't record it) and its reply sections as `sections_json` (NULL: none). An amend of the images or the thinking alone writes that row itself (thinkedit1, **BASELINE CHANGED**, fresh deploy).
  - Entity revisions and summary revisions are immutable.
  - A rollout's context snapshot is frozen once written.
  - State events can only be superseded, not changed.
- **The graph is append-only.**
  - A slot's parent is in the same chat, one level up.
  - A slot never moves.
  - A slot's chain (§3.8) is assigned by the database when it's inserted, never changes, and holds one slot per depth. A state event carries its slot's chain and depth, set the same way and fixed; a chat-wide event has neither (`test/chains.test.ts`).
  - A fork (§3.8) keeps the parent, base and moment it was made at, and its place in its chat's fork tree (`fork_labels`, §3.8 "Fork labels"), and never moves to another chat; a chat starts with one, made by a trigger, whose id is the chat's (`test/forks.test.ts`). A trigger places every fork in the tree as it's inserted; its parent and moment never change.
  - A slot keeps the selection it was inserted with (`slots_selection_frozen`, 0054): a fork's choice is an override (§3.8), so no single write can change what two forks show. An override keeps its fork, kind and target, and in place only takes a newer value and seq (`test/forkSelection.test.ts`).
  - A version's slot, writer and origin never change, and its source can only be cleared.
  - A slot stays inserted or not as it was inserted (`slots.inserted`, `slots_inserted_frozen`; spec/MESSAGE-INSERT.md §2.2). An `insert` override places an inserted slot of its chat: `slot_id` is the slot's parent (its anchor, null above the first message) with the parent's depth, the flag is set (1 placed, 0 not) and there's no value, bin item or changeset, on insert and on update (`fork_overrides_insert`, `fork_overrides_insert_update`).
  - A `move` override (schemafinal, 2026-11-16; **BASELINE CHANGED**, fresh deploy) shows a slot of its chat after another of its slots: `target_id` and `slot_id` are the moved slot (with its depth), `value_id` the slot it follows (null: above the first message), or the slot itself, which leaves it out of the fork (finalwipe1, 2026-11-16: written by a fork made where its parent showed the slot further down, §3.8 "Moves"); flag 1 moves it, 0 puts it back at its own place with no value; no bin item or changeset, on insert and on update (`fork_overrides_move`, `fork_overrides_move_update`).
- **References stay inside their chat.**
  - A slot selects only its own versions, which is what invariant 3 rests on, and so does a fork's selection override; an override is in its fork's chat.
  - A chat's active leaf is one of its slots, and it is the current fork's tip: triggers keep the two equal whichever one a statement moves (`db/baseline.ts`), so what still reads the chat's leaf reads the current fork. A chat's current fork is one of its forks.
  - A fork's parent, base and tip are in its chat, as are the forks slots, rollouts and queued messages name.
  - A version's source ("edited from #7") is a version of the same slot. Deleting the source clears the reference.
  - A state event's slot is in its chat, and its version is in that slot.
  - A summary selects only its own revisions.
