Its Undo is `RestoreBinItems` (1–1,000 item ids, `RestoredItems`): each item still in the bin restored as `RestoreBinItem` would, in the order given, in one transaction; items gone already are skipped, `NotFound` when none is left. The API publishes `Reload` and `Chat` to each chat touched, refreshes the user's cache estimates (any delete can evict a shared dependency) and stops generations whose versions are no longer live, as single delete does. Summaries over the deleted messages go stale as for single delete (`recordReduction`). **Client** (`features/chat/selection/`, registered in `chat/index.tsx`): the message action **Select messages** (`message.select`, order 105, group `delete`, on merged-chat entries too) starts selecting with that message ticked. Each message then shows a tick (`RowTick` in `ui/Choice.tsx`, a 32 px target) before its portrait, in the `message.select` slot (`presentation.tsx`; first in a merged chat's header); the message still being written can't be ticked, and its tick says why. Ticks live in one `MessageSelection` store per open chat (`selection/store.ts`, tab only, gone on reload); each row reads only its own tick through `useSyncExternalStore`, so ticking, or a range of 500, re-renders only the rows whose tick changed, never the list. A range is every message shown between the last tick and the next, with **Select range** on the bar or Shift held while ticking; the store keeps what the confirmation needs of each ticked message (position, version count, copies) while it's scrolled out of the window. The bar (`chat.selection-bar` in the `chat.composer-notes` slot, whose props now carry the session too; in the workshop's side chat as well) counts the ticked messages and offers Select range, Cancel (also Esc) and **Delete…**, which confirms: the count, that they go to the bin with all their versions, that only this branch changes, that copies sent to other threads stay, and that Undo or the bin puts them back. Then one toast, "N messages moved to the bin.", with one **Undo** (`restoreItems` in `features/bin/deleted.ts`), "Delete the copies too" when any had copies in other threads (a `DeleteMessages` per thread), and Open the bin. Showing another branch ends selecting. Tests: server `test/messageSelection.test.ts` (end and middle ranges and their Undo, branch-local, all or nothing, another user's slots, and equal to deleting the same messages one by one), `test/messageSelectionScale.test.ts` (slow: 1,000 of 3,000 messages with 300 branches, at the end and in the shared middle, and Undo), `test/isolation.test.ts`, client `test/messageSelection.test.ts` (ticks, Shift and Select range, the message being written, the limit, a range of 500 among 3,000 in one notification), `e2e/messageSelection.spec.ts` (range, confirmation, delete and Undo at 1440 and 390 px in both themes with the layout audit; Cancel, Esc, Shift-click).
- **Hiding several from the model** (job selecthide1; ST's `/hide N-M`, owner 2026-11-16). `SetMessagesHidden` (same group, handler in `api/messageSelection.ts`) takes a fork, 1–1,000 slot ids (`DeletedSlots`) and `hidden`, and hides or shows each exactly as `SetMessageHidden` would, in one writer transaction (`SetSlotsHidden` in `db/writes.ts`; both share `setSlotHidden`): a `hide` row of the fork's own and, for a hide, `recordReduction`, so summaries and requests treat the messages as the single hide does. All or nothing: every id must be shown on the fork's display path (`pathPieces`/`positionOf`, one query for all of them) and not deleted there, else `NotFound` and nothing written. It returns `changed`, the ids that weren't so already; the same call the other way with those ids is the Undo. When anything changed the API publishes `Reload`, `State` and `Chat` and refreshes the user's cache estimates. **Client**: the selection bar shows **Hide from the model** while any ticked message is shown (and, disabled, when none is ticked) and **Show to the model** while any is hidden, so a mix offers both; each acts at once on the ticked messages it applies to (the store keeps each one's `hidden`), ends selecting, and shows one toast ("N messages hidden from the model." / "shown to the model again.") with one **Undo**. Tests: server `test/messageSelection.test.ts` (branch-local, `changed`, Undo, all or nothing, and equal to hiding one at a time: summary freshness, the next request, the stored overrides and history changes), `test/messageSelectionScale.test.ts` (hiding and showing the same 1,000 of 3,000 messages with 300 branches), `test/isolation.test.ts`, `e2e/messageSelection.spec.ts` (hide a range, Undo, a mix offering both, Show and its Undo, at 1440 and 390 px in both themes with the layout audit).
- **Independent multi-delete review (review-msgactions1, 2026-11-14).** The batch validates ownership, effective deletion state, a non-streaming selected version and membership on the requested branch's display path before writing. It orders bin items by display position even if input ids arrive backwards. Requested ids drive indexed slot/version/payload joins and grouped byte counts. One chain-interval query finds other branches retaining structural messages; inserted messages use the existing display-path probe. Bin entries, overrides, reductions and global marks are written in batches, with the same child-cutoff reuse rule and alternating override/reduction sequences as single delete. The response is read in one ordered query. These changes retain single-message marking, UTF-8 size accounting and reduction records without per-message branch walks or writer round trips. Bulk Undo rejects a set containing another account’s bin item before restoring any of it; already restored or purged ids remain skippable. Undo of one group after a further send recovers the deleted tail on one branch; individual bin restores and unrelated groups retain their own restore behavior. Selection listens to its chat session: switching branches, leaving the chat or a history reload ends it (including choices outside the loaded window), closes its confirmation, and regeneration drops that message's tick. The history-reload policy deliberately also ends selection for unrelated history changes, rather than leaving a stale choice offscreen. Selection registrations declare `source: import.meta.url`, following the existing notice/tool/macro provenance convention; the message-action and slot-entry interfaces accept that optional metadata. This does not add those surfaces to the plugin copy catalog.
- **Forks' tips:** deleting a message moves the tip of the fork that deleted it, if it ended there, to the nearest message that fork still shows; the forks' composers stay theirs. A Reload reads the current fork for a tab that was showing it; a tab explicitly showing another fork keeps it. The header follows the chat's current fork after deleting the one shown. Its menu's **Delete this fork** deletes the fork shown.
- **Chats and entities:** `DeleteChat` and `DeleteEntity`.

**Deleting for good** (`PurgeBinItem`, `EmptyBin`; the UI confirms these):
- **A chat** is deleted, with everything in it and its other bin items.
- **A fork** deleted on its own keeps its row, losing its name and tip (`purged_at`), as forks made from it read its overrides; the messages marked under its item are emptied, so another live or restorable fork keeps its history. A branch deleted before forks keeps its forks' rows the same way.
- **An entity** loses its refs, revisions and tags. The entity row stays, so messages that named it as their speaker still point somewhere.
- **A message, fork's messages or swipe** have their versions emptied: content, reasoning, display forms, amend history and attachments. Slots stay as placeholders, so the conversation's structure and any summaries over it remain valid. This is the one exception to model output being frozen: a version may be emptied only as part of a purge of its own bin item (§3.7). **A message or swipe deleted in a fork is erased in every fork** (owner, 2026-10-27, Q3 (b)), the ones that still show it included, after a warning that names them: the purge marks the slot (or swipe) under its item for every fork (`deleted_at` and `purged_at` mean deleted everywhere, `slotDeletedInSql`), a swipe that forks showed is replaced by another in each (`dropSelections`; one with none left deletes the message in its own view), and a fork whose tip it was moves up. The warning set is `BinItemForks` (`@rp/shared/binApi.ts`: the forks other than the deleting one that show an item, forks in the bin included, each with its name and the start of its tip). What the dialogs list is `BinItemBranches` (owner, 2026-11-01; `binItemBranches` in `db/binForks.ts`, a reader operation): every branch the purge affects, each a `BinBranch` with its state, `shown` (a live branch shows the text), `deletedHere` (a live branch deleted it in its own view: the item's fork, or another whose own message or swipe item over the same text the purge also ends), `branchInBin` (the branch itself is in the bin) or `chatInBin`; `shows`, true exactly for the forks `BinItemForks` names (it's built from that read); the branch-list naming parts (`name`, `original`, `number`: "Branch k" among the chat's live forks made from another, by creation, as `branchLabel` numbers them); its display position of the message (`position`, on its path, or on the path to the slot with its insertions when its tip went up past it); and `link`, the message to open it at: the message itself where it shows it, else the nearest message it shows above it within 200 positions (else below, on its own path), and null for a branch or chat in the bin, which can't be opened. A fork deleted on its own lists itself, since what it takes no other fork has; a chat lists every unpurged fork of it; purged forks never appear. Live branches that show it come first, then `deletedHere`, then those in the bin, each most recently current first. `test/binBranches.test.ts` covers several forks, one showing the message one place down after an insertion, one that went another way, one in the bin, one purged, one whose tip went up past its own deletion, the branch, chat and swipe items, and `shows` against `BinItemForks`. The bin page's Delete for good and Empty the bin dialogs wait for a successful read before they can confirm. Successful purges return affected chat ids from the writer and publish Reload, State and the updated Chat to open tabs, or Deleted for a removed chat. The dialogs send the ids of the entries with `shows` with confirmation; the writer recomputes the set in the purge transaction and returns `BinChanged` if it changed. Internal callers may omit this optional acknowledgement; the regular UI only sends things to the bin. Making room (below) never erases what another fork shows: that item just leaves the bin, its deletion staying in its fork (an item with another bin deletion of the same content is skipped, so eviction cannot destroy that other item's restore). An ST re-import that forks a shared path (§13) copies deleted messages, swipes and branches with the original's bin item: restoring the item brings back every copy, and deleting it for good empties every copy (`test/stImportForkBin.test.ts`).
- `EmptyBin` takes the exact item ids shown for confirmation. In the writer transaction it compares them with the user's current bin; additions, removals or replacements return `BinChanged` without purging anything. The client loads all pages before enabling Empty the bin, captures the ids when the dialog opens, and reloads on closing a changed confirmation. Purging those ids is set-based; unposted queue text is recovered before any purge can remove it.

**Two independent sections**, each evicting its own oldest entries past its own limits, never the other's:
- **Deleted items** (`ListBin`): 10,000 items or 2 GB by default. Eviction deletes the oldest for good, never the item the delete just made, each in a savepoint: a purge that fails is rolled back, logged and skipped, so it never fails the delete that triggered it. If what can go can't make room, nothing goes and the bin stays over its limits (DESIGN §6.2, proposed).
- Sizes are UTF-8 bytes. A deleted item's is what deleting it for good frees: its versions' text columns, amend history and attachment alt text; for a chat also its rollouts and their payloads, summaries, state events and changesets; for an entity its revisions and their search text. Messages and swipes already in the bin count only under their own items.
- **Recovered text** (`ListRecoveredTexts`, `GetRecoveredText`, `DeleteRecoveredText`, `ClearRecoveredTexts`): 2,000 texts or 200 MB by default. It's produced passively by draft commits, discards, history retention and composer text saved after its draft was sent (§3.10), and by removing unposted queue entries, so it never shows a toast.
- Each entry records where it came from: a title, an excerpt and origin details for deleted items, a source label like `Composer in "Harbor"` for recovered text. So text can be copied out without restoring.
- Both lists page newest first, with a cursor of the last entry's time and id, so entries from the same millisecond are never skipped.
- **Configurable capacities** (U13): `GetBinLimits` reads the account's four positive safe-integer limits from user-scoped `settings` (`bin.limits`), falling back to the defaults above. `ChangeBinLimit` changes one field in one writer transaction, preserving the others. The registered `bin.capacity` contribution in the bin page exposes item and byte limits independently for both sections. Saving a limit never purges anything; the writer reads the saved limits on later deletes and recovered-text additions and applies the existing eviction rules, including the oversized-item and shared-fork protections. `Database.layer({ binLimits })` supplies the same fallback to both reader and writer workers; reading or saving a single capacity preserves the other configured limits, including before an account has saved preferences. No new schema is needed. Restart, RPC validation, section independence and ownership are covered by `binLimits.test.ts`, `bin.test.ts` and the isolation matrix.
- **Capacity controls** (`BinCapacity.tsx`, binunits): the registered bin-capacity section uses the shared `Disclosure` (the app’s chevron disclosure). Size limits are a number and MB/GB selector, stored as bytes through the unchanged RPC. GB is chosen when at most one decimal converts back to the same whole-byte count, otherwise MB; arbitrary older byte limits retain their MB precision. Positive decimal sizes round to the nearest byte; empty, nonnumeric, nonpositive and unsafe limits show an inline error and disable Save. Item counts show grouped digits after loading or leaving a field and plain digits as the user types. Each Save is in the control row with an 8 px gap, including on phones; the unit picker keeps its compact width even inside a two-column grid beside the open sidebar. This local field component is used only by bin capacities; no other Settings section shares it.

**The client's RPCs** (`@rp/shared/binApi.ts`, `api/bin.ts`): `ListBin`, `RestoreBinItem`, `PurgeBinItem`, `BinItemForks`, `BinItemBranches`, `EmptyBin`, `ListRecoveredTexts` (every source), `GetRecoveredText`, `DeleteRecoveredText`. Restoring something inside a chat publishes `Reload`, `State` and `Chat` to it, so open tabs read it again, its state included. **The bin page** (`/bin`, linked from the header and every delete's toast; `features/bin/`): deleted items, newest first, a chat named by its readable name and the day ST started it, never ST's file name (`binTitle` in `features/bin/titles.ts`, shared with the toast: labels are built from `kind`, `origin.chatTitle`, branch message counts and, for a message or version, its number in the chat where it was deleted (`origin.position` + 1, its display position in that fork, which inserted messages move off its depth; items binned before it was recorded use `origin.depth`: "Message 12 in “…”"), formatting the whole title with `readableChatTitle`; embedded quotes are preserved. Recovered sources use their known `sourceKind` prefix and one outer quoted title, preserving embedded quotes and leaving library-field labels unchanged), with Restore (then a link to where it went back to) and Delete for good, and Empty the bin, both confirmed with what deleting for good does to that kind. A Delete for good confirmation asks in plain words without nesting the chat's title (`purgeTitle` in `features/bin/titles.ts`: "Delete version 3 of message 21 for good?", the version numbered by its ordinal from 1; "Delete message 21 for good?", "Delete the branch “Side road” for good?") and names the chat in its body ("From the chat “…”."). Under it, both dialogs render the `bin.purge-branches` slot, whose registered `bin.affected-branches` contribution (`features/bin/AffectedBranches.tsx`) lists the `BinItemBranches` entries: a count of the branches affected, how many still show the text and how many hold it only in the bin, then every entry, named by `branchName` (`features/chat/forks.ts`, which `branchLabel` uses too, so the names are the header's Branch list's), with **Shows it** (warning tone) or **In the bin**, its message number or why it's in the bin, the start of its last message and, for emptying the bin, its chat. Each entry with a `link` is an `<a href>` to `/chats/<chat>?slot=<message>&fork=<branch>`, Copy link's scheme with the branch always named (so it opens that branch even if another became current since), which opens the chat there, flashing the message; an entry that opens at a neighbour says so ("opens at message 20, above it"). Links open in a new tab (`target="_blank"`, said in the count line), so a plain click leaves the confirmation as it was; middle-click and the browser's own new-tab commands work as on any link. The list scrolls inside the dialog (at most 22rem or 40% of the viewport), so hundreds of branches keep the dialog within the screen and its buttons visible. `e2e/binBranches.spec.ts` covers the list, the marks, each link's href and the message flashing, then unmarked, in the opened tab, and a 301-branch list within the screen, at 1440 and 390 pixels, with screenshots in both themes when `BIN_BRANCH_SHOTS` is set; recovered text, each shown whole in a dialog to copy, and deleted for good after a confirmation. The `bin.settings` slot (capacity, below) comes after both sections, under a rule.

### 3.12 Connections, models and the usage ledger

The provider layer's storage (spec/PROVIDERS.md §2, §3.1, §9.1), in `db/baseline.ts`.

**`credentials`** (migration `0006_credentials`): keys, each stored once and used by any number of connections.
- **The columns:** `key_enc` (encrypted, bound to `credential:<id>:key`), `key_hint` (its last 4 characters; empty for keys under 12, where 4 characters would be most of the key), a name, `origins_json`, the origins (scheme, host and port) the key may be sent to, and `connection_owned` (0008): the credential was made from a key typed into one connection.
- **The rule** (owner, 2026-10-11): a key is sent only to an origin its credential allows.
  - The origins are recorded when the key is entered.
  - Adding one takes the key typed again (`AllowCredentialHost`). The main thread checks it against the stored key with a constant-time comparison.
  - Code acting as the user without knowing the key (a stolen session, an XSS, a plugin in the page) can edit connections, but can't redirect a key to a new host.
  - Changing a path on the same host needs nothing.
  - **Replacing a key states its origins again** (`ReplaceCredentialKey` takes them). Origins approved under the old key don't carry over: otherwise a stolen session could swap in a junk key, approve its own host with it, and wait for the user to re-enter the real one.
    - **The client must make the user confirm each origin** in the replace-key dialog, starting from the hosts of the connections using the credential. It must not pre-fill and submit the stored list: a stolen session can replace the key and the origins together, and the server can't tell that from the user. A stolen session can also re-point those connections first, so the dialog flags every origin that wasn't in the credential's list before.
  - **Header values are bound the same way.** `headers_origin` (0008) records the origin they were set for, and they're refused anywhere else until set again. Gateway tokens, Azure's `api-key` and Cloudflare Access secrets live in headers. Headers from before 0008 have no origin and must be set again.
  - **A key typed into a connection** (`SetConnectionKey`) is bound to the base URL of the row version the user saw. A stale form is a `StaleWrite`, so a key isn't bound to a URL someone changed in the meantime. `SetConnectionHeaders` works the same way, and both pass the `StaleWrite` to the client as itself. The connection's previous key is deleted if the connection owned it and nothing else uses it, so a rotated (possibly leaked) key doesn't stay at rest. Purging a connection deletes its own key the same way. A credential the user created and attached is never deleted this way.
  - **Redirects stay within the origin** (`Network.fetchFor`). undici strips only `authorization` and cookies on a cross-origin redirect, so `x-api-key`, `x-goog-api-key` and custom headers would follow an open redirect on an allowed host. Same-origin redirects are followed (at most 5), each routed afresh using the request's pinned network settings. A redirect to another origin is a `RedirectRefused` error, reported as `unusable` and never retried. Google uses the same redirect policy and pinned transport.
  - **A connection's own proxy can't carry a key over `http`.** Setting one needs no key, and over `http` the proxy reads every byte. Such a connection is `unusable` until it uses `https` or the instance proxy.
  - **Why:** keys are money, so making them easy to steal makes the frontend worth attacking. ST is a target for exactly this reason.
  - **Switching it off** is possible only from outside the app: `KEY_HOST_BINDING=false`. Most settings are meant to be changeable from inside, including by the user's agent; security settings are the exception.
  - **Server-side code can still read keys** (spec/PLUGINS.md §6.1). This protects against everything that acts through the browser.

**`connections`**: one provider, one provider kind, one wire API, one base URL, and at most one credential per row.
- `provider` (providerchoice, 2026-11-07; BASELINE CHANGED) is the provider the connection was made from (§6 "Providers"), and `provider_settings_json` (`Connection.providerSettings`) holds only the provider defaults the user changed. A connection made by kind alone gets the provider its kind and base URL imply (`defaultProviderId`). A change to the settings advances `cache_revision`.
- `kind` and `api` follow pi-ai's catalog, so the shared schema will validate them rather than a CHECK list.
- `credential_id` references the key the connection sends (`ON DELETE SET NULL`). The database allows only the connection owner's credentials.
- **Other secrets are columns of their own,** written encrypted:
  - `headers_enc`, with only `header_names_json` in the clear, because header values often carry credentials
  - `proxy_url_enc`
- **The database keeps them consistent:**
  - `proxy_mode = 'custom'` always has a proxy URL, and the other modes never do
  - a purged connection (`purged_at`) holds no credential, headers, proxy or base URL; it stays as a tombstone so old messages and ledger rows still name their model
- **The per-connection key columns are retired.** `api_key_enc` and `key_hint` stay in `connections`, but triggers keep them empty. They can go the next time the baseline is edited.
- `cache_revision` (0013) is a non-secret cache identity revision. Endpoint, route, credential, headers, compatibility and deletion/restoration changes advance it; instance network edits advance all connections. Snapshots pin the id and revision, without transport settings or secrets.
- `deleted_at` and `bin_item_id` are for the recycle bin, whose `bin_items.kind` now includes `connection`. The table was rebuilt for that, keeping its rows.

**`models`**: what the upstream reports (`upstream_json`, rewritten by every refresh) and what the user edited (`overrides_json`, never touched by a refresh) are separate columns, merged when read. A model the list stops reporting gets `missing_since` instead of being deleted. A model never moves to another connection or key. Assembly pins the reasoning/developer-role flags and a canonical digest of all resolved request-conversion capabilities (reasoning, vision, tools, thinking levels, output limit, compatibility and sampling). Arbitrary compatibility values stay out of snapshots; any capability change conservatively invalidates the prefix estimate.

**`llm_requests`**: one row per request to a model, retries and failed attempts included.
- **Opened as `running`** before the request is sent, and closed with its status, timings, normalized token counts (`input_uncached`, `cache_read`, `cache_write` with its long-TTL subset `cache_write_long`, `output` with its `reasoning` subset), the provider's raw usage object, any provider-reported cost, and the computed cost with its currency and formula. `running` exactly when `ended_at` is unset.
- **Unknown counts are `NULL`, never zero.** Provider-reported numbers have no CHECKs, so a quirky upstream can never make the closing write fail and leave a billed request unrecorded.
- **A closed request is a record:** only its cost can be recomputed, and a cost always names its currency and formula. Since schemafinal (owner, 2026-11-16; **BASELINE CHANGED**, fresh deploy) a priced request also stores the rates it was priced at (`cost_rates_json`: input, cache read, cache write, long cache write, output, per million tokens; only with a cost and never for a provider-reported one) and its network route (`route_json`: direct with its reason and whether it was pinned, or the proxy, its source and the proxy shown capped at 300 characters), both frozen once closed (`llm_requests_closed_frozen`). `llm_requests_recompute_priced` lets a closed row's cost, currency, formula and rates change only when it was priced from rates and is recomputed from rates (a price table, an override, a price endpoint); a provider-reported or rate-less row's cost is fixed. `pricedCost` (`providers/usage.ts`) returns the amount with its rates; the built-in formula and user formulas (`userCosts.ts`) report them; `requestRoute` (`net/route.ts`) maps the transport's route. Fetched provider or price-endpoint prices will live where model prices live now; there is no separate price table.
- **Attribution stays inside the user's data:** a request names only its own user's chat, a rollout and a version of that chat, and a model of its connection. Attribution can be cleared, never moved.
- **The ledger outlives what it's attributed to:** deleting a chat for good keeps its requests and clears their chat, rollout and version (`ON DELETE SET NULL`, indexed so a large chat deletes quickly).
- Indexed by user and by connection over time, for totals and later limits. The inspector explicitly uses the rollout index, then sorts that rollout's attempts; its query plan is tested.
- A request-local secret inventory is populated when keys, headers and proxy settings resolve. It includes all header values, custom and instance proxy URLs, encoded/decoded usernames and passwords, and Basic credentials. The prepared transport pins the same network settings across redirects and retries, so capture cannot miss a proxy changed between preparation and HTTP. This inventory scrubs both captured text/names and ledger metadata.
- Provider-controlled `response_model` and `upstream` are scrubbed with every nonempty request secret before being capped at 256 characters. The inspector projects only status, displayed counts, usage source and cost, so legacy metadata cannot expose a key through it.

**Operations** (`db/providerWrites.ts`, `db/providerReads.ts`; types in `@rp/shared/providers.ts` and `@rp/shared/usage.ts`):
- **Connections:**
  - `CreateConnection`: the caller picks the id, since secrets are encrypted bound to it
  - `UpdateConnection`: with `expectedRowVersion`
  - `SetConnectionKey` (a typed key or none, with `expectedRowVersion`), `SetConnectionCredential`, `SetConnectionHeaders` (with `expectedRowVersion`), `SetConnectionProxy`
  - `DeleteConnection`: through the bin. A purge leaves the tombstone described above.
  - `ListConnections`, `GetConnection`: secrets appear only as `hasKey`, `keyHint` and header names
  - `ResolveConnection`: the ciphertext and the credential's origins, for the provider layer only
- **Credentials:**
  - `CreateCredential`, `RenameCredential`
  - `ReplaceCredentialKey`: updates every connection using it, with the origins stated again
  - `AddCredentialOrigin`
  - `DeleteCredential`: connections using it are left without a key
  - `ListCredentials`: with how many connections use each
  - `ResolveCredential`: the ciphertext only, for checking a retyped key
- **Models:**
  - `SyncFetchedModels`: adds new models, refreshes `upstream_json`, and marks unlisted ones missing. Models only ever added by hand are never marked.
  - `AddUserModel`, with what the kind's catalog, the registered catalogs and the shims give the id as its upstream
  - `EditModel`: with `expectedRowVersion`
  - `SetLearnedContext`: sets or clears `overrides.learned` (a context size saved from a provider's error), keeping the other edits
  - `SetModelHidden`
  - `ListModels`, `GetModel`
  - `resolveModel` (shared) merges the sources, user edits first. It reports each field's source (`user`, `learned`, `upstream`, `catalog`, `unknown`), and fields no source knows as `unknown` with a safe default. The context window resolves from the user's value, then `overrides.learned`, then what the list reports, then what a catalog matched by id reports (`upstream.catalog` names the catalog, the matched entry and the fields it gave), then `ASSUMED_CONTEXT` (128,000, `modelSettings.ts`), always shown as assumed (owner report 2026-10-31: a window nobody reported was silently 8,192).
  - **The model's settings form** (`ModelSettingsEditor`, `features/connections/models.tsx`: the chat's Model tab, a connection's Edit dialog, the budget note's dialog) has three parts. **Model limits (from the provider)**: the context window and the longest reply as `resolveModel` resolves them under the user's own values, read-only, each with its source ("assumed", "learned from the provider's context-length error", the catalog, or reported), and a pencil that opens the user's own value (open from the start when one is set, or when a link asked for the field), with "Use what's reported" to drop it. **What it can do**: vision, reasoning, tools and prefill, each "as the provider says" unless chosen, the choice naming what the provider says ("As the provider says: yes", or, unreported, "Not known: the provider doesn't say"), one per row unless the form has room for two (a container query: the dialog, not the chat's panel). **Your settings for this model**: context to send and reply length (`samplers.openai_max_context`, `openai_max_tokens`, defaulting to all of the window and up to 4096) and the samplers.
- **Ledger:**
  - `OpenLlmRequest`, `CloseLlmRequest`
  - `InterruptRunningLlmRequests`, for startup
  - `ListLlmRequests`
- **Ownership:** as in §3.8, everything on another user's connection, model or ledger row is `NotFound` (`test/providers.test.ts` runs every operation as a second user).
  - A connection's preset override must be one of the user's own live refs. Another user's ref, and a ref that doesn't exist, are the same `NotFound`, so ref ids can't be probed.
  - A key given at creation is stored in the same transaction as the connection.
  - `ListLlmRequests` pages by `(started_at, id)`, so requests started in the same millisecond aren't skipped.
  - A model list that repeats a key keeps the last entry.
- **Generation rollups** (`db/generationWrites.ts`, `FinishRollout`): the transaction sums the rollout’s `llm_requests` counts and cost into `rollouts` and writes the same totals, request count and currency to its version’s `usage_json` (§15).

### 3.12a MCP servers: remote connections and Check (M1)

spec/MCP.md M1 (job `mcp1`, 2026-11-16), on the M0 tables (§3.7 "MCP storage"). `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.32.2 (exact). Nothing in M1 offers MCP tools to a model or calls one: the only requests sent are a user's **Check** (and the Check that **Add and check** and an address or transport change run).

- **API** (`shared/mcpApi.ts`, `shared/mcp.ts`, `api/mcp.ts`): `ListMcpConnections`, `GetMcpConnection` (with the catalog), `CreateMcpConnection` (settings and an optional typed key or saved credential; checks at once), `UpdateMcpConnection` (row version; checks again when the address or transport changed), `SetMcpKey`, `SetMcpCredential`, `SetMcpHeaders`, `SetMcpProxy`, `CheckMcpConnection`, `SetMcpUse` (allow list and reviewed revision; the Stories and Workshops switches, which workshops read since M2, §3.12b), `DeleteMcpConnection` (to the bin) and `ListMcpCalls` (paged by `(started_at, id)`, 50 a page). Owner-only: a connection someone else owns is `NotFound` everywhere (isolation matrix). All are user-only in the agent's operation exclusions. Settings are checked before anything is stored: a name of 1 to 100 characters, what it's for up to 1,000, an http(s) address up to 2,048, a timeout of 5 to 1,800 s (`McpRefused`).
- **Storage** (`db/mcpRows.ts`, `db/mcpWrites.ts`, `db/mcpReads.ts`, in the writer and reader workers). The key (`mcp_<key>_<tool>`) comes from the name at creation (`mcpKeyFor`: lowercase `[a-z0-9]`, at most 24, a number added when the owner's live or purged-but-unfreed keys or their offered keys have it) and never changes. A typed key becomes a connection-owned credential bound to the address's origin, as a provider connection's key (§3.12); the credentials list counts MCP connections in `usedBy`, and a connection-owned key goes when nothing uses it. Changing the address, transport, timeout, key, headers or proxy bumps `cache_revision`; `SaveMcpCatalog` refuses a listing made against an older `cache_revision` or `catalog_revision` (`StaleWrite`), so a Check that raced an edit is dropped rather than stored. Purging a connection deletes its connection-owned key, its uses (freeing its key) and its shares, and leaves the tombstone M0 defines (no address, program, headers, environment or credential).
- **Client** (`mcp/McpConnections.ts`). `prepare` mirrors `Providers.prepare`: the credential must allow the address's origin, headers must have been set for that origin (else "set them again"), the proxy override and the instance's forced proxy apply, the key goes as `Authorization: Bearer`, and every secret is in the request's scrub list (`requestSecrets`). Requests go through `Network.fetchFor` (same-origin redirects only), with the SDK's `StreamableHTTPClientTransport` (no automatic reconnection) or `SSEClientTransport`. Each request (`initialize`, each `tools/list` page) is one `mcp_calls` row, opened `running` before it is sent and closed with its status (`complete`, `error` for a JSON-RPC error, `failed`, `timeout`, `cancelled`), its bytes each way (JSON message sizes counted at the transport) and a scrubbed error. The connection's timeout applies to each request. At startup, rows left `running` become `interrupted`. The client declares no capabilities and answers any server request with "method not found". Delta from reference-harness's `McpClientPool`: no startup connect and no pool; a client lives for one Check.
- **Catalog** (`mcp/catalog.ts`). `tools/list` is read with the SDK's plain result schema, so one malformed tool doesn't fail the listing; at most 1,000 tools and 2 MiB. A tool whose name isn't valid or whose parameters aren't a JSON-schema object of at most 64 KiB is stored with its problem and can't be allowed. Exposed names are `mcp_<key>_<tool>` with other characters as `_`; a name over 64 characters, or one two tools would share, gets a 6-hex suffix of its SHA-256 (longer on a further clash), and a tool keeps the exposed name it had. Tools are sorted by exposed name. The catalog revision goes up only when the listing changed; a tool remembers the revision it first appeared in. The first listing counts as reviewed, so its tools start allowed; a tool listed later starts off and shows **New** until the user chooses (`mcpToolAllowed`, `mcpToolIsNew`). Annotations are kept and shown as information only.
- **Check** (`check`) stores the listing or the error. When the chosen transport fails for a reason other than sign-in, a timeout or a stop, it tries the other one once (also a ledger row) and says "It answers the older SSE transport: switch to it" (or the reverse), with a one-click switch in the UI.
- **UI** (`client/features/mcp/`): Settings group **Tools** (order 15) with **MCP servers** (`/settings/mcp`), **Add an MCP server** (`/settings/mcp/new`) and each server's page (`/settings/mcp/$connectionId`), whose sections are `mcpSections` slot entries: Server (name, what it's for, transport, address, timeout), Sign-in (bearer token typed or saved, header names with write-only values, the origin warnings with Allow), Tools (Check now, the result, the tool checkboxes with New, problems and annotations), Network route, Recent calls (the ledger, 50 at a time) and Delete. The bin shows the kind as "MCP server".
- **Tests**: `test/mcp.test.ts` against `test/support/fakeMcpServer.ts` (the SDK's own server over both transports on a local port, recording every request): names, keys and catalog rules; Check over both transports with the bearer key and the ledger; the other-transport hint; a key or headers never sent to another origin or through a cross-origin redirect; an echoed key scrubbed; New tools; timeout; bin, restore and purge; interrupted rows; settings refused before storing. `test/mcpSend.test.ts`, the twin of `providerSend.test.ts`: after the Check, editing the server, its key, headers, route and switches, reading, deleting and restoring it, a story reply and a workshop turn send it nothing. `e2e/mcpServers.spec.ts` drives the pages at 1440 and 390 px with the layout audit in both themes.

### 3.12b MCP servers in workshops (M2)

spec/MCP.md M2 (job `mcp2`, 2026-11-17). Workshops use the servers the user turned on for them; story chats do since M3 (§3.12c).

- **Use it in.** The server's page gets the `mcpSections` entry **Use it in** (order 25): **Stories** and **Workshops** switches writing `mcp_uses` through `SetMcpUse`, each with its hover ("Lets workshops use its allowed tools, unless a workshop turns it off. Each call sends what the assistant writes in it to <host>."). Stories applies to story chats since M3 (§3.12c).
- **Per workshop.** The registered capability `mcp` (`agent/capabilities.ts`, modes `off`/`allow`, order 100) is shown as one chip row per usable remote server (`ListWorkshopCapabilities`, in creation order after the built-ins, `WorkshopCapability.target` = the connection id): label the server's name, explanation "Uses <Name>'s tools. Each call sends what the assistant writes in it to <host>.", Off / On (the client labels `allow` "On" for a row with a target), default from the server's Workshops switch, "Use the default". `SetWorkshopGrant { capability: "mcp", target }` writes `workshop_grants (chat, 'mcp', <connection>, allow|off)` only for a row it lists, keeps the other targets, and Off cancels that server's waiting questions (in memory and in `tool_approvals`, matched on the prompt's `rerun.connectionId`). No Ask first: enabling is the consent.
- **Offer** (`agent/tools/mcp.ts`, `ContextGenerator`). A workshop turn reads `McpWorkshopConnections { userId, chatId }` (reader: the user's live remote connections with catalogs, in `created_at, id` order, with this workshop's grant) and offers, after the planner's built-ins, every allowed tool (`mcpToolAllowed`) of each server that is on (the grant, else the Workshops switch), each server's tools by exposed name. Planning never connects. Definitions: `name` = `mcp_<key>_<tool>`, the server's description cut at 4,000 characters, `parameters` = its `inputSchema`; the frozen tool adds app metadata `mcp { connection, connectionName, host, key, catalogRevision, tool }`, effect class `mcp` (`rolloutEffectClasses`, outside the chat; a story admits it through its kind's `outsideClasses`, §3.12c) and the label "<title or name> (<Server>)". Each server on is also a skill `mcp-<key>` (`mcpSkillOf`) whose index line in `load_skill` is the user's own "What it's for" (else "Tools from <Name>."), listed after the registered and card skills (`planToolLoading`'s `skills`) and frozen with them; it loads that server's tools. The workshop profile defers them on a wire that carries deferred tools, and sends them from the start with `load_skill` elsewhere. Resume rebuilds a frozen MCP tool from its metadata (`mcpToolFromFrozen`).
- **Calls** (`McpConnections.call`). Each call opens a client (its `initialize` a ledger row with the chat, purpose `workshop`), sends `tools/call` as its own row (rollout, tool call id, attempt = earlier rows of the call + 1) with the connection's timeout, `resetTimeoutOnProgress` and a 30-minute ceiling, and closes. Stop (the run's abort signal) and a timeout make the SDK send `notifications/cancelled`; the client waits up to 2 s for it to go before closing. The result reports whether the call was sent: a refusal before it (a key for another origin, say) says "Nothing was sent". A timeout or a dropped connection after sending says "It may still have happened." A call is never retried by the app.
- **Permit.** For a tool with an `mcp` ref, `makePermit` reads the workshop's servers at the call: a server gone, Off here or a tool no longer allowed refuses without sending. A fresh call runs without asking, whatever the server's annotations. A dangling call (Resume after Stop, a crash or a restart) reads `McpCallsFor { rolloutId, toolCallId }` (the call's `tools/call` rows in this run and the runs it was resumed from, through `source_version_id` as approvals do): none means it was never sent, and it runs; otherwise it waits in its step with the approval panel, `uncertain: true` and `rerun { connectionId, connection, host, sentAt, status }`. The panel says "The app had sent it to <Name> at 14:02 and got no answer." and offers **Run it again** and **Don't run it** (no Allow in this workshop; the writer refuses `allow_chat` for `mcp`). Don't run it gives the model "This was interrupted and may already have happened; it wasn't run again."
- **Results.** `resultOf` turns content blocks into text (text; an image as an image part, at most 4 of at most 5 MB, only when the run's model has vision, else "[image: type, size]"; audio, resource links, embedded resources as short lines; `structuredContent` as JSON when there's no text), cut at 4 MiB with "[cut: the server sent N MB]", scrubbed of the connection's secrets, framed with `<result_metadata>` (key, tool, bytes). The session quotes it in `tool_data` like any workshop result, error results included, keeps it whole in the transcript and the receipt, and sends the model the 16,000-character projection that `read_run` pages. `ToolOutput.images` become image parts of the tool result (`ToolContext.vision`).
- **Records.** The session writes the receipt and, for a call that reached the server, one `rollout_effects` row of kind `mcp.call` (target kind `mcp_connection`, title "Called <tool> on <Name>", no undo recipe) in `RecordRolloutEffects`. The ledger row is closed in its own transaction just before (delta from the spec's single `RecordMcpCall`: a crash between the two leaves a closed ledger row without a receipt, which Resume treats as sent and asks about). The step shows the outside-effect icon (`effectClass: "mcp"`), its changes list (`StepEffects`), Changes and the regenerate warning include it, `EffectRow` shows "Can't be undone from the app" in place of Undo, and Undo all stops at it.
- **Not in M2:** a client kept per (connection, user) for 5 idle minutes and the reconnect rule (§7.1–§7.2: each call opens its own client), progress on the step's row, the inspector's per-call ledger lines (§10), `tools/list_changed`, story chats (M3), "Send its tools" and server instructions (M4).
- **Tests**: `test/mcpWorkshop.test.ts` (scripted provider, fake server): the offer's order, skill line and byte-identical tools across turns, Off and On over either default, a choice the row lacks refused, planning sends nothing; a destructive-annotated tool runs without asking with its ledger rows, receipt, `mcp.call` change, step class and refused undo; a large result kept whole and paged; Stop cancelling at the server, then Resume asking with the ledger facts and Don't run it; Run it again as attempt 2; a never-sent call running on Resume; a timeout cancelling; Off between planning and the call. `test/mcpSend.test.ts` now also shows a workshop that doesn't call the server, one where it's off by default or by the workshop's Off (a call refused) send nothing, and only the enabled call sends `initialize` and `tools/call`. `e2e/mcpWorkshop.spec.ts` drives Use it in, the chip rows and a call's Changes entry at 1440 and 390 px with the layout audit in both themes.


### 3.12c MCP servers in story chats (M3)

spec/MCP.md M3 (job `mcp3`, 2026-11-17). Story replies with Tools on use the servers the user turned on for them; the account's **Stories** switch (§3.12b) takes effect.

- **Per branch.** The state key `agent.mcp { connection, on: boolean | null }` (positional, branch-owned like `agent.tools`; `null` drops the branch's choice) folds into `ChatState.agentMcp` (by connection id; absent when empty) and `Cast.agentMcp`. Its `connection` is an `mcp_connection` id, checked by `db/stateRefs.ts` against the user's own live servers. `ChangeCast { _tag: "McpConnection", connection, on }` writes it; the agent can't (`change_chat` exposes a fixed list of changes without it, and `operationPolicies`' state keys leave it out).
- **Offer** (`ContextGenerator`, `agent/tools/mcp.ts`). The `rp` kind profile names `mcp` in its new `outsideClasses`, so `admitsEffect` (`agent/effects.ts`) lets a story offer and run `mcp` tools while still refusing every other outside class (planning, the resume filter, and the session's execute and `beforeToolCall` gates all use it). An agentic story reply reads `McpStoryConnections { userId }` (the user's live remote servers with catalogs, in creation order) and offers, after the planner's built-ins, every allowed tool of each server on for it: the branch's choice at the reply's parent (`mcpStoryOn`), else the Stories switch. Then `read_result`. Whether the servers' tools are sent from the start is M4's (§3.12d). The branch's choices are frozen in the snapshot's agent block (`mcpChoices`), so a swipe or Resume keeps the choice it was generated under. Planning never connects.
- **Calls and records.** The call path is M2's, with ledger purpose `story`. Enabling is the consent: a fresh call runs without asking, whatever the server's annotations. The permit's story branch (`PermitDeps.story`) checks at the call that the server is still there, still on for the run's frozen branch choice (else the live Stories switch), and that the tool is still allowed; otherwise it refuses without sending ("turned off for this chat"). A story call writes its receipt through `RecordRolloutEffects` with no effect rows (the `rollout_effects_owner` trigger keeps those to workshops), so a resumed run answers from it. A dangling call asks on Resume with the same approval panel, `uncertain` and `rerun` facts as in a workshop (**Run it again** / **Don't run it**); one never sent runs.
- **Results.** A story's MCP results cross the `tool_data` boundary like a workshop's (the session's `serverData`): stored whole up to 4 MiB, the model sent a 16,000-character page whose recovery line names `read_result` with the call id and offset. `read_result { call, offset? }` (effect `read`) pages a result of an MCP tool in this run's own transcript only (`context.transcript()`), with `<result_metadata>` holding only the offset and total; any other call id is an error.
- **UI.** This chat → Tools (when on) gets the fieldset **From MCP servers** (`McpServersFieldset.tsx`), from `ListStoryMcpServers` (McpApi: id, name, host, allowed-tool count, Stories switch): one checkbox per server, checked by the branch's choice else the account's, with "N tools" under it and **Reset** at the row's end while the branch has a choice ("Goes back to your account setting: on/off."). A server with no allowed tools is disabled with "None of its tools are allowed." No servers: a link to Settings → MCP servers. Each control has its hover text (what clicking does and what each call sends to the host).
- **Not in M3:** a story's "tools now" replacing a changed MCP definition on Resume, and the rest listed under §3.12b.
- **Tests**: `test/mcpStory.test.ts` (scripted provider, fake server): a branch's On with the account off and its Off with the account on, the other branch keeping its own, Reset, an earlier reply keeping the offer it was made with, a server the user doesn't have refused, planning sending nothing; a destructive-annotated tool running without asking with `story` ledger rows, a receipt and no effect rows; a long result paged by `read_result`, which refuses another call id; Stop then Resume asking, Don't run it, and Run it again as attempt 2. `test/mcpSend.test.ts` adds a story branch: off by default and off on the branch with the account on send nothing even when the model calls the tool; on for the branch with the account off sends exactly `initialize` and `tools/call`. `test/stateKeys.test.ts` covers `agent.mcp`'s id; the isolation matrix covers `ListStoryMcpServers`. `e2e/mcpStory.spec.ts` drives the fieldset at 1440 and 390 px with the layout audit in both themes.

### 3.12d MCP deferred loading (M4)

spec/MCP.md M4 (job `mcp3`, 2026-11-17). Each server decides whether its tools are sent from the start, in stories and workshops alike; the kind profiles keep deciding the built-in tools.

- **Send its tools** (`mcp_connections.loading`, built in M0): `auto` (Automatically, the default), `immediate` (From the start) or `deferred` (When the model asks). `mcpLoadingOf` resolves Automatically to deferred when the server has more than `MCP_DEFER_ABOVE` = 5 allowed tools. `mcpLoadingOverrides` maps each offered server tool's exposed name to its server's choice, and in a story adds `read_result`: immediate when any server's tools are, else deferred. `planToolLoading` takes them as `loading` (`LoadingOverrides`), and `loadableTools` and `splitOffer` let an override decide over the kind profile's `immediate` patterns. So only a wire that carries deferred tools (natively or through the dispatcher, TOOL-LOADING) defers anything; elsewhere every tool is sent from the start, with `load_skill` listing the skills of servers whose tools would wait.
- **Skills.** A server is a skill only while some of its tools wait for loading (`skillsFor` drops one that loads nothing), so a small server on Automatically adds no skill and a story whose servers are all sent from the start keeps its exact offer with no loaders. A story's skill also loads `read_result`; a story's cards bring no skills (only its servers' tools can wait).
- **Server instructions** (`mcp_connections.use_instructions`, built in M0, default on): the `instructions` the server gave at `initialize`, cut at 4,000 characters, are appended to the skill's instruction text, so they're returned only when the skill loads and frozen with the run. A server sent from the start has no skill and sends none. The index line stays the user's own "What it's for".
- **Storage and API.** Writer op `SetMcpLoading { userId, connectionId, loading?, useInstructions?, at }` (one transaction; bumps `row_version`); McpApi `SetMcpLoading { connectionId, loading?, useInstructions? }`, user-only in `exposures/exclusions.ts`, refused for another user's server (isolation matrix). Nothing is sent to the server.
- **UI.** The server's page gets the `mcpSections` entry **Sending its tools** (order 35, `LoadingSection`): a radio group **Send its tools** (each option with its one-line description) and the switch **Use the server's instructions** with its hover, and a line saying when instructions are sent, or that the server gave none.
- **Tests**: `test/mcpLoading.test.ts` (synthetic connections, the real registry): Automatically at 5 and 6 tools, a story deferring a large server's tools and keeping a small one's, `read_result` waiting when every server's tools do, no loaders when nothing waits, a no-deferral wire sending everything, From the start overriding the workshop profile, When the model asks through the dispatcher, and server instructions only while on. `test/mcpWorkshop.test.ts` sets Alpha to When the model asks for its skill-index check. `e2e/mcpServers.spec.ts` sets both controls, reloads, and checks nothing was sent; its layout audit covers the section at 1440 and 390 px in both themes.

### 3.13 History edits

Fork independence unit 8 (`shared/historyApi.ts`, `db/historyReads.ts`, `db/historyWrites.ts`, `api/history.ts`) implements DESIGN §10.3's mechanical editing backend and search panel.

- `PreviewHistory` reads only a live owned fork's path. Messages and unselected swipes have separate switches; summaries include every sealed, unsuperseded summary covering that path, using the fork's effective revision. Version reads use the same replacement and deletion overlay as the picker. Pages inspect at most 100 versions within a 100-depth window; a cursor holds depth and version sequence, or summary revision sequence. No whole path of texts is transferred to the main thread. Literal ASCII whole-word searches use FTS5 as a prefilter, also scanning non-ASCII texts because JavaScript word boundaries differ from unicode61. Other literals and regexes scan the windows. Regex compilation, matching and capture replacement run in a reader-only VM with a 150 ms deadline, including a single pathological match. Invalid patterns and excessive per-text match counts return `HistoryRejected`. Multiple pairs match the original text; non-overlapping matches are used, earliest position first and pair order breaking ties. Replacements support captures, named captures, whole-match/prefix/suffix substitutions and preserve case. As in the editor, matching uses Unicode code points and letter/number word boundaries, falling back to plain regex mode for legacy escapes; preserve case leaves uncased matches alone.
- **Inserted messages** (spec/MESSAGE-INSERT.md §3.3, unit 8). A fork that places insertions (`placedInsertions` non-empty) is searched along its display path (§3.8 "Display paths"): `PreviewHistory`'s windows are 100 positions read through `displaySlots` (`db/displayPath.ts`: CTEs `display_pieces` and `display_slots`, one range of `slots_chain` per structural stretch and the inserted slots by id), ordered by position, and the hits' `depth`/`toDepth` and the cursor's `depth` are positions there. A summary is in the fork's history when its first and last messages are on the display path; its `depth`/`toDepth` are their positions (`displayPositionSql`, through the pieces alone). `HistoryEditCost` counts from a position the same way; `retainedDepth` (the history start's structural depth, until assembly reads positions) is taken as a position, so with insertions before the start the estimate counts a few messages too many, never too few. `historyCurrent`, which `ApplyHistoryEdits`, `ListHistoryEdits` and `UndoHistoryEdit` check every target with, uses `onForkPath`, so an inserted message is a target only in the forks that show it: elsewhere, naming its version is `NotFound`. Changesets are keyed by version, so applying and undoing an inserted message's edit are unchanged. A fork without insertions is read by the structural statements as before, where positions are depths. `historyEdits.test.ts` covers a match in X replaced and undone only in its fork, a fork made before the insertion and one made after it, a summary of X found by position only where X is shown, and random appends, insertions, forks and deletions over more than one window, where every fork's search finds its messages in the order and at the positions its path read shows them, and the estimate counts from a position. Review regressions also fork at X through 70 generations, check inherited replacements and independent undo, reject edits and undo in a fork ending before X, and compare unchanged hits, costs and changeset contents in a fork without insertions after another fork inserts a message.
- `ApplyHistoryEdits` validates the preview's identities, text and fork-local deletion state again, then commits all applications in one writer transaction. New versions copy attachments and persisted metadata, with origin `changeset`, the original version as source, and their fork. Each fork gets `replace` overrides, including unselected swipes. A group shares a replacement row for a shared input/version and resulting text across its applications. Summary changes create revisions selected through the overlay. An application that processed summaries marks its replacements `summaries_done`; ordinary edits do not. The item's after snapshot records the input version identities and amend counts preserved through consecutive edits that covered summaries. The summary reader checks these rather than treating a later rename as a repair of an earlier amend or message-only rewrite. Higher-level renamed summaries can follow fresh renamed children only when both revisions came from the same application call; reusing a panel group does not make an independent later child edit fresh; fi7 owns the rest of summary selection and job scoping.
- `changeset_groups` belongs to an account. Each `changesets` application records fork, sequence and group; items record stable target plus before/after identity, text and slot. Repeated writes in an open panel reuse an application while no child can inherit its earlier state; otherwise a new immutable application in the group preserves that child's history. `UndoHistoryEdit` restores before values only while both after identity and text still agree, reporting conflicts. It accepts item ids or a message slot; the latter includes covering summaries transitively. Undo writes only in the viewed fork and records `changeset_reverts`. `ListHistoryEdits` follows bounded fork ancestry (also across lineage flattening), labels inherited records with the originating fork's name, and derives applied/partly undone/undone from effective values. Versions named by before/after snapshots are retained: a subsequent amend copies them even when no other fork currently shows them. Undo also restores the prior `summaries_done` and changeset provenance, so undoing a later message-only edit restores earlier rename freshness. Purposeful purge clears retained version text from item snapshots; deleted state events clear their snapshots too.
- State items use `state_event`, with an existing event target or an empty target/before to add chat-wide state. The after text is a schema-checked foldable event, and referenced entities are ownership-checked. Replacements suppress the previous event and add a fork-owned event; undo suppresses added events and restores earlier suppression locally. Branch-owned event placement is enforced.
- `RenameHistoryTargets` folds effective cast state in every live owned fork: forks count as chats, including ones sharing a tip, while deleted forks and unrelated cast members are excluded. Its result length is the rename-dialog count. `RenameHistory` accepts none/this/all, previews literal replacements in the reader, then applies the matching forks atomically as one group. None creates no history. It changes history only; the card editor's name save is separate.
- **Card rename offers (U18; asked on confirm since cardeditor, owner 2026-11-01).** A card's names are renamed in place in its name header (`CardNameHeader.tsx`, §14.6), and a change of the name chats use (`nickname || name`) asks right there, when the pencil's field is confirmed, never after a later Save: `renameQuestion` (`@rp/shared/cardNames.ts`) says what to ask, and the header hands the `cardSavedContributions` continuation registry (`features/editor/cardSaved.ts`) a change marked `atConfirm` (and `display` for the three-choice case). The dialog answers with a `RenameAnswer`: closing it (`cancel`) cancels the rename and keeps the field open; the names are written only after an answer, as live text (drafts sent at once), so Save asks nothing. `card-rename.history`, registered by `features/cardRename/`, offers No (no history write), only this chat (exact fork), or all N chats using the card (`RenameHistoryTargets`, forks counted separately). A recovered offer names its original chat and fork beside the single-chat choice, even when resumed from another chat. `e2e/cardEditorTabs.spec.ts` covers the owner's matrix on confirm in the character tab (keep, just change, rename everywhere, nickname changed, cancelled by closing, cleared, first set equal to the display name, display name with a nickname set). `e2e/cardRename.spec.ts` covers unchanged model names, none/this/all (including siblings), clearing nickname, diff/undo, failed-action recovery without a second card revision, and a fork-and-rename's isolation. ## 4. Authentication

`auth/Accounts.ts` implements the `Authentication` RPC middleware declared in `@rp/shared/api.ts`. It provides `CurrentUser` to every handler, resolved on every call. Over the WebSocket, the headers are those of the upgrade request. A session is still checked on each call, so a logout reaches connections that are already open. `accounts.test.ts` checks that every RPC in `AppApi` carries the middleware: one added to the group after `.middleware()` would skip it.
- **The isolation matrix** (`test/isolation.test.ts`) has an entry for every RPC in `AppApi`, and fails on an RPC without one or an entry whose RPC is gone. An entry is one of:
  - a probe, run both ways between an admin and a user over real sockets: one reads, changes or references the other's connection, credential, model, preset or ledger row, and is refused or sees nothing. Everything the owner can list (and, for an admin, the users and network settings) is the same afterwards.
  - an admin-only probe: a user is `Forbidden`
  - `global` (no user's data) or `createOnly` (names nothing that exists), with the reason

  The HTTP routes that act on a user's data, `/library/import`, `/library/export`, `/library/avatar`, `/library/media` and `/library/drafts`, have probes of the same kind, run the same way.
- **Message headers are dropped** (`TransportHeadersOnly` in `server.ts`). Effect's RPC server appends the headers a client puts in each message after the upgrade request's, and the later entries win. Before this, any client could name any user in proxy mode by sending `remote-user` in a message. The serialization now empties message headers when decoding, so identity can only come from the upgrade request (`rpc.test.ts` checks this).
- **`AUTH_MODE=single`, built-in login** (DESIGN §10.1):
  - **No account has a password:** loopback and `ALLOWED_IPS` are the implicit local admin `local`, without logging in. That's local use. It's checked on every call, not only when a connection opens: a socket opened from elsewhere while login was required doesn't become the local admin if the last password goes.
  - **Once an enabled user has a password,** a session is required. With `LOOPBACK_REQUIRES_LOGIN=false`, loopback skips login and acts as the oldest enabled admin. Loopback is judged by `x-rp-peer`, which `RequestGuard` sets from the socket's address and which replaces any copy the client sends. Behind a reverse proxy on the same host, every client arrives from loopback, so this setting would make everyone the admin.
  - **Login and logout** are HTTP, since only a response can set a cookie: `POST /auth/login` (JSON `{handle, password}`, at most 4 KiB) and `POST /auth/logout`. A login must be `application/json`, so a cross-site form can't send one, on top of the Origin check. Over plain HTTP beyond loopback, passwords cross the network in the clear: put TLS in front.
  - **The session cookie** `rp_session` is 32 random bytes, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Strict`, `Secure` when the page is on https, and lasts 30 days. The database stores only its SHA-256, so a copy of the database holds no live session.
  - **Login attempts** count before the password is checked, so a burst can't outrun the count. The limits are 10 per address and handle and 50 per address in 15 minutes, then `429` with `Retry-After`; a success forgives its address and handle.
    - Keying by address and handle means nobody can lock someone else out by name. Behind a same-host proxy, all clients share one address, so they also share its limits.
    - At most two password checks run at once. scrypt shares libuv's 4-thread pool with DNS and file reads, so further attempts get `429` instead of queueing.
    - Malformed handles and over-long passwords fail like a wrong password, before any hashing, and count only against their address.
    - A check holds its permit until scrypt finishes, even when the client disconnects, since the hash can't be cancelled.
    - The counts are capped at 10,000 keys: stale ones go first, then the oldest.
    - An unknown handle takes as long as a wrong password (a dummy scrypt check).
    - Checking the current password in `SetPassword` is throttled the same way, so a stolen session can't guess at full speed.
    - The counts are kept in memory.
  - **Passwords** use scrypt (N=2^15, r=8, p=3) on libuv's thread pool, so the event loop stays free. Tests lower the cost (`PasswordCost`, a context reference nothing outside the code sets), since at full cost one test with a dozen hashes took over 30 s at a load average of 75. The hash is stored as `scrypt$N$r$p$salt$hash`. A password needs 8 to 1024 characters, and nothing else (NIST SP 800-63B).
  - **No sign-up:** an admin creates accounts (`CreateUser`, `SetUserDisabled`). An admin without a password of their own can't: the new account's password would make login required, and the admin couldn't log in. Users set their own password with the current one, if they have one; an admin can set anyone's (`SetPassword`). Changing a password or disabling a user ends that user's sessions, and the last enabled admin can't be disabled.
  - **Headless servers:** `ADMIN_PASSWORD_FILE` or `ADMIN_PASSWORD` (with an optional `ADMIN_USER`) gives the first admin a password at startup. The account is the named user, else the oldest enabled admin (so the local admin keeps its data), else a new `admin`. It applies only while no enabled admin has a password, so a password changed in the app survives restarts. Proxy mode ignores it, with a warning.
  - **Caches:** sessions aren't cached, so a revoked one stops working at once. Users are cached per process and cleared on every account change, all of which go through this process. A lookup that started before a change doesn't write its stale answer back.
- **`AUTH_MODE=proxy`:** the user is whoever the reverse proxy names in `AUTH_PROXY_HEADER` (Authelia's `Remote-User`). A missing header is `Unauthorized`, and so is one containing a comma or a control character. Node joins a repeated header with `, `, so a proxy that added its header next to a client's would otherwise produce a name made of both.
  - The header is trusted because only the proxy can connect (exposure, below).
  - Login, passwords and account creation don't apply. Disabling a user does.

**Exposure** (`net/exposure.ts`, DESIGN §11). Who may connect at all, decided per connection from the socket's source address, never from a forwarded header. Configuration is environment-only, as for every security setting.
- **Single mode:** loopback, plus `ALLOWED_IPS`. Without `ALLOWED_IPS`, every address may connect while an enabled user has a password, since everyone then has to log in. This is checked per connection, so if the last password goes, access beyond loopback goes with it. An allowlist stays a restriction even with passwords.
- **Proxy mode:** `TRUSTED_PROXIES` only, or loopback when it's unset. Anyone else who could connect could send the identity header and be any user. `ALLOWED_IPS` is a startup error here.
- **Host names** (`net/addressSet.ts`): an entry of `ALLOWED_IPS` or `TRUSTED_PROXIES` may be a name, since a container's address changes when it restarts and its name doesn't. The `TrustedAddresses` service holds both lists as live sets, shared by the gate and passwordless login (above).
  - A name trusts every address `getaddrinfo` gives it (A and AAAA). It's resolved at startup, before the server listens, then every 30 s, and at most once every 5 s when a connection arrives from an address that isn't trusted, so a proxy that moved is let in within seconds. Connections only read the current set, never resolve.
  - It fails closed. A name that doesn't exist trusts nothing, and the server still starts (the proxy may come up later). A successful answer replaces the name's addresses at once, so an address the proxy left stops being trusted. When the resolver can't answer (a timeout or an error other than "no such name"), the last addresses stand for 5 minutes (ten attempts, enough to ride out a resolver restart), then the name trusts nothing.
  - A name is only as trustworthy as whatever answers for it, so use names your own DNS answers: a container name on a Docker network (its embedded DNS), not a public domain someone else's records could point elsewhere.
  - Changes are logged: a name's new addresses at info, a name that stops resolving or expires at warn. The resolver is the `AddressResolver` context reference, which tests replace.
  - A name has labels of letters, digits, `-` and `_`. One whose last label is all digits (`1.2.3`) is a malformed address and a startup error, as are wildcards.
- **Refused peers** get a `403` written to the socket on connect, which is then destroyed before it's read. Ending it isn't enough: the HTTP parser is already attached, and on a half-open socket it would still dispatch the peer's requests (`exposure.test.ts` checks that no handler runs). The body says the address isn't a trusted proxy (or isn't allowed, in single mode). Each refusal is logged at warn, at most once a minute per address and 20 times a minute in all (anyone who can reach the port may connect from a whole IPv6 /64; the next warning counts the refusals it didn't log), naming the address, the mode and the trusted set with what its names resolve to now, so a moved proxy shows up in `docker compose logs`.
- **At startup,** listening beyond loopback (`HOST` other than `localhost`, `127.0.0.0/8` or `::1`) with nothing beyond loopback allowed is an `UnsafeExposure` error naming the fix. So are entries that aren't IPs, CIDR ranges or host names (a prefix must be 0–3 digits: `Number("")` is `0`, so `10.0.0.0/` would otherwise allow everyone).
- **`ALLOW_INSECURE_EXPOSURE=true`** serves every address. Combined with `ALLOWED_IPS` or `TRUSTED_PROXIES`, which it would silently undo, it's a startup error.

**Cross-site requests** (`crossSiteProblem`, a global router middleware). A page from any site can open a WebSocket to the user's loopback, and a page whose domain is re-resolved to `127.0.0.1` (DNS rebinding) is same-origin with itself. So every request gets a `403` unless:
- **`Origin`**, when present, is in `PUBLIC_ORIGINS`, or names the `Host` the request was sent to. That second route doesn't apply to a public host, so `http://` can't stand in for a public `https://`. Clients that send no `Origin` aren't browsers, so they have no session to borrow.
- **`Host`** is `localhost`, an IP literal (rebinding needs a name), or a public origin's host.
- **Proxy mode with `TRUSTED_PROXIES` set skips the `Host` check.** Only the named proxies can connect, so no rebound page reaches the server. And proxies often forward their own upstream name (nginx's default `Host` is `$proxy_host`). With `TRUSTED_PROXIES` unset, loopback is trusted, so the check stays. A page rebound to loopback is same-origin and could `fetch()` with its own identity header. A same-host proxy forwards `127.0.0.1` or `localhost`, which pass. Behind a proxy under a domain, set `PUBLIC_ORIGINS` to its public origin. Without it the server warns at startup: browsers are refused unless the proxy forwards the `Host` they used.
- **`PUBLIC_ORIGINS` entries** must be exact origins (scheme, host, optional port; a trailing slash is allowed). A path, credentials or a wildcard is a startup error, not something silently dropped.
- Vite's dev proxy keeps `Host` as `localhost:5173`, which matches the page's origin.

Users are created on first sight (`EnsureUser`): the local user, and proxy identities. The first user of an instance becomes `admin`. A disabled user is refused.

**`GetSession`** returns the caller's user and how they're signed in: `session` (logged in, so logging out applies), `local` (no account has a password), `loopback` (`LOOPBACK_REQUIRES_LOGIN=false`) or `proxy`. It's resolved again from the same upgrade headers as the middleware, so it only ever describes the caller (`session.test.ts`). The client uses it to route to login, and to show the login page's "no login needed" state.

In proxy mode, a WebSocket keeps the identity it opened with until it disconnects, so logging out of the proxy doesn't end an open tab's access. That's deliberate (DESIGN §10.1).

## 5. Client

**Account card-list choices (newflows, 2026-11-06).** `DisplayPrefs` adds `sidebarCards`, `homeCards` and `castCards`, each using the switcher's sort/direction/Include personas shape. `useCardBrowse` reads and patches the account's `display` setting through `useViewPrefs`; each place stays independent. Home and sidebar wait for that read before seeding an unqualified URL, while explicit URL choices and history retain their existing meaning. Filters still belong to the view. No baseline change.

**Callout wrapping (review-cardswap).** `ui/Surface.tsx`'s `Alert` wraps its content and action groups when their preferred widths do not fit. Above the phone breakpoint the content has a 15rem flex basis and grows into the available line; the action group wraps within the callout width. Titles and content can wrap long words. A shared note's three banner actions therefore leave readable text in a narrow desktop side panel. `e2e/agentPermissions.spec.ts` retains the linked note for the Notes panel's layout audit at 1440/390, light/dark.

**Header action order (headerswap, 2026-11-04).** The registered saved-chat actions run pin, ⋯ menu, side-panel toggle, placing the toggle at the right edge beside the panel on desktop and phones. Pending card/group chat headers retain their sole side-panel toggle last; other center headers have no side-panel toggle.

**Navigation tiles (navtilesport, owner approved 2026-11-04):** The shell's five destinations (Home, Library, Import, Settings, Bin) use `ui/NavigationTiles.tsx`: route links with the same 16 px icons, text-xs labels, hover and accent selected styles as `ui/PanelTabs.tsx` tool tabs, via shared `panelToolClass`. Route navigation metadata supplies icons and explanations for registered destinations. A ResizeObserver measures the widest natural label and chooses the fewest balanced rows whose equal-width columns fit; incomplete rows retain the same column width. All links remain visible down to the sidebar's 220 px minimum and in the phone menu. The account footer is removed. The editor registers a counted warning above the tiles through `shell.navigation.notices`, visible only when the account has browser copies; it opens the existing BrowserRecovery dialog with its explanation. Committed IndexedDB writes/deletions refresh counts and open dialogs in this tab and across tabs through BroadcastChannel. Account information and password controls live in Settings → Account; Log out appears only in the Account card for password sessions. Settings has no top account box. Ported from approved `ui/next` commits 243e1690 and 8503ce47. Route links select the current destination, including nested pages; Home selects the home page exactly. Ported from `ui/next` commits 8283a6fa and 0444346b, with the owner's equal-width adjustment.

**Center-column headers (centerheader, 2026-11-04).** The shell registers `shell.center-header` in the replaceable `shell.center.header` slot. `ui/CenterHeader.tsx` supplies the chat-height `h-shell-header` canvas header and bottom border. The registered shell route hosts it outside the padded page scroll area (`CenterPage`, also each workbench tab's page); a full editor is a tab of its own with its own header (§5 "The workbench"). `CenterHeaderContent` portals a view's existing title and document actions into its nearest host. Chat and pending-chat headers use the same component directly. Home, library, chat lists, card/group chat pages, import pages, request inspection, bin and settings pages contribute their headings; content toolbars remain in their bodies. `CardHeader center` moves a page heading into that host while retaining its description and creation toolbar in the body.

**Inline label help** (helpalign, 2026-11-03). `ui/AboutHint.tsx` shares the 20 px trigger geometry (14 px help icon) and `LabelWithHelp` inline flow across fields, fieldset legends, switches, checkboxes, slider labels, card headings, card replacement and rate headings. Help follows the final word with a nonbreaking space rather than occupying a separate flex column; captions remain below the label. Wrapped labels place help on their final text line. Choice controls with help use explicit label/control association so clicking help never toggles the control; choices without help retain their full-row label. The Lorebooks placement switch uses this same inline slot and trigger class while retaining its explanatory popover. `e2e/helpAlign.spec.ts` measures the placement switch, a preset switch, a field and a checkbox at 390/1024/1440 px, including card Definition fields in the panel and full editor, and checks label/help click behaviour. The shared editor `FieldLabel` uses inline flex so it does not force help onto a new line (smallfixes4, 2026-11-04).

**Icon toggle explanations (personafilter, owner 2026-11-03).** Include personas, shared by home, sidebar and Add characters, uses Lucide `user-x` geometry in its off state at the ordinary icon colour and `user` with the existing pressed/accent style while on. Its accessible name remains Include personas, `aria-pressed` follows the filter, and the tooltips are exactly “Click to show personas” / “Click to hide personas”. Sort direction, favourite and pin, image concealment and per-image context, guidance, single-image mode, version star/visibility, cast mute, archive, search-panel, block-options and shell/panel icon toggles explain the next click with “Click to …”; disabled image-context controls continue to explain the blocking reason. These controls retain their icons and behaviour.
**New version notice** (macrohighlight, 2026-11-02; stale chunks staleapp1, 2026-11-17; `features/clientVersion.tsx`, `staleBuild.tsx`): `client.version` registers in `appBanners`.
