One tab per item in a frame (`itemKey`): opening an item focuses the focused frame's tab of it, else another frame's (VS Code's reveal if open), at the new URL; an open naming a frame (`OpenOptions.frame`) opens it there even when another frame has it, so two frames can show one item (`openTabAt` also returns the tab). `openTab` puts a new item in the place of the frame's preview tab (VS Code reuses that place for any open), else after the shown tab; `closeTab` shows the tab focused before it and closes a frame it empties unless it's the only one; `splitFrame` gives the new frame a kept copy of the shown tab (VS Code's Split Editor; the store starts the copy at the shown tab's history state), or an empty frame on either side (`before`, `empty`) for a dropped tab; `moveTab` into a frame that has the item already shows that frame's tab and closes the moved one; a split of the same direction joins its parent (one row of three). `restoreLayout` repairs a saved layout (unknown parts, duplicate ids, non-app URLs, empty frames inside a split and bad shares are dropped).
- **Tab kinds** (`kinds.ts`, a registry): `match(url)` names the item (chat: its id, so its branches and messages are places in one tab; `library.editor`: the ref; card, group, request, pending chats; Home, Settings, Import and Bin one tab each), a default `title` and `icon`, `document` (chats, pending chats and library entries: typing in them keeps a preview tab) and `persist` (login is never saved). Unclaimed URLs are one tab per path. `shellSearchKeys` names the search params that belong to the browser's URL rather than a tab's (the sidebar's place, `sidebarSearch`).
- **Each tab its own router** (`Workbench.tsx` `TabHost`): `buildRouter({ history: createMemoryHistory(...), layouts: { app: CenterPage } })` over the registered routes, so every feature's `useSearch`, `useNavigate` and `Link` work inside a tab unchanged, against the tab's URL. The tab renders into an element of its own (a portal), appended to its frame while shown and removed from the page while not: hidden tabs keep their state, drafts and sessions, are never found or focused, and their scroll positions are saved and put back. A tab's history blocks a push to another item and opens that item instead (a link in a message, a document switcher), in the tab's own frame (`store.leaves`, `OpenOptions.frame`): a frame showing that item elsewhere keeps its place, scroll and focus (VS Code opens in the group clicked in); a replace to another item makes the tab that item (a pending chat saved becomes its chat). A push from a preview tab to an item its frame doesn't have open navigates the tab in place, as does an open that reuses the preview (same tab id, same router): a chat switch keeps the outgoing chat on screen until the next is ready, as before tabs. A tab opened from another starts its history at the opener's URL (`takeOpenedFrom`), so Back returns there. Tab metadata (`setMeta`: title, decoration, `region`) is kept per item and dropped when the tab shows another. An editor's tab container is `role=region` named for the editor (`useTabRegion`), so the region includes its header; outside a tab the editor is its own `<section>` (`Region`). `ui/away.ts` `Away` is true inside a tab not on screen: `Dialog`, `ConfirmDialog`, `Sheet`, `Popover` and the phone portrait viewer close while it's away and open again when it's shown (their own state is kept); the side panel portalled beside the frames resets it.
- **The browser's URL** (`store.ts`): while a tab is focused its navigations are copied to the browser's history (pushes push, replaces replace), with the browser's own sidebar params; the browser's navigations (the sidebar's links, Back, Forward, a typed URL) come back: the focused tab's own item navigates it, another item opens (`open`, replacing the entry it came with). A tab's own navigation that changes the sidebar's params (a link that scopes the sidebar, `shellDiff`) carries them to the browser's URL; its history state (a chat's reading place) is copied even when the URL is unchanged. Focusing another tab replaces the browser's entry. A plain click on a bare same-origin link (in a message) opens through the workbench instead of reloading, in the frame it's in (`store.openIn`; the sidebar's links, outside any frame, reveal the item where it's open); a double click on any link keeps its item's tab (`pinItem`). An `input` event inside a `document` tab keeps it, except in search boxes and comboboxes; a page's forms (a new chat's title, settings) don't.
- **Frames** (`FrameView`, `SplitView`): the strip shows when a frame has two or more tabs or the view is split: per tab a small portrait (a chat's first character, `chat/tabPortrait.tsx` through `useTabMeta`) or the kind's icon, the title (`useTitle` names the tab; italics for a preview, in a box as wide as either style so keeping it moves nothing) and a close button; a middle click closes, a double click keeps. Tabs drag between strips and onto frame bodies (`application/x-rp-workbench-tab`; native listeners, since a tab's content is a portal): the outer quarter of a frame on each side splits there (`dropZone`, nearest edge in a corner; `store.moveToSplit` with `before` on the left or top), shading the half the tab takes (`data-drop-zone`); the centre moves it into the frame. **Open beside** (`OpenBeside.tsx`, VS Code's Open to the Side): a chat row's and a character tile's right-click menu (Open, Open beside, Open in a new browser tab; `ForkRow` and `CharacterTile`, the row's corner actions unchanged), where frames fit side by side (tiles have no Open beside button: owner, 2026-11-06); Alt-click on any app link does the same. Both send an `rp:open-beside` event that `useLinkGestures` handles, so they work outside the workbench's context; `store.openBeside` opens kept in the frame right of the focused one, adding an empty one there if none, with the sidebar params the link names (`shellCarried`: a link naming `character`, `forks` or `side` sets that scope whole; the rest stay as the sidebar has them; bare links followed in a frame do the same) (`e2e/workbench.spec.ts` "open beside, one chat in two frames, and a tab dropped on an edge"). The strip's ⋯ (`FrameMenu`, for the shown tab) and a tab's right-click menu (`ContextMenu`, for that tab; tabs aren't text, so the browser's menu isn't needed there) list the same `TabActions`: Pin tab/Unpin tab (`stickTab`: pinned tabs first in the frame, never a preview, a filled pin in place of × that unpins, saved as `sticky`), Keep tab open, Split right/down, Move to the frame left/right/above/below (`neighbours`; each with a frame-and-arrow icon pointing its way, `move-left` … `move-down`), Move to a new frame right/below, Maximize frame/Restore frames, Close tab, Close other tabs, Close tabs to the right, Close saved tabs, Close all tabs (`closeTabs`, each keeping pinned tabs; saved: no unsaved changes), Reopen closed tab (`store.reopenClosed`: the last 20 closed in this page, back in their frame if it's still there) and Close frame. **Maximize** (`maximizeFrame`, `Layout.maximized`, not saved; also a button in the strip while split) renders that frame alone; the others' tabs are away (`useTabShown`), and focusing another frame (an open that lands there) restores them. **Unsaved**: each tab is an `UnsavedScope` (`ui/UnsavedChanges.tsx`) whose tracker the editors' revision state (`SaveRevision`) reports to; a tab with changes not yet saved shows a dot where its × is, the × on hover or focus, and closing asks nothing, since drafts stay with the item. The strip scrolls the shown tab into view, a mouse wheel scrolls it sideways, and its scrollbar shows thin on hover. Dividers are `ui/ResizeHandle` grips (frames at least 320 px wide, 160 px tall; a double click evens the pair). Focus follows a pointer down or focus inside a frame. An empty frame says how to fill it.
- **Header buttons**: `centerHeaderEnd` (`ui/CenterHeader.tsx`) is rendered at the end of every center header; the chat header places it among its actions before the panel toggle (`chat.header-end`, so the toggle stays at the edge). The workbench registers **Split right** and **Split down** there (one Split menu in a header under 40rem), desktop only.
- **Review regressions (2026-11-06)**: moving a tab keeps it open, respects the pinned boundary, and interprets strip insertion positions before removing the source tab. Restore rejects URLs pointing outside the app and repairs pinned ordering and multiple previews. Closed tabs release their metadata and deferred history state; only the last 20 closed URLs remain for reopening. Sessions viewing the same generating version share live atoms with counted ownership, so closing one view leaves the other's stream intact and the last view releases it. Each composer and its description have unique React ids. A chat-bound editor's `chatTab` query identifies its source view for both the editor store and the side panel; live workspaces register by tab rather than chat, so closing a duplicate view leaves the source registered. Older links fall back to a view of their chat and branch. Model, store, session and browser tests cover these cases.
- **Portrait column** (`tab.tsx` `usePortraitHost`, `features/chat/portraitSources.ts`; owner, 2026-11-07, DESIGN §10.1): the portrait column (§14.5a) is a column of the shell, portalled left of the frames (`data-portrait-host`), as the side panel is right of them, never inside a frame, and one for the whole workbench. Each tab keeps its own pictures (its URL's `portraits`) and portrait weights (`ChatPortraitProvider`: per-view `rp.portraitWeights.<userId>.<tabId>` in this browser tab's session storage, falling back to the former account-wide local-storage values), so duplicate views of one card restore independent heights; each chat view in the workbench publishes its viewer to the workbench's `PortraitSources`, which keeps one order over all of them (a view's newly opened picture goes on top, one swapped for another keeps its place). The oldest publishing view renders the column through `PortraitViewerScope` with a shared viewer whose entries carry `tabId + id` ids: a column action (close, move, split, even, Keep one image open) computes the whole stack's next state with `portraitStack.ts` and hands each view its part (`PortraitViewer.set`); a picture opened with Keep one image open on closes the other views' ones. Open as a tab and a drag out use the source view's `useOpenAsTab`, so they open beside the frame the picture came from. Pictures of a tab behind another in its frame stay in the column; a view unmounting (its tab closed) or going narrow takes its pictures out (`e2e/portraitColumnShared.spec.ts`). It takes its width from the shared column layout as before frames, so the frames give way and closing it gives them their widths back. Phones keep the full-screen viewer (`e2e/portraitFrames.spec.ts`).
- **Bars' buttons in tab mode** (owner, 2026-11-07, DESIGN §10.1; `model.ts` `showsStrips`, `stripCorners`; `tab.tsx` `useTabInStrips`, `usePanelTogglePlace`): one view alone (no strip) keeps the hidden sidebar's Show button and the panel's toggle in its header as before. Once the strips show on a wide screen, page headers have neither: `SidebarToggle` (`shell.tsx`, the `sidebarToggle` slot) renders its `strip` place at the start of the top-left frame's strip while the sidebar is hidden (an empty box otherwise, so the first tab starts at the edge), and the chat's `HeaderPanel` portals its `PanelToggles` into `data-panel-toggle-host`, the last of the top-right strip's buttons (after Maximize frame and ⋯), from the tab that owns the side panel (`store.panelOwner`), even while that tab is behind another; with no chat open there is none. A maximized frame is both corners. Phones keep the header buttons. In a frame too narrow for everything (review of sidetoggles, 2026-11-07: four frames at 1024 with both bars open put the toggle under the panel), the tabs give way first (they shrink and scroll); then the strip's Maximize leaves it for the ⋯ menu's own Maximize frame item (`styles.css`, the `tab-strip` container: below 6.5rem, or 9.25rem with the hidden sidebar's Show in it); what still doesn't fit is cut at the strip's start (`justify-end`, `overflow-hidden`), so the ⋯ menu and the panel's toggle stay inside the frame (`e2e/sideToggles.spec.ts`: single pane, tab mode with both bars hidden and only non-chat tabs shown, a split and a maximized frame, four narrow frames with both bars open at 1024, light and dark).
- **Pictures as tabs** (owner, 2026-11-07; `chat/PicturePage.tsx`, `workbench/dropOpen.ts`): a picture can leave the column for a frame. Its tab's URL is `/picture?media=…&name=…&crop=…` (`pictureHref`; the `picture` tab kind, one tab per image and cutout, titled by the name, the image icon), a page that fills the frame with the column's viewer (`PortraitView`: zoom, Fit, 100%, wheel, drag, pinch) and its own Close, so it moves, splits, closes, has the tab menu and comes back after a reload as any tab does. The viewer's header, dragged out of the column (`ViewerHeader` `outside`, pointer events as for reordering within the column), shades what it would take (`dropTargetAt`: a strip, at the place between its tabs, or a frame's body, its outer quarters splitting there as a dragged tab's do, `dropZone`); released there, `store.dropOpen` opens it kept (in the frame, at that place, or in a new frame on that side) and the column closes it. Strip drops retain the boundary's right-hand tab while opening inserts the picture, so tabs following the active one do not shift its destination (`workbenchStore.test.ts`, `e2e/portraitTabs.spec.ts`; review-portraitframes2). The viewer's ⋯ has **Open as a tab** (the view's own frame), as the visible control besides dragging. A portrait click still opens the column. A preview portrait (`Avatar`'s button: messages, the Cast) dragged natively carries `PICTURE_DRAG` with its picture's tab URL (`PortraitViewer.tabHref`, given by `ChatPortraitProvider` inside the workbench); a frame's body and strip open it as they take a dragged tab, and the chat's drop zones (`features/chat/images.tsx`) ignore drags carrying it, so the browser's own image file never becomes an attachment; files from outside still attach (`e2e/portraitColumnShared.spec.ts`). Phones have no frames and no column: their full-screen viewer has neither (`e2e/portraitTabs.spec.ts`).
- **Message images in the column** (owner, 2026-11-07: "Can you open images attached to messages in the image viewer?"; `chat/attachmentPictures.ts`, `chat/images.tsx`): an image in the timeline (a message's or a queued one's) is a picture like a portrait. Its id is `image:<mediaId>:<name>`, so the view's `portraits` URL list brings it back after a reload with no lookup (`ChatPortraitProvider` resolves it after gallery and cast ids); its name is its file name, or "Image from <speaker>" ("Image 2 from Mira" when the message has several) for a pasted one (`attachmentName`). A click opens it in the image column through the view's `PortraitViewer.open`, the same toggle and stack as a portrait's, so it shares the one column with every frame's pictures, the column's width rules and per-view heights, and its ⋯ Open as a tab and header drag; phones get the full-screen viewer. Dragged natively it carries `PICTURE_DRAG` (`ui/appDrags.ts`) with `/picture?media=…&name=…`, so a frame opens it as a tab and the composer's drop zones ignore it. Its app context menu (`ImageMenu`, `ui/Menu.tsx` `ContextMenu`) has **Open in image column** (`show`, never closing) and **Open as a tab** (the view's frame, `useOpenAsTab`), each explained. An image not sent to the model keeps its dimming, toggle and "Not sent to the model: …" tooltip. The separate full-size dialog is gone. A message image's viewer says "image" where a portrait's says "portrait" (`Portrait.image`, set by `attachmentPicture`/`attachmentOf` and carried in its tab URL as `image=1`): the full-size image's alt text, the column viewer's landmark ("<name>'s image") and Close ("Close the image"), and the column's resize handles. An image attached in the composer or the message editor, not sent yet, peeks instead: a click opens `ui/Portrait.tsx` `PicturePeek`, a `ui/Dialog` holding the column's `PortraitView` (zoom, Fit, 100%, wheel, drag, pinch), from the browser's own copy (`src`, a blob URL) while it uploads; it never enters the column on a click. Its context menu has the same two items, and a corner button (`ToggleIconButton` without `pressed`, class `tile-action`, shown on hover and focus and always on touch, as the message images' toggle) opens it in the column; until the upload gives it a media id both are disabled and say why. The peek has no ⋯: the thumbnail's menu has Open as a tab. `e2e/chatImages.spec.ts` (peek, corner button, menus, column or phone viewer, an upload held, hidden images; 1440 and 390, light and dark, layout audits), `e2e/portraitColumnShared.spec.ts` (two frames' images and a portrait in one stack, reload, Open as a tab, dragged to a frame and onto the composer, the phone viewer) and `e2e/portraitTabs.spec.ts` (the context menu's tab, reload, the phone) cover it; `test/attachmentPictures.test.ts` the ids and names.
- **Dragging onto frames** (owner, 2026-11-07, DESIGN §10.1; `ui/appDrags.ts`): what the app's own drags carry is a registry of payload kinds (`dragPayloads`), each a drag data type whose value is a tab URL; the workbench registers three (`PICTURE_DRAG`, the former `PICTURE_TAB_MIME`; `CARD_DRAG`; `CHAT_DRAG`), and a plugin registers its own or disables one. A source puts its URL on the drag with `carryOnDrag` (nothing below 1024 px: a phone has one frame, and a long press stays the row's), or `carryLink`, a link's own `href`: message and Cast portraits (`Avatar`) and a character definition's header portrait (`PortraitControls.tsx` `ViewablePortrait`: the side panel's character tab, the full editor's header and Picture) carry their `pictureHref`; character tiles (`shellData.tsx` `CharacterTile`: Home, the left sidebar, the Cast's Add characters, whose tiles carry their chat-bound editor) and the library's card links carry the card's `/library/<ref>`; chat rows and group tiles (`ShellBrowser.tsx` `ForkRow`, `GroupTile`) and the Chats list's rows (`ChatList.tsx`) carry their link. A frame's body and strip take a tab or any registered kind (`opensHere`), shade the drop zone or strip place only for those, and open the URL with `store.dropOpen` as a dragged picture did; a phone's strip opens nothing dropped. Any other drag that started in the page (`isAppDrag`: a dragstart in this page until it ends, or a registered kind from another browser tab) is refused over a frame outside text fields and editors (`refuseOther`, drop effect none), so its drop does nothing. The composer's drop zones (`chat/images.tsx`), a card portrait's image drop, a card's Gallery (`features/gallery/Gallery.tsx`) and `ui/FileDrop.tsx` (the import pages) never take an `isAppDrag` drag as a file; files from outside still attach (`e2e/dragOpen.spec.ts`: each source onto a strip and into a split, light and dark at 1440 with the drop previews audited, the composer refusing the app's drags while an outside file attaches, a portrait dropped on a frame's Gallery or import drop that opens there and uploads nothing, a 390 long press).
- **Side panel** (`tab.tsx` `useSidePanelPlace`): a chat surface (saved or pending) registers as a panel tab; on a wide screen the panel is portalled beside the frames (`data-side-host`) for the chat focused most recently, shown in its frame or not, or the chat an editor tab was opened from (`panelOwner`, owner 2026-11-07: pictures, library tabs, Home and other tabs never take or hide it). With no chat tab left, `usePanelPlaceholder` keeps the panel's last width there with `features/chat/PanelPlaceholder.tsx` ("Open a chat to see its settings here.", and Hide panel, which forgets the remembered panel tab as a chat's own Hide does) until a chat shows its panel again; only after a chat showed it in this page. When the frames' width changes from their right edge alone (the panel shown, hidden or resized, while the window and the left edge stay), `useKeepDividers` rewrites the shares of the splits along the right edge (`keepRightEdge`, through `store.resize`) so every frame but the last in a row keeps its width and the dividers stay put; it starts with the user's first input on the page, so the panel appearing as the page loads keeps the saved shares, and where room is short the last frame keeps at least an equal share of its row (or the frame minimum, if less), taken from the others (`e2e/portraitColumnShared.spec.ts`); on a phone only the focused tab has its sheet, and a chat whose tab the layout puts behind another closes its sheet (`usePanel`, by `useTabShown`, not by the tab's place on screen, which moves for a moment while a resize remounts the frames). `useTabFocused` gates page titles and chat key commands.
- **Editors opened from a chat** (`PresetWorkspace.tsx`): `workspace.open(ref, focus)` keeps the chat's tab open and opens, in the chat's frame, `/library/<ref>?focus=…&chat=<id>&chatFork=…` (`editorHref`; `workspace.href` gives openers their link). While that chat is open, `EditorPage` binds the editor to it (`ChatBoundEditor`): the chat workspace's `EditorStore` (the panel and the editor show the same text), its preset context, its `current` chat for a card's rename, its cast, the registered `workspaceViews` with the chat's session and view (a chat's note large), and Close, which closes the tab. A chat's workspace publishes itself for this (`publishLive`). Such a tab scrolls on its own (`BoundScroll`, `data-preset-scroll`, the overlay's padding) and shows the chat's surroundings registered in `boundEditorSurroundings` (`workspaceViews.ts`; the chat registers its portrait column, `chat/BoundPortraits.tsx`, so a portrait opens in the column as beside the chat). The document switcher keeps `chat` and `chatFork`. Old `?editor=` links open the editor tab beside the chat, which then is behind it. The editors are named regions ("Preset editor", "Card editor", "Lorebook editor", "Note editor", a view's label).
- **Persistence** (owner, 2026-11-07, DESIGN §10.1: each browser tab's address decides what it shows; `tabLayout.ts`): a browser tab's layout is its own, in that tab's `sessionStorage` (key `rp.workbench.<userId>`), saved when the store starts (including a fresh URL that discards earlier frames), at once after a user's change, 400 ms after a resize or a tab's URL change, and on `pagehide`. A page load restores it only when the load is a reload or a Back/Forward return (`PerformanceNavigationTiming.type`), with the URL's item open (focused where it is, else in the focused frame); any other load (a new browser tab, a pasted or typed URL, a login) opens just its URL as one tab, Home for the root URL. Nothing is saved on the server; the former per-account, per-device layout (`GetWorkbenchLayout`/`SetWorkbenchLayout`, the `rp.device` id) is removed (`e2e/workbenchTabs.spec.ts`).
- **Phones** (below 1024 px): no splits and no split buttons; the focused frame's tab shows, and once two tabs are open a strip lists every open tab of every frame.
- **Links** (`ui/links.ts` `openOnPlainClick`, `ui/Tooltip.tsx` `IconLink`, `ui/Button.tsx` `LinkButton`, `MenuAction`'s `href`, `MenuLinkItem`): sidebar chat rows and group tiles, character tiles (the character: the sidebar on their chats and their latest chat with their card's panel, else a new one; `characterLink` carries `character` and `panel`, so Open beside, Alt-click and a new browser tab open the character too; DESIGN §10.1 [D]), Cast's Add characters tiles, the Prompt preset tab's and a lorebook's Large editor, a card's Full editor, a note's and a shared note's Large editor are links whose plain click runs the opener's own logic.
- **Tests**: `e2e/workbench.spec.ts` (single chat without a strip, previews replaced and kept by a double click or typing, Back/Forward, per-tab drafts, closing; two chats split with the panel following focus, moving tabs from the ⋯, reload; a chat beside its preset editor, two preset editors, a horizontal split; 1024 and 390 in both themes; `SCREENSHOT_DIR`, `LAYOUT_AUDIT`). Each test's page is a fresh browser tab, so it starts from one tab; `e2e/workbenchTabs.spec.ts` covers the root URL and the Home button, the URL following the focused frame, Back/Forward, reloads, and browser tabs of one browser keeping their own frames.

### Restoring places (urlstate, 2026-11-02)

The registered routes keep their existing paths for chats, library entries, settings sections and connection details, import jobs and captured requests. URL choices follow home's conventions: functional search updates preserve unrelated keys, defaults are omitted, place changes push history, filters and sorts replace, and query changes keep the surrounding scroll position. `usePlaceParam.ts` supplies small validated choices, string lists, expansion exceptions and existing-toast notices; features own their keys and registrations.

The sidebar retains its scopes (`character`, `forks`, `side`) plus `sideShow`, `sideSort`, `sideReverse`, `sideQ` and `sidePinsSort` on the same registered chat routes. Its card choices reuse home's parse/write/change helpers under prefixed keys. The existing per-account device sort seeds an unqualified visit once; a browser-history marker protects a default-only entry from later remembered sorts. Grid and scope switches push; all filter/sort/search changes replace. The open-chat branch disclosure stays per account/device.

The library uses `kind`, `show`, `sort`, `reverse`, `view`, `q`, and `presets` (including Archived). Its previous device preferences seed a fresh unqualified entry, with the same history marker as home. Kind switches push; searches, filters, views and sorts replace. Settings connections retain the selected model editor (`model`), hidden-model filter (`models`) and custom-header editor (`connectionDialog`). A linked hidden model remains available to edit, and a missing model produces a notice. The bin's `section` is controlled by the URL, including Back/Forward. Import's existing `into` and server-job `job` queries remain; missing jobs explain that their report was removed. Browser File objects, temporary chooser state, pending uploads and confirmations are transient.

Chat reading uses a per-account/chat/fork anchor and relative pixel offset in the browser history entry. Scroll updates replace the entry while explicitly retaining its search; a copied `slot` link starts at that message. The viewed fork remains explicit even when it is currently the default. Missing fork/message reads retry at the branch bottom, then the current branch, and explain the fallback through the existing toast.

Chat panels use `panel`; an explicit close marks that history entry so device memory cannot reopen it on reload or Back. Links inside a panel preserve the history marker and push a place just as the tab controls do. Panel initialization waits for the cast and checks the current route and requested tab before writing, so an outgoing render cannot overwrite a newer destination. Card sub-tabs are keyed by ref and layout; `book`, `notesCard` and `summary` identify the panel's opened lorebook, note-card focus and summary. Each summary's edit/revisions/children view is keyed by its ID, and draft-history dialogs identify the message edit or summary draft. The workspace uses `editor` and `focus` to reopen a card, preset or lorebook over the mounted chat. `editorDialog` restores its history/search browser; revision selection is per ref and reads older revision pages when necessary. Notes' history browser uses `noteHistory`. A card's book-only/whole-card choice, prompt expansion exceptions, and a lorebook's filters/sort/focused entry are keyed by ref and layout/root. The owner's existing per-device note and lore-entry expansions remain in their original stores. Missing items, prompts, entries, revisions and unavailable tabs use the existing errors or notices.

`chat.portraits` registers `ChatPortraitProvider`, a state adapter over the UI's optionally controlled `PortraitProvider`. `portraits` holds ordered picture ids: character IDs, whose names and images resolve from the current cast, with a notice for an unavailable character; gallery images; and message images (`image:<mediaId>:<name>`, §5 "Message images in the column"). Split weights are per-account device storage. Zoom and pan remain temporary. The inspector keeps turn expansion exceptions in `turns` and each turn's source/whole-text choice in `requestText:<index>`. The saved amendment-history and original-text message dialogs (dialogreload, 2026-11-08) are named in `messageDialog` as `<action id>:<version id>` (a message action's `dialogInUrl`; one registered `chat.message-action-dialog` overlay, `messageActions.tsx`), so a reload or Back/Forward reopens them even when the message is outside the virtualized window. `ReadMessageVersion` loads the exact version through the existing reader-worker operations, checking the account, chat and fork; closing clears the value. `e2e/messageHistory.spec.ts` and `e2e/regexScripts.spec.ts` cover long chats with the target row unmounted. Confirmations remain transient. `e2e/urlState.spec.ts` and `e2e/urlInspector.spec.ts` exercise reloads and browser history across these surfaces, alongside the existing home URL tests.

## 6. Provider layer

`packages/server/src/providers/` (spec/PROVIDERS.md §4, §7, §9). It's the one entry point to models, for the assembler (phase 2) and later the agent loop. Dependencies are pinned: `@earendil-works/pi-ai` 1.0.3, OpenAI 7.19.0, Anthropic 0.129.0 and Google GenAI 2.21.0. Startup scrubs ambient SDK configuration, and requests use the controlled transport. Upgrades require another environment/transport audit; installed libraries are unmodified.

**The provider registry** (`providers/registry.ts`, `providers/builtins.ts`; the generic mechanism is `@rp/shared/registry.ts`, re-exported as `src/registry.ts`). This is the first registry of the structure in spec/PLUGINS.md §3.1: the core registers its features through the same registries plugins will use.
- **A registry** holds entries by id. Registering adds an entry or overrides the one with the same id, and `disable` hides one. Each registration lasts as long as its scope, and closing the scope restores whatever it hid, in any order (`test/registry.test.ts`). Wrapping is `get`, then registering a replacement that calls the original.
- **The `ProviderRegistry` service has these registries:**
  - **Providers** (`providers`; below, "Providers"): what a connection is made from, each offering one or more kinds as its API types.
  - **Provider kinds:** label, pi provider id, wire API id and implementation (pi-ai's `ProviderStreams` or the plugin's own), whether it takes our `fetch`, default base URL, whether a key is optional, a model lister, and an optional catalog. A kind can also wrap the controlled fetch (`transport`, Bedrock's and Vertex's; the SDK is then given a placeholder key, never the stored one, and the transport authorizes from the stored key, so a multi-line service account key file never reaches a header), name the secrets inside a stored key (`secretsOf`, so each part is scrubbed from errors and the ledger), and say its models come from its catalog (`listsCatalog`: Test sends nothing).
  - **Request transforms:** payload rewrites through pi-ai's `onPayload`, applied in registration order to requests whose kind and API they apply to.
  - **Response observers:** readers of the raw stream events.
  - **Cost formulas:** each prices a finished request for the ledger, or passes (null). They're tried newest registration first, so a user's or plugin's formula goes before the built-ins. The ledger records the id of the one that priced it.
  - **Image token counters** (`providers/imageCounters.ts`): an exact count of one image, tried newest registration first; `remote` when it asks a provider (the built-ins), which happens only through a connection the user chose to count with; see "Image tokens" below.
  - **Text token counters** (`providers/textCounters.ts`): the model's own text tokenizer, local or its provider's endpoint, tried newest registration first; see "Text tokens" below.
- **The built-ins** are registered at startup:
  - the providers, in picker order (below)
  - the kinds: OpenAI Chat Completions, Anthropic, OpenAI Responses, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, Google, Anthropic on Bedrock, Anthropic on Vertex, OpenAI Responses and Chat Completions on Bedrock, and System-One
  - Anthropic and Bedrock OpenAI-compatible explicit breakpoints (opted in by a connection's or the OpenAI (AWS Bedrock) provider's `cacheMarker: "prompt_cache_breakpoint"`), as registered transforms
  - the default-layout cache transforms (livefix, 2026-11-07; "Default cache markers" below): `anthropic-stable-endpoint`, `openrouter-cache-control` and `openai-prompt-cache-key`
  - the usage capture, as one observer per wire API
  - the cost formulas, oldest first (`builtinCostFormulas`, prices1): `builtin` (the built-in table), `user-pricing-general` (the user's account-wide and per-type rules), `list` (the model list's or pinned route's endpoint-list price), `endpoint` (the connection's opted-in price endpoint), `reported` (the provider's own figure), then `user-pricing` (the user's rules naming this connection); a later plugin registration can override any of them. "Known prices" below.
  - the image token counters `anthropic-count-tokens`, `google-count-tokens` and `openai-input-tokens`
  - the text token counters `anthropic-count-tokens`, `google-count-tokens`, `openai-input-tokens`, then `openai-encodings` (so it's asked first). The `anthropic-count-tokens` counters skip Bedrock and Vertex connections: neither one's own token counting is wired, so they count locally.

**Providers** (providerchoice, 2026-11-07; owner: "Users should just be able to select something like 'Anthropic (AWS)' and know everything is being done according to what that needs, for caching and everything else"; DESIGN §9). `@rp/shared/providerDefinitions.ts` defines them as data, and the registry's `providers` registers them, replaceable by id. The provider definitions registry is shared by the provider layer and the database client (`providers/definitions.ts` `ProviderDefinitions`). Each private worker request carries the active definitions as a trusted snapshot; worker resolution uses `CurrentProviderDefinitions`, including scoped replacements and their removal, without rewriting stored connections.
- **A definition:** label and description, its API types (kinds, the first the default), the default base URL (null: it must be entered) or a Region address template (with `regionUrls` for Regions whose address doesn't follow it, and `regionFormat` for the Region field's help, example and pattern; AWS's by default), whether a key is optional, its kinds of key (`auth`), its `defaults` (`ProviderSettings`: `auth`, `cacheBreakpoints`, `cacheMarker`, `lookback`, `maxMarkers`, `minTokens`, `promptCacheKey`, `region`, `project`), the settings its advanced section shows, the documented cache contract it uses (`cacheContract`, the provider name `cachePolicy.ts` knows: `anthropic`, `amazon-bedrock`, `openai`, …; a custom server has OpenAI's, which covers only OpenAI's own models, as a gateway serves them; null for the decision model), and its cache lifetime and accounting in the user's terms.
- **The built-ins**, in picker order: `openai` (Chat Completions or Responses; `prompt_cache_key` on), `anthropic` (automatic markers, lookback, 4 markers), `anthropic-bedrock` (markers at each section, no lookback, 4 markers; key type `api-key` or `aws-sigv4`; Region), `anthropic-vertex` ("Anthropic (Google Vertex)": as Anthropic's cache layout; key type `gcp-service-account`; Region, `global` by default, and project), `openai-bedrock` ("OpenAI (AWS Bedrock)": Responses or Chat Completions; `prompt_cache_breakpoint` markers at each section, no lookback, 4 markers; `prompt_cache_key` on; key type and Region as Bedrock's), `openrouter`, `deepseek`, `google` ("Google AI Studio"), `openai-compatible` (custom: no default address, key optional, `prompt_cache_key` off) and `system-one` (the decision model). The form starts on the first, OpenAI with Chat Completions (DESIGN §9, 2026-10-10). Each provider's cache rule and its source: DESIGN §9 (vertexbedrock).
- **Resolution:** a connection's provider is `findProvider(list, connection.provider, kind, baseUrl)`. An id no longer registered falls back to its kind's default provider (`defaultFor`), with Chat Completions and no base URL meaning OpenAI. The settings in effect are the defaults with the stored changes over them (`resolveProviderSettings`). They go to `resolveModel` as a layer under the model's own edits and over its list: `cacheBreakpoints` and `cacheLayout` (`lookback`, `maxMarkers`, `minTokens`) resolve with source `provider`. The send's transforms get them as `request.settings`. The cache contract replaces the kind for `documentedCachePolicy` and `documentedCacheMinimum` (TTL, warmth estimate and minimum), and shims look up the provider and the API.
- **Connections:** `CreateConnection` takes an optional `provider` and rejects an unknown one, an API type it doesn't offer, and a missing base URL where it has no default. A connection's default address is its provider's, or its Region's (`providerBaseUrl`), so the key's allowed origins follow the Region. Only the changes to the defaults are stored (`providerChanges`), from `settings.providerSettings` on create and update. `ListProviders` (a group of its own, `ProviderListApi`, beside `AppCoreApi`, which is at TypeScript's instantiation depth) lists the providers whose API types are registered, with each one's shim labels as `rules`.
- **The form** (`features/connections/list.tsx`, `providerFields.tsx`): Provider first, then the API type where there are several, Name, Region (Bedrock, Vertex), Project (Vertex; its placeholder the loaded key file's project), Base URL (required for a custom server, its placeholder the provider's or the Region's address), Key type (Bedrock), the key (an AWS access key is three fields, ID, secret and an optional session token, sent as `ID:SECRET[:TOKEN]`; a service account key is a JSON file, read in the browser into a hidden `apiKey` field so it's never in the saved draft, at most 100 kB, its account's email shown once loaded), Concurrent requests, and **Advanced**: Cache markers, Finds earlier cached parts, Send a cache key, Most cache markers, Smallest cached size, Cache lifetime (with the provider's documented lifetime), How tokens are counted and Fixes for some models, each at the provider's default until changed, with **Use the defaults**. The connection page's Settings shows the same fields. Its key dialog asks for an access key's parts. Every control has a "?" or hover explanation. `e2e/providerChoice.spec.ts` covers the form, a created Bedrock connection, OpenAI on Bedrock's address, and Vertex's Region addresses, project, key file (a refused file, a loaded one) and a created Vertex connection, with scoped layout audits at 1440/390 px in light and dark.

**Anthropic on AWS Bedrock** (`providers/bedrock.ts`, kind `anthropic-bedrock`, pi provider `amazon-bedrock`). The kind speaks `anthropic-messages` through pi-ai's Anthropic adapter, so every Messages transform, cache marker, shim and usage observer applies as for Anthropic. Its `transport` wraps the controlled fetch:
- **The request:** a `/v1/messages` POST becomes `POST {base}/model/{url-encoded model id}/invoke-with-response-stream` (or `/invoke` without streaming). The body loses `model` and `stream`, gains `anthropic_version: "bedrock-2023-05-31"`, and carries the betas as `anthropic_beta`, keeping only the ones Bedrock documents (interleaved thinking, fine-grained tool streaming, 1M context, token-efficient tools, 128K output). The SDK's key, version, beta and Stainless headers are dropped, and anything else the SDK asks for gets a 404.
- **Auth:** `api-key` sends `Authorization: Bearer <Bedrock API key>`. `aws-sigv4` signs with the stored `ACCESS_KEY_ID:SECRET[:SESSION_TOKEN]` (SigV4, service `bedrock`, the Region from the settings, else the address, else `us-east-1`; `content-type`, `accept`, `host`, `x-amz-date` and the session token signed; paths encoded twice, as for every service but S3). The secret never leaves the server.
- **The response:** AWS's event stream (binary frames, both CRCs checked, across any chunk boundary) becomes the Anthropic SSE the SDK reads: each `chunk` event's base64 `bytes` is one Anthropic event. Exceptions, in the stream or as HTTP errors (`x-amzn-errortype`), become Anthropic error shapes (throttling as rate limit, unavailable as overloaded, validation, access denied, auth, not found), so the error classes and retries are Anthropic's.
- **Models:** pi-ai's Bedrock catalog's Claude IDs (inference profiles such as `us.anthropic.claude-…` and base IDs), with their prices. Listing Bedrock's models is another AWS service, so a refresh and Test send nothing.
- **Caching:** the provider's no-lookback layout (explicit markers, the previous history marker repeated), the `amazon-bedrock` cache contract (5 minutes; 1 hour where marked) and its minimum sizes.
- **Tests:** `test/bedrock.test.ts` checks recorded shapes only: AWS's SigV4 `get-vanilla` vector and two Bedrock requests whose signatures were cross-checked with `@smithy/signature-v4`, the event-stream framing (every chunk size, corruption, truncation), and replies through a mock Bedrock endpoint (address, body, Bearer and SigV4 auth, the repeated history marker against Anthropic's lookback layout, reported cache reads and writes in the ledger, and an access-denied error).
- **Untested live:** SigV4 against real AWS, Bedrock API keys, the betas allowlist, the 1-hour TTL, `amazon-bedrock-invocationMetrics`, the exception shapes, no-lookback cache reads, and the catalog's model IDs.
- `bedrockAuthHeaders` (Bearer, or SigV4 with service `bedrock`) and `bedrockSecretsOf` are shared with OpenAI on Bedrock.

**OpenAI on AWS Bedrock** (vertexbedrock, 2026-11-07; `providers/bedrockOpenAI.ts`, kinds `openai-responses-bedrock` and `openai-chat-bedrock`, pi provider `amazon-bedrock`, provider `openai-bedrock`). Bedrock's runtime serves OpenAI's Responses and Chat Completions APIs at `https://bedrock-runtime.{region}.amazonaws.com/openai/v1` (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/inference-responses-api.html), so pi-ai's OpenAI adapters build the request and read the stream, and every OpenAI transform, shim and usage observer applies.
- **The transport** sends the SDK's request to its own address, dropping the SDK's `authorization`, Stainless, length and host headers. With `api-key` it adds `Authorization: Bearer <Bedrock API key>`; with `aws-sigv4` it signs `content-type`, `host` and `x-amz-date` (and a session token). An error in AWS's shape (`{"message"}` with `x-amzn-errortype`) becomes OpenAI's `{"error": {message, type}}`, with `x-amzn-requestid` as `x-request-id` and `retry-after` kept; OpenAI-shaped errors pass through.
- **Models:** pi-ai's Bedrock catalog's OpenAI IDs by inference profile (`us.`, `global.`, `in.` …`openai.gpt-…`): closed models' base IDs aren't served on the runtime. GPT OSS is listed on Chat Completions only (its Responses API is on Bedrock's Mantle endpoint). Listing sends nothing.
- **Caching** (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-caching.html): for GPT-5.6 and later on Responses, the provider's `cacheMarker: "prompt_cache_breakpoint"` turns on `applyBedrockBreakpoints`, `{mode: "explicit"}` on `input_text` blocks at each section, the previous history marker repeated (no lookback: a request "reads the cache only if it starts with an entire earlier request"), and three of the four writes, the fourth being Bedrock's automatic marker on the latest message. 1,024 cumulative tokens per marker (`documentedCacheMinimum`), at least 30 minutes (`cachePolicy.ts`, 1,800 s), writes billed at 1.25× input. The chat's `prompt_cache_key` is sent, as AWS's example does. Earlier models and Chat Completions cache automatically only: the shims `bedrock-openai-before-5.6-automatic-cache` and `bedrock-openai-chat-automatic-cache` strip the markers, and `bestEffortCache` calibrates the estimate from reported reads. Usage: `input_tokens_details.cached_tokens` and `cache_write_tokens`, read by pi-ai.
- **Tests:** `test/bedrockOpenAI.test.ts` (recorded shapes only): the model list, the documented minimum and best-effort cases, replies through a mock endpoint (address, Bearer and a recomputed SigV4 signature, markers on GPT-5.6, none on GPT-5.5 or Chat Completions, the cache key, reported cache reads and writes in the ledger, an access-denied error).
- **Untested live:** the address, both kinds of auth, `prompt_cache_key`, pi-ai's `include: ["reasoning.encrypted_content"]` and `store: false`, marker acceptance and the read-position rule, the usage fields, inference profile IDs, and whether markers on GPT-5.5 and earlier would be refused or ignored.

**Anthropic on Google Vertex** (vertexbedrock, 2026-11-07; `providers/vertex.ts`, kind and provider `anthropic-vertex`, pi provider `google-vertex`). Vertex serves Anthropic's Messages API (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/claude-on-vertex-ai), so pi-ai's Anthropic adapter builds the request and reads the SSE.
- **The request:** a `/v1/messages` POST becomes `POST {base}/v1/projects/{project}/locations/{region}/publishers/anthropic/models/{model}:streamRawPredict` (`:rawPredict` unstreamed). The body loses `model` and gains `anthropic_version: "vertex-2023-10-16"`; `stream` stays. The SDK's key, version, Stainless, length and host headers are dropped; `anthropic-beta` is kept. The project is the connection's, else the key file's; the Region is the connection's, else `global`. The address follows the Region: `aiplatform.googleapis.com` for global, `aiplatform.{us|eu}.rep.googleapis.com` for the multi-regions, else `{region}-aiplatform.googleapis.com` (`regionUrls`).
- **Sign-in:** the key is a service account's JSON key file, stored encrypted as any key (§3.12); its hint is the end of its key ID. The server signs an RS256 JWT with it (`iss` the account, scope `cloud-platform`, an hour) and exchanges it at `https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token`, a fixed address, never the key file's `token_uri`. The access token is kept in memory by key, one exchange at a time, until a minute before it expires; a refused exchange is forgotten and is the reply's authentication error. The exchange goes through the connection's routed fetch (`KindTransportRequest.aside`), not the observed one, so the ledger, the cache identity and the usage capture see the Vertex request alone. The private key is never sent; `secretsOf` scrubs the key file, the private key in raw and JSON-escaped form, its lines and its key ID.
- **The response:** Anthropic's SSE as is. Errors in Google's shape (`{"error": {code, message, status}}`, at times in a one-element array) become Anthropic's (`UNAUTHENTICATED` authentication, `PERMISSION_DENIED` permission, `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` rate limit, `NOT_FOUND`, `UNAVAILABLE` overloaded, `INVALID_ARGUMENT` invalid request), `retry-after` kept; Anthropic's pass through.
- **Models:** Anthropic's catalog with `@` before a dated ID's date (`claude-haiku-4-5@20251001`), the undated alias of a dated model left out. pi-ai's Vertex catalog has Gemini only. Listing sends nothing.
- **Caching:** Google: caching "behaves as described in the Anthropic documentation" (https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/partner-models/claude/prompt-caching), so Anthropic's automatic layout with lookback, four markers, 5 minutes or 1 hour (not Claude 3.x), the `google-vertex` cache contract and Claude's minimum sizes. Counted as Anthropic counts.
- **Tests:** `test/vertex.test.ts` (recorded shapes only): a synthetic key's JWT verified with its public key, the exchange (form body, one at a time, reuse until a minute before expiry, a refused exchange forgotten), the address for a Region and project, the body and headers, refusals that send nothing, Google's errors mapped, a refused sign-in, model IDs, and a reply through a mock Vertex endpoint with a token taken ahead (the path, Bearer token, `anthropic_version`, cache markers, reported cache reads and writes, nothing secret in the ledger).
- **Untested live:** the token exchange, the address and body, `anthropic-beta` on Vertex, lookback and automatic caching on Vertex, Google's error shapes, the prices and the 10% regional premium.

**Text tokens** (owner, 2026-11-02: "ideally you'd always use the tokenizer of the selected model"; DESIGN §4). The counts the editors show (§14.6: a card's total, permanent and per-field counts, a preset prompt's own text) come from `CountTokens` (`api/generation.ts`), answered by `TextTokens` (`providers/TextTokens.ts`) with the tokenizer of the model chats generate with: the account's current model (`GetGenerationDefaults`; chat locks are described in §15). `Providers.countTextTokens` resolves its connection as a send does and asks the newest registered counter that applies (`TextTokenCounter`: id, label, `remote`, `appliesTo` the kind, API, model and base URL, `count` of many texts):
- **`openai-encodings`** (local): OpenAI's model ids on any host, OpenRouter's `openai/…` too: `o200k_base` for GPT-4o, 4.1, 4.5, 5, the o-series and gpt-oss, `cl100k_base` for GPT-4 and 3.5. Counted off the main thread with **tiktoken 1.0.22**, its Node Wasm binding, loaded lazily (`importer/tokenizer.ts`). It replaces js-tiktoken 1.0.21: 20,000 repeated `x` characters produced the same 2,500 tokens in 0.96 s instead of 45.8 s, preventing context-display reads from blocking a reader for almost a minute. Unbroken whitespace, non-space and combining-mark runs can also merge in quadratic time. `prepareTokenizer` bounds runs of at least 4,096 UTF-16 code units in pieces of at most 4,096 (preserving surrogate pairs), scanning runs linearly and memoizing up to 32 repeated pieces per count. These counts are approximate: boundary merges may change them, without a guaranteed one-token error bound across vocabularies. Display and editor counts say so. Ordinary shorter runs keep the tokenizer's counts. The request text is never rewritten, but changed counts can move history cuts, cache breakpoints and LCM thresholds in existing chats; assembler version 64 fences old assemblies. `test/localTextTokens.test.ts` covers spaces, repeated non-space characters, combining marks, long unspaced lines and Unicode pairs in a time-limited subprocess; `textTokens.test.ts` covers the approximation label including cache hits. Special-token text counts as ordinary text. The dependency stays external to worker bundles and is linked into throwaway test bundle directories; its installed package supplies the Wasm and ranks.
- **`anthropic-count-tokens`**, **`google-count-tokens`**, **`openai-input-tokens`** (remote, `remote: true`), **only where the user chose a provider in the connection's Token counts** (owner, 2026-11-02: "I think this isn't a good idea to do behind the user's back, especially given varying retention policies… We probably should support it but not do it by default"; DESIGN §11): the endpoints the image counters use (below, "Exact counts"), one request per text, two at a time across the server; a text's tokens are its one-message count less a one-token text's (".") count, plus one, so the message's framing drops out. The OpenAI one applies only on `api.openai.com`, for an OpenAI model the encodings don't know.
- **The choice** (`db/tokenCounting.ts`, user-scoped `settings` key `token_counting`, `{ connections: { [connectionId]: viaId } }`; reader `GetTokenCounting`, writer `SetTokenCounting` with `via` null to clear, the same RPCs for the client; either connection not the user's is `NotFound`, and a choice whose connection or counting connection is deleted reads back as none): per connection, local by default, on the connection's page as **Token counts** (`features/connections/tokenCounting.tsx`, registered `connection.sections` part `token-counting`), one picker "Count with": **Local estimate**, **This connection's provider**, or **Another: <name>**, one of the user's other connections used only for counting (owner, 2026-11-02: "It should also be possible to specify a separate token counting endpoint for a connection"). Each option's explanation, and the one under the picker for the current choice, names the provider and address that receive the text and images being counted. `Providers.countTextTokens` and `countImageTokens` take `via`: null skips every remote counter; the connection itself asks its counters in registry order; another connection is asked only where no local counter applies to the chat's own connection, with remote counters that apply to it, and for the chat model under its own name for it (`providers/countingModel.ts`: the same key if it lists one, else the key without a router's `vendor/` prefix, matched with dots and dashes alike); its label says "through <name>". Where a remote counter would apply but none is chosen, the answer is `{ optIn }`, which `TextTokens` turns into the `o200k_base` approximation with a note pointing at the setting. Counts are cached apart by the counting connection, on the server and in the client (`tokenCounts.ts`). Choosing triggers the open chats' image estimates again. Anthropic's old public Claude tokenizer isn't used: it undercounts current models by 30–50% (owner).
- **Open-model encodings** (tokenizers, 2026-11-02): `open-model-encodings` registers after `openai-encodings`. `providers/localTextModels.ts` recognizes published family/version ids in OpenRouter ids and local paths/GGUF names: Llama 3/3.1/3.2/3.3 (`llama3-tokenizer-js` **1.2.0**, no BOS/EOS); Mistral 7B v0.3, Qwen2/2.5, Qwen3, DeepSeek V3/R1 and V4, Gemma 2 (`@huggingface/tokenizers` **0.2.0**). DeepSeek's current `deepseek-flash` uses its separately vendored official API demo tokenizer; unknown legacy aliases remain approximate. `importer/tokenizers/` holds deterministic gzip copies, pinned source revisions, uncompressed SHA-256, licenses and reference-verification instructions. Gemma 2's mirror is byte-identical to Google's published LFS hash. Budgets do not treat Gemma as Gemini: historical reports do not prove current Gemini tokenizer equivalence. Other Mistral versions, Gemma 3, multimodal Qwen and unknown versions retain the marked fallback. Tokenizers load lazily off the main thread; at most one HF vocabulary is retained per worker. The worker builder copies the data next to its bundles and stamps it; throwaway test bundles link the external Llama package beside tiktoken.
- **Text calibration** (`providers/textCalibration.ts`, `db/textCalibration.ts`): the final dispatched text-only payload is counted locally in the format worker when its ledger row closes. `CloseLlmRequest.textEstimate` stores `estimated_input` and `input_tokenizer` in the baseline schema, alongside the existing reported uncached input/cache read/cache write counts. Images and tools are ineligible for text calibration, preventing their extra input from being learned as text. `GetTextCalibration` is an owner-scoped reader operation. For each owner/connection/model/tokenizer it divides total reported input (uncached + cache read + cache write) by total raw estimates over the latest 32 complete reported requests, clamped to 0.25–4. Estimated, failed and interrupted requests never train it. Raw editor counts stay cached; each answer applies the current ratio once, keeps empty fields at zero, and says “Calibrated” in the existing approximate tooltip. A completed model reply invalidates the client's field-count cache; an in-flight answer from before that invalidation is discarded and re-requested. Provider counting choices remain unchanged; remote counts are not ratio-corrected.
- **The cache:** each text's count by owner, connection, model key and SHA-256, 5,000 entries, so typing in one field asks again only for that field.
- **Tests** (tokenizers): `localTextTokens.test.ts` verifies the vendored hashes, seven tokenizer files against independently computed Python Hugging Face tokenizers 0.22.1 reference IDs from those exact model files, Meta's own Llama encode/dialog fixtures, conservative model-id matching, payload eligibility and ratio rounding. `textTokens.test.ts` runs every family through bundled format workers without contacting a provider. `textCalibration.test.ts` exercises a submitted request through the real ledger, including cached input and inspector estimates; `providers.test.ts` checks the bounded 32-sample ratio, read/write cache tokens, excluded usage and owner isolation. Inspector provenance tests retain immutable historical reads.
- **The fallback:** with no current model, no counter for it (an unsupported model or a plugin's kind without one), a provider's counter with no provider chosen for its connection (Claude and Gemini by default), a count that fails or takes over 15 s, the texts are counted with `o200k_base` and the answer says so (`TokenizerInfo`: `exact: false`, the label, and a `note` saying why); a failed model rests for ten minutes. Only if the worker fails too is it the four-characters estimate, saying so. The context budget keeps the assembler's fast estimate (§15 "Token counts"); finalized requests supply calibration samples.
- `test/textTokens.test.ts` covers OpenRouter's `openai/gpt-4o` counted locally without asking the provider, Claude counted here with no request to Anthropic until its connection chooses its provider (and again once it goes back to local), an OpenRouter Claude counted through a separate Anthropic connection under that connection's model name and key with nothing sent to OpenRouter (and local again once that connection is deleted), Claude through a mock counting endpoint once opted in (the framing taken out, the cache asking once per text), a failed count's fallback and rest, unsupported-model and no-model approximations; the isolation matrix's `CountTokens` probe that another user's chat model never counts the caller's text, and the `GetTokenCounting` and `SetTokenCounting` probes (another user's connection can't be chosen, neither as the one counted for nor as the one counting).

**Image tokens** (DESIGN §10.2a: image tokens are part of the prompt, and the estimate is accurate on every provider). What an image costs a model comes, in order, from: the provider's exact count, the provider's documented formula for the model's family, the ledger's calibration for that model, else it is unknown. Every estimate carries that basis (`counted`, `formula`, `calibrated`, `unknown`) to the context view and the composer. The assembly side is in §15 ("Image tokens").
- **Formulas** (`@rp/shared/imageTokens.ts`, pure, registered as image token rules in the assembler, §15). Sources, read and reviewed 2026-10-30:
  - Anthropic (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/vision, https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/vision-coordinates): `⌈w/28⌉ × ⌈h/28⌉` after resizing to the tier's limits. Claude 4.7 and later (and a model name without a version) are on the high-resolution tier: 2,576 px long edge, 4,784 tokens; earlier models 1,568 px and 1,568 tokens. The resize is Anthropic's TypeScript reference implementation verbatim (binary search on the long edge, ties-to-even rounding). Its documented table says 2000×1500 resizes to 1269×952; the reference gives 1270×952. Both cost 1,564 tokens, which is what the tests pin.
  - OpenAI (https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/images-vision): tile models (gpt-4o, gpt-4.1, gpt-4o-mini, gpt-5, gpt-5.1, o1, o3) fit 2048², scale the short side to 768, then base + tiles × per-tile (85/170, 2833/5667, 70/140, 75/150); `low` is the base alone. Patch models (gpt-6-astra, gpt-5.6, gpt-5.5, gpt-5.4, gpt-5.2, gpt-4.1-mini) count 32 px patches after the detail level's size and patch budget, times the model's multiplier (1.2 or 1.62 for models with a documented sizing row). Our requests send `auto` (pi-ai's Responses sets it; Chat Completions omits it, which OpenAI defines as `auto`), so `auto`'s sizing per model is used. Retired gpt-5-mini/nano, gpt-4.1-nano and o4-mini no longer have a documented sizing row: they use counts or calibration, else remain unknown rather than assuming a different model's sizing.
  - Google (https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/image-understanding, https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/tokens, https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/media-resolution): before Gemini 3, 258 tokens up to 384×384, else 258 per tile with a crop unit of `max(1, ⌊min(w,h)/1.5⌋)` (Google calls it rough; the one-pixel floor keeps narrow images finite). Gemini 3/4 bill a fixed figure per media resolution; we send none, which is 1,120. Unversioned aliases and non-Gemini Google models have no assumed Gemini-2 sizing: they use counts/calibration or remain unknown.
  - Mistral (https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/conversations/vision): about `w·h/784` within 1540², Pixtral about `w·h/256` within 1024² (documented as approximate).
  - DeepSeek (https://api-docs.deepseek.com/guides/vision): no formula is published, only a cap of 1,024 tokens per image. The rule returns that as a bound, so the image is calibrated or unknown, budgeted at the cap meanwhile.
  - xAI (https://docs.x.ai/developers/model-capabilities/images/understanding.md) and OpenRouter (https://openrouter.ai/docs/llms-full.txt) publish no formula. OpenRouter passes images to the upstream, so its models (`vendor/model`) use the upstream family's rule. xAI reports `prompt_tokens_details.image_tokens`, which calibration reads. Local servers (llama.cpp, vLLM) document no image-cost endpoint; they are calibrated.
- **Exact counts** (`providers/imageCounters.ts`, `Providers.countImageTokens`, `chat/ImageTokenCounts.ts`). Each counter counts one image as the difference between a one-message count with the image and the same message without it, so framing and the text tokenizer drop out. Anthropic `POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` (base64 images; free, separate rate limits by tier: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/token-counting), Gemini `models/{model}:countTokens` with inline data (cost and limits not stated: https://ai.google.dev/api/tokens), and OpenAI `POST /v1/responses/input_tokens`, only when the base URL is `api.openai.com` (cost and limits not stated: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/token-counting). **Only through the chat connection's Token counts choice** (above, "Text tokens"; DESIGN §11, owner, 2026-11-02: "NEVER send anything to providers users didn't actually choose to"): `ImageTokenCounts` reads it for each request and passes it as `via`; with the default nothing is sent, the images keep their formula, calibrated or unknown basis (never zero), and a model with nothing to count it rests apart for each way of counting, so a choice made later counts at once. Before 2026-11-02 (ftok) the chat provider's endpoint was asked by default, when a chat opened, an image was attached or the model changed. Counting is never on a send's path: the cache-warmth estimate of an open chat (§12) returns the next context's images that aren't counted for its model (`uncounted`, stripped before anything is published or returned by `GetNextContext`), and `ImageTokenCounts` counts them in the background behind one shared permit across all chats and connections, with the with/without HTTP calls also sequential. Each job has a 30-second timeout, with at most 128 pending image jobs. In-flight deduplication uses the storage identity (owner, kind, model, detail, hash); the worker cache is checked again under the permit before HTTP, so stale previews and another connection cannot recount a stored image. It stores each with `RecordImageTokenCount` in `image_token_counts`, keyed by owner, content hash, provider kind, model key and detail (an image is counted once), then estimates that owner's watched chats again. Active composer uploads are included before Send and after model changes, using the owner/fork-scoped server draft; attachment add/remove schedules a new preview. A failed count, or a model whose connection has no counter, rests for ten minutes. `test/providerSend.test.ts` checks that with every setting at its default, opening a chat, attaching an image, reading the next context, counting a card's text and switching the model send no request to either of two providers, and that the submit then sends only the reply request to the chosen one; and that images go only to a separately chosen counting connection, with its key.
- **Calibration** (`providers/imageSamples.ts`). When a request whose final payload sent images finishes with reported usage, the ledger close records a sample with `RecordImageTokenSample` in `image_token_samples` (the newest 20 per connection and model): the images, their total pixels (read from the sent bytes' headers), and their tokens. The tokens are the provider's own image figure where it reports one (`prompt_tokens_details.image_tokens`, Gemini's `IMAGE` modality), else the reported input less the payload's text as the assembler estimates text (`derived`). An estimate fits `tokens = a·images + b·pixels` by least squares once the samples' sizes differ (models whose cost grows with resolution), else uses the mean per image. Zero/invalid reported image counts and zero calibration samples are rejected; a sent image never learns a zero cost. Missing dimensions can still use the observed per-image mean.
- **`kind` and `api` are open strings** (`@rp/shared/providers.ts`), checked against the registry where they're used:
  - an unknown kind can't create a connection
  - a connection whose kind is gone, for example its plugin was removed, is `unusable`
  - `ListProviderKinds` gives the client the kinds in effect
- `test/providerStream.test.ts` registers a gateway kind and a transform in a scope, the way a plugin will. It streams through them, then closes the scope and checks that both are gone.

**Cold-cache parallel requests** (DESIGN §5.5; `providers/cacheStagger.ts`, `providers/cacheIdentity.ts`). After SDK conversion and registered transforms, `stream` hashes the provider-formatted prefix in memory, including tool definitions, structured content and cache configuration. Source provenance locates the last assembly breakpoint in the final payload. For block-explicit caching, its last cacheable block must carry an applicable marker: that reusable endpoint is the scheduling key. Later SDK markers, including a volatile one-turn direction, contribute historical coverage without replacing that key. Automatic-cache requests also schedule on the assembly endpoint. Owner, connection/cache revision, route, model, conversion capabilities and final payload routing fields (including `prompt_cache_key`) participate.
- Gates are acquired at the controlled fetch boundary, where the SDK's actual session-affinity headers are available. Only routing values that reach that boundary enter the identity; an unused Anthropic session ID does not partition otherwise identical requests or historical warmth. Explicit header overrides take precedence naturally. Providers without this controlled fetch boundary bypass scheduling. Sent-context capture still waits until the gate releases.
- Anthropic's top-level `cache_control` enables automatic placement at the last cacheable block (excluding trailing thinking blocks). When no explicit marker was sent at the reusable boundary, that effective endpoint supplies the key. Its TTL/configuration participates in identity; an enabled top-level control is not a markerless request.
- Scheduling pins the final transformed request's documented lifetime (§15), with model/connection overrides taking precedence, just as sent-context capture does. Unknown policies remain unknown. Fixed-lived cache hits do not record a new expiry; historical coverage comes from the original write or miss. Follower hit metadata uses the same normalized read count as the ledger, including header-only Fireworks reads.
- Scheduling has its own **endpoint coverage** predicate. `CachePrefixWarm` checks whether one of the owner's 100 most recent unexpired eligible ledger rows covers the entire requested endpoint with the same identity. A shorter warm history cannot bypass a cold extension. The display comparison (§15) keeps its existing unchanged-old-prefix semantics.
- Migration `0020_cache_identity` stores only endpoint SHA-256 digests and the request's pinned expiry in the worker ledger; no raw tools, images or routing payload are added to storage or client DTOs. Closed records are immutable. Requests predating these hashes are conservatively cold. Without a TTL, simultaneous cold requests still coalesce but historical warmth is unknown.
- No reusable prefix, `cacheRetention: "none"`, disabled model caching, or no applicable marker in an explicit-cache payload means no gate. Unrecognized payload dialects also bypass it. Callers supply the provider-neutral request and model in `inspection`, including future summary jobs.
- The first cold request starts immediately. Matching followers wait for its first **provider response chunk**, including Anthropic's `message_start`, rather than its first text token. All six built-in kinds default to this rule: Anthropic, OpenRouter (Claude included), OpenAI Chat/Responses, DeepSeek and Google. Claude Bedrock/Vertex kinds supplied by plugins inherit the same default. `ProviderKindEntry.cacheRelease` can instead select successful completion and change `timeoutMs` (default 10,000). The reference establishes no different automatic-provider release point; first-chunk readiness remains an assumption to measure for those providers, particularly best-effort caches.
- Timeout, leader failure or stop releases followers too. Stopping a held follower aborts its wait and never sends it. Gates live for one attempt, so retries cannot strand followers. A solitary request has no scheduling wait or timer; caps and rate-limit pauses still apply. Owners cannot hold each other's requests.
- Migration `0019_cache_stagger` adds follower metadata to the usage ledger: leader request id, release reason, and `hit` from the actual provider hit field (null when unavailable). Existing normalized read/write counts and raw usage stay available. This makes first-chunk releases, timeouts and misses distinguishable.
- `test/cacheStagger.test.ts` exercises actual swipe RPCs through assembly, SDK HTTP, worker storage and subscriptions with synthetic providers: one Anthropic write and N−1 reads, automatic-cache followers through OpenAI and the Gemini REST adapter, growing conversations, different one-turn directions sharing cold history, warm requests, timeout, leader/follower stop and owner isolation. `test/providerCacheIdentity.test.ts` checks tools, image blocks, session routing, final routing overrides and disabled/markerless caching at the SDK boundary, including historical warmth, ignored session IDs, actual affinity headers and their overrides, volatile tails, top-level Anthropic control, documented/unknown/fixed lifetimes and normalized header hits. The browser tests cover the waiting label and reconnect.
- **Opt-in live measurement**, never CI: `npm run measure:cache-stagger -- --live --provider anthropic --model MODEL --key-env ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. Repeat for each built-in kind and actual model; use `--base-url` for a gateway, `--release complete` to compare readiness, `--timeout-ms` and `--requests` to vary the cohort. It sends a unique synthetic prefix of roughly 10k tokens, reports follower cache reads/hits and send/hold timings, and closes workers and removes its isolated database under `.cache-stagger-measurements/` (or `--scratch`). It captures the named key before scrubbing provider environment configuration, then imports the application; it never reads production storage. It incurs real provider usage; no live measurement runs as part of checks.

**Calling providers.** `providers/sdk.ts` loads pi-ai's lazy OpenAI and Anthropic wire adapters directly, never its `Models` collection. Production and development entry points first run `providerEnvironment.ts`, then dynamically import the application: SDKs cannot observe ambient provider configuration during import. The scrub mutates only this server process's environment; its parent is unaffected. Server-owned names are declared in `serverEnvironment.ts`, used by configuration readers, and checked against every scrub rule before anything is deleted. An overlap, even for an unset server variable, fails startup. SDK upgrades still require an environment/transport audit; there are no source patches, provider bundles or hash checks.

**Native Google / Gemini API** (google, 2026-11-12; `google` kind and provider, `google-generative-ai` API). The existing provider registry, connection forms, encrypted keys, origin binding, routing, request transforms, usage observer and cost formulas handle Google as they handle the other native providers. The default address is `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta`; custom addresses retain Google's dialect. Test connection fetches `models.list` with `x-goog-api-key`, including pagination; refresh excludes entries that explicitly omit `generateContent`. Resource names lose the `models/` prefix in the picker. List token limits and `thinking` override the pinned catalog; the catalog supplies image input, thinking maps and prices where known. Google's list does not report modalities or prices: unknown models retain unknown capabilities/pricing for the user to edit. There is no route-price endpoint for native Google; OpenRouter's endpoint-price fetching and route rules remain specific to that router.
- **Thinking:** the existing effort setting maps through pi-ai's thinking helpers. Gemini 2.5 uses token budgets (custom budgets or pi-ai's level budgets); Gemini 3 uses `thinkingLevel`. The pinned helper omits Gemini 4, so the Google adapter extends that format selection for Carbon/Argon; the registered `google-gemini-4-thinking-levels` shim supplies their low/medium/high map and forbids off. The `google-gemini-2.5-pro-thinking-on` shim prevents a zero budget (minimum 128). Neither changes another provider's models. `includeThoughts` requests summaries, not raw thoughts; thinking tokens count within output and its cap. See [Google's generateContent thinking guide](https://aistudio.google.com/docs/thinking?generate-content=true).
- **Caching:** implicit caching only. Assembly breakpoints still organize a stable prefix and cold-request staggering, but send no cache marker, `cachedContent` resource, lifetime or session cache key to Google. Turning app caching off suppresses its cache planning; Google's automatic caching cannot be disabled by that setting. No explicit cached-content creation, refresh, deletion, storage billing or expiry management is implemented. The documented native minimums are 2,048 tokens for 2.5 Flash/Pro and 4,096 for 3.1 Pro Preview, 3.6/3.8 Flash and 4 Carbon/Argon; other models remain unknown. Google publishes no implicit-cache lifetime, so the warmth countdown stays unknown unless the user supplies an estimate; reported reads prove only the completed request's hit. A user lifetime is an estimate, never a wire TTL. Gemini 4's documented 2,050-token tail reprocessing rule can reduce reads on small turns. See [Google's generateContent caching guide](https://aistudio.google.com/docs/caching?generate-content=true).
- **Usage/errors/inspection:** `cachedContentTokenCount` is subtracted from `promptTokenCount` for uncached input, cached reads are charged separately, and candidates plus thoughts form output (thoughts also retained as reasoning). Implicit writes have no separate count. Prompt feedback blocks (no candidates) and candidate safety stops become refusals through Google's registered observer, so they do not retry as premature EOF. A natural `STOP` with no nonblank text or tool call fails even without prefill, retaining thought output and usage; empty, whitespace-only and thought-only responses cannot become completed chat replies (`google.test.ts`). Length cutoffs and tool-only responses keep their existing handling. HTTP/stream failures and Stop use the common retry-before-output, ledger and abort paths. Images use pi-ai's inline image conversion. The inspector stores the final sanitized sent transcript and samplers with sources, as for other providers; it does not expose credentials, raw image bytes or an arbitrary full HTTP-body dump.
- **Validation:** synthetic local HTTP only: `google.test.ts` covers catalog pricing, uncached/read/thought accounting, unknown TTL and inspector equality with the sent transcript; `providerStream.test.ts` covers pagination, Test, known/unknown capabilities, auth, retry boundaries, stop and routing; `googleParity.test.ts` compares supported requests to the pinned SDK and checks Gemini 4 levels; `messageImages.test.ts`, `cacheDefaults.test.ts`, `cachePolicy.test.ts` and `providerShims.test.ts` cover images, warmth, minimums and rules. `e2e/google.spec.ts` and the focused Google connection tests in `layoutAudit.spec.ts` exercise the existing forms, Check and Refresh at 1440/390 in both themes. No new dependency, schema or core-provider branch was added. Live API behavior is unverified; Interactions, audio/video output and Gemini 4 continuation-token long decode are outside this adapter.

**Google transport** (`providers/google.ts`). The pinned pi-ai adapter rejects custom fetch. genai 2.21.0's generateContent `HttpOptions` exposes headers, body and retries, but no fetch hook or dispatcher; its fetcher hooks belong to other APIs. Our lazily loaded adapter sends Gemini's REST generateContent stream directly through the request's controlled fetch, reusing pi-ai's exported transcript/tool converters, thinking helpers and event stream. The payload hook receives SDK-shaped parameters, including the request signal; `googleRequest.ts` maps the supported options to REST, normalizes model/tuned-model and cached-content resource names, and rejects unsupported options before HTTP. Generation fields are allowlisted; service tier, system instructions, tools and safety settings live outside `generationConfig`. Full JSON Schema fields are supported; the legacy `responseSchema`/tool `parameters` dialect and unimplemented SDK tools are rejected. Transport settings and cancellation remain request-owned. It preserves thinking and tool signatures, usage, status and aborts. SSE accepts LF, CRLF and CR across arbitrary byte boundaries. Raw JSON and SSE error envelopes retain their details; premature EOF uses pi-ai's recognized retry message, and output still prevents retries. Request, thinking-budget and error parity tests compare against the pinned SDK over local HTTP. No global fetch mutation or library-source patch is needed.
- **Each request gets:**
  - an explicit key: a placeholder for keyless local servers, since pi's direct calls require one
  - `env: {}`
  - `maxRetries: 0`, so retries happen only in our layer and are visible
  - the fiber's abort signal, joined with an idle watchdog (resume1; AGENTIC §12.6): once the request is sent (after any cache gate), the response body passes through a `TransformStream` that restarts a timer on every byte (keep-alive comments and pings count), and pi events restart it too.
