All attempts still pass through the guard, limiter, coalescer and HTTP validator cache. Every card criterion is exposed in the existing Filters panel. Home retains Show on an empty account so cardex is discoverable before an import; filter counts exclude the default rating, and long chips truncate within their container. JSON-only cards fetch their separate full portrait through the guarded image cache when opened; adoption reuses it as avatar media, without a new request while cached, with an initials fallback if it cannot be fetched. No schema baseline changes. `cardex.test.ts` and `cardSources.test.ts` cover synthetic criteria, nullable totals, reset paging, cover defaults and JSON portrait adoption while offline. `e2e/support/cardexCriteria.ts` checks every filter/chip and sort in both surfaces at 1440/390, light/dark; `LAYOUT_AUDIT_CARDEX_ONLY=1` registers the same focused checks in `layoutAudit.spec.ts`. Review regressions additionally cover capped-count wording, paging both picker kinds, URL reload in both surfaces, the explained name-search fallback, and expired-cursor replacement without duplicate cards. The browser suite remains synthetic and never contacts cardex.
- **Long choices and dates (cardex2, 2026-11-12).** A several-choice filter with more than eight options (cardex's Site and Exclude sites, 18 each) is the existing `MultiSelect` picker inside its `Field`, with its search, instead of a row of buttons. A text filter may declare `format: "date"` (cardex: its `date`-typed criteria, the added and created bounds); the panel shows it as a date field and sends `YYYY-MM-DD`. Every other v1 criterion was already offered; the live capabilities were checked again and declare nothing the panel leaves out (the standalone-lorebook kinds came with cardex3, below).
- **Creators (cardex2, 2026-11-12).** A source declares `creators: { filterId, excludeFilterId?, profiles }` in its capabilities (cardex: `author`, `not_author`). A creator view is the browsing view with that filter set to the creator's `site/handle`, so it lives in the URL (`sf`/`sideSf`), survives a reload and opens in another tab, and every filter and sort still applies. Creator and exclusion actions push history entries, so Back/Forward restores the prior creator view; typing and sorting retain the existing replace behaviour. Above the results, `CreatorHeader` (`features/cardSources/creator.tsx`) shows the profile from the adapter's `creator` hook (`SourceCreator` RPC; cardex `/authors/{site}/{handle}`, cached as a page; the avatar is an image key): name, site, card and lorebook counts, first seen, the bio folded, "Not by this creator" (moves the creator to the exclude filter) and a link to the profile on the source. A result's context menu has "Cards by X" and "Not by X"; a source card's "by X" links to the view.
- **Families and recognition (cardex2, reviewed 2026-11-12).** An import (file upload and the ST folder import) collects the card's links, its `source` entries and each extension's `url` (`linksOf` in `importer/importers.ts`, at most 50); registered adapters recognize their own ids and origin URLs. `ImportFile` records these as unverified hints (`recognized_by = 'recognized'`, empty `remote_version`) using the existing baseline shape. Hints do not mark a card as held, block Add, or enable update tracking. Only a trusted archive hash matching an owned import's `source_hash` confirms it: results first use `HeldRemoteCards`' indexed reader lookup; a byte-matched import is bound by the writer's `RecognizeRemoteCards` with the archive version. Opening a source card also checks its actual downloaded bytes, since a derived file can differ from the archive's version hash. Adoption makes the same check in its transaction, returning the existing import rather than duplicating it. Confirmation replaces a conflicting unverified hint and respects the one-origin-per-card rule; verified origins survive later imports. Verified imports support Check for a newer version and Review and merge, while Only tried still counts direct additions only. An edited file with only a Sources link remains an ordinary import until a matching file is available; a Sources link cannot authenticate unrelated definitions. When a held original is in the bin or purged, reads and adoption resolve its newest live fork (including forks of forks, owner-scoped throughout); with no live fork, an import or adoption can take over. A source declaring `families` answers its registered `family` hook (`SourceFamily` RPC, cached as a page): cardex checks the detail identity and family envelopes, then reads `/versions` and `/forks` of up to three origins, at most 60 relatives, each once, enriching sparse detail rows from later family replies while keeping their first relationship, and leaving out the card itself; additional origins or pages set `more`. Archive-content URLs are never followed for these reads: paths are built on the adapter's origin from encoded identifiers, under the shared response caps and network guard. The user's own relatives are marked. The existing `SourceFamily` view lists Chat or Open yours and Inspect on a source card's page and on request in Metadata. Creator envelopes must match the requested site/handle, and summary fields are validated before projection; malformed replies use the existing source error state. `cardSources.test.ts`, `cardex.test.ts`, the isolation suite and the browser creator/family/update specs cover these paths with synthetic data.
- **Successor updates (review-cardex2 follow-up, 2026-11-12).** Check and opening an update resolve the newest live file before fetching it. Cardex's `/origins/<source>/<external_id>` returns the current card and its original file hash in one conditional GET, independent of how many historical slugs precede it. The adapter captures an opaque listing key from the card's primary origin or historical `earlier_origins` metadata; a row without that key first bootstraps it from its historical detail. The one-original-file hash matches the batch version; multiple originals use one canonical batch lookup. With no usable listing key, canonical batches follow only `superseded_by`, at most four hops with cycle detection; one eight-request budget covers bootstrap and all batches. Forks are never successor edges. All paths are constructed on the adapter's configured origin from encoded identifiers; archive-provided URLs are never fetched. Missing or HTTP 451 heads clear the marker and say no newer file is available. Fresh browsing results resolve held historical summaries too, without replacing their historical Inspect files or edited cache entries. Only confirmed imports or additions track updates.
  The baseline adds `current_remote_id` (the slug actually taken), `remote_locator` (the opaque listing key), and `seen_remote_id` (the pending slug); `remote_version` remains the version actually taken and `remote_id` remains the original duplicate-detection identity. An owner/source/current-slug index lets both original and current results find the same owned card. Every worker read and write remains owner-scoped. The downloaded file includes a signed, user/card/source-bound receipt naming its exact slug, version, key and bytes hash. Review and merge and Replace submit it when recording the version taken, so a concurrent check cannot substitute another pending identity; a later pending version stays pending. Add as a separate card records the prepared file's actual identity in its import transaction. The import route receives the current page link, retaining it in Sources through the existing append-only import rules. Synthetic adapter, server and browser tests cover three-version chains, cross-site successors, cycles and request limits, deleted/regional heads, independent forks, inert claims, receipt tampering and owner isolation. The earlier apparent fork timeout came from a functional-test adapter override shrinking its shared rate-limit bucket from 1000 to the production burst of 60, then waiting on Effect's virtual clock; all functional overrides now use the same synthetic burst, with real limiter tests unchanged.
- **Standalone lorebooks (cardex3, 2026-11-12; spec/CARD-SOURCES.md §3.9).** Results carry cardex's lorebooks beside characters: `searchParams` sends `kind=both` unless the Kind choice (four options, in `KIND_ORDER`) says otherwise, and `summaryOf` marks a v1 `kind: "lorebook"` item with `RemoteSummary.kind = "lorebook"` (absent for a card). A lorebook's file is fetched as `mode=original` when listed (World Info JSON, the creator's file that its version hash names); every other path is the card's. `RemoteLorebookTile` (`features/cardSources/browse.tsx`) is the result tile with a **Lorebook** badge on the picture's corner and its own menu: Open, Add to my lorebooks, Open in a new browser tab, Open on cardex, the creator items; no Inspect, chat or Add to my cards. A click goes to `/sources/<id>/lorebooks/<remoteId>` (`RemoteLorebookPage`), which adds it and replaces itself with `/library/<refId>`, so a reload or a second tab finds the same copy; a held tile links straight to it ("You have this lorebook"). Adding is `AdoptRemoteCard`, unchanged on the wire: `CardSources.adopt` sees the parsed file is a lorebook and stores it with no portrait, Sources link or note, named as the source lists it (`withSourceName`: a World Info file names no lorebook, so the importer would take the file's name, the archive's slug), and the writer's `adopt` (`db/cardOrigins.ts`) imports it as `kind = lorebook` (`adoptedKind`: a document with top-level `entries` and no `first_mes`) with the same `card_origins` row a card gets, skipping the hash recognition of imported cards; `newestLiveFork` looks only at forks of the same kind. No new RPC, write op or baseline change. Updates use the card paths as they are (`CardOrigin`, `CheckRemoteVersion`, `/sources/held/<entityId>/file`, successors through the stable listing, `TakeRemoteVersion` with its receipt): the `card-sources.update` editor notice, for a lorebook with an origin in the full editor and the side panel, shows "A newer version is on cardex" with **Review and merge**, which stages the newer file with `/library/import?into=<ref>&mode=merge` (named after the lorebook, so its name stays) and opens the existing merge review. Staging records the exact version/receipt but leaves the active book and its chats unchanged. Cancel leaves it on the import line; the normal pending-merge notice reopens review, and only Merge changes the book. Check for a newer version remains below it. The open route first uses `SourceCard` to record a recent view, including its optional kind; recent lorebook links return to that open route. Lorebook creator actions read **More by <creator>**. The fake archive serves 12 synthetic lorebooks (`syntheticLorebooks`), for `kind=lorebook`, and for `both` only when the words name one ("gazetteer"), so the card tests' results don't change; `publish` adds an entry. `test/cardex.test.ts` and `test/cardSources.test.ts` (adding once, held, origin isolation, update by merge, a successor), `e2e/cardexLorebooks.spec.ts` (1440 and 390, light and dark; also in the layout audit's cardex-only run).
- **Edited cards stay cached (cardex2, 2026-11-12).** The source cache's sweep (at start-up, every 10 minutes, and on a new cap) first reads `EditedRemoteCards`, every user's source cards with active `remote_card` drafts, and passes their card entries to `sweepKeeping`: they count as pinned until the next sweep, past their age and, past the cap, after unpinned entries, so an edit made before adding retains its original past the age limit, subject to the cap. At start-up the cache index is rebuilt with `load` (no sweep) so that first sweep is the one that keeps them. If the drafts can't be read, the round is skipped. Normal cache reads honour the same edit pins as sweeps, so opening an expired original does not delete it. Pinned entries remain subject to the cap, after unpinned entries; add moves drafts to the local card, and discard or deletion ends them, so the next sweep unpins those originals.
- **Workshop tools (cardextools1, 2026-11-16).** The workshop assistant browses card sources through registered operation adapters (`agent/exposures/cardSources.ts`) over `ListCardSources`, `CheckRemoteVersion` and five commands (`agent/cardSourceCommands.ts`, installed with the RPC handlers) that make the browse view's own `CardSources` calls: `list_card_sources` (library.read, never contacts a source), `card_source_filters` (`sources.filters`: the capabilities as the Filters panel offers them, with the user's rating), `search_card_source` (`sources.search`: words, tags, excluded tags, every filter by id or label, choices by value or label, sorts and reverse, the source's cursor as `page`, and `offset` within a page longer than one result), `open_remote_card` (`sources.card`: the listing, then each text field's length and first 300 characters; a named field pages by 8,000 characters, alternate greetings and lorebook entries by entry), `remote_card_family` (`sources.family`), `check_card_update` (your card by name or id, as Check for a newer version) and `adopt_remote_card` (`sources.adopt`). All read, under **Use the internet** (`network`, Ask first by default; its chip now shows in every workshop, whose strip counts it among the Asks), except adding: library.write, effect `library`, `approval: "always"` (`OperationExposure.approval`), so it asks even where library changes are allowed, naming the card, its creator and its id from the recently viewed list (a card must have been opened first). `checkedQuery` maps the assistant's choices to the `SourceQuery` the browse view sends and refuses, in words, what the panel wouldn't send: unknown filters, choices, out-of-range bounds, a min above its max, non-boolean switches, a Chub mark without Site set to Chub alone, non-`YYYY-MM-DD` dates, unknown or non-reversible sorts. The content rating is the user's (`SourcePrefs.rating` else the source's default, as `useSourceBrowse` applies it); the assistant may narrow it only to the source's safe choice (`SourceCapabilities.ratings.safe`, cardex `exclude`), and under a Safe rating `open_remote_card` refuses a rated card. A source the user turned off is refused in the adapter before any approval or request, and the service refuses it again (`disabled`). Results drop image keys; every result passes through the workshop's data boundary (`formatResult`, escaped `<tool_data>`), with source text cut per field. Adding passes a `write` hook to `CardSources.adopt`, so the card's media and thumbnails are handled as for Add to my cards, while the row is written by `RunWorkshopOperation` with operation `AdoptRemoteCard` (now in `creations`; the writer passes the adopt handler to the workshop operations): the document gets the same treatment as a file the assistant imports (scripts and HTML off, no granted edits; a card carrying its own skills is refused), and the receipt replays. A card the user has from there already answers `alreadyYours` with no effect; otherwise Undo bins the card and its notes, after which adding it again makes a new one. Opening a card records it as recently viewed, as the user's own open does. `SetCardSourceEnabled` stays user-only (exclusions); rating, cache, key, tags, suggestions, creator profiles, draft chats and taking an update are not offered. The seven tools form the **Card sources** skill (`card-sources`), registered after the built-ins and every tool deferred: in the loading modes a request carries only its index line, 28 o200k tokens; the definitions, 1,126 tokens in all (search 309), are sent only after `load_skill`, or on every request in Every-tool mode unless Use the internet is Off (`workshopContext.test.ts` turns it off). The opened card's skills are removed before projection (`withoutCardSkills`). Tests: `test/workshopCardSources.test.ts` (the mapping and its refusals, rating narrowing, paging, nothing sent while the source is off or before an approval could be described, the same cards as `SourceSearch`, Safe refusals, field reads, Ask first, the always-asking approval with its title, adding, receipt replay, no duplicate, update check, Undo and re-adding, and a mocked adapter's hostile text quoted inside one escaped boundary), all against the fake archive. Review fixes (review-cardextools1): the adapters' check reads the user's switches and the instance's admin switches (`sources.admin`), takes a source by its id only (a name fails the arguments), and refuses an unnamed source while any source is off, so the command's "only one on" choice can never reach one that is off; `check_card_update` refuses before asking when its card's source (`CardOrigin`) is off. `checkedQuery` follows the panel's `requirementMet` (a switch needs exactly its required choices), sends the source's first sort when none is named, as `queryOf` does, and refuses a tag both wanted and left out. A recently viewed entry records the version opened (`RecentRemote.version`, `versionAt`) and its `rating`; the add's prepared payload carries that version, so a re-open while the approval waits changes the payload and is refused, the approval shows it, and the write hook refuses a file of another version before any write. Under a Safe rating, `sources.card` is told not to record a rated card (`CardSources.card`'s `record`), and adding a rated (or unrecorded) card is refused. `open_remote_card` takes `entry` to read one long greeting or lorebook entry whole (lists show each entry's opening with `whole: false`), and text pages are sized by their quoted length (JSON plus the boundary's escaping), not raw characters. Use the internet's explanation now names only what its tools do (card sources). Measured with o200k over each definition's name, description and JSON schema: 1,080 tokens for the seven after these changes (1,083 before; the builder's 1,126 includes the wire's function wrapper), and the index line adds 27 tokens plus its newline.
- **Sources links for cardex** (`features/cardSources/sources.ts`, `card-sources.cardex`): a `https://cardex.zip/c/<slug>` URL or a `cardex:<slug>` entry in `source`, and the `url` of the `extensions.cardex` cardex writes into its files, link to the card's page there, labelled with the slug; that extension's `origins` link each page cardex found the card on, under the site's name.
- **The fake archive** (`test/support/fakeArchive.ts`): a local HTTP server with synthetic cards only (deterministic names, sites, tags, ratings, forks, lorebooks, generated portraits) in the shape of cardex's API v1, so the real adapter runs against it unchanged (`fakeCardexAdapter(archive)`): v1's capabilities; search with `nsfw` include/exclude/only, `kind`, tags (including alternative groups), tokens (300 at least by default), sites and excluded sites, search fields, creator lists, picture hashes, date bounds, deletion and Chub flags, character-with-lorebook kind, v1's sorts (`relevance` with words, else `newest`, by default), `limit` 1–100 (24 by default, else 400), a cursor for its own query and limit only and page numbers in either mode, semantic mode by page alone and capped at 240, a total capped at 10,000 and then an estimate (or null with `unknownTotal`, as live cursor replies); optional coverless cards exercise the default cover restriction; the tags envelope; a card's detail envelope; a batch lookup that answers anything but its canonical form with a 308; pictures as paths with 512 and 64 px WebP thumbnails; downloads as a mirrored card PNG or JSON with `Content-Disposition`, and a few CHARX-original cards whose mirrored and self-contained files answer 404 `no_derived_download`; `download_modes` on every summary and detail file as cardex lists them (`omitDownloadModes` leaves them out, as a cached answer), and `refuseDownloads(slug)` for a card whose list is empty (403 on a try); misuse answers 400 `bad_request`, a cursor for another query 400 `invalid_cursor`. Errors are v1's `{error, message}`. Control routes count hits and inject failures for tests. The dev server (`dev/main.ts`, which the browser tests run) starts it on a free port unless `FAKE_CARD_SOURCE=off`; a number picks the port. `main.ts` starts it whenever `FAKE_CARD_SOURCE` is set to anything but `off`, whatever `NODE_ENV` says (`dev/fakeCardSource.ts`, imported only then), and logs "fake card source active" as a warning: the development instance (which serves a production build) and previews set it, and production's units never do.

## 12. Chats

Clamped-offset corrections (fix-lows, 2026-11-07) reach TanStack Virtual through its offset-observer callback with `isScrolling: false`, retaining the layout-effect correction before paint and the deferred correction after positioning. Real scroll events keep their normal synchronous updates; correction no longer dispatches a synthetic scroll event that asks React to `flushSync` during a lifecycle. `e2e/scrollOffset.spec.ts` runs the review's three-message development probe through Vite and rejects lifecycle console errors.

**Cold deep links and shell snapshots (perfshell1, 2026-11-13).** The URL's chat can show its linked message before the whole-library shell. `GetSplitChats` validates the owned live chat and requested live fork first. An unsplit, non-importing chat with a nonempty, non-timestamp title, only selection/replacement overrides and visible selected endpoints uses fork/endpoint metadata only. The existing `shownInSql` fork-state probes resolve selected/replaced endpoint versions, including frozen ancestor choices; ordering, recency, empty forks and the current-fork fallback match the complete shell. Other cases use the same group/title construction scoped to that physical chat, with `computeForkOutlines`: selected authors and state still determine cast-derived titles, frozen split ancestry, deletion and threads, while retained-swipe participation and human-author activity are omitted because navigation never returns them. Partial outlines are never persisted. `ListForks` retains its existing own-chat outline projection; `ThreadsOf` checks ownership and the live fork before returning immediately when the chat has no thread sets. Small reads use the reader priority described in §3.1. The saved-chat header retains its existing title placeholder until the viewed cast and split metadata are known; it does not briefly name a split group after the physical chat. `branchControlParts.ready` lets a registered part retain the branch control’s disabled loading state until it can identify the viewed line. The threads part waits for its first thread-set response and cast, preventing a thread from briefly appearing as a branch. Rename requested while this metadata is pending waits for the exact group/name, with a branch-change guard; its dialog or inline editor never starts from the loading label. The message body and composer continue loading independently. `coldMetadata.spec.ts` holds split/thread responses and checks both unresolved and resolved states at 1440/390 in light/dark, plus unavailable/foreign deep links with the catalogue held and a DOM mutation guard against private-content flashes.

`GetSplitChatsFast` and `ThreadsOfFast` are bounded preflight operations. The reader service uses them before the original, potentially long operations; `ListForks` and those fallback operations share the background allowance with full-shell work. Thus a long own-chat outline cannot take the reader held back from browsing. The production policy itself is tested with held requests named `ListForks`/`ShellMaterialize`: `GetDisplayPrefs` and `ListStImports` must finish before either long request is released. Reply reads retain bounded priority, and a running foreground/reply statement still cannot be preempted.

The internal, `OpsOf`-typed reader operations `ShellEpoch` and `ShellMaterialize` coordinate shell display snapshots. `ShellEpoch` hashes owner-scoped chat stamps, fork metadata, card head summaries/persona flags, chat pins, favourites, the pins fold and thread names/versions in a read transaction. It reads no message path, swipe catalogue or card document prose. The coordinator key also includes the current state-module registration snapshot. Worker shell memos additionally include that identity through `ActiveStateModules`; an unchanged database version cannot reuse another reducer stack’s fold. Persisted fork summaries describe core reducers only: active state modules bypass them for shell/navigation folds, and their computed folds are never persisted. Bounded live refreshes defer to the shared path while modules are active. This preserves the core cache after disposal without a database write; `shellPluginEpoch.test.ts` exercises both cold and persisted caches. Unchanged plugin snapshots still share the server-owned materialization. Summary-cache persistence, authentication, draft activity and another account do not change this token. `ShellMaterialize` builds the complete consistent display snapshot in a reader worker, including the labels that thread rows require. The public cards/library/fork APIs use the same pure projections in `shellViews.ts` as the legacy worker reads, selecting only the requested sections/page lengths and their people. The server's per-user coordinator shares pending and completed work within an epoch, drains an earlier epoch before another begins, coalesces not-yet-started epochs into one latest queued read, retries failures, and keeps the computation in the server scope when a navigation drops all its waiters. Completed snapshots retain at most 16 accounts in recency order; running/queued reads remain owned until they drain. Completion is marked and old results trimmed before waking waiters, so immediate sequential callers cannot outrun eviction. A user still has at most one running and one coalesced queued computation. It never holds a gate through persistence. The API queues a shared snapshot's fresh summaries once, using their shared-array identity; a failed store clears that claim so a later view can retry. No SQLite or path folding moved to the main thread. Raw `ShellLibrary`/`ShellCards`/`ShellForks` remain available for independent comparisons; their live variants still provide bounded refreshes.

Epoch readers memoize the metadata hash under their connection’s `PRAGMA data_version`; any visible commit clears that memo before the owner metadata is read again. The hash still excludes summary persistence and unrelated accounts, so those commits do not change the coordinator key. The legacy full-library API retains its pure projection and response by snapshot identity. The application transport (`TransportApi`) preserves the public `AppApi` definitions, request schemas and middleware. Only its full-library response codec changes: a new response is validated normally, its data graph and encoding are frozen, and repeated encoding reuses that immutable value. Decoding retains only the last fully validated response. Parsed network JSON uses canonical serialization for exact-value reuse, with non-finite numbers and signed zero taking the strict path; direct JavaScript inputs compare plain data properties. Changed types/keys/values, accessors, exotic objects and cycles take the original full decoder. Identity caches retain only deeply frozen data properties; freezing an accessor or a Date is insufficient. The wire bytes and full validation of new data are unchanged. This avoids reconstructing, encoding and decoding thousands of unchanged rows on warm tool reads. Weak keys release projections and encodings with their snapshots; decoded reuse retains one response. `immutableJson.test.ts` verifies identity reuse, byte equality, deep immutability, new-state independence, non-finite-number distinctions, changing accessors, invalid incoming/new outgoing rejection, and the transport’s API/middleware invariants.

Full summary folding decodes each shared slot's retained participation/human-author evidence once, skips empty JSON decoding, reuses a parent's structural path, and creates position/prefix maps only where positional events or thread candidates consume them. The existing covering SQL plan remains: tested reordered/record-lookup alternatives were slower. `shellMetadata.test.ts` counts one actual full-tree SQL execution across simultaneous shell views and checks exact projected bytes, bounded navigation, owner isolation, epoch invalidation, and zero discarded path-map entries/empty-evidence parses for an unthreaded cold fold. `shellMaterialization.test.ts` covers abandoned navigation, overlapping views, epoch races/coalescing, account separation and failure retry. The existing shell/split/thread semantic matrices still exercise complete versus stored summaries, and the shell-summary matrix now compares every checked transition with the shared snapshot’s exact projected bytes. `shellEpoch.test.ts` covers chat/branch rename, fork, split/unsplit, threads/labels, chat/branch pin, favourite, card edit/archive/import, workshop creation, branch/chat deletion and preset conversion. Preset conversion creates another preset and changes no cards/forks shell row, so it correctly retains the epoch.

The sidebar subscribes to its requested fork rows alongside cards, before displaying either. Waiting for card delivery first could move the row request into a later metadata epoch behind another own-chat outline; `coldShell.spec.ts` holds the cards and requires the sidebar row request before release. While the shell loads, the existing fixed sidebar area shows “Loading chats…” while cards are pending; rows that are still pending after cards arrive say “Still loading your chats…”. If cards remain pending for 15 seconds, the existing slow-loading notice offers Try again. Navigation stays anchored below the loading area. The linked body is readable; the composer retains its independent draft/cast loading state until its own setup is ready. The final first-page rows, totals and order arrive together; no provisional titles, counts or partially sorted rows are shown. Later pages retain the existing Show more order. On phones the same placeholder occupies the navigation drawer; opening/filling it does not resize the chat beneath it. `coldShell.spec.ts` holds shell responses at 1440/390 in light/dark, verifies the linked message and composer before releasing them, and checks stable chat/navigation geometry and row order. Its geometry baseline waits for the fixture's independent no-model notice, so that notice is not misattributed to the sidebar. Workshop continuity checks count completed logical replies through `ReadPath` and open the requested new/older step by URL; a phone's virtualized DOM need not contain the entire history. Its polling reuses one authenticated test session. No URL/device-layout restoration was added.

The burst performance observation follows the coordinator's post-resize/follow contract: the same fifty 100 ms samples over five seconds retain every corrected distance delivered between polls. The 120 px bound and live-update/render/gap/frame assertions are unchanged. An absolute, geometry-free marker is additionally inspected in Chromium's screencast frames after presentation; a missing marker or displacement over 120 px fails. Before the screencast starts, one screenshot forces the marker’s first presentation; otherwise Chromium can supply the previous compositor surface even after animation frames, falsely reporting a missing marker. Every subsequent supplied frame is still checked. A deliberate painted 300 px jump proves the guard detects a visible failure, including eight repeated negative-control runs. This checks the frames Chromium supplies, not a guarantee that screencast captures every physical display refresh. Image decoding runs in the test driver with the already pinned Sharp version; production UI and model requests are unchanged.

**Timeline mount/layout cost (clientperf, 2026-11-06).** The message virtualizer starts with an estimated offset near the requested destination, avoiding a throwaway mount of the window's first messages before landing at its end. The destination row is the one the positioning scrolls to, including the summary row that holds a linked message. TanStack Virtual learns the list's offset only from scroll events, so after each render and after positioning `MessageList` re-reads `scrollTop` when the two differ (suitegreen5): where the browser clamped an offset to the list's current position (a history too short to scroll, a destination at the top, a row kept in place while rows above it changed), no event fired and the rows between would otherwise never mount. Two neighbouring rows are overscanned; projected rows and key/size callbacks remain stable during scroll renders. Message action toolbars use ResizeObserver's content widths for both the toolbar and More actions button to calculate icon capacity, rather than synchronously querying and measuring each message's buttons during mount. Pins that do not fit keep their menu entries without mounting hidden toolbar controls. Toolbar capacity is retained separately from its visible pinned-action count (`messageActionFit.ts`): ResizeObserver updates the actual measurement, but React subscribes to the visible count, so a resize that still fits the same pins does not render the toolbar again. Newly pinned actions immediately use the latest capacity. `messageActionFit.test.ts` covers retained measurements and subscription cleanup; `messageToolbarFit.spec.ts` counts committed React work, shrinks and grows the toolbar, checks the overflow menu, and audits it at 1440/390 in both themes (review-perfshell3).

**Timeline performance (perfred1, 2026-11-13).** Panel navigation retains the timeline's branch callback in the compiled client. `usePanel` reads the current router through its existing committed ref: reading `router.state.location.search` directly inside the callback made React Compiler infer the changing search object as a dependency despite the explicit `[router]`. `chatPanelSwitch.spec.ts` checks committed callback identity in the production build at 1440/390 in both themes. Positional casts use a recency-ordered cache bounded by the 500-slot window; subscribed bodies retain their positions even outside that window (expanded originals), as do in-flight reads until they settle. `useDisplayed` retains/releases its position with its subscription, and `session.test.ts` checks bounded retention, identity and rereading after eviction alongside the existing generation/fork race checks.

Preset drag handles (`ui/SortableList.tsx`) have stable component inputs; their event callbacks resolve the current item, index and move/select callbacks through a committed ref. Unrelated prompt edits therefore retain the handle's tooltip/button contents without retaining an old reorder index. `presetRender.spec.ts` checks both the prompt control and handle render counts at 1440/390 in both themes; preset/editor browser coverage exercises keyboard, mouse and touch reordering.

Native upward jumps also release bottom-follow during offset correction when they are away from the end, before the browser's deferred scroll event. A clamp at the end keeps following. `scrollOffset.spec.ts` holds the native event while a chat update commits and checks the prepend anchor at both widths/themes; ordinary corrections still use `isScrolling: false` before paint.

Deep window locations also use the existing chain segments (`db/reads.ts`, `ancestorsAt`): follow chain heads down to the earliest requested depth, then seek only those depths. `Around` no longer walks all messages from the leaf to a deep link; `Newer` keeps its single ancestor lookup at a branch. The lookup includes deleted structural slots as before and retains the existing display-path handling for insertions. `ancestorProbes.test.ts` runs the production newer-window helper in a worker against 1,000 and 10,000 messages with the same twenty early branch points, counting real slot probes through a TEMP view. The probe count stays flat; `graph.test.ts` checks the returned windows and branch fallback.

**Large branch lists (clientperf, 2026-11-06).** The registered header branch control and sidebar branch footer use `ui/WindowedList.tsx`: lists above 60 branches mount measured viewport rows with three neighbours on either side, retaining the focused row while scrolling. Small lists keep their complete DOM. The menu opens at the shown branch and exposes full list size/positions to assistive technology. Collapsed sidebar branches unmount their rows and restore their scroll offset on reopening. `perf/clientScale.perf.ts` is an opt-in production-browser measurement (`CLIENT_SCALE_WORK` outside the checkout, run through a check slot): a worker seeds 500 branches with 3,000-message paths and 30 versions per model reply; CDP traces and task/script/layout CPU durations (`threadTicks`, excluding host scheduling delays) cover opening the chat and branch menu, switching branches, scrolling, opening sidebar branches and switching workbench tabs. It checks bounded branch DOM, the selected branch's visibility, browser errors and a 300 ms main-thread CPU budget per action. `CLIENT_SCALE_CPU_PROFILE=1` adds CPU samples for diagnostic runs; timing runs omit that overhead. Task duration includes tasks below the long-task threshold; accessibility selectors are resolved before timing.

Cast-tab opening (casttabscroll, 2026-11-05): `CardEditor` scrolls its field tabs into view only for an explicit `reveal` request, including Show the whole card. An effect replay does not turn an ordinary opening into a reveal, so the cast card opens at scroll position zero. Search Go to retains its separate field selection and scrolling. `e2e/castTabScroll.spec.ts` covers Alice/Sam tab opening and search navigation at 1440 dark; it also accepts `CAST_TAB_CLIENT_DIST` for a development build that exercises StrictMode effect replay.

**Split chats (splitchat, 2026-11-05).** A split is per-fork chat presentation state, `forks.split_chat = 1`, written only through the owner-scoped `SetSplitChat` worker operation. It stays with a binned fork on restore and disappears when the fork is purged; it is not an account setting. `splitChats.ts` assigns each fork to its nearest marked ancestor (or its original chat), so deeper split groups are excluded from their parent's branch list. `shellReads.ts` derives each group's current fork, title, preview, branch count and pins. Shell rows carry their group id in `chat.id` and their unchanged physical chat in `sourceChatId`; navigation always uses the physical chat and explicit fork. A split group's global pin is its root fork's existing pin, while the original chat keeps `chat_pins`. Its title is its root's name, otherwise the original title and split time. `GetSplitChats` supplies the current group, its branches and parent/child links without exposing other accounts' groups. The authenticated split RPC group has its own handler layer to stay below TypeScript's inference-depth limit.

The registered `split-chats` sidebar part follows the registered branch list, reuses the ordinary `ForkRow`, and keeps its size/collapse preference per account/device. Since splitsection (2026-11-05) it is the “Related chats (N)” section with an `AboutHint` “?”: under the caption “This chat was split from”, the source group's ordinary chat row, and under “Split off from this chat”, one row per child group, each a labelled `group`. `ForkRow`'s optional `relation` line (`data-row-relation`) sits under the preview: `splitRelation` formats `SplitChatLink.split` (the split group's root fork's summary split point, from `GetSplitChats`; null for an original group) as “Shares messages #1–N · split <moment>”. The parent row uses the viewed group's split, a child row its own. The section is a list whenever it has a relation, so it collapses and resizes as any foot list; its open height is a max-height, so a list shorter than its size leaves the rest to Chats. Split navigation selects the target's ordinary Chats row; `useSplitReveal` observes its rendering, size and scroll viewport and scrolls only when the full row is clipped, following later measurements until the user moves the list; the split section retains its height and collapse preference. `chat.split` registers the menu action for non-root branches; it opens `SplitChatDialog` (splitconfirm, 2026-11-05), as does the selected branch row's lower-right Split off button in the left panel (foot list and a chat's branch list; never on the group's root). The dialog explains the split and takes the new chat's title, prefilled with the branch's own name, else the current group's title. Confirming sends the title and the observed branch name to `SetSplitChat`; one writer transaction checks the name and marker, updates the title and first-slot version, and writes the marker. Titles allow 200 characters, matching the parent chat title used for unnamed branches. Undo uses the same transaction to remove the marker and restore the previous name, refusing later renames or changed markers. A successful split write publishes Reload to the chat’s subscribers. Naming forms lock submission before draft persistence so two same-turn submits cannot queue two confirmations. Targeted title, rollback and cross-tab regressions are in `splitChatTitle.test.ts` and `e2e/splitConfirm.spec.ts` (review-splitconfirm, 2026-11-05). `chat.split-divider` registers after-message timeline links through `messageStream`, including splits before the first message; they read “This chat was split from “<title>” here” and “Split off from this chat here · <title>”. The existing graph stepper remains unchanged: changing the shown fork naturally changes its derived sidebar group. Header branch lists are filtered to that group, and renaming a split group names its root fork. Grouped chats' Delete menu entry registers `DeleteChatGroupDialog`, showing the branch count and passing its exact fork set to `DeleteChatGroup`. One writer transaction rechecks the group, runs the existing per-fork bin marking against forks outside that group, and records every member in one branch-kind bin item's `origin.forkIds`. Shared history used by outside groups, live or binned, stays in place. Restore reuses `restoreInFork` for each member, repairs the current branch if the last group had gone, and re-derives parent links through surviving ancestor forks. Purge uses the existing branch-bin path and retains surviving groups' shared messages. The physical chat remains as the shared container even if it temporarily has no live groups. The handler stops only generations in the deleted forks and leaves other groups' subscriptions open. The legacy physical `DeleteChat` operation also deletes only the original group when split markers exist; it cannot erase the other groups or close their subscriptions. Ordinary chats without split markers retain their existing immediate delete. Tests: `splitChats.test.ts`, isolation probes, `e2e/splitChats.spec.ts` and the focused split-chat cases in `layoutAudit.spec.ts`; `e2e/support/splitChats.ts` seeds all review scenarios through the app's operations.

**A chat's own picture (families1, 2026-11-15; DESIGN §2.1 [P]).** Optional, in place of the cast's faces. It belongs to the chat as the lists show it, like its name: every branch of the chat shows it, and a chat split off has its own (none until chosen). The writer operation `SetChatPicture { userId, chatId, mediaId | null }` (`db/shellWrites.ts`, one transaction) takes a physical chat id or a split group's root fork id, as `SetChatPin` does, and writes `chats.cover_media_id` or `forks.cover_media_id` (§3.7). The media must be an image (PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP) the user already holds a `media_refs` row for; anything else is NotFound `media`, so another account's media id tells nothing. It returns the chat and the previous media id, for Undo. The RPC is `SetChatPicture` in `SplitChatApi` (`@rp/shared/splitChat.ts`, handler `api/splitChats.ts`), which publishes the chat's hub event; it is excluded from the agent's exposures. The picture is stored through the existing media storage by the existing `POST /chat/image` upload and served by the ownership-checked `/library/media` route: nothing is fetched from a remote URL, at upload or at view time. The saved-media prune counts `forks.cover_media_id` as a reference. Reads: `Chat.pictureMediaId` (`rows.ts`), `ShellFork.chat.picture` and `SplitChatLink.picture` (`shellReads.ts`). Client: the registered `settings.picture` part of This chat (`features/chat/ChatPicture.tsx`: Choose a picture / Change / Remove, each with its explanation, and a toast with Undo), with the default crop and no cutout chooser; `session.setPicture`; `useChatPicture` (`splitChats.ts`). Where it shows: the chats list's rows and group tiles (`ShellBrowser.tsx`, in the first portrait slot of the same reserved cast box, `data-portrait-slot`, so it keeps a 2:3 cutout and the row keeps its layout and height when a picture is set, removed or loaded; a chat without characters also reserves one slot), the chat header (a button opening This chat; the narrow header shows none), the tab portrait and the chat list. Chat export leaves it out and says so (§13b). Tests: server `test/chatPicture.test.ts`, the `SetChatPicture` probe in `test/isolation.test.ts`; browser `e2e/chatPicture.spec.ts` (1440 and 390, light and dark, with layout audits).

**Picture lifecycle review (review-families1, 2026-11-15).** `SetChatPicture` verifies a live navigation group as well as ownership: a physical chat retained for a split group's shared history does not make its binned original group editable. A binned group keeps its picture for Restore; purging a branch clears its picture pointer, and purging the physical chat removes its pointers. Replacing or removing a picture does not delete the upload. Existing `media_refs` are permanent account ownership grants, one per account/file, rather than per-use reference counts; uploads, old avatars and attachments already share that retention policy. Undo and other uses keep working without creating extra ownership rows. The hourly sweep removes unrecorded files after its grace period, not recorded uploads merely because no chat shows them. Accepted-upload garbage collection is not implemented.

A picture is explicit shared chat metadata, like the chat's name: choosing it affects every branch in that navigation group. Branch-local message, cast and state actions still change only that branch; creating a fork, merging together or with separate history, and editing a split group do not overwrite another group's picture. A newly split group starts without one; rejoining hides its own picture and splitting it again restores that choice. Pictures never enter provider inputs. There is no native chat archive/import format: the chat exporter offers SillyTavern JSONL and plain text (and a ZIP of those files for every branch), none of which embeds media. Both export notices explicitly include the chat's own picture among the losses.

`POST /chat/image` now decodes pixels before recording an upload, through `Formats.validateImage` / `ValidateImage` in the bounded format-worker pool. The route retains its 16 MiB limit and signature-based PNG/JPEG/GIF/WebP allowlist (SVG is refused). Corrupt/truncated files are refused, and decoding is capped at 40 million pixels over all animation frames and 20 seconds. A separate transferred copy preserves the original bytes for content addressing/storage; animated originals remain animated and use the existing thumbnail fallback. Tests cover corrupt headers, oversized/wrong-type/SVG input, animated original bytes, deduplication, ownership, the bin/Restore/purge, split groups and both merge modes.

Branch rows use the chat row's corners (splitconfirm, 2026-11-05): the pin at the upper right and, on the selected non-root branch only, Split off at the lower right; the title line ends before that column. Left-panel branch rows (branchrows, 2026-11-05) show only their stored split-relative additions: a leading +, two small full portraits and the shared overflow tile tucked behind the second. Hover/focus lists every added name, including departed participants; no removal row or original-line portraits. Only the selected row has a title-sized pencil opening shared compact `InlineRename` (Enter/Escape and confirm/cancel) through `NameFork`/`SetForkName`; the editor preserves the title's height. The existing registered shell surface remains the replacement point. Home's Group chats and the Chats tab's filter both classify chats by the current branch's cast, requiring two or more characters. Browser coverage: `branchRows.spec.ts`; server classification coverage: `shellForks.test.ts`.

**Merging another chat into this one** (chatmerge, 2026-11-05; spec/CHAT-MERGE.md, owner decisions DESIGN §3.3). A merge is a **join message** J in the destination fork: an ordinary slot below the chosen message M (default the newest), appended when M is the tip and otherwise inserted below M through the MESSAGE-INSERT machinery (`writeInsert`), so a fork made before M never shows it and delete, hide, restore and branch work as for any message. J's single version has origin `merge` (baseline `versions.origin` CHECK), writer `human`, no speaker, and holds the transcript the model reads of the source. The second parent is not a `slot_parents` row (LCM refuses to summarize across those): `chat_merges` (one row per J, `slot_id` UNIQUE, cascade with the chat) records the source chat and fork, the source tip it was pinned at, the merge base, the destination's parallel-span start, title, optional framing line, the cast union (`cast_json`, each `{entity, name, from: both|source|destination}`) and counts; `chat_merge_messages` (WITHOUT ROWID, `(merge_id, ordinal)`) is the frozen copy of every merged source message and summary with how the model reads it (`verbatim`, `summarized`, `left_out`). Source references are soft text, so deleting or purging the source never blocks or changes the destination; triggers keep a merge in its own chat and both tables frozen after insert. **Plan** (`db/merges.ts`, `mergePlan`, shared by the preview and the write): the destination's display pieces to M, the source's display path, their shared prefix (same chat only, `sharedPrefix` over `PathPieces`), and an earlier merge of the same source fork on the destination's path up to M, whose pinned tip becomes the new base, so re-merging brings only what's new. Refusals (`MergeRefused`): the same branch, an empty destination, nothing new, nothing after the shared part. The parallel span starts after that earlier join, else after the shared prefix, else at the request's `start` (unrelated chats), else at M; the budget is the span's tokens clamped to 4,000–50,000. The newest source messages go in as written (`Name: text`) while they fit; the older part comes from the source's own summary layer entries entirely after the base; what neither covers is left out with a note line, or included as written when `includeLeftOut`. The source's own joins are skipped with a note. The cast union is both casts at the merge point (`castAt`); `added` are the source's members the destination lacks. A covering destination summary over M is reported (`rewrites`): it goes stale by the insert rule and is written again with the next reply (§16). The preview's sha256 `digest` covers every input; `MergeChat` recomputes the plan and fails `MergeChanged` with the new preview when it differs. **Write** (`MergeChat`, one writer transaction, registered command `chat.merge`): J, the fork's tip or insert override, `cast_json` of the chat, `participant.join` events at J for the added members (version null), the merge row and its message rows in batches of 200. The API publishes Slot (with position), Chat, State and Lcm. Reads: `PreviewChatMerge`, `GetMerge` (with `sourceLive`), `MergeMessages` (paged ≤ 200), all owner-scoped (`isolation.test.ts`). **Assembly**: `assemblySources` adds each history entry's `merge` (`HistoryMerge`: id, title, framing, start, the source side's cast names), pinned with the entry. The `merge-layout` stage (`assembler/merges.ts`, registered after `roles` and kept separate from the other stages) resolves `merge.layout` (an open id, state key folded to `ChatState.mergeLayout`) against the assembler's own `mergeLayouts` registry (`parallel` "Parallel span", default; `join` "Block at the join"); an id nothing registers records `merge_layout_missing` and uses parallel. It turns each join into two system messages without a name: the section (heading from the merge's framing, else the preset's `utility_prompts.merge_section_prompt`, else the layout's, else `MERGE_SECTION_DEFAULT`, with `{{title}}` and `{{cast}}` filled, then J's text) placed where the layout says (parallel: before the first message read at or after the span's start, taking that entry's slot and depth so the history start and cut treat it as part of the stretch; before the first message read when the start was summarized or cut; at J for an empty span), and the join marker at J (`merge_join_prompt`, else `MERGE_JOIN_DEFAULT`; source kind `merge/join`). Both run through the prompt regex scripts at their new places. `chatLine` sends a `system` projected entry with role system. **LCM**: J is ordinary history, so the destination summarizes it like any message; the `merge-sections` transform, registered after `summary-request`, adds to a summary request whose material holds a `merge/join` piece the instruction to write one section per line, this chat's first, in the instruction piece, the request message and the job's frozen tail. **Settings**: `GetCast` carries `mergeLayout` and `mergeLayouts` (the worker registry's labels, `MergeLayouts` reader op); `ChangeCast` `MergeLayout` writes `merge.layout`. **UI**: the ⋯ menu's "Merge another chat…" (`chat.merge` chat command) and the `message.merge` action ("Merge a chat here…", place group) open `MergeChatDialog.tsx`: a searchable chat list as the sidebar lists chats (`GetShellForks`' `chats` section, so a branch made its own chat is listed and found under its own name, and so is the chat it came from; this chat's other branches, never the branch shown), a branch select when the chat has several (its own branches only, from `GetSplitChats`' `forkIds`), "Merge after" (the loaded messages, default the newest), "It ran alongside" for unrelated chats, what comes in ("Shares #1–N · merges M messages from #N+1", the verbatim/summarized/left-out split and tokens), the left-out notice with "Include them as written" and "Summarize there first" (opens the source's Summaries tab; nothing is sent), the rewrite note, the cast union (added members marked +), the title and framing line ("?" help; an untouched framing is sent as null so the preset's applies), and "What the model reads" as the chat's layout sends it. The `timeline.merges` transform renders J as `MergedChatRow.tsx`: "Merged “title” · N messages", collapsible, the frozen messages paged by 50, "Open “title”" while the source lives. Message actions declare `onMerges` to be offered on J: branch, insert above/below, hide, copy link, delete; editing and versions are not. This chat's settings show "Merged chats" (`MergeLayoutSetting`) once a merge is loaded or a layout chosen; the preset editor's utility prompts gain the two merge templates with their defaults. Tests: `chatMerge.test.ts` (writer/reader: unrelated and same-chat merges, re-merge, mid-history insert and earlier forks, deleting the join or the source, budget and left-out, stale digest), `chatMergeAssembly.test.ts` (request snapshots for both layouts, empty span, start not read, unknown layout, preset templates, causal order, per-line summary sections), `chatMergeLcm.test.ts` (the next reply through the real reader in both layouts, and a real summary job over J through the mock provider), `chatMergeScale.test.ts` (slow: a 3,000-message chat with 20–50 versions on every third message, 200 branches, a 1,000-message source branch and an unrelated 3,000-message chat; 7,200 slots, 41,145 versions; medians on the loaded dev host: preview 133 ms and write 153 ms for the branch, preview 75 ms (160 ms with everything included) and a mid-history write 108 ms for the unrelated chat, the next reply's assembly at a 200k-token window 517 ms after one merge and 986 ms after two, a page of 200 merged messages 5 ms), `e2e/chatMerge.spec.ts` (both entry points, the dialog, the timeline row, the setting, refusals; 1440/390 light and dark), `LAYOUT_AUDIT_CHATMERGE_ONLY=1`. **Limits**: the section's budget follows the destination's span, not the model's window: a section larger than the history budget is cut together with everything before it (the history keeps the newest messages that fit). J takes a display position like any message, so messages after a mid-history merge number one higher (the default merge after the newest renumbers nothing); the source's notes are offered since merge2 ("Notes brought by a merge" below); per-character presence filtering is Phase 4.

**Merges kept separate by origin** (merge2, 2026-11-14; DESIGN "Merging another chat into this one" [D] 2026-11-08: "the timelines remain separate for the characters from chat A and chat B"; audit item 056). In a chat with one shared context, the merge dialog offers the per-join choice the thread joins use ("How the characters see it", now for every merge): **Everyone reads both chats** (together, the default, as before) or **Each character keeps its own chat's past** (`MergeRequest.timelines: "separate"`, stored as `chat_merges.timelines`). With separate contexts the choice is not offered and a line says each character reads what it was present for (C6, unchanged). What a merge kept separate means, per character, in that shared-context chat: a character in this chat's cast at the merge point (`cast_json` `from` "destination" or "both") reads this chat exactly as before (the destination part of the stretch does not apply to it), and of the join only the merged rows it was present for (`knowers_json`; a character in both chats reads both); a character the merge brings in (`from` "source") reads the merged rows it was present for in its own chat and, of this chat before the join, only messages whose recorded presence names it (none, unless it was here once); everyone reads what follows the join; a narrator and the user's own characters read everything, the merge as the labelled section (today's layout, unchanged: CHARACTER-CONTEXT §9.3 / THREADS §16.2 stay Open, Q13/Q14); a character that joins later reads this chat whole and none of the merged rows. **Mechanism**: the existing stretch views (§3.8 "What each speaker reads at a join", "Summaries across splits and joins"). An ordinary merge of another chat records `stretch_before_slot_id` NULL, so its stretch is this chat's whole display path through J (`mergePlan`: a branch of the same chat keeps the slot before its parallel span; another chat's characters lived none of this chat, whatever span the layout reads beside it). `threadStretches(sql, fork, leaf, viewers)` takes the viewer's identities: an ordinary join (`split_id` NULL) contributes only its own slot for a viewer among its destination side, its whole interval for anyone else; a thread join's interval applies to all, as before. The viewer is passed wherever a stretch is resolved for a character: `knowsSql` (summary planning, `firstUnknownPosition`, layers), `readKnowers`, `KnowersOf` (the agent's tools), and assembly's `stretches(leaf, viewers)` source from the `knowledge` stage (a reply's speaker and its aliases; a stretch view's summary job's audience). The pinned `SourcePins.stretches` are the viewer's filtered ranges, the same shape as before, so a rebuild replays them; requests with no separate ordinary join are unchanged. Summaries follow from the stretch views: a character that missed something gets its own (Kai's start at this chat's first message, Mira's at the join), shared summaries stay the narrator's and carry both lines (`merge-sections`), and nothing of one chat enters the other side's summaries. The preview's `views` add `from` (`here`, `merged`, `both`) and the dialog's "What the model reads" names a merged-in character's part of this chat ("[Of this chat before the merge, only what Kai was there for]"). Assembler version **75** (an ordinary separate merge, reachable through the API before, now reads this way). No baseline change. Tests: `mergeOrigin.test.ts` (requests captured per character after the merge: the destination's characters' history byte-identical to before, Wren away across the join in one shared context included; Kai and Lio each read only the rows they were present for and nothing of the Ledger; an earlier merge in the destination and a merge inside the source; own-turn notes stay with their card; a branch merged together beside it is unaffected; a source thread fork merged into another chat and another chat merged into a thread, then a thread join on top; a character in both chats and one who left the destination), `mergeOriginSummaries.test.ts` (summary jobs pending in both chats at the merge; each view's summary requests and stored summaries free of the other chat; replies read their own layers), slow `mergeOriginScale.test.ts` (both chats 3,000 messages, 20–50 versions on every third, 300 branches each; preview, write and each side's request timed beside a together merge), `e2e/chatMerge.spec.ts` (the choice, "For" per character, at 1440 light and 390 dark).

**Notes brought by a merge** (merge2, 2026-11-14; spec/CHAT-MERGE.md §6, audit item 011a). Merging another chat (not a branch or thread of this one) previews the notes it can bring (`ChatMergePreview.notes`, `MergeNote`), listed by `mergeNotes` (`db/mergeNotes.ts`, shared by the preview and the write) from the source's events through its merged end and this fork's through M, with the same switch rules as assembly (`noteSwitches`, a card's `on_by_default` where nothing switched it): the source chat's own notes on there (an agent-written one only where its reply is shown, `agentNotes.ts`), at the revision the source branch has bound (`noteRevisions`), and the source cast's card notes on there but off here, a moved passage and what's left of its field (one `move_group` of a card) as one entry with both entities. Each entry says who reads it (`when`: always, own_turn, turn or not_muted with the cards' `names`, or moved), a 160-character excerpt and, for a chat note whose `replaces` target this fork already has, the refusal text (`replacementConflict` on the destination fork). The list is part of the digest. `MergeRequest.notes` names the ticked entries; `MergeChat` refuses an id not in the recomputed list or one with a conflict, then, in the same transaction after the cast's joins, copies each ticked chat note as a new note of this chat (`insertCopiedNote`: entity, first revision, ref, the document checked like any note; owner this chat, a linked note's text resolved into its own content, and `link`, `covers`, `source_slot_id` and `module_id` dropped) and writes `note.activate` at J for it, or for a ticked card note (its group partner switched with it by `insertStateEvent`). A new chat note's head shows in every branch of this chat but is on only from J on this fork (chat notes start off), so other branches read nothing new; the source keeps its own notes. Thread joins and branches of this chat list none. The dialog shows "Notes to bring" after the cast, each a checkbox (unticked by default, disabled with the conflict as its explanation), its title (a card's note: "‹title› · ‹card›'s note"), who reads it ("Every reply reads it, this chat's characters' too.", "Only replies by Kai read it.", "Only Kai's own replies read the moved passage; every reply reads the rest of the field.") and the excerpt; the hover says what ticking does. No assembler or baseline change. Tests: `mergeNotes.test.ts` (the list and its order, a conflict and an unlisted id refused, ticked notes reaching the exact requests from J by condition, unticked ones not, the moved pair together, the copies owned here, the source's unchanged, a branch from before the merge unchanged; none for a branch of this chat), `e2e/chatMerge.spec.ts` (ticking one of two notes at 1440 dark and 390 light), `LAYOUT_AUDIT_CHATMERGE_ONLY=1` (a long note ticked, separate chosen).

**Separate-origin presence and brought-note revisions.** Ordinary separate-origin merges distinguish a source character merely added to the destination cast from one recorded present for an authored message on its causal display path. The former keeps only its source history; cast changes alone are not participation. Evidence includes retained unselected swipes and previous card identities, matching existing presence rules. The stretch resolver also treats an older ordinary cross-chat merge's saved layout-span predecessor as no common prefix, including after source deletion; same-chat and thread boundaries retain their existing meaning. Assembler version **77** covers the older API-created separate-merge correction and the projected-piece script correction below. Narrator layout and shared-past reset defaults are unchanged (Q13/Q14 remain Open).

Note previews resolve both branches' effective revisions before calculating defaults, groups and readers; a linked note's excerpt uses its linked text, and own-turn placement is recognized even without an explicit condition. The digest includes complete copied documents and card-note revisions/documents/resolved linked content, so edits beyond an excerpt refuse an outdated preview. Brought card notes bind the source revisions at J before activation, retaining the displayed text and audience independently on this branch. Card replacement claims are checked against the destination with their implicit owner filled in, including claims reserved before that card joins.

The dialog's source, position, parallel span, history choice, note ticks and reader are retained in its scoped `mergeSetup` URL value. The command registry's optional `dialogInUrl` restores the merge command through scoped `chatAction`; the message merge uses the existing URL-dialog host. Closing clears the setup. All content remains React text.

Projected script results use a piece-specific cache key, falling back to the original version's result before projection. A merge can expand one stored version into its source rows/section and join marker; those pieces must not overwrite each other's prompt-script text. Lore scans and lore-decision excerpts now read the correct piece, and HTML depth and final composition reuse the same piece's transformed result. This corrects missing lore activation and HTML-depth stripping on joins without changing narrator framing or the existing scan-depth counting. `mergeLore.test.ts` covers both layouts, HTML depth and a shallow scan; `mergeReview.test.ts` proves each separate-origin character triggers only its known side's lore. The layout audit waits for the newly merged row by title and clicks it once; an unqualified last-row selector could click the previous merge before the new row arrived. Synthetic regressions are in `mergeReview.test.ts`; merge fixture database reads now use the fixture worker. No database baseline change.

Merge review regressions (2026-11-05): common-prefix detection checks each fork’s effective version and visibility before excluding shared slots, so a changed swipe or amend copy starts the source’s divergent stretch. Source and destination summary reads are explicitly scoped to their requested forks. Summary ranges are converted from one-based numbers to zero-based merge positions before coverage and boundary checks; rewrite notices retain the summary’s original numbers. The preview digest hashes the complete preview and frozen message rows, including full text and speaker names. Nested joins are recognized by their first version’s origin even after transcript edits. Tests also exercise positional cast union, fork-local delete/restore, history-edit undo, causal regeneration, hidden/deleted joins with historical replay, and byte-identical cache checkpoints for both layouts.

**Overflow tile visibility** (faceplus4, 2026-11-04; DESIGN §10.1). Shared `PortraitOverflow` uses `border-border` around its raised surface, preserving a visible tile edge when selected or hovered rows share that surface. The same edge applies in the header and chat-list avatar stack, in both themes.

**Chat portrait overflow** (faceplus3, 2026-11-04). The header, registered sidebar browser's `ForkRow`, and chat-list `AvatarStack` share `ui/Avatar.tsx` `PortraitOverflow`: a +N tile with the adjacent portraits' radius and muted semantic tokens. Sidebar rows always show up to two fully visible portraits; the count tile sits behind the second, exposing its complete text plus a 4 px trailing inset. The sliver grows with the count. Below 17.8125rem content width, multi-character rows put two 24 × 36 px portraits above the text; otherwise portraits are 32 × 48 px. Only the count tile overlaps. Chat lists retain three portraits followed by a full tile; the header retains its existing four-portrait stack and count. Groups retain every name in their hover/focus tooltip and accessible label. This supersedes faceplus2’s compact slot rule. `e2e/faceplus.spec.ts` covers casts of 1, 2, 3 and 6, both themes, phone, minimum/default desktop sidebar and 1440 px, names, crops, measured visible portrait/count widths and scoped layout audits.


**New chat from the character list** (charnewchat, 2026-11-04). The replaceable `characters.new-chat` contribution in `sidebar.character-chat-actions` renders “New chat with <name>” above the scoped character’s chats, before pins. `NewCharacterChat` opens `/cards/$entityId/chat`, the existing pending first-message flow, with that character chosen; selecting it closes the phone menu. The action is limited to a resolved single-character scope, including lists containing group chats; All chats and chat/group branch scopes omit it. The right panel is unchanged. `e2e/charNewChat.spec.ts` covers the first sent message, scope exclusions and left-column geometry at phone/desktop widths in both themes.

Card identity overflow (identityoverlap, 2026-11-04): `CardNameHeader` reserves the combined minimum width of the name/version pencils and their gap. Its identity row wraps when necessary, retaining normal-width placement and whole rename controls; text still truncates. While renaming, the group reserves room for Save and Cancel as well. `cardHeaderRows.spec.ts` retains the normal-width portrait-height checks and permits wrapping only in its minimum-panel case, where both pencils and Cancel are exercised. The focused header audit supports `LAYOUT_AUDIT_HEADER_MINIMUM=1` to resize the desktop panel to its minimum before sampling character/persona headers.

**Cast navigation spacing** (castgap, 2026-11-04; DESIGN §10.1). `ChatSidePanel` gives the subject strip 4px top padding, matching `SubjectTabs`’ existing 4px bottom padding. Previously the host added 16px above it. The tools row and shared subject component are unchanged. `LAYOUT_AUDIT_CASTGAP_ONLY=1` audits both navigation rows across all tools and character tabs, measures the 12px reduction against the previous spacing, and captures before/after crops.

**Side-panel card header spacing** (headerspacing and personabtn, 2026-11-04; DESIGN §2.2). `CardTokensRow` with `panel` orders Persona above the chats/token line. The text stack stretches beside the portrait: name and nickname remain at the top, the 16 px counts line ends at the portrait bottom, and a flexible Persona row centres its 28 px control between nickname and counts. All row gaps remain at least 4 px; if the identity wraps beyond the portrait height, the stack grows rather than overlapping. The Persona row uses no negative offset. In the panel (`data-persona-align-start`), the off control has no border or background, even on hover; its icon stroke aligns with the text and changes colour on hover, with a pointer cursor. On uses the existing accent-tinted icon-and-label badge with 8 px padding on each side; its box aligns with the text. The on-state inset focus ring surrounds the badge. The bare off-state ring uses a 28 × 28 px pseudo-element centred on the translated icon (8 px before the button edge), while the button retains its hit area and the hidden label remains invisible outside it (focusring, 2026-11-04). Hover/focus explanations remain. Button sizes stay 32/88 × 28 px. Full-editor geometry and the separate group header remain unchanged. `cardHeaderRows.spec.ts` measures both visible edges, portrait/counts bottoms and Persona centring, including the minimum-width fallback.


**Account default persona** (personadefault, owner 2026-11-03; DESIGN §2.2). The optional `GenerationDefaults.persona` field uses the existing `GetGenerationDefaults`, `SetGenerationDefaults` and partial `ChangeGenerationDefaults` RPCs. The writer stores it in user-scoped `settings` as `chat.persona` in the same synchronous transaction as the setting change; non-null selections must be owned, live, unarchived cards tagged `persona`. The reader returns null for an absent, deleted, archived or no-longer-persona card. Other account defaults are preserved by a partial change. No migration is needed.

Single and group pending pages read the account default with their cards before constructing `PendingChat`. It preselects that live persona, or none; there is no first-persona fallback or `rp.lastPersona` storage. Changes on a pending page affect only that pending chat. The existing StartChat selection is stored as chat state on the first send; later account-default changes never alter it. The pending Playing as control adds “(default)” when its selection matches the current account default.

`characters/defaultPersona.tsx` registers replaceable card contributions for the Default badge, picker persona menus, and persona cards' overflow actions through `cardContributions` (`persona-badge`, `persona-menu`, `badge`, `actions`). The library's existing card menu and the chat's `chatCardActions` slot also host that action. The home/left-panel/Add characters grids, and persona/speaker pickers offer the same setting beside each persona; the library rows/tiles and card page/editor menus use their existing action hosts. The menu reads “Set as default persona” or “Clear default persona”, with the owner-specified explanations; badges use the muted shared Badge, sharing the existing Persona row in card headers and a reserved-height metadata row in library lists so setting the default does not move its controls. The persona picker uses 60 px virtual rows to fit its 48 px portraits with padding. `defaultPersona.test.ts` covers persistence, partial updates, unavailable cards, isolation and unchanged existing chat state; `e2e/defaultPersona.spec.ts` covers the user flow at desktop/phone widths and unavailable defaults.
**Chat row corners (2026-11-03).** The shared `ForkRow` in `ShellBrowser.tsx` puts the pin at the upper right and the branch count (when present) at the lower right, aligned with the title and date in horizontal rows. In the narrow portrait-above-text layout (chatrows, 2026-11-04), the pin stays at the row’s upper right, beside the portraits, with branches immediately to its left when present. The top controls have an 8px gap; the pin keeps its position without branches. Title, preview and date use the full text width with a 4px gap between text rows, including when no preview exists; the date has no automatic top margin or reserved branch-control height. Wide rows retain their corner alignment: one column takes the wider button’s width; the title, preview and date use the remaining space. Rows without a count retain the upper-right pin. Button hit areas, tooltips, hover and focus styles are unchanged. This applies to home pins, all and card-scoped chat lists, and shared branch rows. `chatRowClamp.spec.ts` checks corner placement at 390/1440; `chatRowStacked.spec.ts` measures all preview/branch combinations at the minimum desktop sidebar and a 280px phone viewport in both themes, with an opt-in layout audit; `LAYOUT_AUDIT_CHAT_ROWS_ONLY=1` limits the layout audit to these surfaces.

**Responsive chat rows** (chatrownarrow, 2026-11-03; DESIGN §10.1). Every shared `ForkRow` is a named `fork-row` inline-size container. `styles.css` derives the rem queries from Avatar’s md (2 × 3rem) and sm (1.5 × 2.25rem) sizes, the 0.125rem portrait gap, open-control padding, text/action gaps and measured corner-control width. Below 16.5625rem of row content width, two portraits overlap at a one-third-width offset, with the first on top and a 2px surface/raised-surface ring. Below 15.104167rem the pair uses sm portraits on its own line above the full-width text; a single portrait needs that layout only below 14.4375rem. The queries exclude the row’s padding/border; the arithmetic is beside them. At most two cast portraits remain visible. Narrow rows place actions beside the portraits at the top; the date uses its own full-width row directly after the other text. Titles and previews keep their two-line clamps, titles keep normal word boundaries, and dates remain at the bottom. `e2e/chatRowNarrow.spec.ts` measures one-, two- and three-character synthetic chats at the 220px minimum, 320px middle and 360px wide panel sizes and in the 390px phone drawer, including title word ranges, text width, portrait geometry, corners and all filter names. Its opt-in `LAYOUT_AUDIT=1` runs the shared geometry detector on those rows and controls; screenshots and measurements go to `CHATROWNARROW_WORK` when supplied.

**Chats with a card and sidebar split** (chatswith, 2026-11-03; owner decisions 2026-11-02, DESIGN §2.1 and §10.1). `features/characters/chatLinks.tsx` registers `characters.chats-link` in the card surface's `chats` placement and the new `chat.cast-member-navigation` slot, immediately after Write as in `CastTab`'s member menu. Characters show **Chats with <name>**; the card played by the user shows **Chats as <name>**, based on this chat's cast rather than its persona-folder tag. The persona row reuses the same member menu beside Switch for navigation and card actions. The shared `CardTokensRow` joins the `chats` surface to the final muted token line, directly below the Persona toggle; the card page retains its existing chats-link placement above its Persona toggle. **N chats / 1 chat** reads a zero-row `GetShellForks` card section: its total deduplicates chats across branches. The shell read's `CardUsage.chats` (the home and left-panel tiles, the library rows, Most chats) counts the same way, one per chat however many of its branches the card is in (stgapfix1, 2026-11-16; it used to count every branch of a character). It is absent for a card with no recorded chat participation.

Both entry points set the existing `character` scope, clear `forks`, `side` and `sideQ`, and retain the centre's chat and explicit `fork`. The existing All chats breadcrumb clears the scope. Scope changes push history, so Back/Forward and reload restore the list. A hidden desktop sidebar is revealed; phones use the existing navigation drawer, closing the card panel/workspace before showing it. Header links retain a real URL for browser link actions. Hover/focus text on both entries is “Shows every chat with <name> in the left column.”

The upper chat rows already marked the current chat independently of its selected branch, and the bottom branch rows already followed explicit `fork` before the server's current branch.
