Those rules remain; pinned rows now mark the viewed fork too. The lower viewer no longer disappears for a single-branch chat, and still reads its own unfiltered current-chat branch list when the upper list's search excludes the chat. When the upper list is itself this chat's branches, it remains the branch viewer rather than duplicating it below; the Characters grid has no lower chat viewer. A branch's “opens here” badge still indicates the server's default branch, independently of the viewed-branch selection.

`OpenChatBranches` and `SplitChatSection` remain registered through `sidebarFoot`. `SidebarFeet` (`useBranchHeight.tsx`) provides responsive heights but reserves no extra space: the main `[data-shell-list]` remains `flex-1`, and each footer contribution occupies only its actual section. A list defaults to two standard rows (221 px for branches; 356 px for Related chats, whose two groups have captions and whose rows a relation line), or the existing device preference (`rp.branchHeight.<user id>` / `rp.splitHeight.<user id>`). An absent split section occupies zero height; an open Related chats section is never taller than its rows (splitsection). The three first Chats rows, including intervening list headings, are measured to determine the available footer space. On shorter columns the preferred heights shrink, stopping at minimum expanded heights of 147/231 px that accommodate a complete row, including wrapped branch dates and stacked chat portraits. If those minima still do not fit, Split off collapses to its header first, then Branches. A ResizeObserver tracks column changes; a MutationObserver updates the main-row measurements and list/header/absent section classification. Responsive shrinking/collapse and restoration never write saved sizes or manual collapse preferences (`rp.openChatBranches` / `rp.splitChatsOpen`). Explicit dragging, arrow keys (10 px; Shift 40 px), Home/End and reset retain the ordinary `ui/ResizeHandle` behavior. Split-off lists keep their chevrons and the ordinary Chats-row portraits, insets and timestamps. Branch rows retain master's d67a8cf8 rename layout: the pencil follows the name rather than filling the line to its end. `test/sidebarFootLayout.test.ts` covers two-row defaults, shrink-before-collapse, full-row minima, parent-only/absent space recovery and preserved preferences. `e2e/splitChats.spec.ts` navigates through parent-only and no-split chats and checks the main list's available height. The focused `e2e/layoutAudit.spec.ts` asserts at least three complete Chats rows and a full row in every expanded foot list, checks Hills (source only) shows one source row with no space below it and gives its surplus to Chats, and saves only the four owner-requested dark screenshots (Journeys/Harbor/Hills at 1440×1000 and Journeys at 390×844). `e2e/chatsWith.spec.ts` retains pinsplit's branch-local pin expectations and covers resizing/reset/persistence through window changes. The header toggles always remain enabled. If a click opens a section that the normal height rule would collapse, `SidebarFeet` gives that section a temporary focus override: reserve one full Chats row instead of three and keep the other footer collapsed. The override uses the existing chosen size within the larger available space, without changing saved sizes or the other footer's manual-collapse preference. Clicking the open header closes it and clears the override; clicking the other header transfers priority. `e2e/support/phoneFooters.ts` is shared by the normal `splitChats` browser regression and the focused layout audit: it checks both headers start auto-collapsed/enabled at 390×844, opens each with a complete footer row and a complete Chats row visible, switches priority, clicks each closed, and verifies saved sizes are unchanged. The audit saves `branches-open-390x844-dark.png` and `split-off-open-390x844-dark.png`.

**Shared chat reads** (tabperf3, 2026-11-02). The registered Cast and character panels use `chatCards.ts`: one query for all live participant/persona definitions, keyed by chat, fork, tip and sorted entity ids, invalidated by `library` and `chat-cards:<chat>`. Loading/empty casts issue no query. Opening a new tip reads the cast once, and its initial context does not schedule a second LCM read when one already started. `composerWorkspace.ts` synchronizes the text draft once per fork/tip/open generation, retaining its queue through surface remounts and rereading after a moved tip or new open generation. The registered image provider waits for that draft's resolved id instead of issuing its own OpenComposer; its attachment replay and image operations remain separate. Snippet scope changes in one React commit coalesce into a read of the final scope; a refresh after a write still starts a new read and supersedes older responses. These data helpers leave panel/provider/control registrations in charge of their surfaces.

**Sidebar row widths** (branchwidth, 2026-11-02). The shared `ForkRow` in `features/characters/ShellBrowser.tsx` fills the available width up to `max-w-controls` (40rem), aligned at the start, as the chat-list wrapper already does. This covers all-chat rows (including group chats), scoped named/pinned and unnamed branch lists, the bottom open-chat branch section, pinned chats, character-scoped chats (Just, With others, Was in), and filtered search results. The same row on character pages and home pins follows this cap. The bottom branch header shares the cap so its expand action stays beside the rows. Character and group portrait grids retain their responsive columns. `e2e/sidebarRowWidth.spec.ts` measures the rows and their alignment with the sidebar at its default 320px and dragged to 1020px in light and dark, with optional screenshots and geometry through `SCREENSHOT_DIR`; `ROW_WIDTH_BEFORE=1` captures the original geometry without enforcing the cap.

**Chat row title clamp** (chatrowclamp, owner, 2026-11-02). `ForkRow` titles and secondary branch labels stop at two lines with an ellipsis, using normal word breaking and overflow wrapping; an unbroken token is clipped with an ellipsis instead of wrapped character by character. The existing open tooltip includes the complete title, and a secondary label has native title text. The shared row covers all chats, group chats, character scopes, scoped and bottom branch lists, home pins and character-page lists. Group tiles on the home page and sidebar also clamp their titles to two lines and expose the full title on hover. Avatars, branch counts and pins retain their fixed sizes and vertical centering; preview, time and detail lines retain their existing limits. At the 220px sidebar minimum, the responsive row described above moves small portraits above the text; the full-title hover remains available. `e2e/chatRowClamp.spec.ts` checks the owner's example and an unbroken token at the sidebar's 220px minimum and in the 390px phone drawer, including title and total row bounds, accessory geometry and full-title hovers, plus home pins and group tiles. The separate `/chats` list already truncates titles to one line.

The chat RPCs, live updates and generation. Contract in `@rp/shared/chatApi.ts` (merged into `AppApi`), handlers in `packages/server/src/api/chats.ts`, the services in `packages/server/src/chat/`.

**Left-panel name filter** (leftsearch, 2026-11-04). The registered `ShellBrowser` places Chats / Characters and Find by name in one row at 26rem of available content width: an 11rem switch, 0.5rem gap and at least 14rem for search. Below that width both fill separate rows; the two segments share the switch equally. Fixed grid tracks keep hover, focus and selection from shifting the controls. `e2e/leftSearch.spec.ts` checks both views at phone, minimum, default and maximum sidebar widths in both themes, including the scoped layout audit. `e2e/shellNavigation.spec.ts` checks the actual input width plus the message-search toggle and CSS gap against the stacked row, including aligned edges and no wrapping, at 1440/390 in both themes with the toggle off/on/off and absent in Characters. It retains detection of unused input space inside a full-width wrapper and runs the scoped layout audit in each state.

**Finding a message** (search, 2026-11-12; DESIGN §6.2 "Search … everywhere", ST-COMPARISON item 21). The left panel's chat search widens from names to message text in all of the user's chats.
- **Where.** In the list of all chats, a pressed toggle (`MessageSearchToggle`, a chat icon, "Search message text") sits beside the Find by name field in the field's own grid cell (the field and the toggle share the cell's row; `e2e/leftSearch.spec.ts` measures that row). On, the field is "Find in messages", the Show/Sort row and the chat rows give way to the results (`MessageResults`), and its explanation says how to go back to names. Both are registered contributions to `sidebar.search-tools` and `sidebar.message-results` (`features/characters/MessageSearch.tsx`), so a plugin can replace or drop them. A character's or a chat's own list has no toggle: the search covers every chat.
- **URL.** `sideIn=messages` says the search looks through messages; `sideQ` keeps the text, as for names. Both are in `sidebarSearch`, so they stay while chats open from the panel and a reload shows the same results. A result links to `/chats/$chatId?fork=…&slot=…`: the chat opens on that branch at that message, and a reload returns there (`ChatPage`'s `slot`).
- **What a result is** (`@rp/shared/messageSearch.ts`, `MessageHit`). One message version, the text as written, with the live branches that show it: a message a hundred branches share is one result, never one per branch. A branch's own copy (a Search and replace in one branch writes one, §3.13) is a result of its own, on that branch and the branches made from it after. An unselected swipe is not a result until a branch shows it. Deleted messages, versions, branches and chats, and messages still being written or failed, are left out. A result names its chat (`chatName`: its title, else its current branch's cast), the speaker (the card's library name, else "You" or "Model"), its number on the first branch, when it was written, an excerpt of about 180 characters around its first match with every match marked, and its first three branches (as the left panel names them, `forkLabel`) with the count of all of them. The first branch, where it opens, is the chat's current branch when that shows it, else the one chatted in last.
- **Matching.** Each word typed (letters and digits, at most eight, two characters at least in all) must start a word of the text, in any order, folding case and accents, through the version full-text index (`versions_fts`, §3.7): `light` finds "lighthouse", `house` doesn't. `markWords` marks what the index matched, on the text with the same folding. Template messages (greetings with macros) match their stored text.
- **Phrases** (stgapfix1, 2026-11-16; `parseQuery`, `matchPhases`). Words in quotes (`"…"`, `“…”`, `„…`; an unclosed quote runs to the end) are a phrase found exactly: whole words, side by side, in order, punctuation between them ignored (an FTS5 phrase); other words beside it are still required as word starts. Two or more words without quotes are read in two phases, each newest first: first the messages where they stand side by side in the order typed (an FTS5 phrase of prefixes, `"a"* + "b"*`), then those with all of them apart (`(…AND…) NOT (phrase)`), so "handwriting was unmistakable" lists the message with that phrase above newer ones with the words scattered. A phrase hit's excerpt is centred on the phrase (`findPhrase`, `focusPhrase`) rather than the first word found. The cursor carries `phase: "words"` once the side-by-side matches are used up; a page that finishes the first phase goes on into the second, and the client keys its pages by phase and `before`. The search toggle's explanation says what quotes do. The index (`versions_fts`, unicode61 with `prefix='2 3'`) is unchanged; FTS5 checks phrases with its position lists.
- **The read** (`SearchMessages`, `db/messageSearch.ts`, reader worker; `TextSearchApi` in `@rp/shared/textSearchApi.ts`, its own authenticated group). Matches are read newest first (by version `seq`, which follows writing order), 5,000 per statement. Each is checked in that statement for the caller's ownership, deletion and whether any branch can show it (its message's own selection, a branch's `select` override naming it, or a `replace` override naming it as a branch's copy), so the swipes that make up most matches cost one indexed row each. For the rest, the chat's live forks are read once per search, those whose tip reaches the message are checked with `shownIn`, slot and version deletion in one statement, then against their display path (`pathPieces`, cached per fork; it places inserted messages and gives the message's number). Only an unnamed branch made from another needs its split for its name: from its stored summary, or worked out once per search. A page holds 20 results and stops after 20,000 matches, whichever comes first, with a cursor (`before`, a version `seq`) to go on from, so a word that matches only other users' or unshown text still answers in bounded time ("Search older messages"). Every statement is separate, so an interrupted read stops at the next one.
- **Cancelling.** Each page is its own `AppClient.query` atom keyed by text and cursor; the text is read 300 ms after typing pauses. A changed text unmounts the old pages, which interrupts their RPCs: the reader pool drops a queued request and a running one stops at its next statement (§3.1 `readerPool.ts`).
- **Time budget.** Every page under 1 s on the owner's scale. `test/messageSearchScale.test.ts` (server-slow) builds a 3,000-message chat with 300 branches and 20 swipes on every message (63,000 versions with the common word, each branch selecting swipes on twenty early messages) and checks every page of a word in every 50th message and all its swipes, and the first page of a word in every version, against that budget (medians of seven; measured 350 to 750 ms a page for the rare word, which scans 20,000 matches a page, on a shared 48-core host).
- **Tests.** `test/messageSearch.test.ts`: a shared message once with both branches, branch-only messages, word starts, case and accent folding, a swipe found only once a branch selects it, a branch's replaced copy, deleted messages and chats, and paging without repeats; `packages/shared/test/messageSearch.test.ts`: words, marks (accents, astral characters) and excerpts; the isolation suite's probe (another user's messages are never found); `e2e/messageSearch.spec.ts` at 1440 and 390 in light and dark: the toggle, results with chat, branch, speaker and marks, a shared message listed once, the URL through a reload, no results, opening a result on its branch at its message and reloading there, and the layout audit of the panel with results.

**Column header alignment** (headeralign, owner 2026-11-03; DESIGN §10.1). `styles.css` supplies `--spacing-shell-header` (65 px): the centre header's existing 48 px portrait plus 8 px vertical padding and its 1 px divider. The sidebar's title/actions, saved and pending chat headers, and the panel's tool-tab bar all use `h-shell-header`, including narrow columns where the centre hides portraits. Their bottom borders line up whenever the columns sit side by side. Sidebar title/actions and chat controls are centred with matching 8 px vertical padding; the sidebar no longer adds an outer top inset. Chats / Characters starts 16 px below that divider, matching the message list's leading inset; the panel's cast tabs also sit below the common line. Existing action slots, tab registries and sidebar rows are unchanged. `e2e/headerAlignment.spec.ts` measures all three dividers within 1 px, sidebar title/button centres, matching padding and tab spacing for saved/pending chats at 1440 and 1024 px in both themes, and the phone header's fit at 390 px. `HEADERALIGN_WORK` saves geometry and header crops; `HEADERALIGN_BEFORE=1` records the old layout without enforcing the new measurements.

**Finding a branch** (stgapfix1, 2026-11-16). A chat with more than six branches gets a **Find a branch** field (tooltip "Shows the branches whose name or last message has these words.") in the header's branch list (`BranchControl.tsx`) and in the left panel's foot list of the open chat's branches (`OpenChatBranches`). Both filter rows already read in full (`ListForks`; the foot's shell sections, up to 5,000 each), so typing asks the server nothing: a branch is listed when every word typed is in its label or its last message's first words (`branchMatches`, `@rp/shared/branchNaming.ts`), and "No branch has those words." replaces an empty list. The foot keeps its text per chat. When the left panel lists one chat's branches (its ⑂ count), its search field becomes "Find a branch", with text of its own for that chat (the words that found the chat by name would match none of its branches), and the paged shell read matches it within one chat against each branch's own name, "Original" and its preview (`sectionRows`), keeping the chat's name in the breadcrumb while nothing matches. Tests: `packages/shared/test/messageSearch.test.ts` (`branchMatches`), `test/shellForks.test.ts` (the chat-scoped search), `e2e/branchSearch.spec.ts` (the menu and both panel lists at 1440 and 390, with the layout audit).

**Last live fork.** The header's branch list (`BranchControl.tsx`) disables a branch's delete while it's the only live fork, saying “The only branch: delete the chat instead”; with one branch the header shows no control and ⋯ Branches… lists it. The server still refuses deleting the last live fork. `e2e/branchNaming.regression.spec.ts` checks the disabled action after deletion and reload/rename at 1440 and 390 pixels; deletion and Undo remain covered on a fork with a survivor.

**Independent navigation shell (2026-10-26).** `/` shows account pins above the characters' filter and sort (below), with a separate Recent / Created / Name sort for the pins. Groups shows each multi-character chat once (by its current fork), rather than combining chats by title and cast. The older group RPCs remain for existing group pages. **A card's Recent has one definition, computed in one place** (`db/shellReads.ts`): `ShellCard.recentAt` is the latest `recentAt` of any fork with recorded version participation for the card, that is its last shown message, else its chat's start (an imported chat's ST date), or the user's last activity in it (below, fheader), so imported dates count and an import's own time never does, as ST sorts by `date_last_chat`; null for a card in no chat. (`CardUsage.lastMessageAt` stays the card's own last turn, including turns written by the user. Persona Recent follows that last turn, falling back to chat activity for an imported selected persona without a turn.) Editing a card doesn't move it. The home grid, the left panel's grid sort by it with `features/characters/cardRecency.ts` (`sortCards`: never-used cards last, newest first) (`test/shellNavigation.test.ts`, `test/shellForks.test.ts`, `client/test/cardRecency.test.ts`, `e2e/homeRecent.spec.ts`). Created is `entities.created_at`: a full ST import's CCv3 author creation date, else its best arrival evidence (updated if stronger evidence is later found), otherwise when the card came in (§13). Personas are the shell's `personas` (personausage), each also marked `ShellCard.persona`; the lists leave them out but under Personas or with Include personas (below).

**Grid controls (homecontrols, 2026-11-03).** Home and the sidebar Characters grid share `CardGridControls.tsx` inside their registered surfaces. Each instance uses an inline-size named container and container queries: wide puts filters left and the sort/direction/persona group right with bounded search below; medium puts filters above search left and sort right; narrow puts scrolling filter segments above sort right and full-width search. A ResizeObserver measures the intrinsic filter and sort groups and a 20rem search sizing marker, adding the actual column gap to generate the container-query thresholds in a constructed stylesheet (inline style elements are blocked by the app CSP). Each instance removes its sheet and observer when unmounted. Counts, fonts, selected labels and toggle presence can change those thresholds. Filter choices never wrap; the platform handles horizontal scrolling. The sort group can also scroll at exceptionally small panel widths. Its unbordered toolbar has a narrow inset-audit exception: its controls align with the segmented row without a surrounding panel inset. Start a chat and Add characters retain compact pickers. `e2e/homeControls.spec.ts` asserts all three layouts for each surface at a fixed viewport, plus alignment, scrolling and selection.

**Card families (families1, 2026-11-15; DESIGN §4 [P], off by default).** A family is a card and the cards forked from it, at any depth: `entities.forked_from_entity_id` followed to its root, the only lineage recorded. Cards imported separately are not related, whatever their names. `cardFamilies` (`db/shellReads.ts`) resolves the root of every forked card in one query, and `ShellCard.family` carries the root's entity id for a card with a recorded parent; a root learns its family from its forks. A binned member still links its descendants to the root. Grouping is the client's, over the cards the list already holds (`features/characters/cardFamilies.ts`, `groupFamilies`, one pass): a family with two or more members in the list becomes one tile where its first member stood, shown by the member used last (the first in the list's order when none was used), with an “N cards” pill under it (`FamilyToggle` in `shellData.tsx`) that opens its other members after it, in the list's order. So filters decide the members there are, a family with one member left is that card alone, and a search lists each card it finds, ungrouped. The choice is the account's display preference `cardFamilies` (default false), switched by the “Group forks” button (`GroupFamiliesToggle` in `cardBrowse.tsx`) in the grid controls of the Characters page and the left panel's grid; the open family is in the URL (`family` on the page, `sideFamily` in the panel; one per place). Add characters and Start a chat stay ungrouped. The `cardGrouping` client registry (`features/characters/cardGrouping.tsx`) registers the `forks` tile grouping and its control together; replacing or disabling the entry updates both grids live, without rewriting account preferences. Family open/close changes push URL history in both places, so Back restores the previous family, reload preserves it and another tab's open choice stays independent. Tile menus and archive/favourite actions target only that tile's member. Bulk archive always opens its explicit, ungrouped per-card selection list; collapsed families never expand a silent bulk target set. Tests: `packages/client/test/cardFamilies.test.ts`, server `test/chatPicture.test.ts` (`cardFamilies`, `ShellCard.family`), browser `e2e/cardFamilies.spec.ts`.

**The characters' filter, sort and favourites (2026-11-01).** One set of parts (`features/characters/cardBrowse.tsx`) lists characters on the home grid, in the left panel's Characters grid and in the Cast tab's Add characters (`CharacterGrid` in `shellData.tsx` takes the cards in order, the date sort and a `pick`: what a click does instead of opening the character's chat, each tile's accessible name and tooltip, and its state, a mark over the picture, done (dimmed, a click doing nothing, still focusable for its tooltip) or pending, all from a status word per tile (`status`, by entity id), so a change re-renders only the tiles it changes):
- **Filter** (`CardFilterControl`): All / With chats / Never used / Favourites / Personas / Groups, each with its count, muted and outside the choice's accessible name. The counts are over all the user's characters, whatever the search, as before the shell (the shell commit 8e201904 had dropped them); Groups counts the `groups` section (`useGroupCount`, a limit-0 read). Start a chat has no Groups. Home and the sidebar grid lay it out as a scrolling segmented control; the other narrow places use a picker (`compact`, `CardBrowseBar.tsx`).
- **Sort** (`CardSortControl`): Recent, Created, Added, Name, each with a tooltip saying what it orders by (in the compact menu, a line under each). **Added** is `ShellCard.addedAt`, the upstream ref's `created_at`: the best inherited ST arrival for a full-folder import, otherwise when it came into this app (§13). A **direction toggle** beside it (an icon button whose tooltip names the order, "Newest first" / "Oldest first", "A to Z" / "Z to A") turns the order round; a new sort starts its own way (dates newest first, names A to Z); Recent keeps never-used characters last either way (`sortCards` in `cardRecency.ts`). For Groups, `GetShellForks` takes `reversed`, and Added sorts groups by `ShellFork.addedAt`, inheriting ST group arrival (§13). Each place remembers its own sort and direction on the account in `display` (`useCardBrowse(place)`: `home`, `sidebar`, `cast`), since a narrow panel and the home page are used differently. Outside home, the filter starts at All on each visit. Home instead restores its filter and sort from the URL (below).
- **The date** a date sort orders by ends each tile's last line (`SortDate`), right-aligned and muted beside "N chats" / "Never used", short ("3h ago", "2w ago", then "Mar 2024", `shortAgo`), its tooltip the full date and time and what it is (Last message, Created, Added); tiles keep their height, and the date truncates on a narrow tile. Name shows none. Start a chat's rows already show their last chat's date, so they add it for Created and Added only.
- **Favourites**: a star on each character tile (over its picture), each library row and grid tile, and beside a card's name in its editor (`FavouriteStar`), a toggle with a tooltip that never opens the card. They are the user's, per card, stored in the existing user-scoped `settings` table under `cards.favourites` (`db/cardFavourites.ts`: `{ on, here }`), so a database made before them needs no migration. `SetCardFavourite` (a writer transaction; NotFound for another user's or a deleted card) sets one and records it in `here`. **ST's favourite flag** (`fav`, kept in the card as `extensions.fav`, which ST writes alongside the top-level copy the format drops) is applied by `ImportFile` in the import's own transaction on every first import and re-import, unless the user set that card's star here since; a card file without one changes nothing. The shell read carries it as `ShellCard.favourite` (`e2e/characterBrowse.spec.ts` at 1440 and 390, `client/test/cardRecency.test.ts`). The star is only a favourite character's: chat and branch pins (`PinButton` in `ShellBrowser.tsx`) use a pin icon (`ui/Icon.tsx` `pin`), outline when unpinned and filled when pinned. Chat rows and group tiles toggle the global chat pin; branch rows and the chat header toggle the branch-local pin. Tooltips say “Click to add this chat to Pinned” / “Click to remove this chat from Pinned” or explain pinning/unpinning the branch within its chat.

**Personas in the card lists (personalists, 2026-11-02; DESIGN §2.2).** `GetShellCards` answers the persona folder's cards as `personas` beside `cards` (personausage), each marked `ShellCard.persona` (the `persona` tag); the lists browse both (`browsable` in `shellData.tsx`). Every list built from them (`browseCards`) leaves them out but under the **Personas** filter, which lists them alone (its count beside it), or with **Include personas** (`CardBrowse.withPersonas`, `IncludePersonas` in `cardBrowse.tsx`: an icon toggle, off by default, shown only while the filter lists characters, not under Personas or Groups, its tooltip "Include personas" off and "Personas included" on, with `aria-pressed` and a raised background and accent icon while on), which mixes them in, the filter's counts counting them too. The toggle uses the existing `people` icon and the same 32 px `IconButton` as the sort direction; the compact filter shrinks with truncated text to keep the bar on one row (personatoggle, 2026-11-02). In a mixed list (`mixesPersonas`) each persona's tile has the shared "Persona" badge on its picture's lower left (`ui/PersonaBadge.tsx`, tooltip "In the persona folder: a card you can play in chats."; the tile's accessible name ends "(persona)"). Where: the home grid has both, the toggle after the sort direction; the left panel's grid and the Cast tab's Add characters have both, the toggle after the sort direction in their compact bar (`CardBrowseBar` `includePersonas`; personaswitch added it to Add characters, marking the personas it mixes in); Start a chat has the Personas filter only, and Add characters' separate persona rows are gone. The toggle is remembered with the place's sort in `rp.cards.<place>.<user>` and is in the URL: `personas=true` on home, `sidePersonas=true` for the left panel, seeding a fresh visit from that memory as the sort does. The library page keeps its All / Characters / Personas. `e2e/homePersonas.spec.ts` (1440, 390), `e2e/castAdd.spec.ts`.
**Branch navigation and previews (splitlink, 2026-11-05).** The registered header branch control uses `ListForks.startSlotId`: a recorded base when available, otherwise the last shared display-path message with its parent (the first message when no shared prefix exists). Imported branches with null bases and nested branches retain the start link and its existing explanation. Readers select the latest displayed, non-deleted message with non-whitespace text and a non-failed selected version for branch/header/chat previews. Shell summaries retain the latest usable preview independently of the actual endpoint and time; format 7 recomputes stored previews. Preview slots reserve two lines, including “No messages yet”. The selected left-panel branch’s compact InlineRename fills its title width, retains title font size and measured height, and shows its own name or the “Branch name” placeholder; the optional placeholder leaves other callers’ defaults intact.

Branch-list titles occupy one fixed 20 px line: the text truncates with an ellipsis, the selected row’s pencil follows it, and the non-shrinking “opens here” chip stays at the end. Adding or removing the pencil/chip does not change row height, including at the minimum sidebar width and on phones. Compact rename uses the title’s remaining width alongside the chip.

Branch-list row boxes share chat rows’ full available width and 40rem cap, including the open-chat branch list. The sidebar-width regression measures the outer `data-fork-row` boxes; branch text containers have their own padding and are not row edges.

**Chats tab browsing (chatsort, 2026-11-02).** Under Find by name, `ChatBrowseBar.tsx` uses the Characters row's layout and UI parts: a counted Select, a compact sort Menu and the shared `SortDirection`. The characters feature registers it in `sidebar.chat-browse`, a replaceable slot. The filter keeps its option name at its intrinsic width; below 22rem of browse-row width it hides only the closed picker’s count (the popup retains counts). The sort menu and direction stay together and wrap right-aligned when the filter and sort cannot fit. The shared Select’s `shown` renderer accepts React nodes so the count can hide without changing option labels. The shared Select keeps its 8px option gutter on its scrollable list, so the inner scroll boundary retains padding. Filters: All, Pinned (any live branch pinned), Group chats (at least two model-written characters in the current cast), One-on-one (exactly one), With branches (more than one live fork), and Workshops. Workshops appear only under All and Workshops; all other choices and their counts exclude them. Empty story casts appear under All. Filter, sort and reverse read only the tab’s URL (`sideChatsShow`, `sideChatsSort`, `sideChatsReverse`); an unqualified visit uses defaults and never restores per-account localStorage. Counts are chats, once each within the current scope, before the search and selected filter. Sorts: Recent (the existing `chatRecentAt`: latest message or activity across live branches, including Branch from here, else chat start), Started (chat start, including imported historical dates), Name (readable current chat name), Messages (current path's visible count) and Branches (live fork count). Dates default newest first, Name A–Z, counts most first. Direction reverses only the primary metric; ties use chat id ascending, then fork id. A new sort resets direction.

The sidebar pages **`GetShellForks`**, not `ListChats`. Its optional `ShellForksView.browse` is applied in the reader worker to `chats` and character-scoped `just`/`with`/`was` sections before slicing their first 100 rows; the response includes `filterCounts`. Search and scope retain their existing behavior. A changed filter/sort/direction resets the requested page length. Current-path metrics come from existing `fork_summaries`, with one chat map and pinned-id set added to the existing per-user, per-database-version shell cache. Counts/deduplication are linear in the scoped forks; only deduplicated chats are sorted. Chat pins use one bulk query; no per-row subqueries or message walks are added; the existing `forks_chat` and summary primary-key indexes support the bulk read. The existing invalidation still refreshes changed paths. `chatBrowseScale.test.ts` exercises 1,000 chats with 100 cached branches each and bounded response size.

**Pinned stays above Chats** in its existing section, listing globally pinned chats once on their current branch (a pinned chat also remains in the ordinary chat list). The section retains its own Recent / Created / Name sort, independent of the new list sort, and follows the new chat filter. A scope narrowed to one chat lists Pinned branches / Named branches / Branches, each by last message; the chat browse row is for lists of chats. The Characters tab and its persona controls are unchanged.

`useChatBrowse.ts` remembers all three choices per account in this browser (`rp.chats.sidebar.<userId>`). `sideChatsShow`, `sideChatsSort`, `sideChatsReverse` travel in sidebar destinations' retained search keys, independently of the Characters tab's choices; defaults are omitted, a fresh unmarked visit seeds memory, explicit URL choices win, and changes replace history without resetting scroll. Search continues using `sideQ`. `chatBrowse.test.ts` covers all filters/sorts, both directions, stable ties, current-path versus other-branch messages, scope, search, counts, paging and pin invalidation. `e2e/chatBrowse.spec.ts` covers the row, top pins, URL and account memory, reload/fresh-visit restoration and geometry at 1440 and 390. `layoutAudit.spec.ts` supports `LAYOUT_AUDIT_SIDEBAR_ONLY=1` for sidebar scopes and the two browse menus.

**Personas in the card lists (personalists, 2026-11-02; DESIGN §2.2).** `GetShellCards` answers the persona folder's cards as `personas` beside `cards` (personausage), each marked `ShellCard.persona` (the `persona` tag); the lists browse both (`browsable` in `shellData.tsx`). Every list built from them (`browseCards`) leaves them out but under the **Personas** filter, which lists them alone (its count beside it), or with **Include personas** (`CardBrowse.withPersonas`, `IncludePersonas` in `cardBrowse.tsx`: a checkbox, off by default, shown only while the filter lists characters, not under Personas or Groups, its tooltip "Shows the cards you play as among these characters"), which mixes them in, the filter's counts counting them too. In a mixed list (`mixesPersonas`) each persona's tile has the shared "Persona" badge on its picture's lower left (`ui/PersonaBadge.tsx`, tooltip "In the persona folder: a card you can play in chats."; the tile's accessible name ends "(persona)"). Where: the home grid has both, the checkbox beside the sort; the left panel's grid and the Cast tab's Add characters have both, the checkbox under their compact bar (`CardBrowseBar` `includePersonas`; personaswitch added it to Add characters, marking the personas it mixes in); Start a chat has the Personas filter only, and Add characters' separate persona rows are gone. The checkbox is remembered with the place's sort in `rp.cards.<place>.<user>` and is in the URL: `personas=true` on home, `sidePersonas=true` for the left panel, seeding a fresh visit from that memory as the sort does. The library page keeps its All / Characters / Personas. `e2e/homePersonas.spec.ts` (1440, 390), `e2e/castAdd.spec.ts`.

**The Persona control (saveflow follow-up, owner 2026-11-03; DESIGN §2.2).** `useSetPersona` in `features/characters/personaFolder.tsx` still runs `SetPersona` and invalidates `library`, so lists, filters, counts and badges update live, with an error toast if it fails. Its registered `characters.persona-folder` header contribution binds the shared controlled `ui/PersonaToggle.tsx`, in the panel/full card header and on the card page. The library item's Persona menu tick retains the same action and stays a menu item. The button is a muted person icon when off; pressed, its accent state grows from 32px to 88px to show “Persona” after the icon. Width transitions take 150ms and are disabled for reduced motion. `aria-pressed` follows the optimistic state until the shell agrees. Off explanation: “Mark this card as a persona: a card you play as, listed under Personas.” On: “Remove the persona mark: this becomes a regular card again.” The binding still renders nothing for a card the shell does not list. The full editor's Persona row is third; the side panel's character tab puts it last, below the chats/token line (smallfixes4, owner 2026-11-04). That panel portrait omits Persona membership badges and keeps You for the played card; other views retain their badges. The Persona row retains the registered account-default badge beside its toggle, shrinking its label with an ellipsis at the panel minimum while preserving the full accessible text; the combined chats/token line precedes Persona in the side panel and follows it in the full editor. Card actions no longer include Switch persona; persona switching remains under the composer. `e2e/personaSwitch.spec.ts` checks live membership across the panel, editor, card page and lists; `e2e/cardHeaderRows.spec.ts` guards row structure, height, button states, width and exact explanations.

**Persona badges (personabadge, owner correction 2026-11-02; DESIGN §2.2).** `ui/PersonaBadge.tsx` supplies one accent style, hover/focus explanations and a portrait-overlay option. Outside the chat's cast and speaker/persona controls, the marker always reads **Persona**, explained "In the persona folder: a card you can play in chats." This includes home and left-panel mixed grids, library rows/tiles and Add characters pickers, the standalone card page and full editor. A list that shows only personas (the Personas filter or tab of any grid, picker or the library) marks none of them; badges appear only where personas are mixed with other cards (owner decision via coordinator, 2026-11-03). In the chat's cast, This chat and character/persona tabs and the composer's speaker/persona switcher, **You** marks only the selected persona, explained "You play this card in this chat." The full editor opened over a chat also reads that chat's cast: its selected persona gets You, even without folder membership; another folder card gets Persona. Speaking as a different character does not move the You badge. The card-header portrait renders the shared overlay directly so the badge remains hoverable and focusable. Add characters identifies the selected card as already in the chat while its folder marker remains Persona. The badge-surface layout audit also enforces an 8 px inset around picker controls and speaker options, removes the full editor back button's negative left margin, and declares the intentional membership and sticky picker overlays. `e2e/homePersonas.spec.ts` and `e2e/castAdd.spec.ts` cover the labels, contexts and explanations at 1440 and 390.

**Card archive surfaces** (cardarchive, 2026-11-06). Home and sidebar offer Archived (`show=archived` / `sideShow=archived`); every ordinary filter and picker excludes these cards. Under All, a nonempty name search adds a collapsed Archived (N) group after the ordinary results. Archived includes personas, marked with the existing Persona badge in the mixed grid and in archived search matches, independently of Include personas. The registered card archive control is beside Favourite in headers and in its own corner of a tile (§5 "Tile toggles"), with an entry in a tile's right-click menu; card ⋯ menus have none, since each sits beside a visible toggle (the library row's direct Archive, the panel's star and archive) (archivebtn, 2026-11-06). Each manual change offers Undo. The shared registered `archivedCardActions` slot hosts “Archive unused cards…” on both Archived surfaces. Its dialog renders the shared registered criterion list, defaults to never used/30 days, previews matching cards with dates and checkboxes in a windowed list, excludes favourites, and archives the checked subset in one operation with Undo. `e2e/cardArchive.spec.ts` checks 1440/390, light/dark, Home, sidebar, search, selection and both Undo paths, with scoped layout audits and screenshots. The review preview uses `e2e/support/cardArchive.ts`: 200 synthetic cards with mixed dates, stars, archive state, edits and chat activity.

**Home URL state (homeurl, 2026-11-02).** The existing Show tabs are the home filter: `show=used|unused|favourites|personas|groups` (All is the default). `sort=created|added|name` (Recent by default), `reverse=true`, `q` (the search text, kept as typed) and `pinsSort=created|name` (Recent by default) describe the other controls. `features/characters/homeSearch.ts` parses each key independently, falls back on unknown values and writes explicit `undefined` to clear retained defaults; `useHomeBrowse.ts` reads and updates them through TanStack navigation. The home route declares these keys as `retainSearch`, so changing the sidebar on home preserves them, while other destinations do not inherit them. Show switches push history; sort, direction, pinned sort and search replace it without resetting scroll. Reload, copied links and back/forward restore the controls. The existing `rp.cards.home.<user>` sort/direction memory seeds only a fresh visit without any home params; an explicit home query wins as a whole. A `homeBrowse` history-state marker prevents that memory from overriding a previously visited default-only entry, including after reload. No new device memory is added. `PinnedChats` accepts optional controlled sort props for home; its other hosts retain their existing local sort. `e2e/homeUrl.spec.ts` checks both widths, copied links with conflicting memory, all Show tabs, both sorts, reversed direction, search, history length, default-only history and hand-edited bad parameters; `test/homeSearch.test.ts` covers query round trips, invalid types and sort-direction resets.

`GetShellLibrary` (`ShellLibrary` reader operation, `db/shellReads.ts`) reads owner-scoped graph metadata and bounded 160-character excerpts at visible endpoints, folds selected-version state on each visible path, and returns card dates, individual fork rows, message counts, present cast, characters with recorded version participation and each character's last speaking slot/time/category. Character lists and jumps use that character's speaking activity, so other characters' turns cannot advance it. Just X excludes other present characters written by the model; With others includes them; departed characters appear under Was in. The iterative walk handles deep imported paths without recursive JS calls. Metadata reads start with the live owner chats using `chats_owner_live` (migration `0046_shell_owner_reads`), then indexed slot/event lookups, enforced by CROSS JOIN order. Query-plan regressions use the production statements in `shellQueries.ts`. Metadata work grows with the user's graph size; it is performed in a reader worker. Fork rows carry only the chat's id and title, and their cast as entity ids; `people` describes each cast card once, and the client's `shellAtom` puts the cards back on each row. At 1,000 cards / 5,000 chats / 50,000 slots this halves the response (3.8 MB to 1.9 MB without excerpts). Fork rows carry departed participant ids independently of the model cast; silent departures use those ids, so a present character played by the user keeps its present classification.

**Stored fork summaries (fux1, 2026-10-31).** The walk above costs every message the user has: on the owner's real ST import it grew from 0.3 s to 25–28 s a read, and those reads, abandoned by clients that asked again, held both readers so every other read (a card page, a chat) queued behind them. Now each fork's walk result is kept in `fork_summaries` (`db/forkSummaries.ts`): preview, visible-message count, endpoint, end time, and the cast, joined, departed and activity lists as entity ids only, so names, avatars and the fork's display name stay the read's and a rename never invalidates one. Each summary also says where its fork parts from the fork it was made from (`split_at`, `split_after`, format 3): walking its shown path against its parent's path (else against its base, while the parent is gone), the time of its first own message, else the fork's making, and how many shown messages come before it; null for a chat's first fork. `ListForks` reads the same from the stored summaries while they're valid, else computes them for the chat without storing (`chatForkSummaries`), and `BinItemBranches` reads what is stored. A summary is valid while its chat's `chats.shell_stamp` and the owner's `shell_user_stamps` row are what they were when it was computed, and its `format` is the code's `FORK_SUMMARY_FORMAT`. **Triggers move the stamps** (`db/baseline.ts`) on every write the walk reads: slots, versions, the walk's kinds of `fork_overrides`, state events and forks move the chat's; entity purge/deletion and deletion of its refs or revisions move the owner's, since `withoutPurged` depends on them. Bin/restore and archive are projected from live library metadata; they do not change the stored fold. No write path can forget it. A read (`ShellLibrary`) takes cards' names, avatar and lorebook flags from their head revisions' `card_summaries` rows (§3.9, "Card summaries"; before decisions1, `json_extract` on each head document, which parsed every document, megabytes with a lorebook, on every read), joins live forks, chats and stored summaries in one query, walks only the forks whose summaries are stale (`shellSlotsQuery` and `shellEventsQuery` take a JSON array of fork ids; per-fork validity below), and builds card usage in one pass over the forks. What it walked comes back in the read's `fresh` field, which the `GetShellLibrary` handler strips and stores after answering (`StoreForkSummaries`, in parts of 250 chats, each kept only if its stamps haven't moved). `StImportFinishChat` stores the finished chat's stale summaries in its own transaction. A chat an ST import is still writing (titled "import unfinished") is never walked by a read, since every batch makes it stale and it can be tens of thousands of messages long: it shows its last stored summary, or none, until its finish stores one (`test/shellSummaries.test.ts`). `recompute: true` ignores every stored summary; `test/shellSummaries.test.ts` compares the stored and recomputed reads after each kind of write. Measured at load average 92–96 on 48 cores (`test/shellScale.test.ts`, 1,000 cards / 5,000 chats / 50,000 slots): the reader's warm read 1.2 s against master's 6.6 s, 3.8 s end to end against 9.0 s; the test's 2 s budget fails on both at that load. At a heavy user's scale (420 cards, 1,885 forks, 500,000 imported messages; synthetic, fux1) a warm read takes about 0.4 s of CPU and 0.3–0.9 s wall at load 85–90, against 25 s before; during the import itself its median was 137 ms while cards and the first chats went in and about 0.5 s near the end. **The app reads it in parts** (fux1r): every fork's row was 1.7–1.9 MB of JSON per read, encoded on the main thread and decoded and laid out in the browser. `GetShellCards` (`ShellCards`) is the cards alone, with each card's Recent and where its tile opens (`open`: the fork and line it last spoke in, else its latest chat's end, which the client used to work out from every fork). `GetShellForks` (`ShellForks`) takes a view (a card's chats, one chat's forks, given chats, or all; a search over the fork's and its cast's names; a sort) and named sections, each with a limit, and answers each section's first rows, its total and the cards the rows name: `pinned`, `chats` (All chats), `just`/`with`/`was` (a card's), `current`/`peers`/`other` (a chat's), `groups` (home), `card` (a card page's list) and `all` (a header's or a list page's pins). The left panel, home's pins and groups, the card page, the chat header and the chat list each read only what they show (`useShellForks` in `shellData.tsx`, one atom per view; a longer list or another search keeps showing the last answer until the new one, another scope doesn't). Lists show 100 rows and "Show N more of M" asks for the next 100 (every row made the home page 33,000 elements, 7.8 s of script and 2.6 s of layout per visit). `GetShellLibrary` stays the whole read, for tools and tests. A reader worker keeps its last computation, with what it walked, while `PRAGMA data_version` (which moves with every commit of another connection, the writer's) is unchanged, so a screen's several reads cost one; any write recomputes it (`test/shellForks.test.ts` writes between reads). Measured on the UI audit's synthetic dataset (437 cards, 2,142 chats, 210,000 messages) at load 56–60 on 48 cores, page loads in a fresh browser and after a reload: home 0.97–1.27 s and 0.44–0.66 s, the left panel 0.67–0.97 s and 0.45–0.65 s, a 5,800-message chat's link 1.22–1.29 s and 1.03–1.15 s; before, at load 67–75, home took 6.6–31 s and 4.1–7.3 s, the chat 4.3–7.9 s and 12.6–13.7 s. The first read of a data directory with no stored summaries (one made before them, or after `FORK_SUMMARY_FORMAT` changes) walks every chat: 23.5 s there, once. Each character tile's fork badge reads one `CardFamilyIndex` for the whole grid (the cards in a fork family and their own forks' count, by `entities_forked_from` both ways) instead of a `CardFamily` tree per tile (1,257 reads on one home load at 420 cards); the tree is read when the badge opens it. **A chat's Recent across its branches (fheader):** a fork's `recentAt` is the later of its last shown message (else its chat's start) and the user's last activity in it (`forks.last_chatted_at`: a send, a reply, a swipe, a continue, an edit, and making it with Branch from here, which `CreateFork` stamps), so branching counts as activity; an import never chats in a fork, so an ST branch file merged into its chat (a fork made at import time) keeps the chat's ST dates (`test/shellRecency.test.ts`); `chatRecentAt` is the latest of its chat's live forks', and `branches` their number, both computed by the read from the forks' columns and stored summaries (no new stamps: creating, deleting or restoring a fork already moves the chat's). The lists that stand for chats (`chats`, `just`/`with`/`was`, `groups`, `card`) show each chat once: its current fork's row when that one is in the list, else its first there, sorted by `chatRecentAt` (character lists still by that character's turns); each row carries its chat's readable name (`chatName`), which those rows show, with "N branches" (`ShellBrowser.tsx` `ForkRow`). `pinned` and a chat's own lists (`current`, `peers`, `other`, `all`) stay per fork. A card's Recent counts its forks' `recentAt`, branching included (`test/shellRecency.test.ts`).

**Per-fork summary validity (importperf, 2026-11-01).** The stamps are per chat, so any write made every fork of its chat stale: an ST chat with hundreds of "Branch #N" files (merged as its forks) walked every fork at each file's finish (O(N²) paths; on the owner's import `StImportFinishChat` grew to 10 s a file by the hundredth) and every shell read walked them all again while the import ran (ShellCards 3–10 s, past the client's limit). Now the writer's own connection notes what each write touched, in TEMP triggers and tables (`db/summaryValidity.ts`), and before each write transaction commits (`transaction` in `db/tx.ts`) it records which forks the touched rows reach (since perfshell2, by moving those forks' `fork_shell_stamps`, below; before, by moving every unreached summary's `stamp` on to the chat's new one): a slot's shown fields reach the forks whose tip is it or below it (a new slot reaches none until a tip moves to it; a new version of an existing slot contributes participation and human-authored activity even before it is selected); a fork's row reaches that fork, and since a fork's split reads its parent's path, a tip's move reaches the fork's children whose tips are at or below a slot one of the two paths holds and the other doesn't (walked up from both tips to their common ancestor; an append reaches none), and a fork's deletion, restore or removal all its children; an override or state event of a fork reaches the forks whose lineage holds that fork at least up to its sequence number (those whose points lie from the writer's point at that number, `pointAtSql`, to its range end: one range of `fork_labels_point`); a removed slot, an insertion, a slot write in a chat with insertions, a chat-wide event or one removed or changed in place reach the whole chat. Each fork a write's overrides and events name is resolved once, not once per row (before fork labels, a transaction of 100 events in a fork of a 650-fork chat with 64-entry lineages settled in 20–35 ms, 2 s before that). A summary stale when the write began stays stale; a write on another connection notes nothing, so older summaries of its chat are invalid until reconciled. A summary computed at the chat's current stamp is valid immediately, including before tracking begins; storing such a claim reconciles tracking, as does the next noted write reaching every fork. Reads walk only stale forks and `StoreForkSummaries` replaces only the rows it was given. A walk of more than eight forks of a chat (or one whose tree is already held) resolves them from one read of that chat (`db/forkPaths.ts`, below; before perfshell2, only forks whose lineage selects, replaces or deletes nothing, `shellPlainForksQuery`, shared the chat's tree), and folds a fork's own events once per state change rather than per message. `test/summaryValidity.test.ts` checks each rule on a written database, `test/shellSummaries.test.ts` which forks real writes leave stale (and that stored equals recomputed after each), `test/shellSummariesModel.test.ts` seeded random sequences of real writes over a forked chat (appends, branches, swipes, selections, edits, deletes, restores and purges in one fork or all, insertions, hides, state events, fork deletion), after each of which a read from storage must equal one from scratch (one seed in `npm test`, more in `npm run test:slow`), `test/stImportBranchResume.test.ts` an import cancelled inside a branch family and run again, and `test/stImportBranchScale.test.ts` (slow) 650 branch files of a 300-message chat: about 60–150 ms a file from first to last at moderate load, against master's growth to over a second by file 200; shell reads under 1 s while it runs and after. A write that does reach every fork of such a chat still walks them all at the next read: 2 s for 201 forks at load 120.

**Incremental shell updates (shellrefresh, 2026-11-06).** `WatchShellCards` and `WatchShellForks` use the same owner-scoped reader operations and stored summaries as the one-shot APIs. They subscribe before their first snapshot; one pending signal per stream coalesces writes, and a change during a read queues another read immediately. ChatHub listeners receive writes and deletions even when nobody subscribes to that chat. Post-write stream reads share a per-user gate. The shared materialization below publishes its snapshot before asynchronous summary persistence; the gate no longer waits for those writes. Initial and concurrent views share that snapshot, including while persistence catches up. `ShellCardsLive` and `ShellForksLive` run in the ordinary foreground lane only after a worker-side preflight in the same read transaction: at most 5,000 live forks, at most two stale summaries, paths and live parents below depth 5,000, and no insertion placements on stale chats. Wider or deeper work returns null and the handler uses the original background read, preserving its reserved reply reader; initial snapshots remain background reads. This lets bounded sidebar work proceed while a cache estimate is in flight. Subsequent messages contain changed card/fork rows plus ordered IDs, section totals and cast metadata, so movement across a page boundary, removals, filters and counts agree with a fresh query. The shared `shellUpdates.ts` reducers retain unchanged wire rows and discard removed rows. Card updates carry separate changed rows and ordered IDs for characters, personas and archived cards (including archived personas); snapshots, reconnects, archive/unarchive moves and empty collections retain the same shape as `GetShellCards`. The client stream seed declares all three collections without a type assertion. Reconnects and explicit library/pin/favourite invalidations start with a complete snapshot. Ordinary ChatSession events refresh the legacy chat/group lists and split-chat links (`chat-lists`); the shell streams update independently without the former one-second delay or query restarts. `ChatSummaries` reads only the endpoint's depth before its separate bounded last-text read. `shellUpdates.test.ts` covers push, movement, deletion and reconnect without a chat subscription; the isolation matrix covers both streams; `e2e/shellRefresh.spec.ts` checks an edit from another client appearing on Home without another shell request. The bigchat benchmark records edit-to-sidebar-stream latency alongside its forced one-shot refresh timings.

**Settlement during swipe-heavy imports (importspeed2 round 2, 2026-11-02).** The `kept` CTE is explicitly materialized: eligibility is decided once per moved chat and reused by the slot, tip and lineage reachability walks. Without the fence, SQLite inlined its correlated `NOT EXISTS` scan of `shell_touches` into each touched-version row; pinning thousands of swipe versions repeatedly scanned the same touches, quadratic in the batch's changed versions. Settlement still runs inside every write transaction and before an import computes summaries, preserving live validity, rollback and cancellation behavior. It processes the new suffix's touches without deferring validity until an import ends. `stImportBatch.test.ts` compares all stored fork summaries, exact chat/owner/summary stamps and validity flags before any shell read can repair stale rows, through both cached-prefix and positional imports.

**Touch-driven settlement (slowfix1, 2026-11-15).** Settlement uses explicit `CROSS JOIN` order from `shell_touches` to version identities and then their slots, for participation discovery and touched-path projection. Adding `versions_lcm_inputs` changed SQLite's cost estimates so the human-activity arm otherwise scanned every version on every import batch, including when that batch had no human-version touches. The indexed probes bound this work to the transaction's touches; the planning index and both shell and LCM stamp triggers remain intact. `summaryValidityPlan.test.ts` inspects the actual settlement statements against the full baseline in a worker and requires version-identity searches, avoiding a host-dependent timing assertion. Existing validity/import comparisons and `bigchatScale.test.ts` cover results and owner-scale live costs. No schema, invalidation rule or model request changes.

**Large imported chats (bigchat, 2026-11-03).** Slot-touch settlement deduplicates touched chain/depth pairs and walks each affected chat's fork-tip chain segments, testing interval membership rather than enumerating every descendant message of an old touched slot. The existing indexes serve the lookups; conservative whole-chat invalidation for moved slots and insertions, tip-move reachability, frozen lineages, and settlement inside the transaction are unchanged. A refresh of at most two views, including reads after a send or reply, reads only those paths and their live parents, using the existing small-import-refresh strategy; it does not load the chat's entire tree just because the changed fork has no overrides. The shell's plain-fork check also respects each lineage entry's frozen sequence: a parent's later selection, replacement or deletion cannot disable the shared-tree read for branches made before that choice. `test/shellPlainForks.test.ts` checks older nested forks and a choice inherited at its exact bound. `test/bigchatScale.test.ts` imports one synthetic chat at 100/200/400 branches, 750/1,500/3,000 messages per complete path and 40 swipes on roughly 30% of messages, then measures WebSocket open, old-page, send, fake generation, swipe, old fork, branch navigation and old edit RPCs with the shell refresh after each. It runs in `test:slow`; `BIGCHAT_SIZES` selects fractions of the full shape and `BIGCHAT_OUT` writes timing JSON and worker-backed synthetic snapshots outside the checkout. `BIGCHAT_REUSE` replays live operations from those synthetic snapshots, in another imported full-length fork, retaining the original import timings separately. The fixture uses short prose to isolate graph/version counts; the benchmark reports RPC/server latency, excluding browser paint and real-model inference.

**Independent summary review coverage (review-perfshell2, 2026-11-14).** The stored-versus-from-scratch model also mixes chat/fork renames, split markers, card archive/bin/restore, thread starts/renames/Undo, chat merges and thread joins (and deletion/restoration of their join messages), and writes by another account. Each check compares both accounts; a foreign write must preserve the first account's complete read, including the set requiring recomputation. Unexpected defects fail the model instead of counting as refused writes. Typed operation refusals and choices with no applicable target remain part of the random sequences, so a successful model step is not necessarily a committed mutation. This complements the SQL/path oracle and import/re-import suites; it is not proof of arbitrary out-of-process SQL mutations.

**Dense chats (perfshell2, 2026-11-14).** A chat with hundreds of long branches (synthetic: 200 branches of 1,000 messages, 30% of messages with 20–50 swipes) cost one shell read about 10 s per 1,000-message depth; at 200 branches of 5,000 messages, 91 s. The walk read every fork's whole path again (`shellSlotsQuery`, one query per batch of forks), since nearly every imported branch selects something; and every write to any branch moved the chat's stamp, so a walk that outlasted the next write (a streaming reply writes every few hundred milliseconds) could never be stored. Three changes, none to what a read answers:
- *Batch path resolver* (`db/forkPaths.ts`, `makePathResolver`). A walk of more than two forks (`computeForkSummaries`, `computeForkOutlines`) reads each chat's slot tree once with each slot's selected version (one indexed `json_each` read per batch of new chats), each lineage fork's `select`/`replace`/`delete_slot`/`suppress_event` rows once (unused lineages are evicted after loading toward a 400,000-row cache target; the current batch's required lineages stay even when they exceed it), the chat's events once in event order, and the evidence of the slots walked. Each fork's path is then followed in JS from its tip by parent while depth falls, applying its lineage's overrides at their frozen sequence bounds, ending where the version it shows is missing, exactly as `shellSlotsQuery`'s rows end; events apply `fork_labels` visibility, supersession, suppression, slot deletion and version scope as `shellEventsQuery` does. Message slots shared by forks that show their own selection share one row object. A refresh of one or two forks keeps the per-fork SQL, and so does a chat with at most eight of the forks walked (`PATHS_ALONE`) unless the resolver already holds its tree: on chats of 5,000 messages the tree read cost as much as walking 8 (200 branches) to 16–32 (600 branches, 3.6 M overrides) forks alone; three forks 1.4–1.7 s alone vs 4.5–8.0 s from the tree, and 3.6 s vs 17.6–26.5 s. Digests of every fork's paths and events matched the SQL path on both dense seeds; `test/forkPaths.test.ts` compares each live fork's summary and outline from one batch against each fork walked alone after a seeded run of appends, branches, swipes, selections, message and swipe deletion, insertions, hides, fork-only replacement copies, event suppressions, scoped joins/leaves and fork deletion. Measured cold (no stored summaries, reader only, load 30–60 on 48 cores): 200×1,000 from 10.5 s to 5.5 s, 200×5,000 from 91 s to 35–39 s (tree read 8 s, override rows 6 s, JS the rest).
- *Validity per fork, persisted* (`db/baseline.ts`, `db/summaryValidity.ts`). `fork_shell_stamps` holds, per fork, the chat stamp at which a noted write last reached it; `chat_shell_tracked` holds the chat stamp after the last write whose reach the writer noted. A summary is valid (`summaryValidSql`) when its format and owner stamp are current and either its `stamp` (the chat stamp it was computed at) is the chat's stamp now (nothing it reads changed since, noted or not; summaries stored before the chat was tracked stay valid), or it is before the chat's, at or after its fork's, and the chat's tracked stamp is the chat's stamp. Settlement upserts the reached forks' rows (all forks of a chat a write reaches whole, or whose stamp moved unnoted) instead of moving every unreached summary's stamp, so a write costs the forks it reaches, and a summary computed while another branch was written can still be stored. `StoreForkSummaries` stores a row only while its chat is tracked and its stamp is at or after the fork's; a chat never tracked (a database from before, or one written only by another connection) is reconciled by a store whose claim is the chat's current stamp. `FORK_SUMMARY_FORMAT` is 10, so older stored summaries are recomputed once.
- *Materialization in parts*. Before `ShellMaterialize` reads the library, the reader service stores stale summaries part by part: `ShellSummarizeStale` (a background read) computes stale forks (excluding unfinished imports) ordered by chat, 16 a batch, batches until about one second has passed, and returns them with how many remain; `StoreForkSummaries` stores each part. The worker keeps the part's resolver for the next part while the owner's stamp is unchanged, with each chat's stamp from before its tree was read: a write since reaches only some forks (their `fork_shell_stamps` pass that stamp), the others are walked from the kept tree and stored as computed at that stamp, and the reached ones wait until no unreached fork is left, when the trees are read again (`test/forkPaths.test.ts`, "a kept tree", compares them with each fork walked after the writes). So a reply streaming into a long chat doesn't make every part read its tree again (perf fixture, 200 forks of a 120,000-message chat: parts of 5 s, each rereading the tree, became parts of 1.1 s). It stops when nothing is left or two parts in a row leave no fewer forks than the fewest so far (`storeStaleParts`; one write can cost a part: the first noted write to a chat never tracked stales all its forks, which on the 200×5,000 seed made the materialization compute 170 forks itself, 39 s); the materialization then computes what remains, and stores it under the same gate before answering, so a branch read waiting there finds it stored. The one-second target is checked between batches, not within a statement or a batch: a first tree read or a dense batch can hold its reader much longer. Stored completed parts survive writes to other branches and a restart; the in-memory resolver itself does not survive a restart. Parts take only chats with more than two stale forks, which share a tree: one or two (a chat after a write, a small chat) are walked by the read that wants them, by their paths, once, since a reply streaming into the chat would waste every part's walk of them. A chat's branch reads (`ListForks`, and `GetSplitChats` and `ThreadsOf` when their bounded preflight declines; `GetSplitChats` first tries the stored summaries, below) first store that chat's stale summaries the same way (`chatId`). Every part, computed and stored, holds a per-user gate, so a part queued on another reader starts after the previous one is stored and never computes the same forks again. So they read stored rows instead of each computing every fork's outline again without storing it (on the 200×1,000 seed, cold: `ListForks` 4.7 s and 2.9 s, `GetSplitChats` 2.6 s and 2.4 s, all repeated work, before).
- *Measured with the development fake generator* (`perfshell2` dense matrix: a fresh server on a copy of the seed, a link to the middle of the long branch with the chats panel open, one append during the cold load and one after it settled, then a restart; times from opening the link; load 40–100 on 48 cores, so ±30%). 200×1,000: text 1.3–1.5 s, composer 1.6–2.5 s, every panel row 11 s (before: 43 s), the next append's row 0.8–1.3 s, after a restart all of it 1.5–1.7 s. 200×5,000: text 1.4–2.4 s, composer 4.7–7.5 s (`GetLcmState`, 4–5 s at that depth, is most of it), panel 52–61 s (before: first row 91 s, the current row 394 s), the next append's row 2.9–5.4 s (3.3 s before), after a restart 3.1–3.3 s. 600×5,000: text 1.7 s, composer 6.6 s, panel 227 s (master: 1,064 s for the first row), the next append's row 8.3 s, after a restart 4.7 s. A part's first batch reads the chat's whole tree, so on a 600×5,000 chat one part holds a background reader for up to 35 s; the panel lists no rows until the last part is stored. The perf fixture on a fresh server (no stored summaries; 200 forks each in a 120,000- and a 40,000-message chat) with six replies started in the long chat at once: the panel's first answer at 36–37 s against master's 35–38 s, but the replies start in 1.6–1.8 s, where on master `Regenerate` waits 31–37 s behind the one shell read. The development generator bypasses `ContextGenerator`; normal context planning, assembly and provider first-token latency require separate measurements.
- *Indexes*. Of perfred1's four covering indexes, `versions_shell` (9% of the 200×5,000 file) makes the resolver's tree read 4–5× faster (1.0 s against 5.0 s) and the evidence and two-fork path reads 20–40% faster, and `versions_slot_human_authors` (partial, near zero bytes) the evidence read 2–3× faster. The covering columns of `slots_chat_depth` and `slots_shell_chain` (17 MB and 30 MB there, 1.7% together) showed no difference beyond noise on the shell's reads, warm or with an 8 MiB page cache, now that the shell no longer reads the plain tree by chat; they stay, since the chain-range reads of the rest of the app (display paths, history, bin, the summary planner) use them and weren't measured without them. Writer cost: alternating six-run passes of 100 `AddVersion` and 100 `AppendMessage` on the 200×1,000 seed, each variant without one index against all four, differ by under 1.5 ms (median 9–12 ms) in either direction. A bulk rewrite is another matter (perfshell3): a workshop publication adds one swipe to each of 5,000 slots, so every slot-keyed version index dirties about one leaf page per slot, and the wider its entries the more of them there are. perfred1's `versions_shell` (slot, id and eight metadata columns) beside the `UNIQUE (slot_id, ordinal)` constraint's index did that twice over (`workshopRewriteScale`: publication 2.6 s, profiled, against master's 1.4 s: the `versions` insert 595 ms against 174, `COMMIT` 782 against 392). It is split now. `versions_shell (slot_id, ordinal, id, purged_at)` holds only what participation reads of every swipe, and it is the slot's only version index: the constraint is gone and the `versions_slot_ordinal_unique` trigger keeps ordinals unique by probing it (`slot_id` and `ordinal` never change, `versions_identity_fixed`). The shown version's shell fields moved to `versions_shell_meta`, keyed by id: a new version's id (UUIDv7) sorts after the others, so a rewrite appends to it instead of touching a page per slot. The shell's joins (slot and id) search it by id, covered. A synthetic 5,000-slot, 175,000-version table, one new version per slot in one transaction (sqlite3, three runs each): master's indexes 0.52–0.60 s, master's plus perfred1's 1.12 s, the split 0.47–0.56 s. What it still cost was `versions_shell`'s `id` column. One new version per slot of the test's 5,000-message chat, on a copy of its database after the rename: master's indexes take 220–240 ms to insert and 175–190 ms to commit, these 320–380 and 270–300 ms, and these without `id` in `versions_shell` 235–270 and 185–210 ms. **Since stack4** (2026-11-15) the column is gone: `versions_shell (slot_id, ordinal, purged_at)`, and participation reaches a swipe's cast by its seq (every index entry's rowid) through `version_participants.version_seq` (`version_participants_seq (version_seq, entity_id)`, appended to as versions are, set by the same triggers); settlement's evidence check joins the same way. And the bulk publication states each copy's `content_length` (`length` of its text) in the `versions` insert, so `version_texts_length_insert`, which now fires only when the stored length differs, no longer updates 5,000 fresh rows and their indexes. Replaying the publication's statements on copies of each tree's test database just before its first rewrite (`synchronous = FULL`, five alternating rounds, load 25–29): job/stack3 909 ms (commit 303 ms, 5,824 WAL pages), stack4 before this 1,090 ms (commit 433 ms, 7,994 pages), with the stated length 1,012 ms, with both 938 ms (commit 320 ms, 6,271 pages). Merging `versions_shell_meta` into `versions_lcm_inputs` saved 150 pages and nothing measurable, so both stay. The whole `workshopRewriteScale` publication (rewrite and rename), five alternating rounds against job/stack3, loads 15–47: stack4 1,007–1,196 ms (median 1,125) against 1,149–1,302 ms (median 1,225), none near the 1.5 s limit. The rename also paid 300 ms of settlement, now gone (§3.7, summary-stamp settlement). Unprofiled and alternating, under load averages of 20–40 from other jobs. Against master with slowfix1 (`e693ec88`), two rounds: first publication 1.50 s and 1.50 s against 1.37 and 1.46 s, rename 1.53 and 2.31 s against 1.63 and 1.33 s. Against `d97da4ae`, three rounds before that merge: 1.13/1.37, 1.89/1.69 and 1.59/1.33 s against 1.19/1.36, 1.70/1.84 and 1.22/1.05 s. Both trees miss the 1.5 s budget at times under these loads. The publication's guard against a generating reply (`generatingIn`, `db/forkState.ts`) reads the partial `versions_generating` index first; the planner had taken a covering slot/version index and scanned the chat's every version (360 ms there).

**Branch lists while the first pass runs (perfshell3, 2026-11-15).** A cold library's branch lists don't wait for its first pass (`ShellMaterialize` after every part is stored: minutes at 300 branches of thousands of messages). `WatchShellForks` waits `PARTIAL_AFTER` (300 ms) for the shared snapshot, else reads `ShellMaterializePartial` (an ordinary read; it reads metadata and, for thread candidates, indexed display-path intervals): every live fork is listed, and one without a valid stored summary is a `pending` row with only what its fork record says (name, pin, chat, creation) and an exact `endAt` for ordering. The usual endpoint is one indexed tip lookup; the maximum insertion anchor is read once per chat, so checking for possible after-tip insertions does not rescan all its anchors for each pending fork. A deleted tip or a possible insertion at its end seeks backwards through indexed display intervals to the last undeleted slot. `shellProgress.test.ts` counts actual anchor inspections and compares pending endpoints with full computation, including a first insertion with no structural tip. Its preview, length, cast and split are empty. Thread membership is resolved from split labels and indexed path intervals before projecting rows, so pending threads retain their group and do not inflate branch counts. Its chat's name is `""` where that name comes from the cast of a pending current fork, and the snapshot is never memoized. `forksView` adds `loading: { ready, total }` while any fork the view lists is pending (a chat's forks for a branch list; in a chat list a chat is ready only when every branch is ready), and a search matches pending forks by their own name and their chat's only. The browse control shows unknown filter counts as ‘…’ until all branches are read. A stream whose answer is still loading reads again once the full snapshot is ready or a second later (`PROGRESS_EVERY`), whichever is first; the shared materialization goes on regardless of who waits. Parts read each chat's current fork first, alone and by its path (no tree read), most recently used chats first, then each chat's forks by their distance from the current one in its branch list. `GetSplitChats` answers from the stored summaries when that is exact (`GetSplitChatsPartial`: a chat with no split chats whose name doesn't need a pending fork's cast), else after one part of the chat, and only then after all of it; meanwhile it starts that chat's parts in the background (`ahead`, once per chat), between the library's under the user's gate, so the open chat fills in first. `SHELL_PASS_PAUSE_MS` (default 0) waits before every part but the library pass's first (a chat's parts, read ahead or for a branch read, wait before their first as well); tests use it to hold a pass half done. The client draws a pending row in the same boxes as a read one (title line, two preview lines, the when line). A branch row that has been pending retains space for added portraits and its date until it unmounts, including the narrow row’s portrait band, so filling those fields changes neither row nor text geometry; rows first mounted complete keep their usual compact layout. A chat row in a chat list that has been pending (stack4, 2026-11-15) holds two portrait boxes from the start: the chat's picture shows at once in the first when the chat has one (the shell's own owner-scoped `pictureOf`, which needs no stored summary, so a pending row never shows another chat's picture), else the faces fill the boxes as the row is read, with the overflow count beside them; before that the boxes are quiet bars and the hover list is off. `chatPicture.test.ts` checks pending rows' pictures against the full read (a split chat's own, none for a plain or another account's chat); `branchProgress.spec.ts` checks pictured and unpictured, one- and three-character cold chat rows keep their boxes as they fill, at 1440/390 in both themes.
