The macros that number messages count positions (the omitted count is the first entry's position less the cursor's). `historyStart` translates the recorded start (`previousStartIn` in `db/historyStart.ts`): the candidate walk stays structural, and the start's depth becomes its position on the display path through the leaf (a start at the target: its rollout's message); `rollouts.history_start_depth` is recorded as the start slot's depth (`generationWrites.ts`), since the snapshot's is a position. `historyRevision` counts the fork's reductions at positions before the boundary (`displayHistoryRevision`: the depth index bounds the changes read, since a position is never below its slot's depth, and each is placed among the pieces), so deleting or hiding an inserted message before the start is a reduction there; an insertion writes no `history_changes` row. So an insertion before the start leaves the start, the revision and the cached prefix as they were, and one after it cuts nothing and changes the prefix from the inserted message on. The warmth estimate names it ("Message N was inserted.", when a message the next request reads, marked `inserted`, comes before the first message that moved), and the inspector numbers messages by the positions the snapshot pinned. Captured requests and their replays are unchanged. Not yet: an inserted message's own rollout isn't a candidate for later replies' history start (the walk is structural; a skipped candidate costs a fresh cut). LCM (§16 "Inserted messages") gives the layer's cursor, summaries' and failed ranges' `from` and `to` as display positions in a fork that shows insertions, so the stages compare positions with positions: `historyOmitted`, the retained-history minimum and the omitted ranges, the failure markers and the image omission locations. A summary request's `summaryBefore` and a condensation's cursor are positions too, and since `history` reads strictly after `after`'s position, a cursor on an inserted message, which isn't a structural ancestor of the leaf, fences the history. `NextContext.summarizedThrough` and `historyStart.depth` are positions, which the message list compares with each entry's `position` (§16 "Client data"). `test/lcmInsertRequests.test.ts` runs real summary requests through the summarizer and the mock provider: inside a range, with the cursor on an inserted message (and one inserted below it, raw), at a seam, above the first message, condensations over and across insertions, and a failed range holding an inserted message. Each request renders its whole chunk or parts in display order and completes, and the next reply sends the summaries, then the raw history after them in display order. The insertion-path target also pins `displayPositions`, so macro message arrays retain the positions of summarized history and deleted gaps; absent on paths without insertions and older snapshots, it preserves their numbering and replay keys. A next-context preview at a null structural tip still reads the fork’s above-first insertions. `test/insertionAssemblyReview.test.ts` covers that empty-tip preview, regeneration after an insertion, bounded event inheritance at X, raw history immediately after a summary cursor and a byte-identical synthetic request captured from master’s assembler version 38. `test/steppedHistory.test.ts` ("stepped history with inserted messages", over the database), `test/forkStateEvents.test.ts`, `test/inspector.test.ts` and `test/imageExclusion.test.ts` cover it.

`history_changes` holds sparse reductions keyed by slot, fork and sequence (`fork_id`, `''` for every fork). A fork's entry carries its fork's label (`label`): it counts in that fork and the forks made from it afterwards (`labelVisibleSql`), so earlier entries stay readable in descendants after further parent reductions, and making a fork copies none. Local deletion marks do not also increment a global counter; explicit global purges do. Worker-side triggers count deletions and hiding; content and selection writers compare JavaScript UTF-16 lengths in the same transaction to count shortening, including emoji and embedded NULs. Ordinary appends do not enter the index. `historyRevision` sums only changes on the requested path before the boundary, with an indexed empty-set exit. The cut state stores the budget, configuration digest, admitted example count and reduction revision. `SourcePins.historyStart` and `historyRevisions` pin the reads, including null/zero, so replay ignores later changes. Worker tests replay every recorded generation after interval sends, branch changes, pre-boundary reductions and raised budgets; unit tests compare complete prefixes across ST, concat and swap-tail layouts and four post-processing modes.

**Own-turn card notes** (ownturn1, 2026-11-13; CHARACTER-CONTEXT §4.2–§4.3, built using its [P] mechanisms). A card note’s `{ when: "own_turn" }` condition refers to its owner card, without a library id. It holds only when that card is the target version’s speaker, including persona, narrator, regenerated/swiped and agent turns. Card swaps change the owner through the existing copied-note mechanism; the self condition needs no remapping. Separate contexts and card rotation remain independent. The agent’s note lookups hide another viewer’s self-conditioned notes, as they hide explicitly turn-conditioned notes.

The `section: own_turn` placement goes at the preset’s `ownTurnNotes` marker, sent in its chosen role (system by default) in the card’s `<Name>…</Name>` wrapper. It holds only the speaker’s notes whose conditions are due; skipped notes produce provenance without expanding macros. Built-in and imported ST presets insert the marker after history and its adjacent Newest message, before tail prompts. The preset editor reuses the marker rows and drag handles, offers Insert Own-turn notes below in each block’s menu, allows removal, lists the slot’s notes and warns when moved above history. A missing/disabled effective marker falls back to the start of the tail, recording “Own-turn notes sent at the start of the tail: this preset has no Own-turn notes marker”. A self-conditioned note can instead use any ordinary placement. A note before history bounds reuse whether it is due or skipped; the default marker leaves the entire prefix before it identical between speakers. The existing cache popover additionally names both speakers when own-turn notes precede history and their mapped requests differ: “Mira's turn starts differently from Tobin's: ~36,400 tokens are written again when Mira's cached copy has expired.” It counts the affected suffix of the actual mapped request with the selected local text counter and image estimates. Names come from the owner-scoped pinned card revisions. This conditional notice is separate from warm/cold status and can appear without a known TTL. As a delta from reference-harness’s cache-control checkpoints, it adds information only: existing breakpoints, TTL rules and final checkpoint stay in effect. Assembler version **68** pins these changes and the independent own-turn review fixes (above both merged parents at 67). The inspector labels each self-conditioned source **Own-turn note**; a skipped one is in **Not sent this turn**, with “only on Mira’s turns” (the actual card’s name).

**Move to an own-turn note**, a registered field view (`own-turn-notes.field`), appears in the text strip for Description, Personality, Scenario, Example messages, System prompt and Post-history instructions, in both card editor layouts. Select a passage and press its note action. `MoveToOwnTurnNote` (its own authenticated API group, to stay below the core handler group’s type-size bound) checks the saved card revision and exact selected text and writes both notes in one writer transaction. It leaves the card field untouched: an ordinary self-targeting replacement note holds the remaining text; the own-turn note holds the selected passage after the editable `OWN_TURN_FRAMING` background sentence. Repeated moves from a field update its same replacement and add separately titled own-turn notes. An existing unrelated replacement refuses the move. A linked shared replacement also refuses a further move until unlinked, since its slot content is not the text it sends. Text edited in the source is checkpointed through the existing editor before moving. No model is contacted. The stored JSON adds the self condition, placement and optional `move_group`; no SQL tables or columns change.

The field uses **As replaced / Original** tabs and a local-tokenizer line, for example “~1,000 every turn · ~2,000 only on Mira’s turns · SillyTavern gets the original”. Replacement edits use the note’s normal drafts and leave guard. The Notes tab groups all notes of a field move under **Moved from Description**, with one per-chat switch. `graphWrites.insertStateEvent` writes the group’s switches in the same transaction, with the same position, version and origin, restricted to the same owner card and account; swipes and forks retain ordinary state semantics. Portable group ids are scoped by owner, so a copied card does not switch its source’s notes. Export carries the group with the condition and self-target; import restores them without granting agent permissions. Every card Export… goes through the common notice when notes replace fields, offering **Export** or **Open the notes** before downloading the original card text. The workshop exposes `move_card_text` through the same `MoveToOwnTurnNote` operation and its registered `changeset.apply` undo policy (`library.write`, library effect). `read_card` includes the saved card notes; `edit_card_note` uses `AgentReviseEntity` and its existing library revision Undo, preserving the note’s condition, placement and replacement target. These tools belong to the Cards skill. Library list/read tools are marked `replyTool: false`, so a story’s tool settings cannot offer `read_card` or `list_library` to bypass replaced fields or note filtering. The user’s workshop assistant, including a side chat, may read their owned library’s original fields and all own-turn notes; this is an out-of-character user agent, not a character’s knowledge boundary.

**Independent own-turn review** (review-ownturn1, 2026-11-13). Note-tool audience is carried as `Generation.speaker` / `ToolContext.speaker`, independently of separate-history and thread viewers. Narrator and persona runs therefore cannot list, edit or switch another card’s own-turn note; every title lookup filters before producing errors. Shared summaries omit all own-turn text; a private summary may include it only for its single owner audience and when notes are enabled. Summary inputs keep moved field replacements even with notes disabled, so the original passage cannot return through definitions. Frozen summary prefixes compare sent card/note pieces before reuse in shared contexts too; ordinary volatile preset prefixes retain their existing freezing behavior. Field macros (including example dialogue), template history and lorebook description/key scanning read replacements rather than raw fields. Stored originals and exports remain unchanged.

Moves refuse cut macros, cut HTML tags and unbalanced selected elements; text inside an element, whole elements, whole fields and paragraph-spanning plain text are supported. Each move records both before/after note revisions in the existing library edit history. **Undo move** uses `UndoLibraryEdit`; the same record remains accessible in Search and replace’s recent list after reload. Initial note revisions are off, with an empty own-turn note and the full shared source. Undo restores those revisions, retaining the moved passage in immutable History. Later moves record the existing shared replacement before changing it. If either note has a later edit or active draft, the whole paired inverse is refused with an explanation; ordinary library replaces retain their per-entry conflict behavior. Deleting either side first explains whether the original field returns or the passage stops being sent, and how to restore it. Both card editor layouts use the same controls. `noteSwitches(events, notes)` projects a card-scoped group’s last explicit switch onto all its current members, including passages moved later; assembly, the chat list and agent tools use that projection. The fold is linear in events plus members. A move after Undo reactivates the restored shared replacement; a deliberately disabled group with retained private text refuses a further move until turned on, preventing missing passages. Empty historical placeholders do not supply a group’s visible switch when a later moved note has text. No new tables or SQL columns; move history uses existing `changeset_groups`, `library_edit_items` and revision `origin_ref` metadata.


**Note slots.** Notes support explicit `context_start`, `tail_start` and `tail_end` sections as well as existing card sections, before/after-main placement and depth injections. The tail starts after history and an adjacent newest-message marker, or directly after history when newest was moved later. Several notes in one slot keep their order (rank, then id). Tail-end notes precede generation control directives; a newest-message marker moved after the tail follows those directives. Legacy `tail` remains ST depth zero, preserving imported behavior. The editor lists active sent notes at those positions, including their actual depths.

**The snapshot** (`types.ts`, DATA-MODEL §7.1, invariant 6) holds:
- the assembler semantics version (`ASSEMBLER_VERSION`, currently 80; historical changes: 40 is fctx's context window, 41 Continue without a prefill, 42 the regex scripts from every list and the reasoning scripts on reply sections sent back, 43 no author's note, 44 preset lorebooks in place of global books, 45 structural cache breakpoints, 47 agent replies' assembly, 48 notes that replace prompts; absent means 0)
- what it was built from: chat, slot, version, the leaf, the clock and time zone, type, speaker, mode, the preset's ref, revision and scope, each card's ref and revision, the model
- the request and its resulting history start and movement reason
- every piece with its source and the messages it went into (a card block's fields included)
- the enabled preset prompts their condition or their ST triggers left out this turn (`skippedPrompts`, by preset source with the condition, or with the triggers it is sent for), for the inspector's "not sent" list; absent in older snapshots and when none were
- the issues the user should see: a prefill dropped, a piece left out, history or examples cut by the budget
- the values drawn per piece, and the variable writes

- what the sources read, pinned (`SourcePins`): the state events by id, the path's versions with their amend counts (and the rest of what was read of them, but their text), and each card and note read by revision, keyed by what it asked for. Revisions and state events never change, and an amended version keeps its earlier texts (`version_history`), so the pins hold everything else the context depended on.

`RebuildContext` checks the recorded assembler version first [P: the assembler code is an explicit input]. The integer constant is bumped whenever assembly output for the same inputs changes; version 1 was the first bump; version 2 fixes note expansion dependencies and skipped-note composition; version 3 moves cache boundaries for variable readers after intermittent notes; version 4 activates and places lorebooks; version 5 bounds lazy previews, reserves stable tail capacity, resolves primary sources, pins path counts and fixes ST example ordering/empty wrappers; version 6 makes frozen macro work replay identically, pins legacy import filenames and caps the tail reservation by eligible stored content; version 7 records historical note activation and interval decisions on source pieces; version 8 pins stepped history state and counts every reserved consumer toward both thresholds; version 9 pins durable restoration inputs and example admission; version 10 preserves full note text, shares unused note capacity and pins observed expansion sizes; version 11 adds the LCM layer and cursor; version 12 adds frozen summary requests; version 13 fixes summary placement and framing; version 14 pins triggering reply prefixes and integrates LCM with stepped history and historical cache lifetimes; version 15 loads the persona's notes, places notes at the author's note's top and bottom and with a card's definition, and sends a persona placed by its note instead of by the persona-description marker; version 16 preserves persona card-section notes in our layouts and treats an activated interval-zero author's note as off for attachments; version 17 preserves stepped raw-history starts with LCM and omits zero-content lineage from rendered summary prose; version 18 expands the summarization instruction’s `{{words}}` with the job’s target; version 19 budgets and pins failed-range markers after raw history overflows; version 22 uses CCv3 nickname fallback for the model’s card names throughout assembly; version 23 takes generation settings from the model and global selections rather than the prompt preset; version 24 separates the newest-message marker, adds explicit note slots, and records root pieces’ prompt slots for editor annotations; version 25 keeps several notes in one slot in their order and bounds the default response length by the context size in use and, for a schema continuation, by the model's output limit less the source prefix; the RP loop's version 26 sent preset prompts by their conditions with `{{speaker}}` and `{{direction}}`, replaced the tail directive and the verbatim system direction with the imported group nudge, impersonation and direction prompts, and closed a request that would end on the model's side with a user turn; the assembly unit's version 26 removed ST-compatible mode for the one assembly path (per-field joins, the Definitions marker, the speaker's card overrides, global books, lorebook placement by the chat's setting, pinned lore and the breakpoint priority); version 27 combines both units' version 26 changes on one path (conditioned prompts with the per-field joins, the Definitions marker, the card overrides and lorebook placement); the summarization unit's version 26 added the summarization pairs, the explicit `{{summary}}`, summary notes placed by their switch alone, and summary requests without the preset; **version 28 combines it with version 27** (the pairs and the explicit `{{summary}}` on the one assembly path, where the layer always takes the `<summaries>` block and ST mode's layer placement is gone); the notes unit's version 26 sent notes by their conditions instead of intervals, added the lorebook scan switch, `on_by_default` in place of the first-note rule, linked shared notes and what rides on a switched-off author's note; **version 29 combines it with version 28** (notes' conditions, links and `on_by_default` on the one assembly path, where the imported summary note is a chat note switched on like any other and `{{summary}}` reads only one that is on and due, and "with the definitions" stays after the main prompt, owner question 2, whatever unit 3's Definitions marker does with the cards). Version 30 is the RP loop of PHASE1-DECISIONS §2: the closing user turn right after the last chat message, and only without a user-role message after it; ST triggers as a filter beside conditions; the speaking card's prompts on impersonation turns; departed speakers naming their messages; version 30 also, from the notes fix batch, wraps the persona's part like every cast card's and puts each card at the Definitions marker in that wrapper, places a card's note "with the definitions" inside its card's part (volatile when conditioned), never leaves a persona's description out for a note's kind or title, and reads ST's Character's Note from a card's in-chat notes that are on; version 30 also, from the summarization fix batch, sends each summary as its own message before the history, `{{summary}}` reading only the summary notes (DESIGN §8, owner 2026-10-28), summary requests without notes unless the chat includes them, and the summary length in words. Version 31 makes Main a permanent slot, adding it first and off when an older preset lacks it, so notes beside that empty slot are sent. Version 32 resolves chat-scoped shared-note/snippet links through the viewed fork’s revision binding. Version 34 enforces one selected persona and scalar `{{user}}` expansion, retaining historical requests from earlier versions without replaying them through the new fold. Version 48 sends a note that replaces a preset prompt or card field in its place (Replacements, below). Version 49 expands a replacing note's `{{original}}` at its own position and keeps conditional replacement slots outside the cached prefix even when empty or overridden by a card.

Version 41 continues on a model without a prefill (§15 "Continue") and moves ST's continue nudge into the end-of-request texts. Version 42 runs prompt scripts from every registered list (global, preset, character) and on world-info entries, records which scripts changed each piece, and runs reasoning (placement 6) scripts on reply sections sent back. Version 38 adds image token budgeting, explicit oversized-newest/chunk failures and image content/detail cache digests. Version 39 assembles a fork's display path by position (§15 "Inserted messages"); chats without insertions assemble byte for byte as in version 38. Version 35 combines the end-of-request instruction with version 34’s single-persona bindings: the turn and direction remain one separate final user message after post-processing; summary instructions also use the final user message with or without the preset; the empty-text fallback checks the actual final role, including system prompts. Raw summary cache markers and estimates cover continuity only. The built-in preset and new prompt presets use the balanced end-of-request defaults. End-text macros expand after other text and before prefill, preventing end writes from changing the prefix.

Version 43 drops the author's note (DESIGN §4.1, owner 2026-11-01): no note carries what's placed at its top or bottom, and a chat without an author's note gets no default one; old requests keep their recorded assembly.

Version 44 reads a preset's lorebooks in place of the user's global books (owner 2026-11-01): there are no global books, and the preset's enabled `lorebooks` are read after the chat's attached ones; old requests keep their recorded assembly.

Version 36 makes the explicit `author_note.set` choice override an imported author-note kind and treats an explicit null as no author's note, so old requests keep their recorded assembly rather than replaying through the changed precedence.

Version 37 adds the registered `images` stage: an image the user took out of the context in a fork, or one a rule leaves out, is left out of the request with its reason recorded.

An older snapshot returns `EarlierAssemblerVersion` with its version, the current version and the original snapshot intact as `storedSnapshot`, without attempting replay or claiming missing chat data. The stored request remains available internally; the public inspector requires a sanitized final capture. A current-version snapshot returns `Rebuilt` with `snapshot` (callers must narrow the tag to access either field) and builds again from its pins, its inputs (the model as resolved, the preset's revision), its clock and the values drawn, rather than from the chat as it is now: after the user amends a message, a card or the preset moves on, or a state event is added, it still gives the same snapshot (`test/assemblyStorage.test.ts`). A card, note or preset in the bin still rebuilds, since its revisions are kept and never change; it fails, with the reason, only when something pinned was deleted for good. Only the chat's owner can rebuild it: every pinned read is the owner's. A context whose prompt regex scripts ran out of time can come back different where the deadline fell; lore activation’s emergency result is pinned.

**Where scripts come from** (`scriptSources.ts`, `Assembler.scriptSources`). Each list is a registered `ScriptSource` (`id`, `scope`, `scripts(assembly)`), run in registration order; the built-ins are ST 1.19's, in its order (engine.js `SCRIPT_TYPES`: global, preset, scoped): `regex.global`, the account's global list (`AssemblySources.globalRegex`, pinned in `SourcePins.globalRegex`, no approval, as ST's global scripts), `regex.preset`, the preset's once `regex_approved`, and `regex.character`, the character's (`CardDoc.regex`) once that card's `regex_approved`. The character is ST's `this_chid`: in a prompt, the speaker when the model writes as a character, else the chat's one character; for text being written, its card on the model's side, the chat's one character on the user's (a group has no current character when the user sends). A plugin adds a list, wraps one or disables it by id. Each script compiled carries its `ScriptRef`; the issue for one left out names its list ("The global regex script …"). The pieces a script changed record it (`Piece.scripts`): history messages, templates and lorebook entries, and the inspector lists them on the source (`ContextSource.scripts`, names scrubbed), shown as "Changed by regex: Name (scope)". **World info** (placement 5): prompt-only scripts run on each activated or pinned entry's content as it goes in (`loreStages.ts`, as `world-info.js`), with the entry's depth when it's placed at one and no depth otherwise.

**Regex scripts** (`regex.ts`, §9). Once the user approved the preset's scripts (`regex_approved`), its prompt-only ones (and those of the other lists, above) run on the chat as ST runs them when it builds a prompt: on the user's or the model's side, within their depths, in order, before names are added. A pattern comes from a file, and `(a+)+$` takes exponential time on some inputs with a backtracking engine, so every script runs on V8's linear-time engine: the `l` flag, with `--enable-experimental-regexp-engine` set when the module loads, for the whole process (V8 calls flags set after startup unsupported; Node 24.15 honors it in the main thread and in workers). V8's fallback from the backtracking engine after too many backtracks (`--enable-experimental-regexp-engine-on-excessive-backtracks`), which would run ordinary patterns about 50 times faster, is not used: it doesn't fall back on some patterns the linear engine takes (`(?:(a?)(a?)…x){16}` over 1,000 `a`s ran for minutes), and a VM timeout doesn't stop it there (fregexr). That engine takes no `i` or `u`, so a case-insensitive pattern is rewritten with both cases of each ASCII letter, in classes and ranges too (`caseless`, tested against V8's own `i` on sample patterns), and `u` is dropped unless the pattern uses `\p{…}` or `\u{…}`. What the engine refuses (backreferences, lookaheads, nested counted repeats) is left out and reported, never run. The linear engine's time still grows with the pattern times the text, and no count of that predicts it (a review measured a 902-character nested pattern over 43,000 characters at over 8 s), so the scripts run with a deadline: each batch of messages is a `vm` script with a timeout, which V8 enforces by stopping whatever runs, a regex included, in the main thread or a worker. Matches are found with `exec` in a loop rather than `String.prototype.replace`: V8 13.6's `replace` with a function loops forever, where no timeout reaches, on an empty match of a global linear-engine pattern with 32 or more groups. A context gets 200 ms in all; past that the rest of its messages go without scripts, and the issue says so. Every character the scripts make, replaced or copied, is charged to 8 million per context, so neither a long replacement nor a script copying long messages can grow without bound; a script that runs out, or throws, is skipped for that message and reported, never a failed assembly. A message a script was skipped for, for time or output, is volatile for the cache breakpoints (below): what ran out depends on the messages read before it, newest first. Each context also allows at most 100 scripts and patterns of 2,000 characters after the rewrite. A context built again can differ from its snapshot only where the deadline fell, which a busy host moves: the issue is recorded either way. The rewrite only ever matches less than `i` would: non-ASCII letters, letters in escapes, and ranges between cases match as written. Without `u`, a character class or `.` sees an emoji as two characters. V8's fallback to the linear engine after too much backtracking was tried first: it skips every pattern with an `i` or `u` flag, and a review measured `(a+)+$` with `i` taking 6.7 s on 26 characters.

**Lorebook activation** (`loreStages.ts`, `lorebook.ts`). Registered stages run inside the assembler’s reader transaction. Books come from the chat's attached books that are on (`ChatState.lorebooks`, below) on the selected path, then the preset's enabled books (`PresetDoc.lorebooks`, below) the chat hasn't attached (one in both is read once, as the chat's), and the cast’s embedded `character_book`s, personas included. Attached and preset books are read alike, through `sources.lorebooks`: the ref head of a live lorebook of the chat owner's (a chat's own copy only in its chat), so an id that names anything else is read as nothing. Attached books use the ref head; its id, entity and revision are pinned, including an empty read. A card’s bound primary attachment replaces its embedded book; the embedded book is the fallback when the primary is unavailable, unless the chat turned it off (`lorebook.embedded` with `on: false`, which an ST import writes where ST never sent it, §13, and the chat settings' "<name>'s own lorebook" switch writes through `ChangeCast`'s `CardLorebook`). With no such event it's on. Earlier imports without a binding resolve `extensions.world` against the retained import filename (`entity_refs.source_path`, basename without `.json`), never the mutable document name or label. Variants inherit the upstream import identity. The resolved filename is pinned with each book so replay does not consult mutable ref metadata. No content-based deduplication is used. The association comes from pinned state/card/book revisions, and embedded fallbacks use the card’s pinned revision. Rebuilds read those revisions even after edits, detaches or binning. The preset's revision is pinned with the preset, so a rebuild reads the same list. Earlier snapshots are retained without running this assembler (`ASSEMBLER_VERSION`, above).

ST folder imports attach chat-bound, primary character and extra character books, and attach ST's `globalSelect` books to ST's selected preset (§13); persona-bound book selection has no representation. There are no global books (owner, 2026-11-01).

Lorebook replacement review coverage (`assembler.test.ts`, `assemblyStorage.test.ts`, `e2e/lorebookReplaced.spec.ts`) checks independent group-card links, swapped card forks, case and whitespace mismatches, display renames, deletion fallback and pinned replay, with the browser rows audited at 1440 and 390 in both themes.

**A chat's books stay listed when off.** `lorebook.attach` turns a book on, appending it to `ChatState.listedLorebooks` if it's new and keeping its place if it's listed; `lorebook.detach` turns it off and keeps it listed; `lorebook.remove` takes it out of the list, on or off (`removes`, like `detach`, so it may name a book in the bin). `ChatState.lorebooks`, what the stage reads, is the listed books that are on, in listed order. `ChangeCast`'s `Lorebook` writes attach or detach and `RemoveLorebook` writes remove; `Cast` carries both lists. `test/state.test.ts` covers the fold, `test/forkStateEvents.test.ts` the events per fork.

**Preset lorebooks** (`PresetDoc.lorebooks`, `@rp/shared/docs/preset.ts`): a list of `{ id, enabled }` by lorebook ref id, unique by id (drafts address an element as `["lorebooks", "id=<ref>", "enabled"]`), absent when none. They're sent with the preset whenever it's in use, each by its own switch. ST has no such field: the ST export leaves them out (`exportStPreset`) and an ST file never sets them. `LorebookPresets { ref }` (reader `LorebookPresets`, `db/lorebookSettings.ts`) lists the user's live presets whose head lists the ref, a chat's own copy while its chat isn't binned, with its switch there (`{ refId, label, enabled }`), owner-scoped. Cross-user probes cover the events (`stateKeys.test.ts`) and ops (`isolation.test.ts`); `test/assembler.test.ts` and `test/lorePins.test.ts` the reads (on, off, read once with the chat's, another user's ref read as nothing, rebuilt exactly).

The scan uses eligible path messages newest first, with speaker names and approved prompt regex transformations. Hidden, failed and empty messages do not enter it; swipes already end their path before the replaced reply. History loading supplies the greatest requested scan depth independently of the request budget (at most 1,000 messages). Message-count delays use a separate count of eligible messages on the full path, pinned independently of that bounded window, and read only when an entry of the books read has a delay (the count walks the whole path: 0.2–0.9 s on a 5,800-message chat); edits, hidden messages and branches cannot change it on rebuild. Templates are resolved against their position as usual. Description opt-ins read the first character and persona, including the first character’s active Character’s Note. Notes have no retained `scan` flag, so general scannable extension injections are left out. Resolved templates run their prompt scripts before lore scanning; composition reuses the result.

[P] Defaults follow a fresh ST install: depth 2, case-insensitive, whole words, recursion on, and a lore allowance of 25% of the assembler’s available context budget; the estimator counts four characters per token. Book depth, recursion and absolute budget overrides apply as the matcher defines below. ST global scan preferences and insertion strategy have no runtime representation. Probability has its own deterministic RNG hashed from the pinned target, time, book/card revisions and read message identities/text; it consumes no macro RNG. Keys and descriptions use read-only macro previews; content is previewed lazily only after trigger, delay, key, secondary, group and probability gates, and an already-exhausted budget. All previews share a deterministic 4,000,000-unit work allowance, charged before allocating repeat output or parsing/hash-reading input. Exhaustion leaves candidate content out with an issue. Logical handler work declared by a macro (`MacroSpec.work`, e.g. dice count for `roll`) is charged from its arguments before choosing a fresh or frozen value, so preview-limit outcomes replay exactly without rerolling. Draws are frozen by book/uid/field, but variable writes do not persist or affect other pieces. This avoids skipped entries writing chat state; it differs from ST’s content macros. If the emergency regex deadline fires, the partial matcher result and its content-preview draws/issues are retained in the snapshot and reused by RebuildContext, so the timeout does not change activation on replay.

**With "only below the history" off** (`lorebook.below_history` with `on: false`; absent is on, DESIGN §1.3), entries go where their positions say, as ST places them: at `worldInfoBefore`/`worldInfoAfter` with the preset’s `wi_format`, at depth with their role, and before/after example dialogues. Blocks and `em_bottom` reverse descending admissions, including equal-order ties; `em_top` keeps descending admissions because ST prepends those examples. Empty joined lore skips `wi_format` while retaining activation provenance. Outlets have no consumer and produce an assembly issue. World Info regex postprocessing and `placement_override` are not implemented.

**Pins.** With the setting off, entries placed above `chatHistory` in the preset's order (`before_char`/`after_char` at markers before it, `em_top`/`em_bottom` when `dialogueExamples` is before it) are recorded in the cut state as `pinnedLore` (book, revision, uid). The next generation on the path loads them when its configuration digest is unchanged and keeps them activated and placed (activation `why: pinned`), whether or not they match again; a new match above the history is added at once and pinned. When the history's start moves (a cut, a restore, LCM's cursor: the start's depth or the movement changes), entries kept only by their pin are dropped (their piece records `pin released`) and what matched this turn is pinned in their place; the cut chosen with them stays valid, as the context only shrinks. A changed configuration (a book switched, an entry edited, the preset, the setting) loads no pins. Entries after the history are never pinned and are evaluated every turn, as in ST; author's-note entries ride on that note and aren't pinned, so an author's note outside the chat is `volatile` whenever an enabled entry could ride on it. From the first place pinned lore can go, the prefix's messages are `pinned` (an empty boundary keeps that even on a turn with no entry there). The pins live in the snapshot's `historyStart.state`, which `SourcePins.historyStart` pins, so `RebuildContext` replays them exactly (`test/lorePins.test.ts`).

**Only below the history** (on, the default): **all** activated entries, constants included, whatever their position (depth entries too), go in one system block at the start of the tail: after `chatHistory`, and after `newestMessage` when that is right after it (G's `tail_start` slot), before the tail's notes, in descending admission order with stable input ties. That block is volatile and follows every cache breakpoint. History and examples reserve the smaller of 25% of available context and the estimated joined size of eligible stored content (enabled constants and entries with primary keys), including one lore message’s overhead. Empty or ineligible books reserve zero. This calculation never expands content or depends on this turn’s matches or draws, so the allowance is identical whether any entry activates or not. Macro expansion beyond that stored-text allowance is subject to the same overflow cut. An entry that would exceed it is skipped with a budget issue, even with `ignore_budget`; it cannot borrow from history. Thus activation changes neither retained history/examples nor the cached prefix. With the setting off, ST's budgeting applies. Constants stay there because probability, groups and budgets can make them change too. Retention until a compaction boundary remains deferred with LCM; activation is evaluated each assembly.

Measured alone on this host (2026-10-12), the real worker assembled a synthetic 1,000-message path with 500 entries in 101.3 ms cold and 41.9–66.2 ms warm (median 44.4 ms); `uptime`: 46 days, 13:35, load averages 24.48, 26.21, 21.71. The probe is in `assemblyStorage.test.ts`. The review’s 887 KB, 1,000-entry unmatched macro book used about 1.0 MB additional heap in 54.8 ms (previously 203 MB); the preallocation regression also verifies that a repeat exceeding the shared allowance never allocates its output.

Every activated and skipped entry has a `lorebook` source tag naming book/revision/uid, status, recursion pass and matched primary/secondary keys or skip reason. Skipped pieces have no text or request-message indices. Matcher issues (construct and suggested regex fix, unsupported controls, work/recursion limits) and exhausted token allowances become `lorebook_issue`s in the inspector.

The pure matcher takes identified books, messages newest first, descriptions, scannable injections, settings, a replayable random source and a token counter. The caller resolves names, keys and descriptions, supplies the full path count separately, and optionally supplies a lazy content-preview callback for candidate admission. The scan window is independent of final request budgeting. Results identify the book, matched keys, recursion pass, skipped entries and issues. The initial pass is numbered 0. The [ST 1.19.0 reference](spec/ST-WORLD-INFO.md) has 166 numbered compatibility tests. Additional synthetic tests cover safety limits and review findings.

Enabled constants need no keys. Other enabled entries need a primary match. Selective entries then apply one of four secondary conditions: any match, every match, no match, or not every match. Trigger and message-count gates apply before matching. Plain keys use literal string search. Whole-word mode requires that neither neighbor be an ASCII letter, digit or underscore, as ST does. Keys containing whitespace use substring matching. Case sensitivity defaults to false and whole-word matching defaults to true. Only ST's `/pattern/flags` syntax invokes regex matching; `use_regex` is ignored.

Scan depth comes from the entry, then the book, then settings, then defaults to 2. Messages are trimmed and capped at 1,000. The buffer preserves ST's sentinels and interior empty slots, but skips trailing empty strings. Selected descriptions and scannable injections follow the messages. Only requested message depths are prepared. Each depth's chat text is built once. Completed buffers and their lowercase forms are reused for entries with the same depth and description flags within a pass. ASCII whole-word keys use a word index built once per buffer and case mode. Case-sensitive regexes such as `/\bcat\b/` share that index when they are not sticky. Exact non-sticky patterns such as `/(?:cat)/` use substring search when their entire rewritten body contains only ASCII letters, digits or underscores. Their results, and other regex results, are cached per buffer. Duplicate key slots still contribute separately to group scores. Unscored constants need no buffer.

Admitted content can activate further entries on later passes. Recursion defaults to enabled and honors book overrides and the exclude/prevent flags. Delayed recursion levels are pass thresholds; they never force recursion when it is disabled. Recursion defaults to 16 passes and cannot exceed 64. Probability uses the supplied random source and ST's inclusive comparison, so probability 0 passes an exact-zero draw. A failed draw is not retried.

A group admits at most one entry. Scores count matching key slots, including empty slots. Positive secondary logic adds secondary matches whenever primary slots exist, even if none of those primary slots matched. The all-match mode adds secondary scores only when every secondary slot matches. Selection uses score, override, descending order and stable input ties. Each entire group string is treated as one name. Admission and returned entries also use descending order with stable input ties.

The token counter receives content with appended newlines. Counts are cached for each distinct input, including invariant content from earlier passes. Combined content is still counted together, so tokenization need not be additive. An entry that reaches the allowance exactly is rejected. Global exhaustion stops ordinary admissions. A positive book budget applies only to that book; its rejected content does not spend another book's allowance. An `ignore_budget` entry bypasses both checks but its content remains charged. All content stays charged across recursion, including `prevent_recursion` content, avoiding ST's undercount.

Regex keys use the scripts' linear-time engine and its ASCII-case and Unicode limitations. Both the original and rewritten pattern have a 2,000-character cap. Regex execution charges an estimated expanded pattern size times input length. One evaluation may spend 250,000 units, and an activation may spend 500,000. Indexed word matches and exact ASCII substring matches spend scan work instead. Invalid syntax falls back to literal matching and produces an issue. Oversized slash patterns are refused before syntax validation. Refused constructs produce a specific explanation and a suggested edit. An untestable secondary condition excludes the entry, including negative conditions.

Compilation has separate memory limits, checked before invoking V8. At most 4,096 patterns are cached. Their keys and estimated rewritten source together may use 131,072 characters. Compiled programs may use 262,144 estimated expansion units in total. The estimate multiplies source size by every counted repetition's upper bound, including nested repetitions. It deliberately overcounts disjoint repetitions. Escaped braces and braces inside character classes are literal. Case rewriting is included in the estimate. This prevents short sources with large repetitions from retaining unexpectedly large programs. Ordinary literal keys are not kept in the pattern cache.

These memory limits were measured on Node 24.15 with synthetic fixtures in October 2026. The review's 1,000-pattern repeated-literal case previously added 234 MB of heap. It now stops after eight compilations and added 2.24 MB in the measured run. Nine stress variants exercised literal patterns, repeated groups, nested counts, the cache-count ceiling, case rewriting, captures and alternatives. The combined case reached 4,096 cached patterns and 261,440 expansion units. Its 7.5 MB heap increase was the largest observed. Tests assert the deterministic count, character and expansion ceilings, rather than a heap reading affected by garbage collection.

Retained scan data has its own bounds. An activation allows 4,096 buffers, 8 million characters of prepared buffer and index text, 100,000 indexed words and 20,000 cached regex results. Lowercase storage is charged conservatively before allocation. Each activation also allows 100,000 key evaluations, 128 million characters of text preparation and scanning, and 8 million characters sent to the token counter. Indexed lookups charge the key spelling without charging another traversal of the buffer. Substring searches and uncached general regexes still charge their traversed input. Candidate content and literal boundary checks also spend scan work. Scanning and general regex execution share an additional allowance: scanned characters plus 256 times regex work may not exceed 128 million. The charge is checked before the work runs. This prevents an activation from spending both full allowances independently.

The work allowances leave room for ordinary books. The measured 500-entry book, with three keys per entry and ten 2,000-character messages, activates its five expected entries. It charges 74,653 scanned characters without recursion and 131,778 with recursion. Tests also cover 300–1,000 entries, depths 2–10 and messages of 2,000–4,000 characters. The largest indexed case charges 256,778 scanned characters and 378,656 retained characters. A 500-entry substring case charges 123 million scanned characters. A mixed book with exact ASCII substring regexes on 50 of its 500 entries charges 11.6 million scanned characters and no general regex work. Both use ten 4,000-character messages and recursion. These cases run without limit issues.

The CPU allowances target roughly one second on the measured host. The earlier independent allowances permitted 28.2 seconds of work on a combined synthetic input. On Node 24.15.0 and an EPYC 7402, the new combined limit stopped that input in 449–489 ms over 20 worker-thread runs. The slowest run had host load averages of 10.24 / 13.62 / 18.71 over 1 / 5 / 15 minutes. A scaled nested-regex and scan input took 123–188 ms. Both produced identical results over 20 runs, reported a work-limit issue and remained replayable. A scan-only input spending 127.97 million characters took 926 ms at load 10.33 / 13.49 / 18.58. The 500-entry word, mixed, substring and boundary-regex books took 4.8–26.1 ms and admitted their five expected entries without issues. Each typical variant also replayed identically over 20 runs. These measurements exclude fixture construction and use a synthetic token counter. They are observed times under load, not a guarantee for arbitrary host scheduling or caller-supplied functions.

At most 1,000 diagnostic occurrences are collected. Repeated issues collapse to a count and the first three examples, with key excerpts capped at 160 characters. Callers may lower the limits. Reaching an aggregate limit stops work with one limit issue and the admissions already completed. Candidates still awaiting admission are left out. Results include work counters and explain unfinished entries.

A five-second VM deadline remains as an emergency guard around activation. It can interrupt a regex engine call. If it fires, the result explicitly says it is not replayable. Evaluation failures become issues and preserve completed admissions. Ordinary activation depends only on its inputs and the injected functions. Regex scripts keep their separate cumulative 200 ms deadline and existing behavior.

**Timed lore and speaker filters** (lorebooktimed, owner 2026-11-02). The registered lore stages implement ST 1.19.0's `WorldInfoTimedEffects` rules. Sticky bypasses primary/secondary keys, probability and recursion admission flags, while enabled/trigger/character/delay gates and budgets still apply. Sticky group members displace non-sticky members and bypass score/override selection; ST's unusual sticky-plus-cooldown group exclusion is retained. A sticky interval ends exclusively at its start plus its message count. Cooldown starts on admission too; sticky wins outside groups, and observing sticky's expiry starts a fresh protected cooldown. Re-admitting an active sticky does not extend it.

- **Causality and counting.** `StartRollout` inserts the snapshot's `loreTiming` admissions in `lore_activations` in its existing writer transaction (no separate write operation, no chat counters). Each admission holds the unresolved entry's SHA-256 identity, book included, and its two durations. The reader's `AssemblySources.loreState` walks the selected path once, counting visible, non-failed messages with text or images, and folds only those versions' compact receipts, never whole context payloads or historical keyword scans. Original and continued/edited versions follow their source-version lineage; sibling swipes are excluded. A normal reply uses its preceding message count; swipes use that same prefix; Continue also counts the existing reply and retains its original admissions, without restarting sticky. `message_offset` records that Continue evaluation's extra message. Only current entry identities enter the fold. The current effects, bounded by the enabled books' entries, and count are frozen in source pins for inspector rebuild. Edits invalidate an entry's previous identity. Hidden, deleted, failed, empty (without images) or off-path messages contribute no receipts or count. Existing above-history pins remain the owner's separate retention rule; character filters still gate those pins.
- **Long paths and forks.** The pure fold (`loreTiming.ts`) hashes compact receipt prefixes, finds the latest cached ancestor before doing interval work, and shares immutable checkpoints across branches. A reader keeps at most 512 checkpoints, spaced every 32 admissions and at the requested end. Cold reads fold admissions once for all entries; warmed reads only advance the uncached suffix. Snapshots retain current effects, not an ever-growing receipt history. Source records and cache keys contain no message text. All SQLite stays in reader/writer workers.
- **Filters.** Name inclusion and tag inclusion are separate gates (both must pass); exclusion rejects either match. ST's exact avatar stems resolve to `character_filter.cards` (entity plus original filename), and installation-local tag IDs resolve to card tag names, with the original IDs retained for export. Unresolved filenames stay visible as unavailable picker choices. Evaluation uses `cast.speaker`, independently of cast-wide `{{char}}`; single and multi-character chats use the same gate. All cards have a tag array here; an empty array fails an inclusion filter. The pure matcher retains ST's bypass for a missing mapped tag array. `ListLibrary(withFilterData)` supplies owner-scoped filenames and tag choices for the existing `ui/MultiSelect` fields. The folder parser maps filters and card tags in a format worker before storing a revision, and mapping changes enter reimport hashes. World Info export restores filenames/tag IDs; our extension preserves the resolved filter on our own round trips, including embedded books.
- **Deliberate differences.** Previews use the same current effects as generation, while ST's dry runs ignore sticky/cooldown. Imported messages and manually written messages have no generation admissions to invent: imported chat-wide timed metadata is not copied, and timers start with an actual generation here. Stored admissions remain evidence of the selected version even after an ancestor text edit; earlier prompts are not regenerated. Other established matcher differences below and above-history pinning are unchanged. Automation ID requires an external automation engine; memo and export name/priority are metadata, and `use_regex` is legitimately ignored in favor of slash syntax.
- **Verification.** `loreTiming.test.ts`, `loreTimingStorage.test.ts` and `loreFilterImport.test.ts` cover windows, protection, probability/delay/recursion, previews, Continue, siblings, branches, compact replay, 3,000 messages/200 branches, mapping and reimport. `test:st`'s `lore-timing` section uses stock ST's actual `checkWorldInfo` and timed-effects implementation with a synthetic entry source/metadata. `e2e/loreTiming.spec.ts` checks the existing fields and card/tag pickers across reload at desktop and phone widths.

Weighted or overlapping groups, expanding history, source tiers, decorators, external/vector activation, World Info postprocessing remain deferred. Unsupported retained entry controls produce issues. Tail-block persistence and exact tokenizer/global settings resolution come later.

**Generation** (`chat/ContextGenerator.ts`; DATA-MODEL §1, principle 7: every generation is a rollout). The chat's generator:
- assembles the context in a reader worker. A context that can't be built fails the version with the reason (`no_model`, `budget`, `invalid_document`); a locked chat uses its model binding, and a missing bound model fails visibly.
- opens the rollout (`StartRollout`, one write): the row (`running`, role `narrator`, the model), its frozen snapshot in `rollout_payloads`, the version's rollout, connection and model, the variables the preset's and cards' macros wrote as `var.set` events of the version (origin `rollout`), and the values template messages drew, kept on versions that had none (`frozen_macros`, `{}` when a template drew nothing but wrote variables), with the variables each wrote as `var.set` events of its own version, recorded unless that version has some already, so a `{{time}}` in a greeting stays what it was. The version must be the user's and still generating, and the model one of the user's live connections'.
- maps the request to the provider (`wire.ts`). Chat Completions gets the assembled messages exactly, names included, in `payload` (§6), since pi-ai's own conversion drops names and moves later system messages to the top. Anthropic and the other APIs get a context pi-ai converts, as ST converts for Claude: the leading system messages as the system prompt (always, except for Anthropic and Google without `use_sysprompt`), later ones as the user's with names folded into the text, one message each so a breakpoint covers nothing after it, the prefill last, and the samplers pi-ai doesn't set in `payload` (Google's in `config`, as ST sends `topP` and `topK`). Breakpoints go only to models whose breakpoints are `explicit`.
- streams through the provider layer (§6), which writes a ledger row per attempt, attributed to the chat, rollout and version. Text deltas become the version's text. Ordinary replies omit the preset prefill from saved text, as ST does; Continue starts with the source version's full text and appends the returned suffix; a provider error fails the version with its reason (`bad_request`, `context_overflow`, …).
- fails a prefilled reply that streamed no text after its prefill (`emptyAfterPrefill`, class `empty_reply`, "The model returned no text after the reply's prefill."; liveapi F12, a schema prefill returning only its prefix): the version shows the error and offers Retry, on every provider and prefill kind. Continue and agent replies are left out.
- closes the rollout (`FinishRollout`) on every exit, as a resource of the stream's scope, so a stop before the first token closes it too: `completed`, `failed` with the message, or `stopped` (a user's stop or the server's), with the usage its ledger rows add up to, on the rollout and the version's `usage_json`, in one transaction. At startup, rollouts left `running` become `interrupted`.

The production server, and the development server without `FAKE_GENERATOR_TPS`, generate this way. Tested against local mocks that record what they're sent (`test/generation.test.ts`): an OpenAI-compatible one, whose body must hold exactly the assembled messages and samplers (pi-ai adds the model, streaming and usage options around them); a failing one; an Anthropic-shaped one with a made-up key, checked for the system prompt, the prefill, the samplers and a breakpoint; Google's and OpenAI's o-series samplers; and 40 generations stopped 0 to 7 ms after they start, none of which may leave its rollout running (`test/generationEdges.test.ts`).

**Continue** (`ContinueVersion`, `features/chat/ContinueAction.tsx`; DESIGN §7.5). The latest message's selected version offers Continue beside Regenerate when its text is finished and nonempty, whoever wrote it: an edit of a reply (a `human`-written version, `origin: edited`) and a version the user wrote continue as a generated one does, and a persona's turn continues as an impersonation (parity finding 1). The client action and `ContinueVersion` apply the same rule (`NotContinuable` only for a version still being written or without text); the button stays in place, disabled with a reason for earlier, unfinished or empty messages, a missing model, or an unresolved model capability. When the next context has not arrived yet, Continue waits for it and rechecks the selected message before acting. **Without a prefill** (owner, 2026-10-31; ST's continue nudge): a model whose capability is `none`, or whose endpoint can't take one (`continueUnavailable`: DeepSeek without `/beta`, tool-schema prefill without its adapter), gets the text it continues as its own last message (an assistant message whose piece is the source message, so the inspector names it "Message N"), and the end-of-request instruction after it is the preset's `continueNudge` with the direction, if any (§15 "Who writes, and the direction"). The second kind adds a `prefill_dropped` issue saying why no prefill was sent. The new text is appended as with a prefill; when the text continued doesn't end in whitespace, the registered reply parser `continue-join` (`chat/continueJoin.ts`, before `reply-sections`) puts the preset's `continue_postfix` (ST's; a space by default) before the first text the model sends, unless that starts with whitespace. The budget reserves the message as it reserves a prefill. It adds a selected generated version in the same slot with `source_version_id`, the original text and speaker, and only the `direction` given with it (the composer's guidance), not the source's. It also copies the source reasoning, appending any new reasoning a paragraph apart [P], and its reply sections: the prefill is the reply as it came (`originalReply`: its sections in their tags, then the text), as ST's prefix, and a source cut off inside a section resumes inside it. A version whose text is empty but whose section has text continues too. The source remains unchanged. Streaming offsets begin after that starting text; only the wire prefill trims trailing whitespace, which Anthropic refuses. The assembler recognizes the source as a continuation, sets generation type `continue` for preset triggers, excludes the target from ordinary history and budgets its text as the trailing assistant prefill. The frozen inspector capture identifies it as “Message N as it was, continued from its end.” The source text replaces the preset's ordinary prefill [P]. Tests: `test/continueReasoning.test.ts` (an edited reply continued into a third, generated version, both originals kept; a blank edit refused; a model that takes no prefill: the request's last two messages, the joined result, the inspector's labels), `test/replySectionsGeneration.test.ts` (a section cut off continued without a prefill), `test/reviewContinue.test.ts` (only DeepSeek's own host is held to `/beta`, with the reason; another host's address gets the prefix), `e2e/continueReasoning.spec.ts` (Edit → Save → Continue at 1440 and 390 px; Continue on a model without a prefill and the inspector's "End of request: when you continue a reply").

Resolved `prefill: assistant` models use a trailing assistant message: Anthropic and native-prefill OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions. DeepSeek additionally marks only the final prefill message `prefix: true`. On DeepSeek's own host (`api.deepseek.com`, also the default when no Base URL is set) the Base URL must end in `/beta`; with another endpoint there, Continue goes without a prefill (above), and the context's issue explains the endpoint it needs. Another host is a router or compatible server in front of DeepSeek, which is the one that decides where the request goes, so it gets the prefix on its own address (liveapi2, 2026-11-07). The endpoint is never changed automatically. Capability and adapter availability are retained independently of context budgeting, so a budget failure cannot enable an unsupported model. An unresolved capability keeps the action unavailable.

`prefill: tool_schema` supports OpenAI Responses and Chat Completions. Like reference-harness's anchored strict-schema `analysis` argument, it forces a single function call with an anchored string pattern; the delta is a dedicated `continue_reply` tool with a `text` argument containing the whole reply, including the exact original prefix [P]. The schema includes that prefix and regex-escapes it. It replaces the trailing assistant prefill, disables parallel calls, streams parsed argument text after stripping the prefix, and validates the provider’s original tool-argument JSON, the final call and unchanged streamed text before completing. Raw Chat Completions argument deltas and authoritative Responses completion arguments are retained separately from pi-ai’s permissively repaired preview objects. When provider usage is absent, the forced reply tool’s serialized arguments contribute estimated output counts, including on stop or failure; ordinary tools retain their existing usage semantics. Preambles are ignored; malformed or prefix-changing replies fail with `bad_prefill`. The assembler reserves the serialized tool/schema input and the repeated prefix’s JSON output, in addition to the configured continuation length. The wire maximum includes that prefix allowance, and a known output ceiling that cannot fit it fails with an explicit budget explanation before dispatch. No tool is executed and no agent loop is needed. On other APIs Continue goes without a prefill (above), and the context's issue says their schema adapter is unavailable. Ordinary preset schema prefills use the same mapping. The source version retains its exact text, including trailing whitespace; native wire prefills trim trailing whitespace for Anthropic, while schema prefixes preserve it.

The model editor distinguishes absent provider information, explicit no support, native assistant support and schema support. Users can declare either supported prefill method. Frozen inspection captures only the dedicated forced schema tool's parameters and prefix as a message with continuation provenance, or DeepSeek's prefix flag; these fields are scrubbed with the rest of the display. Arbitrary tool definitions remain excluded. The picker refreshes when the selected version's status or saved row version changes; opening a list with a generating record also refreshes it. Completion status and preview stay current after switching to the original version. Tests in `reviewContinue.test.ts` cover budget-independent capability, DeepSeek protocol/endpoint validation and Responses schema suffix streaming; browser tests exercise both protocol adapters and unavailable capability at both widths.

**Reasoning** (`features/chat/Reasoning.tsx`; DESIGN §7.4). Provider `thinking` deltas are saved in the existing `version_texts.reasoning` column, also used by ST imports; no migration is needed. Stop, failure, orderly shutdown and periodic saves retain it. `ReadPath`, `GetVersion` and `ListVersions` expose it; `Hello` restores live reasoning after reconnect or reload. A separate atom per version batches reasoning independently of reply text. The new component renders a Markdown block above the reply, expanded while generating by default, folded when done and expandable in one click. Toggling during a run saves the user's streaming choice through `GetDisplayPrefs`/`SetDisplayPrefs` to user-scoped `settings`, key `display`; later runs and other devices read it. A completed block's local fold choice does not alter the streaming preference. Switching versions resets the local choice. The header beside the toggle renders the `message.reasoning-actions` slot (`reasoningActions` in `presentation.tsx`, props: the version, the raw text, streaming, the panel's kind and the session), whose defaults are registered in `reasoningActions.tsx` (parity finding 7): **Copy reasoning** (`reasoning.copy`) copies the raw text, stored or streamed so far, never the rendered Markdown (`copy.ts`, shared with Copy text, toasts the outcome); **Collapse all** (`reasoning.collapse-all`) bumps a module counter every mounted block watches, closing each as a local choice for that block, so the streaming preference in user-scoped `settings` is untouched. A plugin can replace, disable or add to either by id. Tests: client `test/reasoningActions.test.ts` (order, replacement, removal, the counter); `e2e/continueReasoning.spec.ts` (two replies opened, Copy's exact text, Collapse all closing both, the preference unchanged, at 1440 and 390 px).

Reasoning is display-only in these plain chat generations: the assembler and `wire.ts` replay text blocks only, and never add stored reasoning (`versions.reasoning`, text without a signature) to history, so no plain chat request carries a thinking block. Signed blocks are replayed only inside agent rollouts, checked by the provider layer (§6 "Signed thinking"). `FAKE_GENERATOR_REASONING=<tokens>` adds a synthetic reasoning phase ahead of the fake generator's text at `FAKE_GENERATOR_TPS`; production does not wire it. Tests: `continueReasoning.test.ts` checks Chat Completions and Anthropic prefill, exact old-text preservation, independent reasoning, inspector provenance and unsupported dispatch; `session.test.ts` checks live delta/reconnect handling; the isolation matrix covers the new RPCs; `e2e/continueReasoning.spec.ts` checks stop/continue, the old picker entry, persisted reasoning, sticky preferences and unsupported explanations at 1440 and 390 px.

**Thinking in a message's edit** (thinkedit1, 2026-11-16; SillyTavern's reasoning edit, "Add reasoning block" and its removal). A message's Edit (`Message.tsx` `Editor`) shows its thinking (`editableThinking`, `@rp/shared/replySections.ts`: `versions.reasoning`, the provider's reasoning or ST's imported `extra.reasoning`; without it, its reply sections' text, which is also how ST's imported `parsed` reasoning and the auto-parse's sections are kept, review-thinkedit1) in a second field above the text, as the panel sits above the reply; the registered `message.editor.thinking` slot (`features/chat/editThinking.tsx`, entry `message.editor-thinking`) renders it with the shared message text editor, a "Thinking" heading whose `AboutHint` says it is saved as plain text without the provider's signature and that plain chats never send thinking (for sections: that the model sees it again only where the preset sends thinking back), and Remove thinking (trash) in the field's strip. Without thinking (or after Remove), **Add thinking** (`message.editor-add-thinking`, a `messageEditorTools` entry beside the image button) shows an empty field, focused, or the removed text again. The field is a server draft of its own: target `EditThinking { versionId }`, the edit's `version_edit` draft with field `reasoning` (`EDIT_THINKING_FIELD`), whose start state is the version's thinking; `MessageDrafts` lists it while active even when empty (emptied means removed), and typing into it saves the text field's draft too (`MessageDraft.keepOpen`), so a reload reopens the edit with both. Save sends `reasoning` (`""`: none) and `reasoningDraft` with `EditVersion`/`AmendVersion`; Cancel discards both drafts. `messageEditorTools` props gained `session`, `entry` and `source`.
- **Server.** `EditVersion` keeps the source's thinking unless `reasoning` differs from it (before, an edit dropped it, its reply sections too); a changed thinking goes through the edit scripts with the text (`rewriteText`'s reasoning, `raw_reasoning`). For a version whose thinking is its sections (`thinkingInSections`: no provider reasoning), the change goes to the sections instead (`sectionsWithThinking`: one section in the first one's tags with the typed text, before the same gap; `""` none), so the thinking stays tagged thinking that the preset's send-back sends, as ST's edited reasoning is still sent by `add_to_prompts`; the scripts see it as sections (`raw_sections`). With both, the field is the reasoning and the sections stay. `AmendVersion` (the user's own versions) changes it in place, the earlier thinking in `version_history.reasoning_json` and `sections_json` (its sections before; the trigger records both), the row version counting up as for an image-only amend; when another fork shows the version, the copy takes the new thinking and the other forks keep theirs. Unchanged thinking sent again amends nothing. `VersionAmendments` returns each state's `reasoning` and `sections`; `RestoreVersionAmendment` restores them with the text. The writer commits the thinking draft by id, session and the exact text typed (`commitReasoningDraft.text`), matching only its field (the text commit now matches only field `""`), and moves its history to the version saved, as the text's.
- **Signed thinking.** A version keeps no provider signature; signed blocks live only in the source's run transcript. The edited version is a new version without a run (an amended one is the user's and never had one), so Resume, agent continuity and later requests can't replay the signed original through it, and plain chats never send stored reasoning (above). The export maps it to `extra.reasoning` as before (`stReasoningExtra`), typed `edited` or `manual` as ST would (`stReasoningType`, §13b).
- Tests: server `editThinking.test.ts` (kept/changed/removed on edits, the ST line's `extra.reasoning`, in-place amends with history and restore, another fork unchanged, the draft's start state, listing, commit and move, and a signed Anthropic agent reply edited sending no thinking in the next reply), `editThinkingSections.test.ts` (a synthetic ST chat with every `reasoning_type`: parsed reasoning shown, kept by a text edit, changed and removed as sections, amended with its history and restored, exported with ST's types and imported back the same; with provider reasoning too, the sections stay); browser `editThinking.spec.ts` (field, hover text, change, Remove, Add, reload before Save, export, layout audits at 1440/390 in light and dark).

**Reply sections** (spec/REPLY-SECTIONS.md; DESIGN §7.4 [P]; owner request 2026-10-31). SillyTavern's reasoning Auto-parse, with its pattern pairs and both-at-once limits lifted. A reply that starts, after whitespace, with a section in the preset's tags (`reply_sections`, §9) has it taken out of the body into its own field, whether or not the provider also sent reasoning; several consecutive leading sections are all taken, tags later in the text are left alone.
- **Settings layout** (thinkingsection, owner 2026-11-03): `ReplySectionsSettings` has a heading-adjacent + (Add another tag pair). The + appends an empty pair. (No ⋯ menu: its "Add the default pair" was removed, owner 2026-11-03: "What even is the point of this? Just remove it".) Each bordered pair contains its two tag inputs, Match case and Treat as a regex, with a corner X (Remove this pair). Zero pairs are valid, so every pair retains its X. The header and corner controls reuse HistoryPanel’s shared `IconButton`, and additions call shared `revealAdded` after mounting to scroll the new box into view and flash it. The tag-pair list is followed by "Move tagged thinking into its own panel", then "Send thinking back for the last replies". Opening and Closing tag use shared single-line `Input` controls; their grid stays within 40rem and wraps below two 14rem columns. The existing registered preset settings surface is unchanged. `e2e/replySections.spec.ts` checks input type, dimensions, wrapping, control order, corner removal through zero pairs, adding/revealing/flashing a box, restoring all or only missing defaults without changing retained pairs, saved literal values, and scoped geometry audits (including header controls, added boxes and the menu) at 390/1024/1440 in both themes.
- **Storage:** `version_texts.reply_sections` (JSON, baseline schema; `Version.replySections`, `@rp/shared/replySections.ts`): `{ sections: [{ lead, open, text, close, prefilled? }], gap }`. `content` is the body. `lead`/`open`/`close`/`gap` are the exact text around it, so `originalReply` rebuilds the reply byte for byte (`prefilled`: how many leading characters a preset prefill supplied). `close: null`: the reply ended inside it. The provider's reasoning stays in `version_texts.reasoning`. Copies of versions (amends in a fork, history edits, fork imports, inserted messages) carry the column; the bin purges it.
- **The parser** (`chat/replySections.ts`) is a registered stage, `ExecutionRegistry.replyParsers` (built-in `reply-sections`); `ContextGenerator` runs every registered parser over the reply strategy's chunks, in order (`throughParse`). A pair's tags are **literal text** unless the pair sets `regex: true` (DESIGN §7.4 [D], owner 2026-11-02): a literal tag is escaped (`literalPattern`), so `<think|plan>` or `[plan.*]` match only as written. Both kinds compile with the assembler's linear-time engine (`compileLinear`, anchored opening `^(?:…)`, case-insensitive unless `case_sensitive`); an empty tag, or a regex that doesn't compile, is unsafe or matches empty text, skips its pair. States: before a section it holds the start of the reply while it may still become an opening tag: for a literal tag, exactly while the held text begins it (so `<b>` goes through at once; a tag may hold line breaks, as ST's default `<think>\n` does, or start with one); for a regex, until a line break, 64 characters, the end, or a first character its literal first character rules out. Once an opening tag has fully arrived, everything after it streams to the section (owner, 2026-11-02), holding back only what may start the closing tag (the opening pair's; after a Continue, any pair's): for a literal tag, the earliest tail that begins it (`</thi`, not `a < b`); for a regex, from the first character in the last 64 that its literal first character allows, or all 64 when it has none. After a close it holds whitespace until it knows whether another section opens (else that's the gap); then it passes the body through. So a tag split across chunks parses, section text never shows in the body first, and the saved result is the parse of the whole reply at once; a regex tag is at most 64 characters. A reply that ends inside a section keeps its text there with an empty body, as ST's streaming does (`ReasoningHandler.finish` leaves it as reasoning). Its chunks are `{ sections, text }` (the state, and what the panel gains) and `{ held, into }`; `Generations` keeps the latest `held` and settles it into the body or the section when the reply ends without the parser's end (`settleHeld`: stop, crash, failure, periodic saves), and publishes `Section` deltas of `sectionsDisplay` (section texts a blank line apart). `Hello` carries the live panel text. A preset prefill that opens a section starts the reply inside it. Prefills and streamed replies use the same opening matcher: a literal tag keeps its own leading whitespace, even after additional whitespace before it, and partial tags are held using that same boundary. The fake generator runs the parser with the default pairs (literal `<think>`/`</think>` and `<thinking>`/`</thinking>`); `FAKE_GENERATOR_SECTION=<tokens>` starts its text with a synthetic `<thin`+`king>` … `</thin`+`king>` section.
- **Sent back** (§15): history sends the body; the `reply-sections` assembler stage (after `history`) prepends a message's sections, in their tags as they came, for the last `send_back` replies that have them, as ST's add_to_prompts/max_additions (a reply by another card than the one being written, both known, is skipped without counting, as ST does in groups). Those messages are volatile for the cache prefix. Pinned history windows keep neither text nor sections; a rebuild reads both again. Summaries and the refusal judge see the body only (the stage does nothing for a summary job).
- **Regex scripts** (fregexs; §12 "Rewrites", "Live rewrites"): each section's text goes through the reasoning (placement 6) scripts as the reply finishes and while it streams, and the `reply-sections` stage runs the prompt-only placement-6 scripts on each section's text, at the message's depth, before putting it back in its tags (ST's `getRegexedString(reasoning, REASONING, { isPrompt, depth })` before `addToMessage`); the scripts that changed it join the message's record for the inspector. History entries carry the sections (`HistoryEntry.replySections`), not their joined text.
- **Hidden from the model** (thinkhide1; reviewed 2026-11-14): `SetThinkingHidden` (§3.8) stores an independent override per version, thinking part and branch. Forks inherit the choice as of their fork point; other branches and swipes keep their own. The captured-section stage omits exactly the saved leading sections (including their saved tags and separating gap), leaving the body byte-for-byte; it still consumes that reply's send-back allowance. Later pattern changes never reparse the old spans. Continue also omits hidden sections from its prefill. On Resume, `RebuildContext.thinkingForkId` overlays just these choices onto the frozen source pins, including a saved request, and returns the identical snapshot if no choice changed. Other pinned prose/settings and completed tool receipts remain fixed. `GetThinkingHidden` reads unselected swipes too; ownership/branch isolation is tested. Hidden provider reasoning changes no plain-chat request, because those requests never replay it. It controls agent transcript replay instead; manual-thinking tool turns retain required blocks until the active turn ends. Workshop continuity rejects a hidden carried message and rebuilds. Summary inputs and model-facing search/read tools use message bodies, never provider reasoning or captured sections; workshop compaction also filters thinking.
