Display/search storage is retained: hiding is not deletion. A future complete chat export should retain the thinking plus its branch/version hidden flags so reimport preserves both; there is no such export in this branch, and ST export mapping is unchanged.

  Each registered panel offers Hide from the model while streaming or finished, and Show to the model again once hidden. A short toast offers Undo tied to the original branch even after navigation. The header retains the thinking with a ghost mark. Tooltips distinguish provider reasoning replay from plain chat and captured-section send-back. The action and panels remain replaceable registry entries, use the shared UI controls and semantic tokens, and wrap at phone width. `hideThinking.spec.ts` and the focused `layoutAudit.spec.ts` mode (`LAYOUT_AUDIT_THINKING_ONLY=1`, grep “thinking hidden”) cover streaming, Undo, reload, exact version choice and geometry at 1440/390 in light/dark.
- **Display** (`features/chat/Reasoning.tsx`): the registered `message.reasoning-panels` slot renders `reasoning.provider` ("Reasoning") then `reasoning.reply-sections` ("Thinking in the reply"), the same block with the same open/closed streaming preference and Collapse all; a panel whose section was never closed says so. While the reply streams and its body is still empty (the body starts only after the last section closes), the sections panel's header reads "Thinking…", pulsing (`data-thinking`; `aria-busy` on the open region), folded or open as the streaming preference says, its text live when open; once the body starts it reads "Thinking in the reply". The header toggle explains itself on hover and focus (open/fold, and that a choice while streaming sticks). The `message.reasoning-actions` slot's props gained `kind`, `first` and `session`: Copy reads "Copy thinking" there; Collapse all shows once per reply, on its `first` panel; and `reasoning.show-as-text` ("Show as reply text", finished versions with sections only) calls `ShowSectionsAsText`, which adds a selected `edited` version whose text is `originalReply`, keeping the reasoning and images; the parsed version stays among the versions. Selection copy maps the panel's prose through `MessageBody` as it does reasoning.
- **Setting** (`features/editor/ReplySectionsSettings.tsx`, the preset editor): each pair's Opening and Closing tag, "Match case" and "Treat as a regex" (off by default; on, the tags are checked as patterns); the copy says tags match exactly as written. Opening and closing tags use the shared textareas, so real line breaks in ST's literal tags remain visible and editable, and survive Save and reopening the editor. An ST folder import maps `power_user.reasoning`'s prefix and suffix to one literal, case-sensitive pair, as written (`formats/stData.ts`). Preset documents are JSON, so the `regex` key is no schema change; a preset stored before it with a regex pair now reads it as literal text (no real data yet).
- **ST chats:** `stReasoningOf` imports `reasoning_type: "parsed"` as a section (§13), which a message's edit changes as its thinking (§12 "Thinking in a message's edit"); `stReasoningExtra` is the export mapping (sections without provider reasoning → `extra.reasoning`, `"parsed"`; with it, provider reasoning as `"model"` and the sections left in `mes` in their tags), used by the chat export (§13b).
- Tests: `test/replySections.test.ts` (both spellings, mixed closes with a regex pair, every two-chunk and per-character split, several sections, tags mid-text, never closed, stop settling, Continue inside a section, a prefill, reasoning beside, literal/case-sensitive/rejected pairs, literal tags with regex metacharacters, ST's tags with line breaks, regex tags split anywhere, a partial tag let through once it stops matching, and 400 generated replies in random chunks parsing as the whole reply does); `test/replySectionsGeneration.test.ts` (a mock provider's reasoning plus a split `<thinking>…</think>` section, `Section` deltas, send_back 0 and 1 in the next request, Show as reply text, a length cutoff inside a section continued); `test/formats/stReasoning.test.ts`, `test/stImportTextSwitches.test.ts` (ST import/export and settings); client `test/reasoningActions.test.ts`; `e2e/replySections.spec.ts` (two panels in order, a clean body, open/Collapse all, Show as reply text, the literal default pairs and Treat as a regex, at 1440 and 390 px, light and dark); `e2e/replySectionsStreaming.spec.ts` (folded while streaming with "Thinking…", opened it streams live, the body only after the closing tag, folded when done, the saved sections).

**Current account settings** (`GetGenerationDefaults`, `SetGenerationDefaults`, `ChangeGenerationDefaults`; `db/generationSettings.ts`): `generation.model` holds the connection/model pair and `generation.preset` the prompt ref. Each is independent. On changing to another connection, its optional `presetOverrideRefId` sets the current prompt preset; another model on that same connection does not reapply the lock, and later prompt switches remain possible. The connection's settings show the lock. Selection checks, the previous-connection read, and lock adoption run in the same writer transaction. Ownership checks return `NotFound`; deleted choices read as unset.

**Model settings** (`@rp/shared/modelSettings.ts`, `ModelOverrides.settings`). Samplers, context/reply limits, history target, thinking effort, verbosity, stop strings, logit bias, streaming display, cache retention, provider routing and wire names/squashing/system formatting belong to the connection's model. Existing model overrides retain capabilities, image limits, prefill support, cache policy, compat and sampling. Assembly uses a transient ST compatibility view containing those model settings plus the prompt document; this view is never stored as a prompt preset. The model's context size and response length (`samplers.openai_max_context`, `openai_max_tokens`) are settings, apart from its reported limits (`context`, `maxOutput`), which assembly still reads as the model's window and output ceiling. Without its own, the context size is the model's window as `resolveModel` resolves it (`ASSUMED_CONTEXT`, 128,000, when nothing reports one) and the response length is at most 4096, within the reported output limit and half the context size in use (the model's own when set, within the window) (`withModelSettings`), so a model reporting an output limit as large as its window, or one given a small context size, still leaves room for history. A schema continuation with that default response length shortens it to the output limit less the source prefix; only a response length set on the model can fail the continuation's output-limit check. Sampler defaults are temperature/top-p 1, penalties 0 (repetition 1), no seed, other optional samplers off. The preset's old budget never supplies these values. Streaming off buffers the generated chunks until completion while preserving the controlled SDK stream for transport and cancellation.

Model settings live on models, not in prompt presets: no preset sampler is copied onto a model, and chat binding events never change the account model or preset. New library writes strip model fields from prompt documents. Assembler version 23 pins the new semantics; older saved request snapshots remain inspectable through the existing version-mismatch path.

**Composer and settings panels.** The composer's strip shows the effective model and prompt preset as chips (`ModelChip`, `PresetChip` in `GenerationControls.tsx`), each opening its picker with one click (below, **Preset and model pickers**). Model lists leave hidden models out except the current one, which stays named and marked hidden (`modelChoices.ts`), here and in Settings → Chats. The popovers end with **Model settings…** and **Edit preset…** (when those panel tabs are registered), which open the Model right-panel tab which edits the model the chat's next reply uses (`NextContext.model`, the same one the budget note and the refusal open; the account's current model before the estimate arrives), named at its top with its connection, and the Prompt preset tab (`PresetTab.tsx`, below under **Preset overlays**); the model editor is reused on the connection page, and the prompt editor retains only prompt content. The pickers offer a per-chat lock (below). Settings → Chats also edits the current account selections. The built-in preset is displayed as “Default (built-in)” (`BUILTIN_PRESET_LABEL`), apart from ST's own Default preset, which a folder import brings in under its library label. The model editor's number fields keep text as typed until it parses (“0.” on the way to “0.7”); an empty field means the default, and Save refuses text that isn't a number.

**Chat preset/model locks** (lockchat, built 2026-11-04; **[D]** owner, 2026-11-03, personadefault): preset and model "are universal settings", account-wide; a per-chat selection is "an exception, not the rule". The existing registered picker bodies include **Lock for this chat**, with hover "This chat keeps this preset when you change it elsewhere." / "This chat keeps this model when you change it elsewhere.". The switch row contains only its normal control label (14 px, text colour), with padding before the divider and no scope description in either state (lockline2, 2026-11-05). Locked chips show a small lock state icon, never another button. An unlocked choice changes the account default, followed by other unlocked chats; a locked choice changes only the chat binding. Turning the lock off removes the binding and follows the account selection again. No separate lock buttons were added to the row.

The existing `preset.binding` / `model.binding` and unbind events store locks through `ChangeCast` and worker `AddStateEvent`; no database schema changed. `Cast.presetLocked` distinguishes an empty binding (the built-in preset) from no binding. The registered model/preset assembler stages and reader sources resolve chat bindings before account defaults; assembler version 46 records this behavior. Pending chats continue to choose account settings. `e2e/lockchat.spec.ts` covers account propagation, independent locks, unlock, reload, chip markers, absence of picker scope text in both states, the built-in preset and actual next-request selection at 390/1440. The layout audit's `LAYOUT_AUDIT_LOCKCHAT_ONLY=1` covers chips and open pickers at 390/1024/1440 in both themes.


**Preset and model pickers** (`features/pickers/`; the owner, 2026-11-01, DESIGN §6.1). One picker for each, opened by the composer's chip and by a dropdown at the very top of the side panel's Prompt preset and Model tabs (`PanelPickers.tsx`, mounted above each tab's own content in `registerPanels.tsx`), the current choice selected. Choosing in either changes the account selection through `ChangeGenerationDefaults`, or the chat binding through `ChangeCast` when locked; both read the same queries (`presetSelection.ts`, `modelSelection.ts`, `defaults.ts`: `GetGenerationDefaults` under `settings`, the two preset lists under `library`, `ListModelUse` under `models`/`settings`), so a choice or an archive in one shows in the other at once. The bodies are registered slot entries, `preset.picker` and `model.picker` (`pickers/index.tsx`), so a plugin replacing one changes the chip's popover and the tab's dropdown together; the popover around them (`PickerPopover`) puts focus in the filter, or on a touch screen on the current row so no keyboard opens. Rows are radios with a muted line under the name (its full text the row's description) and a tooltip saying what choosing does and the exact times. Above 60 rows the list mounts only the rows in view and three either side (`ui/WindowedList.tsx`, opened at the current row). Down in the filter moves to the current row (else the first), Enter takes the first row; Up, Down, Home and End move between rows, and Up from the first returns to the filter.
- **Presets** (`PresetPicker.tsx`, `presetList.ts`): a filter (case and accents ignored), then **Name**, **Modified**, **Used** and **Archived** (`Segmented`, each with a tooltip; Archived counts them). The first three list presets that aren't archived, Default (built-in) first; Archived only archived ones, the most recently archived first; the text filters every view. The line says "edited 3 days ago", in Used "used 2 hours ago · edited …" (never used last), in Archived "archived yesterday · edited …". The sort is remembered per account on the server (`DisplayPrefs.presetSort`, default Name, shared with the library); Archived never is, so the list reopens on the last sort. Each row has an archive icon button ("Archive: hide it from these lists; nothing is deleted"), in Archived an unarchive one; it neither chooses nor closes, moves focus to the row that takes its place, and a status line says what happened with **Undo**. The preset in use can be archived: it stays in use, and in the other views stays at the top, checked and badged Archived, with its unarchive button; the chip and the tab's dropdown name it ("(archived)" in the dropdown). The list ends with **New preset…**, as the tab's header does beside the dropdown (**New**): the dialog (`NewPresetDialog`, shared with the library's New prompt preset) says it starts as a copy of the built-in default and suggests "New preset" (numbered when taken); Create makes it (`CreatePreset`), chooses it as a row would, and opens it in the preset editor over the chat (or its page with no workspace). Settings → Chats and a connection's locked preset keep an archived choice listed, marked "(archived)" (`selectablePresets`).
- **Models** (`ModelPicker.tsx`, `modelList.ts`, `VirtualModelList.tsx`; modelpicker, 2026-11-06): the registered `model.picker` body serves the composer, Model tab, first-run chooser, account default, refusal judge, summary model (account and chat), fallback summarizer and decision-connection field. Presets have no additional model selector; this checkout has no summary retry-with-model field. A permanently visible connection filter applies to every section; punctuation/accent-tolerant subsequence search matches the upstream id, resolved display name, provider prefix and connection name. Pinned models come first across connections, then up to twelve recent choices/replies, then the remaining catalog grouped by connection; Name/Used sorts the remaining models. Each row shows its resolved name, connection, id and last-use line. Catalogs over sixty rows mount only a viewport plus three neighbours; fixed row heights bound layout, and arrow/Home/End navigation reaches unmounted rows while retaining the focused row during pointer scrolling. Small lists retain every row. Search-field Down reaches the current model (or the first match), Enter chooses the first match regardless of scroll position, and Up from the first row returns to search. Pin controls keep their position until reopening; the icon and account setting change immediately. Every opening starts a fresh search and connection filter and reapplies pin order, including when reopened during the closing animation. Hidden models stay excluded except selected models, labelled hidden; decision connections remain excluded from reply choices and their own picker lists only their models.
- **Model picker preferences** use `DisplayPrefs.modelPins` (connection/model-pair keys, booleans, at most 500), `modelRecent` (selection times, at most 100, newest first) and the existing `modelSort`, merged in the writer's `SetDisplayPrefs` transaction under user-scoped settings key `display`. Independent pin/recent patches preserve other devices' choices; older timestamps cannot replace newer ones. `ListModelUse` still supplies actual reply times from the owned request ledger; the client takes the newer of selection and reply times. Opening, searching, pinning and choosing read stored models and send no provider request. No baseline change.
- **Model catalog validation**: `test/displayPrefs.test.ts` covers account/device isolation, pin patches, sort, bounded recents and stale timestamps; `test/pickerLists.test.ts` covers fuzzy search and section/filter ordering. `e2e/modelpicker.spec.ts` serves three loopback mock catalogs (3,000/10/40), plus forty manually added decision-only models, checks selections and bounded DOM at 1440/390 in both themes, and measures production Chromium main-thread CPU with CDP `Performance` thread ticks (`MODELPICKER_PERF=1`, one worker, enforces 100 ms opening and 50 ms per key; ordinary browser runs check behavior). The focused `model picker catalog layout` group of `e2e/layoutAudit.spec.ts` audits open and filtered states at both widths/themes.

- Tests: `test/pickerLists.test.ts` (each view's order and filter, an entry read in both lists, the lines, the selects' archived choice, the model sorts); `e2e/pickers.spec.ts` at 1440 and 390 px (the tab's picker selects and the chip agrees; filter, each sort and the remembered sort; archive from the list without closing it; Archived by archive time; unarchive; the archived current preset; New preset from the tab, chosen and opened; the library's hidden archived presets and Archived view; the Model tab's picker, Used sort and the connections link; the empty Model tab), screenshots of each view in light and dark.

**What a version shows of its context.** `StartRollout` keeps the snapshot's issues on the rollout (`context_issues_json`), so a path window reads them with each version (a lookup by the version's `rollout_id`, as `versionExtras` in `db/rows.ts` adds it to every version read) without reading a snapshot. Migration 0016 backfills valid issue arrays using the kinds from `ContextIssue`, including lorebook warnings; malformed arrays remain null. Snapshot presence is checked independently of issues, including legacy rollouts without a snapshot. `Version.context` is null when nothing recorded a context (typed and imported messages, greetings, a generation that failed before its rollout opened), and otherwise holds the issues.

**The request inspector** (DESIGN §7.4; `GetRunContext`, `@rp/shared/inspectorApi.ts`, `api/inspector.ts`; the reader op `RunContext`, `db/inspectorReads.ts`). From a generated version, the context it was generated from, as it was sent: its rollout's stored snapshot, not a rebuild, so it's exact whatever changed since, a card or preset deleted for good included [P]. Only the chat's owner reads it, and a version, message or chat in the bin is `NotFound`, like every read (the isolation matrix).
- **The sent provider mapping** (`wire.ts`) is captured in the SDK's `onPayload` hook, after SDK conversion and registered transforms. Before HTTP, `RecordSentContext` is queued on the writer, which then writes only text messages, numeric samplers, source indices, server-only content digests, sanitized display metadata and the capability identity actually used to `rollout_payloads.sent_context_json`, in one owner-checked transaction. The request doesn't wait for that write: it commits beside the HTTP request, ahead of the rollout's later writes (the writer serves in order), and the attempt's stream ends only once it has. It isn't stopped with the request, so a reply stopped just after sending keeps its record; a failed write is logged, and the inspector then shows the capture as unavailable (`test/sentContextRecord.test.ts`). Assembly reads the complete display metadata in the same reader transaction: model and preset labels, source labels and identities, issues and activation decisions. Capture scrubs every display string (including lore keywords) on the main thread with the complete effective request inventory (§6), including catalog and authentication components resolved before capture, and excludes headers, keys, proxy settings and arbitrary payload fields. SDK environment defaults are disabled; Google uses the same controlled transport. Ordinary provider errors published in Version events use this inventory too. Retries replace this projection with the latest attempt's mapping. Responses' `developer` and Google's `model` roles are preserved. Combined system blocks retain all their sources. Before transforms, wire messages receive explicit provenance on JSON-invisible symbols, retained through object spreads and moves. Inserted or replaced messages without that provenance have no assigned sources; source labels never fall back to row position [P]. Missing final captures, including legacy captures without sanitized display metadata, return `capture: unavailable` with empty messages, samplers and issues and an explicit “Not sent / unavailable” notice. The inspector never falls back to raw assembly text or reconstructs labels from mutable refs. Database workers receive no decrypted credential inventory. Display metadata annotates the captured wire messages without storing their text twice.
- **Each message** with its role, name, text, estimated tokens (the assembler's estimate: four characters a token, three a message, plus its images), each image's estimate with its basis and detail level (`ContextMessage.images`: tokens or unknown, what the budget counted, whether it was sent; captured wire messages are text, so the images come from the snapshot's request messages through each wire message's `inputs`) and its sources, named for the user from the pieces that went into it: `Preset prompt “Main Prompt”` (the name in the preset revision the context used), `Preset: new chat prompt` for the preset's other text, `Card “Mira”: description` (the name in the card revision it read), `Note “…”`, `Message 12` (by depth, linking to the message), `One-turn direction`, and the assembler's own blocks. A message squashed from several pieces lists each. A history message's source carries its `version` (its place among the slot's versions when sent, from 1), shown as `Message 12, version 2`; a lorebook entry is `Lorebook “Harbor”: entry 3 “The lighthouse”` with the entry's title (ST's comment) in the book revision read; a card's, lorebook's or preset's source carries its library `ref` to link to; notes take their title.
- **Parts** ("debug symbols", PHASE1-DECISIONS §1). Each captured message records where each source's text sits in it: `parts`, character offsets into the sent (scrubbed) text, in order and never overlapping, each naming one of the message's sources. The reader hands the main thread each request message's pieces as a tree of text by source id with the inspection inputs, never stored: each outermost piece, and inside a labelled block the pieces it holds (a card's wrapped field holding its join prefix, field and suffix; the characters' definitions holding each card's; a lorebook block its entries; a prompt with `{{summary}}` its summaries). A preset prompt that read `{{description}}`, `{{personality}}` or `{{scenario}}` holds the joined fields' recorded `cards:macro:*` piece when its text contains it, so a format prompt shows which card each line came from. Final capture (`inspectWire`, `locate`) scrubs each text as the content is scrubbed and finds it in the sent message, searching from the end of the previous sibling, else at its first free occurrence, and a block's pieces only inside the block. Leaves become `parts`; blocks become `groups` (same offsets, nested ones inside their outer ones). A card join prefix or suffix inside a block is marked `frame`. Assembler-side rewrites are per piece and recorded as the piece's text (regex scripts' output for a history message, `collapse_newlines`), so their spans are found as any other. A piece whose text isn't in the sent message verbatim (a registered provider transform rewrote the whole message after assembly, which no per-piece span survives) takes the text between the siblings found around it, trimmed of edge whitespace, marked `rewritten`; a run of such siblings shares that text, the first as `source` and the others (including nested sources in inseparable blocks) as `also`, and a lone rewritten block's pieces are searched inside it. When located neighbours moved out of order, the remaining unclaimed text is boxed with all unresolved sources instead of being attributed to the assembler. These shared fallback boxes may include joins: they identify the candidate sources without claiming an exact division after a whole-message rewrite. Wrappers and blank pieces never take text, and an empty gap (a rewrite removed the text) produces no box: then the source is listed under "Also from" as before. Text between parts is the assembler's joins, wrappers and folded names. Only offsets are stored, never the text twice.
- **Not sent.** The capture's display lists what this turn left out (`notSent`): notes whose condition didn't hold (`due: false`), lorebook entries skipped, and the snapshot's `skippedPrompts`, each a source like any other, with its activation decision. A prompt left out by its ST generation-type triggers (§9) is listed like one left out by its condition, reading “(sent only for normal generations)”; a prompt excluded by both is listed once, by its triggers. Notes have no hidden kinds, so none is special-cased here.
- **The fix batch's request shapes.** Each summary of the layer is its own system message, shown as its own turn under a titled group (“Summary of messages 1–2”, an assembler piece around the summary's text, so the `<summary …>` framing is the group's wrapper); `{{summary}}` shows only the imported summary note's text, as a note part. A persona's description is its own wrapped `<Name>…</Name>` block under “Tobin's persona”, inside the characters' definitions. The end-of-request pieces are labelled by their three editor labels; the empty-text fallback is labelled “End of request fallback: who writes next”.
- **Older captures** (before parts, versions, refs and `notSent` were recorded) open the same way: their verbatim messages with the sources they recorded, one box per message, and a "not sent" list collected from the skipped note and lore sources those messages carry. Nothing is reconstructed from current references.
- **The cache breakpoints** between the messages, with why each is there (the end of the preset's part, or the end of the history the next request repeats), and whether they were sent: only to models whose breakpoints are `explicit` (§6).
- **The model, the preset** (its label and scope), the generation type and mode, the rollout's status, the effective samplers after provider mapping, and **the usage the provider reported**, per attempt (an inspector-specific DTO: status, uncached input, cache read, cache write, output, usage source and cost). The SQL uses an explicit column projection. On phones usage appears as a two-column list of labelled values per attempt, keeping numbers and “unknown” on one line without horizontal page scrolling; desktop retains the table. `e2e/inspector.spec.ts` checks all six labels and unbroken values at 390×844.
- **The issues** in the inspector come from the sanitized final display capture. Version warnings still use the validated rollout column; malformed legacy arrays display as none.
- **Source explanations and identity.** Lore sources retain status, step and constant/keyword reasons, with secondary-key logic. Notes retain explicit versus default activation, their condition in words, whether it was due, and in snapshots from before intervals were dropped the interval and its user-message count. The client renders these historical decisions beside the source. Deduplication and React keys use stable hashes of book/ref + revision + UID for lore, entity + revision for notes, and the other source references for other kinds. Equal labels remain distinct.
- **The client** (`features/chat/ContextPage.tsx`, `/chats/$chatId/context/$versionId`, a lazy route). Every version with a recorded context, a swipe included, has a "Request it was generated from" button among its message actions (`Message.tsx`), beside the same item in its "More actions" menu. The page shows the request summary (model, preset, generation type, breakpoints, samplers), the issues, then one block per sent message in request order, headed by its number, role, name and tokens; inside, each group is a titled box holding its parts and inner groups, and each part is a titled box: the title says what the text is and where it came from (linking to the chat message or the library item), with the activation decision under it, and the text follows exactly as sent. A group's text outside its parts is its framing, shown verbatim without a box: quiet when an assembler block's (with `frame` wrappers labelled by their preset source), as plain prompt text when a preset prompt's own; line breaks at the framing's edges are left to the layout. Prompt text is set in the monospace face on the canvas colour; the inspector's own titles, labels and links are in the interface face on the raised surface, so they can't be mistaken for prompt text. A rewritten part or block is boxed like any other, its title "<source> (rewritten)", so a transform's output is never attributed to the assembler. Text outside every box shows as quiet framing labelled "Added by the assembler" (whitespace-only joins are left to the spacing); "Show as one text" shows a message's whole content in one box. Then "Not sent this turn", then usage: per attempt the counts and cost, and its times from the ledger (`InspectorUsage.startedAt`/`firstTokenAt`/`endedAt`): Time (start to end, "running" or "unknown"), First token (start to the first text or reasoning delta) and Tokens/s (output over first token to end), each "unknown" when a figure is missing. A context of at most 60 messages and 120,000 characters opens with every turn expanded; a larger one opens collapsed to previews of the first 200 characters; "Expand every turn" / "Collapse every turn" switch all. Rows are TanStack Virtual rows measured as they expand, following the chat list's approach. Visible rows, a small overscan and the focused row mount. List items expose their full-list position and size. Expansion state lives above the virtual rows, keyed by version and message index. Browser coverage scrolls and opens a later row in a 100k-token context and the last row of a dense 10,000-message context, retains keyboard focus through PageDown, and restores expanded rows after unmounting. A version under another owned chat's URL redirects to its canonical chat; the back link uses the returned chat id. Both inspector offers carry the fork the message is viewed in (`?fork=`, the session's resolved fork, which needn't be the fork that generated the version nor the chat's current one); "Back to the reply" and every history source's link carry it on, so returning, or following a source, opens that fork at the message (`e2e/inspector.spec.ts`: two forks showing different versions at a shared slot, at 1440 and 390 px).
- **Generation time and tokens on a reply** (parity finding 5). The reader operation `VersionMetrics` (`inspectorReads.ts`; RPC `GetVersionMetrics`, at most 200 versions a call, another user's versions left out as if they had none) reads the `generation` ledger rows of each version that has rows of its own, together with those of the versions it was continued from, following the complete `source_version_id` chain with deduplicated identities (an edit continued counts the reply it was edited from; the edit itself, having no rows, shows nothing). `versionMetricsOf` (`@rp/shared/inspectorApi.ts`) projects them: requests, whether the last is still running, the summed start-to-end time of ended requests, the summed first-token-to-end time (unknown if any request lacks its first-token time), the output tokens of the ended requests that have a count with the number that have none (`outputUnknown`), reasoning tokens (null if any request reported none), whether any count is the app's estimate, and the last request's figures apart. Cost and input (msgcost1, 2026-11-16; no schema change): each request's figures also carry the ledger's `cost` with its currency and `cost_formula`, `reported_cost`, `input_uncached`, `cache_read`, `cache_write` and `cache_write_long`; the metrics sum the ended requests' costs per currency (`costs`, never added across currencies), count those with none (`costUnknown`), list the formulas (`costSources`), flag a cost priced from estimated counts (`costEstimated`; a `reported` cost never is), sum the reported charge (`reportedCost` over `reportedRequests`), and sum each input count (null when any ended request lacks it). The client shows them under the portrait as two message details (`versionMetrics.tsx`, §5 "Message details"): `message.timer` ("9.3s") and `message.tokens` ("209t", "~" for an estimate, "+" when some request had no count; absent when unknown), ST's forms, each a button named "Generation: 9.3 s · 209 tokens" ("tokens unknown", "time unknown") whose tooltip and click-open panel list generation time, time to first token (the last request's), output tokens, speed, reasoning tokens and "Reasoning time: not recorded" (the ledger has no reasoning end time) when the version has reasoning, and the request count explicitly saying it includes the original generation, retries and continuations, with the last request's time, tokens and cost (labelled estimated when applicable) when there is more than one. The panel also lists (`costDetails`) the cost ("$0.012 (estimated); 1 request had none", amounts in different currencies joined by "+"; "unknown (no price for this model)" when none has one), "Priced by" (the provider's charge, the model's price list, or your cost formula), "Provider charged" when the provider's charge differs from the cost or covers only some requests, "Input tokens" (the total, then uncached, cache read and cache write, with the long-lived part of the writes when there is one), "Cached" (cache read over all input) and output tokens "reasoning included" (pi-ai's output includes reasoning for every supported provider). The header detail `message.cost` shows the cost short (`formatCost`/`shortCost`): three decimals ("$0.012"), two from a dollar up ("$1.23"), two significant digits under a cent ("$0.0041"), another currency's label after the number; "~" first when estimated, "+" after when a request had none or was priced in another currency. It opens the same panel, and an import or a user's turn shows none. Reads are batched per microtask per chat session (`metricsLoader.ts`) and repeated when the version's status changes; a failed read or one that still finds the last request running is repeated a second later, up to five times, independently of React effect changes. The metrics panel uses balanced columns and scrolls within its available height so the last request remains reachable on phones. Nothing shows while generating. An imported version shows what SillyTavern recorded instead (`Version.recorded`, §13; `recordedFigures`): started, finished, generation time, time to first token, reasoning time, ST's token count and speed, each only where recorded; an imported user message has its count alone. The speaker's name keeps its width (up to 12 rem) so the model label truncates first. Tests: shared `test/versionMetrics.test.ts` (cost sums per currency, missing costs, input sums), client `test/versionMetrics.test.ts` (texts, unknowns, recorded figures, the registration, the cost's short forms and rows), server `test/versionCost.test.ts` (a reported cost with cached input through a continuation, then recomputed costs in another currency and none), `test/continueReasoning.test.ts` (an edit continued sums two requests; the inspector's times), `test/isolation.test.ts` (`GetVersionMetrics`), `e2e/continueReasoning.spec.ts` (the figures under the portrait, their panel and the inspector's columns at 1440 and 390 px), `e2e/messageCost.spec.ts` (the cost after the time and before the mark, its hover and panel rows, unchanged heights and the layout audit at 1440 and 390, light and dark, both spacing modes, solo and group, its switch).

**The cache-warmth estimate** (DESIGN §5.5; the reader op `CacheWarmth` in `db/assemblyReads.ts`, the pure comparison in `assembler/warmth.ts`, the service `chat/CacheWarmth.ts`). Whether the provider's cache for a chat is likely warm for the next reply, labelled as an estimate.
- **History budget explanation.** `NextContext` adds an optional `budget` with the effective context maximum (clamped to the model), stepped target, response reserve, and estimated tokens taken by everything except raw history, plus the preset's name and whether it is ST's built-in default. The maximum and target include the response reserve. Assembly records these counts in new snapshots; a fixed-content budget failure also carries them, so the next-context read can explain it without a successful assembly, a model or an earlier send. Other assembly failures return a null budget. The chat's virtualized list shows one explanation before the first retained raw message, or at the end when none fits, only in the loaded window containing that boundary; while an assembly refusal shows, the refusal explains instead and the list shows none. It names the preset and these token amounts, including the built-in fallback. Hidden and summarized messages keep their separate marks.

`NextContext.assemblyError` carries an assembler refusal through the reader’s next-context estimate and Cache events, including a newest message that cannot fit the history target while fixed prompts still fit the maximum. The registered `chat.composer-notes` contribution `composer.assembly-error` (`AssemblyRefusal.tsx`) shows the refusal before Send, in the composer's column (`max-w-3xl`) like the chat's other inline alerts; a successful estimate clears it. `NextContext.assemblyErrorReason` names the refusal's kind. A `budget` refusal is a notice in the warning tone ("The next reply doesn't fit the context size"), not an error: when the fixed content and the reply reserve exceed the context size it says so with each number's source; otherwise (the newest message, a summary chunk) it shows the assembler's reason and the same numbers without claiming they overflow. It offers the history notice's action as its primary button. Other refusals keep the danger tone. `NextContext.budget.origins` (`budgetOrigins` in `assembler/budget.ts`) says where the budget's numbers come from: the context size from the model's own context size setting, or else its window's source (your setting, learned from the provider's error, the provider's list, a catalog and its match, or assumed); the reply reserve and the history target from the model's settings or the defaults. The history notice (`timeline.history-budget`) names each, turns to the warning tone when the size is assumed, and offers **Set the context size** (assumed) or **Change the context size**, which opens the model's settings in a dialog (`ModelSettingsDialog`) focused on the field in use: the window, or the context size setting when that's what applies. The model list marks an assumed window "(assumed)" and a learned one "(learned)", with each source in its title; the settings form describes what an empty window field resolves to and from where, and shows a learned size with **Forget it**. The existing history boundary continues to describe the last successfully assembled cut. Server `test/stPresetContext.test.ts`, client session/contribution tests and browser `stPresetContext.spec.ts` cover the refusal, its removal after repairing the budget, registry replacement/disablement, and both widths/themes.
- **From the last request** of the chat that reached its provider: the newest ledger row with the chat's attribution that is running, complete, or got a first token [P]. Its start is when the cache was written or read. Verified when the provider reported a cache read or write on it; assumed otherwise [P].
- **TTL eligibility:** model override, connection override, then the documented catalog policy (`providers/cachePolicy.ts`), with a source URL per value. pi-ai's `promptCache` guesses are not defaults. After transforms, capture pins the actual requested mode and its TTL, including extended retention and OpenRouter upstream model namespaces. Editing a TTL cannot extend an existing cache: expiry uses the historical captured TTL. An explicitly unknown final policy stays unknown through capture and readback; only absent legacy policy metadata permits fallback. Intentional user overrides still take precedence. Marker discovery checks shaped controls only at the selected API’s control locations, never inside schemas or tool arguments/results. Unknown policies have no default; the user can set one. Gemini cachedContents resources are not created by this app, so its explicit resource default is not a sliding timer here.

| Provider / mode | Built-in seconds |
|---|---:|
| Anthropic; Bedrock Claude; Vertex Claude | 300; 3600 when all requested markers use 1h |
| OpenAI GPT-5.6+ / later families; GPT-5.5 | 1800 |
| Earlier cache-enabled OpenAI, in-memory / requested 24h | 300 / 1800 (typical, not the 24h ceiling) |
| Azure GPT-5.6+; earlier in-memory / 24h | 1800; 300 / unknown |
| Moonshot K3 (including regional API), default / requested 1h | 300 / 3600; K2 and Coding unknown |
| Qwen / DashScope explicit | 300; implicit and token-plan contracts unknown |
| Groq supported GPT-OSS, including Safeguard 20B | 7200 |
| Bedrock OpenAI-compatible GPT-5.6+ / 6.1 | 1800 |
| MiniMax explicit Messages | 300; passive Chat unknown |
| Cerebras Chat | 300 from write |
| OpenRouter Claude with markers, default / 1h unpinned / one pinned upstream (none without markers) | 300 / 600 / 3600 |
| OpenRouter Gemini implicit / explicit | 180 estimate / 300 fixed |
| Vercel known Claude / MiniMax route | 300; 3600 with requested 1h controls |
| Other policies, including direct Gemini implicit, DeepSeek, xAI, Mistral | Unknown |

**Minimum cacheable size** (livefix, 2026-11-07): a prefix below the model's minimum is never cached, so the estimate claims nothing warm below it. The minimum is the model's `cacheLayout.minTokens`, else `documentedCacheMinimum` (`providers/cachePolicy.ts`): Claude per model as Anthropic documents it (512 for the 5.x generation, 1,024, 2,048 or 4,096 for earlier ones; Haiku 4.5 4,096), on Anthropic, OpenRouter, Bedrock, Vertex and Vercel; OpenAI 1,024 (direct, Azure, OpenRouter `openai/`); OpenRouter Gemini 1,024, Pro 4,096; unknown elsewhere. When the last request's prefix (assembler estimate through its last breakpoint) is below it: no estimate if the next one is too; else a cold estimate, "The last request was below the model's minimum cacheable size (N tokens), so nothing was cached.", with the next prefix's tokens.

**OpenAI's best-effort cache** (`bestEffortCache`: OpenAI models direct, on Azure, and OpenRouter `openai/`), calibrated from the live suite (gpt-5.4-nano, 2026-11-07, with `prompt_cache_key`): a request a few seconds after the first read nothing; later ones read 1,792 tokens, the first prompt's 128-token floor, not their whole previous prompt; an edit of the first user message read none of the unchanged start. So the estimate's cached prefix is the last request's reported read, never more (none before the first read), and a changed prefix re-sends the whole next prefix. The live suite records OpenAI's reads without requiring them and checks only that the estimate claims no more. Through OpenRouter pinned to OpenAI (liveapi2): a 1,700-token chat read nothing on turns 2 and 3, while a 3,200-token prompt sent three times read 2,816 tokens from the second on, with or without `prompt_cache_key`.

Fixed lifetimes (Cerebras, OpenRouter explicit Gemini) use both the matching prefix's original write/miss time and that write's stored TTL, found in the chat's last 100 write/miss requests. Subsequent hits, TTL edits and transformed mode changes never renew them. Without a known origin there is no countdown. Sliding estimates conservatively start at request start. A changed prefix still produces a rewrite estimate without a TTL; a countdown requires both a historical expiry and a next-request TTL. No model, a missing connection or a next request that cannot be built yields no warmth estimate, while its recorded history boundary can still be published.

- **Whether the prefix still matches:** the reader assembles the next request as a new reply at the requested leaf (the active path for pushed estimates) [P], maps it through `wire.ts`, and compares the provider-formatted prefix with the pinned previous mapping. Connection id and cache revision, model identity and capability digest, an OpenRouter model's routing setting (each provider caches on its own; liveapi2), roles, names and text must match. New captures compare SHA-256 digests of the actual final role/name/text and each sent image's content SHA-256 and detail before redaction; only display text is scrubbed. Digests stay in worker storage/comparison and are excluded by the explicit `GetRunContext` projection. Older captures without digests fall back to their stored text and can conservatively read cold after redaction [P]. Unassigned transform insertions inside the reusable prefix also participate in comparison. The next Responses request uses the installed SDK's message converter with pinned reasoning and developer-role flags; the historical comparison uses the final captured mapping. A capability change is conservatively cold even if its effect on these particular messages is unknown [P]. Legacy snapshots without a pinned connection revision are cold until a new request records one [P]. Without a reusable breakpoint the estimate is cold, never warm by default. A mismatch reports the first changed source, including piece membership and positions, and estimates the **next** prefix's uncached suffix through its last breakpoint [P]. A combined system block is counted as one wire message. A history cut caused by reaching the maximum says “The context reached its maximum; older messages left.” History movement under a changed budget is identified through emitted piece membership/start and the pinned history; unchanged retained turns with moved offsets are instead attributed to notes or the reusable-prefix endpoint/layout; an amendment requires changed text at the same version, while a changed version is reported as an edit. Image changes, removals and exclusion toggles also invalidate the prefix. Final capture hashes inline bytes transiently and persists only the digest; image bytes never enter the stored wire or client DTO. Model, connection route, system conversion, edits, branches, hidden messages, preset/card/note revisions, macro values and layout changes all invalidate the estimate.
- **Pushed, not polled.** `SubscribeChat` watches the chat for its owner once the subscription is allowed, and asks for an estimate. The hub calls the service for every event it publishes to a chat someone subscribes to (`ChatHub.listen`; not deltas, not `Cache`), which estimates again 250 ms after the last such change, never two at once for a chat, and publishes `Cache` with the estimate (null for none), path leaf and next request’s history start, independently of TTL or a previous provider request. An inactive-path client uses that event to invalidate its path-specific `GetNextContext` read; both RPC and worker validate the leaf against the owned chat. Editor commits, restores, regex approvals and merges, connection/model edits, model refreshes, connection credential/key/header/proxy changes, dependency deletion (`DeleteConnection`, `DeleteCredential`, `DeleteNote`), all bin restorations/purges/emptying, and generation defaults re-estimate the user's open chats too. Graph deletions (`DeleteChat`, `DeleteMessage`, `DeleteFork`, `DeleteVersion`) also refresh the user's other watched chats, since any delete can evict a shared dependency from the bin. Instance network edits refresh all watched chats, since they change what a chat sends without an event of its own [P]. A change from elsewhere (a re-import) shows with the chat's next change. **Off a reply's path:** an estimate assembles the whole next request, as a reply does, so it waits while a reply is prepared and written in the chat (`CacheWarmth.hold`, taken by `Generations` for each running generation, and `expectReply`, taken for up to 2 s by a posted message whose sender asks for the reply next, until the reply's hold replaces it). Changes meanwhile make one estimate when the last hold ends. `GetNextContext` goes through the service (`CacheWarmth.next`): while the chat is held it first checks that the chat is the caller's and the leaf and fork are in it (`NextContextAccess`, a cheap reader read), so a refusal never waits on the chat's reply or shows its timing (`test/isolation.test.ts`, whose fixture replies stream for the whole suite), then waits the same way, then is worked out from what is stored then, never taken from an earlier estimate, since a change written without a chat event (a writer call from another service) would leave that one stale (`test/cacheWarmthHold.test.ts`, `test/nextContextFresh.test.ts`).
- **The indicator** (`features/chat/CacheIndicator.tsx`, the strip's `composer.cache` chip; fcomposer 2026-10-31): one compact chip whose popover says why in plain words. A changed prefix is an amber "↻ 2.9k uncached" (`compactTokens`), its popover "Your next reply re-sends about 2,926 tokens at full price, instead of reading them from the provider's cache." and "Why: " the server's reason; this shows with or without a TTL (DESIGN §5.5). Warm is "Cache warm 4:12", counted down in the browser from the request's start and the TTL, its popover saying whether the provider confirmed it; when it runs out it becomes "↻ N uncached" with the prefix's tokens and "More than 5 minutes passed since the last request, so the provider's cache has expired." No chip shows when the tokens round to 0, or without a TTL and with nothing changed (`cacheState`). Other parts of the chat add notes to its popover through `cacheNotes(session)` (the insertion editor's re-read); with nothing else to show, the chip shows the first note's short text. The countdown can be hidden from the popover, remembered per browser [P]; hidden, the chip still turns cold on time, from one timer. While a reply is written on the path shown, and until the first estimate after it arrives (30 s at most, as a failed estimate sends none), a chip that had something to show reads a neutral "Cache after reply" instead, its popover saying the estimate is worked out again when the reply ends, since the server makes none meanwhile (`CacheWarmth.hold`; `e2e/cacheAfterReply.spec.ts`).
- Tested over a real server (`test/inspector.test.ts`): the inspector against the request the mock provider received, with sources, breakpoints, usage and issues; warm after a reply, cold after an earlier message's edit, on another branch, and after the default preset changes; no countdown without a TTL, but a rewrite estimate on a changed prefix. `e2e/steppedHistory.spec.ts` checks dropped versus hidden messages, the pushed boundary before a first send, warning without TTL, truncation retained in the inspector, and two tabs with an inactive-branch deep link. The isolation matrix probes the final `GetRunContext` projection, the writer op `RecordSentContext`, and the reader op `CacheWarmth`, both ways. In the browser (`e2e/inspector.spec.ts`), against the production server and a fake provider: opening a reply's context and its sources and breakpoints, an earlier reply's and a swipe's request from the message's button, the indicator warm then cold after an edit, the long context (its chat with summarization off), and the phone width. New captures name macro-joined descriptions, personalities and scenarios by their fields, and label persona fields as **Persona “<name>”**. History sources pin their one-based position among the generating fork’s undeleted swipes at send time, matching the swipe counter after deletion; later deletions do not renumber a captured request. Older captures retain their recorded labels and optional-field fallback. `test/inspectorProvenance.test.ts` covers persona attribution and deletion before capture, and checks the groups (a card's wrapped field inside the characters' definitions, its wrappers as frames; a personality format prompt holding the card it read) and a part and its source for each kind (preset prompt with its preset link, card field, note, lorebook entry with its title, history message with the version sent, the closing user turn, a skipped note and a skipped conditioned prompt as not sent) and that a capture stripped of parts and `notSent` still opens verbatim; The provenance regression also restores and deletes a preceding swipe, checks the current picker’s numbering, and verifies that captured numbers and exact snapshot replay stay frozen. `test/assembler.test.ts` checks all three macro-join titles (descriptions, personalities and scenarios). `test/lcmAssembly.test.ts` checks the summary's part. `test/inspectionParts.test.ts` checks `locate`'s order, nesting and overlap rules and its rewritten fallback (one piece, a run, a removed text, a rewritten block's parts); `test/inspectorCapture.test.ts` a registered transform's rewrite captured as its card field's rewritten part; `e2e/inspector.spec.ts` the "(rewritten)" box at 1440 and 390. `e2e/inspectorWalkthrough.spec.ts` walks a realistic synthetic chat (a preset with conditioned prompts, two cast cards, a persona, notes with one on another card's turn, a lorebook hit, a summary, a swipe) at 1440 and 390, light and dark, including each card's box and a personality format prompt's per-card boxes.

`test/stPresetContext.test.ts` HTTP-imports synthetic 50-message chats with 3,500- and 5,000-token card descriptions and ST's selected 32,000-token preset. It checks that the whole history fits after adoption, all three preset report messages, re-import preservation of a chosen default, and the built-in budget on fixed-content overflow. Without adoption, the smaller fixture's history start is depth 50 (past its last message at 49); the larger fixture fails assembly and has no boundary. `e2e/stPresetContext.spec.ts` checks the explanation at the end in both cases and its disappearance after importing the selected preset, and the side panel's This chat tab naming ST's built-in preset and its 4,095 tokens, then “Roomy” as the user's default with 32,000 and a link to the editor; the server test checks `preset` (name and scope) in `GetNextContext`; `e2e/steppedHistory.spec.ts` checks its position before retained history. The new writer operation has lease and cross-user preset probes in the isolation matrix.

**Known limits:**
- A message whose speaker has left the chat is named as the first card of its side.
- Reasoning streams and persists separately on the version (see Reasoning above); it stays out of ordinary text history. A reply's leading tagged sections are sent back only by the `reply-sections` stage, as the preset's `send_back` says (§12 "Reply sections").
- With `use_sysprompt` and a greeting first, Anthropic gets an assistant turn first, as ST sends it; not checked against the real API.
- ST's per-model sampler rules are its model-name patterns, copied: they'll need updating as ST's do, until models carry them.
- The time zone is UTC: the client doesn't send the user's yet.
- The cache estimate assumes the next request is a new reply at the displayed path’s leaf: a swipe, another speaker or a generation type a preset prompt triggers on can differ from it.
- Each estimate assembles the next request in a reader, after every change to an open chat: what an assembly costs (above), up to a few hundred milliseconds of a reader at 100,000 messages with state events.


**Source descriptors** (`assembler/sourceDescriptors.ts`). The assembler's scoped `sourceDescriptors` registry names provenance kinds; all eight built-in kinds register through it and keep their existing labels, identities, activation metadata and library/message links. A plugin stage can record a `PluginSource` with kind `<plugin-id>/<kind>` and plain JSON `data` in a piece. Its descriptor maps that pinned source to the inspector's title (`label`) and optional existing library (`ref`) or chat-message (`slotId`) link, using pure code and the owner-scoped built-in label lookups where relevant. A plugin needing other metadata pins it in its source data; it does not query SQLite from a descriptor. Source identity and activation remain in the fixed projection. Missing or disabled descriptors fall back to the kind as a readable title, without inventing a link. Descriptors install through trusted `AssemblyModules` in source and bundled readers; inspection copies the active entries within the request's module scope. The final request capture freezes and scrubs the resulting title with the rest of the display, so closing the plugin's scope does not alter historical inspector output. The shared contract admits built-in and namespaced kinds; the existing inspector renders their titles and typed internal links without another client registry. `test/inspectorSources.test.ts` exercises a scoped custom stage and descriptor through generation and the inspector RPC, fallback, built-in override/disable/restoration, and identical built-in output in source and bundled workers. `e2e/inspector.spec.ts` also renders a captured namespaced source with its title and library link at 1440 and 390 pixels. Cache-expiry comparisons need only whether a prefix differs and use the fallback label without querying source names.

**Assembly modules in readers** (`assembler/modules.ts`). The server exposes the scoped `AssemblyModules` registry alongside `Reader`. A trusted entry (`id`, absolute `module` URL, `exportName`) names an `InstallAssemblyModule` function. That function receives the assembler and registers projections, stages, macros, source descriptors or final transforms through the same APIs the built-ins use. Every reader RPC carries the server registry's current snapshot in an internal header, overriding inherited headers. The worker validates that snapshot and provides it in the request's Effect context. Each assembly (reply, rebuild or summary) and projection-metadata read installs those modules in a scope around the operation, then removes their registrations. No plugin code or SQLite runs on the main thread. Requests already admitted retain their snapshot; new requests after a scope closes see the previous modules, including after worker respawn. ESM modules stay cached, so changed code needs a new module URL. This supplies trusted worker module execution, not a plugin installer or consent UI. `test/assemblyStorage.test.ts` verifies scoped additions, overrides, disablement, metadata and missing-projection fallback through source and bundled readers.


## 16. LCM: hierarchical summaries

Phase 3 slices 1–7 implement summary storage, freshness, context assembly, planning, provider-driven summarization, refusal handling, condensation, re-summarizing, the summary UI, and enabling LCM on a chat that has history already with its backfill and cost estimate. `spec/LCM.md` records the design; its remaining unbuilt UI items are cost/model per summary and summarization rollouts in the panel (§2.13).

**The summary schema** (in the baseline) is the five summary tables and their indexes, reference guards, immutable revision triggers, draft cleanup and FTS triggers. Summaries add `failed`, error JSON and a batch id; revisions add `imported`; L1 inputs allow a null version for an absent effective message; higher-level lineage pins each child's revision. Jobs add an indexed batch and a leaf inside their chat. All foreign keys are indexed. Inputs, lineage, revisions and summary identity are immutable, including INSERT OR REPLACE, and may be deleted only with their chat. A new summary starts unsealed. Insert guards require its declared primary-parent chain, ordered L1 inputs or contiguous children at strictly lower levels, with sealed children and no self-reference. With insertions the range may instead follow display order (below). `summaries_chain` keeps the primary-chain check first, then permits ancestor endpoints spanning inserted children or endpoints ordered across an inserted subtree. It never bypasses endpoint checks just because the chat has an insertion. `summary_inputs_chain` and `summary_parents_chain` also permit returning through inserted ancestors to an older inserted sibling (UUID descending) or the anchor’s ordinary successor; they cannot return from an ordinary branch or reverse inserted siblings. Input guards reject merged slots. Sealing checks the count and last slot; together the guards preserve ordered lineage, allowing skipped insertions in a stale summary. These graph guards are independent of current fork placement: the layer and completion additionally validate membership and order in the viewed fork. Sealing checks complete coverage and closes both lineage tables to further inserts. A sealed summary cannot be reopened. Its base selected revision is frozen; per-fork selection and absorption status are overrides.

**Writes** (`db/ops.ts`, `db/lcmWrites.ts`) run in the writer, one transaction each:

- `CompleteSummary` requires an owned processing job and running summarize/condense rollout. It walks the job's primary-parent chain, refuses merges, requires L1 inputs in exactly chain order, or lower-level children that partition it in declared order with revisions belonging to those children. In a job's fork that shows inserted slots it checks the job's display range instead (below): inputs, or parts, in display order with only inserted slots between them, so a job claimed before an insertion inside its range still completes, and its summary is stale there at once; `slot_count` is the inputs' count, or the parts' sum. It saves and seals the summary, generated revision and inputs or lineage, then saves permitted absorption supersessions, the completed job and finished rollout with ledger usage atomically. An invalid reference or chain rolls back everything. Claimed jobs also bind completion to their frozen request.
- `EditSummary` writes and selects a user revision with `expectedRowVersion`, and commits only the named draft/session holding exactly that text, returning recovery metadata. `SelectSummaryRevision` selects a revision of that summary or of a completed replacement linked to it by its job, with the same concurrency guard. Choosing a replacement records a `summary_choice` override; choosing or editing the original restores it in that fork. `lcm_summary_choices` remains shared base state only. Replacement revisions appear in the original's Revisions list. Both refresh the caller's cache estimates.
- `GetSummary`, `EditSummary` and `SelectSummaryRevision` are authenticated RPCs (`@rp/shared/lcm.ts`, `api/lcm.ts`). Every new storage operation and RPC has cross-user probes in both directions. References reach their owner through the chat; foreign or deleted chats are `NotFound`.

**Freshness** (`db/lcmReads.ts`) is derived in the read transaction, in a fork (§3.8: the fork in view, `ForkView`, else the current one). A summary is shared by every fork whose path holds its chain, and is fresh in a fork when its inputs match what that fork shows, so a swipe or an amend that copies in one fork makes it stale there only, and only that fork's planner (`PlanSummaries`, run in the fork named, a reply's own, else the fork through its leaf) has work for it (`test/forkSelection.test.ts`, `test/forkVersions.test.ts`). An L1 is fresh when every input still matches its slot's effective version: the version the fork shows (its selection, or its copy standing in for it, §3.8) if it's nonempty, nongenerating and nonfailed, of a live, unpurged, unhidden slot, otherwise null. The input also records the amendment count because human versions can change content without changing id. An L1 is also fresh only if the fork would send the images it was written with (below, "Images"). A higher level is fresh only if every child is fresh and selects the recorded revision. A completed explicit rerun makes its generated source inactive for live freshness, so generated ancestors must incorporate the new child; historical contexts retain the old immutable child pins. Edits, swipes, deletes, restores and hides write nothing to summaries; selecting the old version or restoring visibility can make them fresh again. Reading a summary never starts a generation.

Tests: a bare-schema oracle for each new trigger and foreign-key indexes, a real-server hand-built branching graph with recursive freshness, amendment and revision selection, completion rollback, and the isolation matrix. Fixtures use synthetic data only and write SQL in a worker.


**Selection and partition** (`db/lcmLayer.ts`, registered `assembler/lcm.ts` stage). The reader walks the primary-parent path and considers sealed complete or truncated summaries ending on it. Before freshness recursion or cursor advancement it independently checks each candidate’s real slot chain, ordered inputs and recursive lower-level child partition, including pinned revision ownership. An inconsistent candidate is ignored, retaining usable earlier coverage and the remaining raw text; a visited-node memo bounds malformed cycles. At an endpoint, a user-written or imported revision wins until the user chooses a replacement; other candidates prefer freshness, then higher level, then newer id. A queued absorption cannot displace a protected same-level summary even when its new range extends beyond it. Empty summaries with changed inputs are excluded so restored effective messages return as raw history. It walks candidates backwards, retaining only a continuous prefix from the root: a gap leaves the original messages raw, matching the baseline's no-loss rule. A stale summary remains usable when no fresh candidate ends there. Summaries in a pending or processing batch are withheld; overflow can use completed members, as described below. The selected layer is in path order and its last slot is the cursor. History reads strictly after that cursor, including an empty read when it is the target's parent; covered originals are neither sent nor pinned. Failed rows do not replace raw messages while those fit. Summary freshness reads share a memo within selection, so repeated child lineage is read once.

**Batched planning proofs** (planperf1, 2026-11-14). The existing `readingOnce` scope now keeps input/child facts, structural validity, lightweight selection projections and selected layers for one read transaction only. Ordinary primary paths find ending-slot candidates by indexed chain spans, then include their pinned descendants. A grouped input query checks ordinal/count/endpoints, primary-parent adjacency, version ownership and effective version/amendment freshness; a child query checks the same lower-level partition and revision ownership as the individual validator. Ordinary message overrides are resolved once over the fork's bounded lineage, with nearest-writer/newest-row precedence. Published hide ranges and preserved-input applications retain their original effective-input proof. Images, audience knowledge, inserted display paths and changeset application/group checks retain their existing specialized checks. Full summary DTOs are still returned to assembly and registered maintenance policies; lightweight projections stay internal to selection. Partial and whole batches share a selected layer only when the gathered candidates have no batch ids.

Mutable summary facts are reused only behind the LCM stamp ("Kept planning facts" below). One per-connection LRU (`lcmLineageCache.ts`) retains only sealed structural validity and pinned child links, shared across forks because these facts are immutable. Current owned summary headers are still read before consulting it; the key includes the sealed identity/range/count/base revision/status. The cache has at most 4,096 entries and 4,000,000 serialized key/header/child characters. It clears on `schema_version` changes and is disabled if the required immutability/retention/closure guards are absent, including corruption fixtures. Completed read operations publish newly checked structural proofs; no writer or freshness update participates. Jobs, settings, models, view boundaries and assembly are never cached. Every operation starts a read snapshot, and no writer updates either cache, so there is no writer-side invalidation/update window. Concurrent edit/plan attacks and missing-guard corruption/repair probes are in `lcmPlanning.test.ts`. Live jobs, settings and models are read normally in that snapshot. Retained planning state is proportional to the planned forks' summaries, not the chat's unrelated branches. Retained bounds per reader are the kept facts (8 forks, 64M estimated characters), a 4M-character/4,096-entry structural LRU and the tokenizer bound below, in addition to the reader's existing 256 MiB SQLite page cache. Maintenance slices stale ranges from the effective path when it read it, falling back to the original range read when endpoints do not match. Completed/failed coverage starts from requested path slots and uses a position map, removing the former per-summary linear search. Each plan still returns at most four jobs of each existing class; selected-path scans are linear work, not a constant-time bound for arbitrarily long histories. Maintenance explicitly retains ending-slot/insertion order, including serialized maintenance pins; its faster join cannot reverse the order of repairs or explicit requests. Requests, assembler version and registered planning policies are unchanged.

**Kept planning facts** (planperf2; reviewed 2026-11-14) replace the fact snapshot above. Each reader connection keeps, per (user, chat, fork) and at most 8 forks and 64,000,000 estimated characters across them (`db/lcmFactStore.ts`, least recently used first), what `primeSummaryReads` read of that fork's summaries: headers, input proofs, child links, validity, lightweight projections, full summaries of pure rows (no audience, images or changeset application), and the level-1 range inputs maintenance signs. Flat-row accounting includes every string (including failed-summary error, audience and image metadata), input identities and child identities, with allowances for scalar fields and references (`lcmFactWeight.ts`); these estimates bound retained cache accounting, not V8 heap bytes. They are valid while the chat's LCM stamp (§3.7) and `schema_version` stay; a moved stamp drops them, and the next plan reads them again (with the structural LRU still warm). The baseline's `summaries_chat(chat_id)` index includes SQLite's implicit rowid suffix, so the watermark stops at its last matching entry and the new-row query seeks directly above the saved rowid; `(chat_id, level)` alone would scan unrelated forks' summaries. The per-summary facts don't depend on the leaf, so a plan at another leaf of the fork reads only the summaries the kept ones lack. Per kept leaf (the four most recent) the store holds the path's summary ids; a request whose path passes a kept leaf reads only the summaries ending past it (one indexed span) and those sealed since, with their pinned parts (rowid above the kept floor: ordinary summaries are inserted and sealed in one transaction, and never deleted while their chat exists). Imported-summary adoption can prepare an unsealed row across transactions, below an already kept floor; its final publication writes a hide-range override and sets the enable run published, moving the chat stamp before that row is visible. So send → reply appended → next send reads a few new slots, not the 1,404 summaries again. Inserted-slot display paths and corruption fixtures without the guards or stamp triggers bypass retained facts. Audience/image rows can retain headers and structural inputs, but never retain their complete projections across operations: audience knowledge and image exclusions are checked live. The store is a copy: nothing is written for it, a crash or restart starts empty, and writes publish nothing to it. Jobs (batch withholding), settings, models, reruns, choices and assembly are read live on every plan; summary choice/revision overrides also move the stamp before cached headers can be reused. No settings digest is needed because no settings-dependent plan or request is retained. A change confined to another fork still moves the chat stamp when it touches existing summary facts; ordinary append/finish writes on either fork leave it unchanged.

Maintenance (`maintain`) completes pure candidates' full summaries in one grouped input read, and signs level-1 ranges from the kept range inputs; it reads the ranges it lacks one by one, or the whole effective path once when more than 32 are missing. Structural paths in a fork with message overrides join the fork's resolved overrides (`messageView`) as a table instead of probing fork steps per slot (`lcmPath.ts` `choiceColumns`), unless a published LCM range's hide needs the probe. Inserted display paths retain indexed fork-step probes: SQLite underestimates their windowed outer path and otherwise scans the first materialized choice alias for every position (stack2 review). `planCache.test.ts` runs every write kind (append, recent and summarized swipe/amend/select/hide/delete/restore, a second tab's fork and swipe, summary rewrite/revision/rerun/completion, settings, queued and claimed jobs) and checks whether the stamp moved and that the kept facts plan exactly as a fresh read; during the job, every plan of the LCM corpus was also compared with master's frozen reader (outside the repository). `lcmPlanningScale.test.ts` (slow tier) adds five send → append → send turns on the 200-branch fixture with the 200 ms budget on the median. `planCacheSeams.test.ts` (combine1115) checks the features built beside it the same way on warm readers: the account's summary model set, revised, overridden by the chat's, taken off, a branch's own choice (the other branch's plan unchanged) and that model's connection deleted, none of which moves the stamp; and a merge of another chat kept separate (merge2) into a warm destination with a branch made before it, then messages after the join, then its Undo (deleting the join), each compared with fresh facts for every view the plan lists (the characters' stretch views exist only while the join does) and the earlier branch planning as before throughout. The merge's `chat_merges` row moves the destination's stamp; the notes it brings (`entities`, `entity_revisions`, `entity_refs`, state events) and the summary-model choices (`settings`, scoped state events, `models`, `connections`) are no kept fact and are read live on every plan, so they need no trigger. The same file checks the request side of msgactions1's deleted-input exclusion with warm readers: deleting two inputs of a summary under a condensation on one branch moves the stamp, plans as fresh, and leaves neither summary's text in that branch's next request while a branch made before keeps it; restoring them brings it back. After a separate merge, deleting a summarized destination input does the same for both the destination's and the source's character.

Local tokenizer preparation also shares an exact `(encoding, text)` LRU in each worker (`importer/localTokenMemo.ts`), capped at 4,000,000 key UTF-16 code units and 20,000 entries across all local encodings. An edit is a different key, an encoding switch is a different namespace, failures are not cached, and oversized keys are not retained. This holds token counts only; it caches neither model settings nor assembled requests. Custom counter preparations keep their existing per-assembly cache. The graph/settings attacks are in `lcmPlanning.test.ts`, and `lcmLineageCache.test.ts` checks header mismatch and bounded eviction; tokenizer namespace, failure and hundreds-of-branches eviction attacks are in `localTokenMemo.test.ts`. `lcmPlanningScale.test.ts` belongs to the slow tier and compares the same 20,000-message/1,404-summary path with one and 200 branches (447,962 versions in the latter), recording cold initialization and three steady-state samples with the 200 ms before-reply guard. Other summary scale, graph, audience, thread and workshop tests remain gates.

**Per view** (contexts C7; §3.8 "Summaries kept per view"; in a chat with one shared context, a separate join's stretch views, §3.8 "Summaries across splits and joins"). In a chat set to separate contexts, a character that missed something has its own summaries (`summaries.audience_json`, its identities) after the shared ones that end before its first missed message; selection with a `LayerView` reads that layer, and every read without one (planning the shared summaries, the UI without `viewer`, coverage, failed holds, maintenance, the claim gate) reads only NULL-audience rows, so a shared chat is unchanged.

With the default two ordinary readers plus maintenance, the fact accounting cap totals 192M characters; the structural and token LRUs add 12M characters each across those three readers. At two bytes per character that is about 412 MiB of string payload allowances, plus object/array/map overhead and transient plans. SQLite may additionally cache 768 MiB across those readers. Their three 2-GiB mmap limits reserve up to 6 GiB of virtual address space, not 6 GiB of anonymous heap; resident file pages and WAL/page-cache memory must still be included in process/host measurements. Increasing `DB_READERS` multiplies all per-reader bounds, and the writer/format workers and application memory are additional. `lcmFactStore.test.ts` covers aggregate-weight eviction, oversize refusal, 400 branch keys, LRU promotion, schema/stamp changes, missing triggers and a fresh connection.

**Literal rendering and placement.** Model and user summary text is never macro-expanded. Each summary of the layer is its own system message, `<summary level="N" from="A" to="B">` around its text (`summaryBlock`), oldest first, immediately before the history and its failure markers, placed like the history's messages (DESIGN §8, owner 2026-10-28): a new summary is a message after the earlier ones, which stay as they were sent, so their cached prefix holds. `{{summary}}` is ST's one summary: it reads only the chat's switched-on summary notes that are due by their condition, never the summaries, in every chat (the one assembly path, §15). The imported summary note is sent only by its own switch, also beside the summaries. A `{{summary}}` prompt is volatile (never inside a cached prefix) while any summary note with text has a condition, since what it reads can change from turn to turn. With LCM off, existing imported-note behavior and the ST differential oracle are unchanged.

**Inserted messages** (`db/lcmDisplay.ts`; spec/MESSAGE-INSERT.md §3.4). In a fork that shows inserted slots (`insertionPieces` in `db/displayPath.ts`, null otherwise: one probe of `fork_overrides_point` per lineage entry), LCM reads its display path (§3.8 "Display paths") and every number is a position there: a summary's `from` and `to`, the layer's cursor (`cursorDepth` in the assembler's `SummaryLayer`, a position, equal to the depth without insertions), job ranges, failed ranges and `LcmSlot.position`. A fork that shows none runs the structural code unchanged.

**Moved messages** (schemafinal, 2026-11-16).
