**Inserted-path planning cost (stack2).** The batched choice join introduced in planperf2 (`8e8f688d`) caused a separate read regression beside slowfix1's settled-write fix. On a synthetic 5,008-position display path with dense overrides, SQLite chose `SCAN so LEFT-JOIN`; the full path query took 2.74–3.14 seconds warm, and complete first-reply reads were about three times deployed baseline even though the relative fork-depth assertion passed. `wholePath` now selects its existing indexed `lcmPathColumns` probes for inserted display paths, retaining batched choices for structural paths. On the same saved database, the warm path read took 372–406 ms and all 5,008 serialized rows had the same SHA-256 before and after. Warm reply planning returned to 1.31–1.41 seconds, within the independently replayed baseline range. No cache bounds, stamp rules, ownership/view checks, planning policy, returned data, baseline or operation contract changes. `lcmPathPlan.test.ts` executes the production reader in a worker against the full schema, checks the selected and inserted messages, and requires indexed fork-step lookups instead of the choice scan; it fails on the previous query form without a timing threshold.

### Compact reading and marker seams on the combined branch (stack3, 2026-11-15)

The registered chat-settings marker also reads `agent.send_presence` and `decision.points`.
Reply presence mode says whether replies may or must name who is in the scene. A change in the
branch’s disabled-decision set says “Decisions changed for this chat”, with the number turned
off and the existing fallback/consent rule in its explanation. The comparison uses set identity:
changing one disabled decision to another marks the change, while reordering the same set or
undoing a change at the same message does not. This does not enable a decision connection.
Account-level decision connection settings remain outside positional markers.

A `send_message` present list and `set_presence` effects write version-attached `away.set`
events and recorded presence, already displayed by the dedicated away/return rows. They do not
also get a cast/mute marker: muting is automatic reply eligibility and does not remove a card
from requests, while away presence controls each character’s causal view. Auto’s run handle
is transient authorization and is not a chat-setting event. Auto’s own state tools and presence
effects still follow the same selected-version and net-change rules as manually started replies.

`stackMarkerSeams` exercises destination cast markers at separate-history joins, exclusion of
source-only settings and selected-swipe effects alongside slot-attached settings. Import seam
coverage compares imported marker events with effective assembly state and verifies unpublished
`st_import_stage` rows do not affect markers. `stateMarksPlan` executes the production reader in
a worker against the full baseline (including `versions_lcm_inputs`, `chats.lcm_stamp` and import
staging), requiring indexed event-chain/position and fork-override probes. Marker labels remain
outside all assembly, summary, export and draft-generation input paths.

The copied-display/selection/Auto/draft seam, re-import preview, swipe find/sort and card-version
browser fixtures accept `STACK_DENSITY=compact` for the same width/theme and layout assertions;
the default remains Comfortable. Both use semantic tokens and existing registered controls.
No baseline object or operation contract changes in stack3; assembler version 81 is above both
merged sides (stack2 80, master 75). No Proposed/Open decision status changes.

The picked-folder re-import browser fixture waits for the newly selected import job to complete
before asserting its exact committed message count. A prior Imported report or a cleared refusal
list can appear before the asynchronous upload publishes; reusing a fixture session exposes this
ordering independently of login latency. The count/refusal assertions and deadlines stay intact.

**Prepend anchoring correction (stack3).** The text-reading resize predicate retains TanStack’s
native first-measure compensation for an unmeasured row above the fold (`adjustForReading` in
`readingPlace.ts`). A fast older-page prepend can measure new rows before the DOM’s previous
row indices commit; comparing only those indices suppressed estimate-to-actual corrections.
Already measured rows keep the existing reading-text anchor for late marker/footer growth.
The helper reads the installed virtualizer’s public size cache and logical offset/adjustment;
it does not clear or write caches. A real-Virtualizer unit and eight ordinary-client quick
prepend cases at both spacings, widths and themes guard this handover and retain one marker
read. The 6,000-message/99-page prepend study verifies the unchanged 2 px anchor bound in both
spacings; delayed-marker and density-switch frame bounds remain unchanged.

## 18. Files and commands in workshops (sandbox1, sandbox2, 2026-11-17)

What is built from spec/FILES-AND-ENVIRONMENT.md: the server half of A0 (§10's migration, the registry kinds, `FILES_DIR`, `safePath.ts`, the `file_versions` operations), L0 (measured on the test host and in the server image), A2's core (`commandSandboxes`, `linux-bwrap`, `bash`, `search_files`, the after-command scan, `shell.run` rows, the `commands` and Internet capabilities, the image's tools and seccomp profile, a cgroup per command), A1's file tools with versions, effects and Undo, and the Files quota and version retention (§1.2, §1.3; sandbox2). Not built: the folder chip and its popover, card folder memory, upload and raw HTTP routes (the quota's check is ready for the upload route), the bin, `ListFiles`/`AuthorizeFilePath` as named operations, Restore on `shell.run` rows, Settings → Assistant tools, `toolchains`, `bash_output`/`bash_stop`/background jobs and full-output paging, PDF text in `read_file`, attachments (A3), `/app-source` and plugin working copies (A4), host folders and `none` (A6), and every desktop unit.

**Storage.** An account's Files are the directory `FILES_DIR/<userId>` (`FILES_DIR` defaults to `DATA_DIR/files`), its home folder `DATA_DIR/env-home/<userId>`, both mode 0700 and made on first use (`files/environment.ts`: `accountEnv` refuses an id that isn't a plain name, `prepareAccount`, `accountMounts`). The app reaches them only through `files/safePath.ts`. Each path is split into checked segments (no `.`, `..` or NUL; names ≤ 255 bytes, paths ≤ 4,096). Every folder on the way is opened with `O_DIRECTORY|O_NOFOLLOW` relative to the one before (through `/proc/self/fd/<fd>/<name>`), so a link anywhere in the path, swapped in at any time, is refused (`FilePathRefused`) instead of followed. A file is read only when the opened descriptor is a regular file (opened `O_NONBLOCK`, so a FIFO doesn't block). Writes go to a temporary name in the same folder, are synced, then renamed over the target: a link at the target is replaced, never written through. `resolveFilesPath` turns a tool's path (absolute under `/files`, or relative to the run's directory) into segments and refuses `~`, other roots and anything that climbs out; when the run's directory is outside `/files` (a command's `cd /tmp`), relative paths resolve from `/files`.

**Migration `0002_files`** (`db/migrationFiles.ts`, the first after the frozen baseline): `file_versions` (immutable by trigger; `rollout_id`/`tool_call_id` both set or both null, with no foreign key, so provenance outlives the run), `file_shares` (unique per owner, path and grantee; a trigger refuses sharing with oneself; no operations yet), `version_attachments.name`/`path`, `composer_images.kind` (default `'image'`) and `name`. Registries: `rollout_effects.kind` gains `file.write`, `file.edit`, `file.create`, `shell.run`; new `file_versions.origin` (`upload`, `editor`, `agent`, `command`, `restore`, `delete`). Writer `RecordFileVersions` (one transaction: the content-addressed `media_assets` row on conflict, its `media_refs`, the version rows) and `CompleteFileUndo` (marks a `file.*` effect undone after the host put the file back); reader `FileVersion`. `migrations.test.ts` upgrades a 0001 database holding synthetic rows; `schema.test.ts` runs baseline plus 0002, so its foreign-key index check covers the new tables. `preSquashSchema.json` still records the baseline alone, since that test runs only `0001_baseline` (delta from §10, which said to regenerate it).

**The sandbox seam** (`sandbox/registry.ts`): `commandSandboxes`, a `makeRegistry` of `CommandSandbox { id, label, explanation, platforms, available(): Promise<Availability>, run(spec, signal): Promise<RunResult> }`. `RunSpec` is `{ command, cwd, mounts, env, network: "public" | "none", limits }`; `RunResult` is `{ exitCode, timedOut, outputCapped, diskLow?, memoryCapped?, head, tail, outputBytes, cwd, durationMs }`. The optional `note()` is user-facing text the `commands` row adds when commands run with less protection ("Commands run with weaker limits here."), and `start()` runs at server start (cleanup, and lines for the log). `selectSandbox` takes the one `COMMAND_SANDBOX` names, else the first available for the platform. When none is available, commands aren't offered and the `commands` row's explanation ends with "Not available here: <reason> <fix>"; the file tools still work. Deltas from §3.3: promises with an `AbortSignal` instead of Effects (the run is one child process, and the tool wraps it with `Effect.tryPromise`), no `prepare` (the host makes the folders) and no `describe` yet.

**`linux-bwrap`** (`sandbox/linuxBwrap.ts`) drives bubblewrap directly, not through `@anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime` (0.0.83 checked: maintained, Apache-2.0). Its Linux mode binds the host's `/` read-only and hides a deny list at the host's own paths, from one process-wide configuration. Here each command needs its own allow list, with the account's folders remapped to `/files` and `/home/user`, which is a different bwrap argument list rather than a configuration of that one. Each run gets a fresh `bwrap` with new user, PID, IPC, UTS, cgroup and network namespaces, `--disable-userns`, `--die-with-parent`, `--new-session`, `--cap-drop ALL`, `--clearenv` and a read-only root. It sees `/usr`, `/bin`, `/lib*`, `/sbin` and selected `/etc` entries read-only, a synthetic `/etc/passwd`, `group` and `hosts` (uid 1000 `user`), Node's prefix read-only when it isn't under `/usr`, a private `/tmp` (tmpfs, `limits.tmpBytes`, default 1 GiB), `/dev` read-only with a `/dev/shm` of at most 256 MiB, its own `/proc`, `/files` and `/home/user` writable, and `/run/rp` holding the network bridge. It sees no `/data`, no other account, no host home and no server process. On x86_64 and aarch64, bwrap gets a seccomp filter (`seccompFilter(arch)`, `deniedCalls(arch)`, `--seccomp 3`) refusing with EPERM the kernel calls commands don't need: io_uring, keyrings, userfaultfd, bpf, perf events, file handles, mount and namespace calls, modules, kexec and the like, and on x86_64 the x32 ABI. The aarch64 numbers are the generic table's, checked against a Linux host's headers; the program's shape is tested, but it hasn't run on an aarch64 host. Docker's default filter refuses these too, but a development server has none. bwrap's options (the host folders it binds, the environment, the end marker) go through a descriptor (`--args 4`, a NUL-separated file in the run folder), so the sandbox's `/proc/1/cmdline` is `bwrap --args 4 /bin/bash -c <prelude> rp-sandbox <command>`: no host folder and no marker. The marker comes as `RP_END` in the environment and is unset; the command shares that shell and could still read it (`trap -p`), which only lets it choose its own next directory, inside the sandbox. Limits are set by `ulimit` inside the sandbox before the command (process count, data size, file size, open files; a failure exits 125), after `oom_score_adj` 1000 so the kernel kills a command before the server when memory runs out. The data-size limit doesn't count shared mappings, memfds or tmpfs pages, so on its own it isn't a real memory cap.

**A cgroup per command** (`sandbox/cgroupLimits.ts`, registry `bwrapLimiters`, part of `linux-bwrap`; the first available entry is used, checked again each minute). Each command runs in a cgroup v2 of its own: `memory.max` = `limits.memoryBytes` (all its processes together, shared mappings, memfds and `/tmp` included), `memory.swap.max` 0, `pids.max` = `limits.processes`. Two entries:

- `cgroup-delegated` makes a child group under `COMMAND_CGROUP` (a subtree the server may write; the image's entrypoint makes one, `docker/entrypoint.sh`), with `memory.oom.group` 1, and starts bubblewrap through a small `sh -c` that writes its own pid to the group's `cgroup.procs` and then execs it, so it begins inside. After the run it reads `memory.events` (`oom_kill`), writes `cgroup.kill` and removes the group.
- `systemd-scope` (a host with a systemd user manager: a development server) runs `systemd-run --user --scope --unit=rp-cmd-<random> -p MemoryMax=… -p MemorySwapMax=0 -p TasksMax=…` around bubblewrap, which runs in place, so its parent is still the server and `--die-with-parent` holds. Afterwards `systemctl --user show -p Result` says `oom-kill` when the cap stopped it, and the failed unit is reset. Its availability probe checks that a scope really gets `memory.max` and `pids.max`: a user manager without the memory controller delegated accepts `MemoryMax` and ignores it.

A command stopped by the cap has `memoryCapped`, and its result says it used more than the command's memory. Where neither is available, commands keep the per-process limits, the log says why at startup, and the `commands` row ends "Commands run with weaker limits here." Delta from §3.6, which left per-account memory limits for Later. With `limits.reserve` (bytes and inodes), a command doesn't start when a writable mount's filesystem is below it, and is killed when it goes below while running (checked every 500 ms); the result has `diskLow`. The process limit has to be set inside the new user namespace, where it counts only the sandbox's processes. The spawned `bwrap` leads its own process group. The timeout, Stop and Resume kill that group with SIGKILL, which kills the namespace's init and with it every process the command started, daemons and `setsid` children included. Output (stdout and stderr together) keeps a 1 MiB head and a 1 MiB tail. The command's final directory comes back through a random marker printed by an EXIT trap, and is cut from the output. Each run's support files live in a temporary directory (`rp-sbx-<server pid>-XXXXXX`) removed when it ends. At startup `sweepRunFolders` removes those of a server process that is gone (a server killed outright leaves its bridge and socket). Folders of a live process, such as a test run sharing the temporary folder, stay; ones named before the process id was added go after a day.

**Network** (`sandbox/network.ts`, registry `sandboxNetworks`, entry `public`). The sandbox has no network interface but loopback. With network on, the app opens an HTTP proxy on a Unix socket for that command (mode 0600, in the run's directory). A small Node bridge inside the sandbox listens on 127.0.0.1:3128 and pipes to it, and `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY` and `ALL_PROXY` point there. The proxy handles `CONNECT` and absolute-URL HTTP (no shared agent pool), both to ports 443 and 80 only (`CONNECT_PORTS`: no SSH, SMTP or other raw TCP from the server's address, and no HTTP body carrying another protocol to its port; 403 "Commands can reach HTTPS (port 443) and HTTP (port 80) only."), resolves each name once, and dials the address it checked. It holds at most 256 connections at once (`PROXY_MAX_CONNECTIONS`), since each costs the server's process two descriptors. Private, loopback, link-local, metadata, CGNAT, multicast and reserved ranges, the host's own interface addresses and its public addresses behind NAT are refused with 403 "Only public internet addresses can be reached from commands." (`sandboxMayReach`, built on `isPublicMediaAddress`). The public addresses are `PUBLIC_ADDRESSES` (IPs, CIDR ranges or names) and what the hosts of `PUBLIC_ORIGINS` resolve to, kept resolved by `net/addressSet.ts` and installed with `setPublicAddresses` by the files host. A name with any refused answer is refused, so DNS rebinding gains nothing. The proxy resolves every name a command asks for through the host's resolver, so a command with Internet on can leak data in the names it looks up (DNS exfiltration); that comes with having internet at all, and isn't prevented. A program that ignores the proxy variables has no route out. With **Internet from commands** Off the proxy isn't started. Delta from §3.4: no `socat`; the bridge is Node, already in the image. The proxy runs on the main thread's event loop (async socket I/O only).

**Agent tools** (`agent/tools/files.ts`, registered by `files/WorkshopFiles.ts` into `execution.rolloutTools`; workshops only, offered from the start in the workshop's tool profile). Every call first proves the run may use the tool (`AuthorizePluginTool`, the same reader proof plugin tools use) and makes the account's folders.

- `read_file` (`read`): numbered lines with `offset` and `limit` (default the first 2,000 lines; files up to 10 MiB). An image goes as an image block when the model takes images, otherwise it is described; other binary files are described. It records the content's hash for the run.
- `list_files` (`read`): names, kinds, sizes and times to a depth, with an optional glob, at most 500 entries. `search_files` (`read`): ripgrep in the sandbox with network none, or, where commands aren't available, an in-app literal search (30 matches); results at most 15,000 characters.
- `write_file` and `edit_file` (class `files`, capability `files` "Change your files", Allowed by default). Replacing or editing an existing file needs a read of its current content in this run (a hash check; an earlier write or edit in the run counts). The earlier content is stored as a version (origin `agent`), and one effect is recorded: `file.create`, `file.write` or `file.edit`, target kind `file`, undo `{ path, before, after, inode }` (`before` the version id or null, `after` the new hash). `edit_file` takes one replacement or `edits[]`: exactly one match unless `replace_all`, all or nothing, with a hint when only CRLF differs. Writes of one account are serialised.
- `bash` (class `outside`, capability `commands` "Run commands", Allowed by default; at most 4 at once per account and 16 per instance) takes `command`, `description?`, `timeout_ms?` (default 120,000, at most 600,000) and `cwd?`. The run's directory carries over between calls (from the last result's "Directory after:" line, else the `workshop.folder` state, else `/files`). Network follows **Internet from commands** (`commands.network`, Off / On, default On, listed alongside Run commands). Limits: 512 processes, 4 GiB of memory (with a cgroup, the whole command's; without one, each process's data), 4 GiB per file, 4,096 open files, 1 GiB `/tmp`, and a reserve of 2 GiB and 100,000 inodes on the Files disk (the quota keeps accounts from each other; the reserve keeps the disk the database shares from filling). A command stopped at the reserve says the server's disk is almost full. Over the account's quota, a command is refused before it starts. Before and after the command, the app scans the account's tree (`scanTree`: no links followed, `SCAN_SKIPS` such as `node_modules` and `.git` skipped, at most 2 s and 50,000 entries). It stores each changed or created file of at most 16 MiB as a version (origin `command`, 256 MiB per command, less when the data folder's disk is near the reserve) and each deletion as a version without content. The result has `exit: N` or the timeout, "Directory after: …", the files changed, created and deleted (with "not all are listed" past the scan's budget), a line when the internet is off, a line when the command left the account over its quota, then the output as a head and tail of at most 30,000 characters. The command records one `shell.run` effect, target kind `command`, with no undo; its row says "Can't be undone from the app".
- Results go back as tool data, like every rollout tool. A call left without a receipt when the app stopped is never re-run silently: Resume asks first, as for every non-read call (`approvals.ts`).

**Quota and retention** (`files/quota.ts`, owned by `WorkshopFiles`; spec §1.2, §1.3).

- **Usage** is the account's Files, its home folder and the bytes its versions hold (`FileVersionBytes`: each stored content once). The folders are measured by `measureTree`: no links followed, each inode once, disk blocks rather than sizes (a sparse file counts what it uses), at most 2,000,000 entries and 60 s. They are measured when nothing is known yet, after each command, and every 10 minutes for accounts used in the last day.
- **The quota** is `FILES_QUOTA` (default `10G`, binary units; an invalid value stops the server at start), or an admin's per-account value in the app setting `files.quotas` (`{ [userId]: bytes }`).
- **Enforcing:** `check(user, adding, what)` fails with `QuotaExceeded`: "Your files use 21.3 GB of 20 GB. Delete files you don't need to <what> again." Over the quota it first removes versions older than 7 days and measures again. `write_file` and `edit_file` check the new content plus the version they keep, and count what they wrote until the next measurement. `bash` checks before it starts and is measured after (a command can't be stopped mid-write). Reads, Undo and deleting still work. The upload route will call the same check.
- **RPCs** (`filesQuotaApi.ts`): `GetFilesUsage({ userId?, fresh? })` (your own; another account's for an admin) returns used, quota, files, versions and home bytes, when it was measured, `over` and `partial`. `SetFilesQuota({ userId, quotaBytes | null })` (admin) sets or clears an account's quota. Both are excluded from agent exposure and have isolation probes.
- **Retention:** every hour from startup, the writer's `PruneFileVersions({ userId?, before, limit })` removes versions older than 30 days, in batches of 2,000. Each batch is one transaction that also deletes the `media_assets` rows nothing names any more (no other version, account reference, saved address, cover, attachment or composer image). The hourly media sweep removes their bytes later, outside any transaction. `RecordFileVersions` no longer adds a `media_refs` row, which would have kept the bytes after retention. Undo of a change whose earlier version is gone says "Its earlier content is gone." The spec's "newest version of a deleted file until its bin item is emptied" waits for the bin.

**Undo of file changes.** The writer refuses `UndoRolloutEffect` on a `file.*` effect with `FILE_UNDO_ON_HOST`, and `api/workshop.ts` sends it to `WorkshopFiles.undoEffect` instead. The file must still have the hash the change left (else "Changed since"). Its current content is stored as a `restore` version, the earlier version is written back from the media store (or the made file is removed), and `CompleteFileUndo` marks the effect undone. "Undo all of this reply" therefore works newest first over file changes and stops at the first refusal, as built. The client's Undo hover explains each `file.*` kind.

**State.** New chat-state event `workshop.folder { path, inode }` (`ChatState.workshopFolder`), read by `bash` for its starting directory. Nothing sets it yet.

**Deployment.** The image adds bubblewrap, git, python3 (pip, venv), ripgrep, curl, procps, xz-utils, unzip, less and file (about 170 MB). The container needs `--security-opt seccomp=docker/seccomp-userns.json` (Docker's default profile plus `clone`, `unshare`, `mount`, `umount2`, `pivot_root` and `sethostname` without `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`; each checked to be needed, `setns` not) and `--security-opt systempaths=unconfined` (so the sandbox can mount its own `/proc`), plus, where AppArmor is on, the shipped profile `docker/apparmor-rp-harness`, loaded on the host and named with `apparmor=rp-harness`: `docker-default` with `deny mount` replaced by `mount`, `remount`, `pivot_root` and `userns`. It compiles (AppArmor parser 4.1.7) but hasn't been enforced anywhere yet, since the test host has AppArmor off; see `docker/README.md`.

The image's entrypoint (`docker/entrypoint.sh`, `/usr/local/bin/rp-entrypoint`) runs the server as it is when started as node. Started as root (compose `user: "0:0"`, with `cgroup: private`), it:

1. enters a user namespace mapping root and node to themselves, with new mount and cgroup namespaces;
2. mounts a read-write cgroup2 view of the container's own cgroup at `/run/rp-cgroup` (util-linux with `LIBMOUNT_FORCE_MOUNT2=always`: the seccomp profile allows `mount(2)`, not the new mount API);
3. moves itself to `rp/server`, hands the memory and pids controllers to `rp` and gives `rp` to node;
4. drops to node with no capabilities (`setpriv`), with `COMMAND_CGROUP=/run/rp-cgroup/rp`.

Any step failing, it runs the server as node without it. `docker exec` and the health check still work: Docker puts them in the server's group. a development server needs nothing: the test host has bubblewrap 0.12.0, unprivileged user namespaces and a systemd user manager that delegates the memory and pids controllers.

**Tests.** `sandboxEscapes.test.ts` skips with a message when bwrap can't start. It covers:

- own files only, as an unprivileged user;
- no data folder, database, secret, other account or host home;
- no server process or environment in `/proc`;
- no links or `..` out of Files;
- no writes outside Files, home and a private `/tmp`;
- no nested namespaces;
- no network without the proxy, and the proxy refusing 127.0.0.1, localhost, ::1, 169.254.169.254, 192.168.1.1, 10.0.0.1, 172.17.0.1, 100.64.0.1 and a `--noproxy` attempt, plus resolution checks;
- a fork bomb, and memory and file-size caps;
- killing at the timeout, after a normal exit that left daemons, and on abort, with no process left behind;
- no capabilities, `NoNewPrivs`, and setuid programs (sudo, su, mount) gaining nothing; no `/sys`, `/var`, Docker socket, inherited descriptors or terminal; no hard links into its folders from outside;
- sized `/tmp` and `/dev/shm`, a read-only `/dev`, the OOM score, the disk reserve before and during a run, and the seccomp filter (with node still running);
- numeric, octal, hex, zero and IPv6-mapped forms of loopback, a loopback Host header, tunnels to ports 22 and 25, the proxy's connection cap, and no command left behind when the server process is killed outright;
- with a cgroup limiter (skipped, saying why, without one): 1.5 GiB of shared mappings, of memfds, and of four 400 MiB processes, each stopped under a 1 GiB cap with `memoryCapped`, while 256 MiB works; the process cap for the whole command;
- `/proc/1/cmdline` without host folders or the end marker; plain HTTP to ports 25, 22, 587, 6379 and 8080 refused; the server's public addresses refused once installed; stale run folders removed only for processes that are gone; the seccomp program's shape on x86_64 and aarch64.

Also: `filesQuota.test.ts` (sizes; `measureTree` with a hard link, a link out and a sparse file; a scripted run over a 1 MB quota: a command goes over and says so, the next command and a write are refused, a read works; `GetFilesUsage`, and an admin's quota lifting it and clearing it; `PruneFileVersions` per account and for all, keeping content another account's version names); `safePath.test.ts` (links, FIFOs, renamed parents, writes over links, the scan, a folder swapped for a link in a tight loop while the app reads and writes through it, long, unicode and case-different names); `workshopFiles.test.ts` (a scripted run: write, read, edit, replace, list, a refused path, two commands with the directory carried, effects, Undo in order and the refusal out of order, and Undo refused when the file or a folder on its path was swapped for a link); and the browser test `workshopFiles.spec.ts` (the chip's three rows and the internet switch; a run that writes a file, reads it back and runs a command offline; its Changes rows and Undo; layout audit at both widths and in both themes).
